10079-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-:
This July 1858 Atlantic Monthly concludes its article on the catacombs of Rome, quoting Paulinus of Nola and the psalm on God's dwelling in peace. Rome, the writer says, is preeminently the city of monuments and inscriptions, and the lapidary style is the one most familiar to her.

Republic, Empire, Papacy, heathens, and Christians have all written their record on her stones, and the catacombs hold the earliest Christian chapters. The article guides readers underground, through tombs and inscriptions. It is a learned, atmospheric piece, suited to readers who love Rome and early church history.
10560-the-last-of-the-foresters-or-humor:
John Esten Cooke published this Virginia frontier novel in 1856, subtitled humors on the border. Cooke, author of The Virginia Comedians, sets the tale at Apple Orchard and Winchester, where Verty, a young hero, thinks, plays, and dreams his way through border life. The tone is comic, romantic, and full of local color.

A legal porcupine, Mr. Roundjacket and his poem, a white pigeon, a pedlar and a necklace, and Miss Sallianna's love for Verty fill the chapters. Violin playing, taverns, and horseback revenge add fun. Readers get a lively, antebellum portrait of the old Virginia frontier.
11007-jemmy-stubbins-or-the-nailer-boy-i:
Elihu Burritt edited this 1850 story of kindness, centred on Jemmy Stubbins, a nailer boy in an English wayside smithy. Burritt met Jemmy while walking in England in 1846, determined to meet working people face to face. The boy could not read a letter, but American boys and girls, giving half dimes, sent him to school for two years.

Letters from Jemmy after schooling show a mind opened to new ideas, and Burritt dedicates the book to the American children whose gifts paid for it. The tale argues that small gifts, joined together, can change a life. Short and earnest, it belongs to the literature of benevolence, where one child's story stands for many poor children helped by charity.
11154-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for July 1861 opens with Our Orders, a poem for the Civil War's first summer. Lyons looms must weave no more silks to deck girls for gay delights, since the crimson flower of battle blooms and solemn marches fill the nights. Instead they must weave the flag drooping over early dead, and homely garments, coarse and grey, for orphans who must earn their bread.

Viols must keep back tunes that pour delight from other lands, while the trumpet leads warrior bands, and the Sibyl Arts must combine in one stern knot while Courage draws the lot. The issue continues with Agnes of Sorrento, where Mother Theresa embroiders an altar-cloth in a convent room frescoed with the Virgin's life, while nuns sing an ancient Latin hymn. The number shows the Atlantic turning its arts to war.
11170-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-:
Boston's monthly magazine for May 1861 opens with a serialized tale set in Sorrento, Italy, where a young girl named Agnes sits beneath an old gateway guarded by a stone saint. The issue carries the magazine's usual mix of literature, art, and politics, printed at the moment the American Civil War was beginning. Its pages pair fiction with essays and commentary for a general educated readership.

Readers get a window into both a fictional Italian town and the concerns of an American audience in 1861. The Sorrento opening leans on vivid place description, from orange stands to wayside shrines, while the surrounding magazine matter shows what editors thought worth printing alongside it. Together they make the issue useful for anyone tracing mid-century American periodical culture.
11196-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for July 1859 opens with Thomas Paine's Second Appearance in the United States, on party bitterness in the early republic. Modern readers, the writer says, can hardly conceive the violence of party feeling under the early Constitution, when two hostile camps pitched against each other and every man stood in his tent. Original Federalists sought a strong central government, while Anti-Federalists feared consolidation would prepare monarchy.

Later pages follow the poet Percival, who answered a phrenological lecturer with a newspaper pasquinade, A Lecture on Nosology, headed by a wood-cut of a gigantic nose. Percival, quoting Humboldt, held phrenology a discovery which, stripped of charlatanry, shows but a meagre portion of truth. The issue shows the Atlantic joining political history with literary biography in the years before the Civil War.
11604-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for July 1860 opens with meteorology, presented as a glance at the science rather than a teacher's lesson. The writer notes rapid progress in thirty years, yet many phenomena still unexplained and learned men still divided.

Meteorology, the essay says, now ranges beyond vapour and air to heat, light, electricity, magnetism, winds, water, vegetation, geology, and climate. Climate, in turn, controls pursuits and affects character. Later in the number, a sick boy named Clarian begs Dr. Thorne to let him have his way for an hour. The issue mixes science with fiction.
1165-the-little-book-of-modern-verse-a-s:
Jessie B. Rittenhouse edits a compact anthology of modern verse, choosing poems that show the new poetry of the early twentieth century at its best. The book aims to be small enough to carry and strong enough to keep. Rittenhouse, a poet herself, edited anthologies that introduced modern verse to schools.

Rittenhouse selects lyrics that are clear, musical, and modern in feeling, without academic bulk. For readers new to modern poetry, the little book works as a friendly first shelf, and for lovers of verse, as a keepsake. Her little book, small and cheap, aimed to put new poetry into ordinary readers' hands.
11658-a-williams-anthology-a-collection-:
Edited by Edwin Partridge Lehman and Julian Park in 1910, this anthology gathers verse and prose of Williams College from 1798 to 1910. Washington Gladden's song to the mountains opens the book, with snows, summer clouds, autumn scarlet, and spring garniture.

Later pieces include a play scene where a monk tells of the wandering Jew, condemned to walk until Christ comes again. Faces grow solemn in firelight as voices lower. The volume mixes college songs, poems, and prose, and it preserves a century of student writing from a small New England college in the Berkshires.
1166-the-second-book-of-modern-verse-a-s:
Jessie B. Rittenhouse follows her Little Book of Modern Verse with a second book, again choosing modern poems for general readers. New voices and new forms appear beside poets from the first volume. Rittenhouse's second book answered readers who wanted more modern poems after the first.

Rittenhouse keeps her taste for clear, musical lyrics, and the second book widens the survey without losing its small, handy shape. Together the two volumes give a portrait of modern poetry as readers first met it. New poets of the 1910s join the earlier voices, widening the modern survey.
11725-a-ramble-of-six-thousand-miles-thr:
S A Ferrall's Ramble of Six Thousand Miles appeared in London in 1832. It began as letters to friends in Europe, written for amusement and not first meant for print. Ferrall says he skipped seaboard city statistics, already well covered by others.

He hoped to note what other travellers passed over. Chapters run through the country in order, with a facsimile of the Cherokee Phoenix of July 1830 as frontispiece. A passage on rivers describes bluffs and bottom land alternating. Hills recede from the water, and soil shows an old river bed. The book is a traveller's sketch of young America.
11727-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for May 1859 opens with the gymnasium, tracing Greek education to two branches: music for the mind and gymnastics for the body. Plato, the essay says, puts grammar, poetry, eloquence, and history under music, with the Muses presiding over all arts and sciences.

Architecture and sculpture, the writer notes, reached a perfection no later civilisation has matched, though knowledge was less divided into professions than in modern times. Later in the number, Alice meets Mrs. Sandford, a motherly woman who becomes her kindly adviser and wins the girl's heart. The issue pairs classical learning with new fiction.
11751-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for June 1859 opens with Shakespeare's art, quoting Ben Jonson: nature gives the matter, but art gives the fashion. Whoever would think clearly and speak earnestly, the essay says, should give days and nights to Shakespeare.

His ear, the writer argues, learns phrases whose only mannerism comes from fullness of thought and directness of expression. Loose, careless prose drifts around its subject for paragraph after paragraph, never landing with the brevity and force a handful of direct statements could achieve. Later in the number, a lover pleads against ungenerous pride. The issue is literary criticism at its most earnest.
11990-shakespeare-s-insomnia-and-the-cau:
Franklin H. Head's 1887 pamphlet Shakespeare's Insomnia and the Causes Thereof is, as its transcriber notes, a literary hoax, and the letters it quotes are fictitious. Head opens by calling insomnia, the lack of tired nature's sweet restorer, the chronic terror of men of active life past thirty-five or forty.

The hoax imagines Shakespeare himself suffering sleeplessness, with invented letters explaining its causes, a joke that depends on readers knowing both Shakespeare and the Victorian cult of the bard. As a piece of literary play, it shows how readily a famous name attracts forged documents. It also shows how a hoax can reveal, through its very invention, what an age wanted its greatest writer to have felt.
12107-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-:
The May 1862 number of The Atlantic Monthly, volume nine, number fifty-five, appeared in the second year of the American Civil War. The magazine, founded in Boston, mixed literature, art, and politics for a Northern readership.

Its lead essay compares the human race to a warship under sealed orders, sailing toward a purpose it cannot yet read. Other pieces weigh weather in war, arguing that storms, frost, and drought have decided battles and toppled dynasties. Poems, reviews, and political comment fill the rest. The issue shows a serious magazine thinking aloud in wartime, using history and science to make sense of a conflict whose end no one could foresee.
12285-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-:
The June 1861 Atlantic Monthly, volume seven, number forty-four, appeared two months after the Civil War began. The Boston magazine mixed literature, art, and politics for Northern readers who wanted sense made of the crisis.

Its fiction lead is Agnes of Sorrento, chapter five, in which Elsie wakes at dawn in a bristling state of caution, like a hen who has seen a hawk over her brood. Spirits in the gorge, priests, and Italian scenery carry the romance. Other pieces in the number address war, science, and letters. The issue shows a literary magazine holding its course in wartime, publishing romance and reflection while the nation split.
12299-the-mechanical-properties-of-wood-:
This technical study of wood sets out the mechanical properties of timber species, with photomicrographs and long tables of test results. The frontispiece shows a small block of western hemlock at thirty-five diameters, with cross, radial, and tangential sections.

Chapters explain strength, stiffness, and elasticity, with tables giving modulus of elasticity in compression parallel to grain and in bending, species by species. The text teaches how to read grain, rays, and early and late wood, and how moisture and defects change strength. Written for engineers, builders, and foresters, the book turns a familiar material into measured science. It remains useful for anyone who works wood by numbers as well as by hand.
12310-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-:
The June 1862 Atlantic Monthly, volume nine, number fifty-six, leads with Thoreau Walking, his plea for nature, absolute freedom, and wildness against a freedom and culture merely civil. Thoreau asks readers to regard man as part and parcel of nature, not merely a member of society.

Other pieces in the number address the war and domestic life. One passage treats a girl constitution that lays up nothing for emergencies, and cannot endure accidents trivial to an active boy. The mix is typical of the Atlantic in wartime: high literary essays beside social observation. The issue is prized today for Walking, which became a founding text of American nature writing.
12374-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-:
The May 1858 Atlantic Monthly opens with an essay on American antiquity that questions comfortable certainties about the past. Herodotus, Gibbon and the old schoolbook landmarks, from Romulus and Remus to the Flood and the discovery of America, no longer stand as firm as students once thought. A decade of new research, the writer argues, has shaken them.

The rest of the number follows the magazine's pattern of essays, stories, poems and political comment for a thoughtful American audience. Together the pieces show a culture re-examining its history even as it argued over its present. The issue is most useful as a record of that mid-century mood: learned, unsettled and eager for fresh evidence.
12675-sketches-and-tales-illustrative-of:
Mrs. F. Beavan drew this 1845 book from seven years living in New Brunswick, then a young British colony. She describes spring floods, log huts, sugar making, lumber camps, and the hard work of clearing land, alongside schools, churches, and neighbourly frolics. Short tales break up the sketches of daily life.

Among the set pieces are the burning of Miramichi, a lost traveller's tale, and the story of an Indian bride told by a refugee. Beavan writes as a settler, not a tourist, and her eye for housekeeping detail gives the book its value. It remains a vivid first-hand picture of backwoods life in the 1830s and 1840s.
1271-bygone-beliefs-being-a-series-of-ex:
H. Stanley Redgrove was a chemist with a taste for the occult. He tours the byways of old belief: alchemy, astrology, magic, and the doctrine of signatures. Each chapter takes one belief and follows it through history, tracing how it grew from honest wonder and hardened into error.

Redgrove writes with a scholar's patience and a skeptic's smile, neither mocking nor credulous. The book gives a clear, readable history of ideas that science left behind. It suits readers who like the odd corners of thought and the roots of modern science.
12839-the-young-wireless-operator-as-a-f:
Lewis E. Theiss published this 1921 boys' book about Charley, a young wireless amateur who becomes a fire patrol in the mountains. A summer holiday turns to work when forest fires threaten timber, and Charley uses his radio skill, pluck, and steady habits to help the forester. A bear, a secret camp, and timber thieves add danger.

The forester praises Charley not for what he knows but for his habit of being prepared, with tools and records in order. That lesson anchors the adventure. The book blends new radio craft with old forest lore, and dedicates itself to forester Gifford Pinchot.
12877-the-first-hundred-thousand-being-t:
Ian Hay's First Hundred Thousand, the unofficial chronicle of a unit of K(1), tells how Kitchener's first volunteers became soldiers. Captain Ian Hay Beith, born in 1876 and just inside the age limit, enlisted in the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders in 1914, trained at Aldershot, and reached France in April 1915. His junior sub's voice carries the book.

A camp debate on nursing shows the tone. Bobby praises girls who gave up clothes fuss for nursing, while Kemp warns against amateur ministering angels who nurse a man to death for a day. Hay mixes humour with the grind of training. The book is a classic of First World War humour and comradeship.
12941-the-scranton-high-chums-on-the-cin:
Donald Ferguson's Scranton High Chums on the Cinder Path mixes school sport with a haunted quarry mystery. Hugh, Thad, and their chums forage for nuts on a bright October Saturday, train for a great tournament, and prowl a quarry road where ghosts are talked of. A marathon race and a final mile build the sporting climax.

A night scene catches a prowler with a flashlight trying a locker key, seized by Hugh while Thad covers retreat. The prowler's muffler falls, and faces are glimpsed in the dark. Ferguson blends track athletics with boy-detective fun. Note: the file warns readers that a cleaner edition exists elsewhere.
13026-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-11-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for May 1863, volume eleven, number sixty-seven, offers literature, art, and politics in the middle of the Civil War. It opens with Charles Lamb's uncollected writings, recalled through a small New England bookshop where a young man first met Chaucer, Spenser, and Sir Thomas Browne. Book talk and old authors share space with war-time pieces.

Other pages carry a strange tale of arrest for high treason, with a torch, a vine-clad opening, and a hand on the shoulder. A sketch of an old soldier muses on pensions, patriot feeling, and the courtesy of veterans. The number captures a magazine trying to hold culture steady while the nation fought, month by month.
13215-edwy-the-fair-or-the-first-chronic:
Rev. A. D. Crake's Edwy the Fair, first chronicle of Aescendune, is a tale of the days of Saint Dunstan in tenth-century England. Chapters run from the forest primeval and the house of Aescendune to London in olden time, temptation, coronation, Glastonbury Abbey, and the flight of Dunstan. Crake writes for young readers who like history dressed as story.

One scene turns on a forged letter, as Redwald writes a false message in Dunstan's hand to send a boy home for his health. Another hero, facing his first battle, feels gloomy forebodings and prefers Valhalla, with hunting by day and feasting by night, to priestly talk of heaven. The tale mixes Saxon kings, monks, and warriors in a plain, earnest romance.
13826-a-gunner-aboard-the-yankee-from-th:
Russell Doubleday, Number Five of the after port gun, kept this diary aboard the Yankee in the Spanish-American War. H. H. Lewis edited it, with an introduction by Rear Admiral W. T. Sampson. The Yankee, manned by naval reserves, cruised and fought off Cuba. Chapters cover the bombardment of Morro Castle at Santiago and life on the gun deck.

Doubleday describes searchlights sweeping the black horizon, lively fusillades, and temporary confusion on deck. The diary gives a sailor's view, not an admiral's strategy. It honours reserve crews who learned war at sea. The book serves historians of 1898 and of naval life. Its plain, vivid entries still read fresh today.
14294-new-ideas-in-india-during-the-nine:
Rev. John Morrison, late head of a Church of Scotland mission school in Calcutta, gave these Gunning talks in 1907 on new ideas in India. Chapters treat leading witnesses, old Indian ways, new social ideas, what dissolved old ideas, woman's place, and the words reformers use. Edinburgh's lectureship aimed to give ministers the gains of study in science, thought, and social life.

Education and faith carry the argument. Morrison urges required Indian history and political economy in colleges, abler teachers, and Anglo-Indians who take interest in India beyond business and exile's end. Hindu reform appears in Chaitanya's followers, who call their lord Gauranga and declare Christ a prophet Hindus may accept like Krishna. Loose doctrine and free choice of teacher, Morrison notes, make such a view bold yet possible. Mission work and study, kind yet keen, mark the book.
14424-the-eventful-history-of-the-mutiny:
Sir John Barrow's 1831 history recounts the 1789 mutiny aboard HMS Bounty, when Fletcher Christian seized the ship from Captain William Bligh in the Pacific. Barrow, a naval administrator, worked from Bligh's account, court records, and later reports.

The narrative follows the breadfruit voyage to Tahiti, the seizure, Bligh's open-boat voyage to Timor, and the fate of the mutineers on Pitcairn Island. It also covers the trials of men later captured and returned to England. The book mixes adventure with official record, and it fixed the popular shape of the Bounty story for later writers.
14446-a-supplement-to-a-compilation-of-t:
George Raywood Devitt compiled this 1904 supplement to James D. Richardson's collection of presidential messages and papers, covering 1789 to 1902. It fills gaps left in the McKinley section of the main set.

The volume prints messages, proclamations, and executive orders of William McKinley not included earlier, plus those of his successor, Theodore Roosevelt, to date. Topics include the Philippines, trade, and the workings of federal departments. As a reference work it preserves official language intact, useful for tracing policy in the years around 1900. Researchers still consult it today for exact presidential wording on policy, diplomacy, and war.
14633-the-transgressors-story-of-a-great:
Francis A. Adams's political novel The Transgressors, subtitled Story of a Great Sin, was published in Philadelphia by the Independence Publishing Company as a novel of the twentieth century. Adams had earlier written Who Rules America?

The plot opens in the coal country around Wilkes-Barre, with a sheriff, a young attorney named Harvey Trueman, and a secret syndicate. An anti-trust conference, a secret oath, a list of transgressors, and the birth of a new party follow. Adams aims his anger at greed and corporate power, and at conscience standing against both.
14665-through-the-air-to-the-north-pole-:
Roy Rockwood's 1906 boys' adventure sends a crew north in the Electric Monarch, an airship built to seek the North Pole. Rockwood wrote many boys' series tales.

The boys are driven from town, chase a runaway train, meet a strange rescuer, and rise in the airship past eagles and electric perils. Ice caves, sea lions, tornadoes, Eskimo captors, and magnetic fire worshippers follow on the way to the pole. The story is brisk Edwardian science romance, full of gadgets, dangers, and plucky comradeship. Rockwood's airship tales thrilled boys before airplanes were common.
15016-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-:
Six monthly numbers of a Boston magazine from the summer and autumn of 1863 make up this volume, issued in the midst of the American Civil War. Essays, stories, poems, and reviews share space with science, history, and political debate. Names such as Hawthorne, Alcott, Holmes, and Thoreau appear through its pages.

War themes run deep: pieces on freedmen at Port Royal, Harvard's fallen soldiers, and the claims of labor sit beside Agassiz on glaciers and Parkman on French Florida. The mix captures a nation thinking aloud in wartime. For readers today, the volume is a rich window onto American minds in a year of crisis.
15344-grace-harlowe-s-sophomore-year-at-:
Jessie Graham Flower's 1911 school story follows Grace Harlowe through her sophomore year at high school, with girl chums in work and athletics. A frontispiece shows sophomores refusing impositions, and chapters open with a declaration of war, a generous appeal, and an unfortunate aviator. Battle, disgrace, and friendship follow.

Grace and her friends face rivals, gather clouds, and learn the price of friendship through sports and school spirit. Flower writes in the cheerful series style for girls. Young readers who like school stories will enjoy Grace's pluck, loyalty, and high-school fun.
15484-the-care-and-feeding-of-children-a:
L. Emmett Holt, professor of diseases of children at Columbia and physician to New York's Babies' and Foundling Hospitals, published this catechism in a fourth revised edition in 1907, with Appleton. It is written in question and answer form, for mothers and children's nurses, so a reader can find a rule fast in a nursery crisis.

Part one covers care: bathing, eyes, mouth, skin, clothing, napkins, nursery, airing, weight, growth, and teething. Part two covers feeding: nursing, weaning, artificial feeding, care of milk, modification of cow's milk, and food for healthy infants in early and later months. Rules on intervals, regularity, overfeeding, and common mistakes follow. The book shaped American infant care in its day, plain, strict, and practical.
15810-the-age-of-erasmus-lectures-delive:
A set of lectures on Erasmus and his age by P. S. Allen, Fellow of Merton College, Oxford. Allen gave them at Oxford and London, and the Clarendon Press issued them in 1914. Erasmus, the Dutch scholar, stands at the hinge between medieval and modern Europe. Allen uses him to light schools, monasteries, and universities of the time.

Lectures treat the Adwert Academy, schools, monasteries, and universities, then Erasmus's life-work in full. Force and fraud, private life and manners, pilgrimages, and the transalpine Renaissance follow. A final lecture joins Erasmus to the Bohemian Brethren. The book gives a vivid, humane portrait of learning on the eve of reform.
15860-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for May 1864, volume thirteen, number seventy-nine, issued by Ticknor and Fields in Boston. In the Civil War years the Atlantic mixed travel, letters, and politics for a Northern audience. This number opens with a cruise, not a battle. A letter to Dear Q sets the voyage in motion.

The steamer Valamo leaves on a Tuesday for Serdopol, at the head of Lake Ladoga, stopping at Schlusselburg, Konewitz Island, and Kexholm. The island monastery of Valaam crowns the route. Other pieces treat literature and the war. The issue shows the Atlantic's range: even in wartime, readers travelled by print to Russian lakes and monks.
16097-the-pursuit-of-the-house-boat-bein:
John Kendrick Bangs's 1897 comic fantasy, illustrated by Peter Newell, imagines the shades of great authors in trouble. Dedicated to Conan Doyle with thanks for the untimely death of his detective, the book sends a search party after a stolen house-boat under the leadership of Sherlock Holmes. Chapters cover the Associated Shades taking action, a stranger who unravels a mystery, and conferences on deck and below stairs.

Captain Kidd, Dr. Johnson, Boswell, and Hamlet all turn up, with cheers, warnings, and a marooning before the escape and the end. Bangs writes light, learned farce, poking fun at literary fame. Readers who like Holmes, literary jokes, and gentle fantasy will enjoy this playful sequel.
16226-a-journey-to-katmandu-the-capital-:
Laurence Oliphant's 1852 John Murray book describes a journey to Katmandu, capital of Nepaul, with the camp of Jung Bahadoor, including a sketch of the Nepaulese ambassador at home. Dedicated to his father, Sir Anthony Oliphant, chief justice of Ceylon, the book answers English interest in Jung Bahadoor's recent visit to England. Oliphant notes no work on Nepaul had appeared in Britain since Dr. Hamilton's of about 1819.

Through the ambassador's friendship, Oliphant visited Katmandu under most favorable terms, seeing court, country, and camp at first hand. His narrative mixes travel, politics, and portraiture. Readers of Victorian travel will find a rare, romantic glimpse of a closed Himalayan kingdom.
16230-fat-and-blood-an-essay-on-the-trea:
S. Weir Mitchell's Fat and Blood, in an eighth edition of 1911 from Lippincott, edited with additions by John K. Mitchell, treats neurasthenia and hysteria. First copyrighted in 1877 and revised in 1883, 1891, 1897, 1900, and 1905, the book enjoyed favor in Europe as well as America. Its preface promises a thorough, clear statement of the treatment as carried out in Mitchell's practice at that time.

Mitchell, a member of the National Academy of Sciences, writes for doctors facing worn, nervous patients with little to offer them. The essay sets out his method case by case, with the confidence of long experience. Modern readers will find a landmark of nineteenth-century nerve medicine, dated in theory but humane in intent.
16737-international-language-past-presen:
W. J. Clark wrote this 1907 London book on a world helper language, issued by J. M. Dent. It gives the past, present, and future of the quest, with samples of Esperanto and a grammar. Clark notes that when he says international language, he means an auxiliary tongue, a second language for all, not a replacement for home tongues.

Clark weighs past schemes, then sets out Esperanto's case with samples and rules a learner can test. He writes for readers who want nations to talk without giving up their own speech. The book remains a clear, early guide to the world-language dream, useful for Esperanto learners and for historians of language reform.
16807-falling-in-love-with-other-essays-:
Grant Allen wrote this 1889 book of essays, issued by Smith, Elder in London. The title piece defends falling in love against Sir George Campbell, who had set his face against it, while parents through the ages had only fought single cases. Other essays take up evolution, sleepers of seven years, a fossil land, thunderbolts, honey-dew, ants, and desert sands.

Allen mixes science with wit, turning from love to beasts, foods, pots, and old barrows with the same bright curiosity. He writes for a general reader who likes facts served with jokes. The book gives a lively sample of Victorian popular science, where a love essay sits quite at home beside a piece on the milk in a coconut.
16947-wyandot-government-a-short-study-o:
J. W. Powell, director of the Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology, wrote this short study of Wyandot government and tribal society. It names four groups in Wyandot social order: family, gens, phratry, and tribe. The family, nearly the household, shares one lodge or one section of a communal longhouse, built oblong of poles and bark, with a fire down the center for two families.

Powell sets out Wyandot kin, council, and rule in plain, systematic terms, as a model of tribal society. The study is short but dense, meant for scholars of Native America. Modern readers should read it as a period ethnology, noting that Wyandot voices and later work have deepened and corrected its picture.
17865-the-meadow-brook-girls-in-the-hill:
Janet Aldridge wrote The Meadow-Brook Girls in the Hills in 1914, printed by Saalfield in Akron, as one more in the Meadow-Brook Girls run. The girls, led by Miss Elting, camp in the White Mountains, where a pilot has gone missing and a guide named Janus Grubb joins them.

Chapters bring a man with green goggles, a start that comes to grief, a burning bridge, horses that give alarm, and a climb up high cliffs. The girls face storm, height, and the tale of Chocorua with pluck and teamwork. It is a cheerful camp tale for girls, full of fresh air, fun, and loyal chums.
17959-the-hand-of-fu-manchu-being-a-new-:
Sax Rohmer wrote The Hand of Fu-Manchu as a new phase in the deeds of Fu-Manchu, the devil doctor, his great villain of the age. The tale opens in a London hotel in November fog, where the narrator hears a strange sound, half drag and half tap, and finds the corridor choked with yellow mist.

Nayland Smith soon joins him, and a man with a limp bursts from a door, white-faced, in a panic. From there the chase runs through fog, hotels, and hidden foes, with Fu-Manchu's hand ever near. Rohmer's pulp tale is tense and lurid, and it shows the era's fears in stark form, best read now with a critical eye.
18136-the-mysteries-of-free-masonry-cont:
Captain William Morgan wrote The Mysteries of Free Masonry, containing all the degrees of the order conferred in a master's lodge, sold for one dollar. Morgan's exposé, printed in the United States, vows to lay bare the secrets of the lodge, from the lost word to the rites of Hiram.

Morgan notes that few Masons advance past the third degree, and fewer still learn the great word lost by Hiram's death. Solomon, Hiram of Tyre, and Hiram Abiff swore to guard it. The book is a famous, fierce exposé, and its author's fate made it legend. It stays a key text for readers who study Masonry and its critics.
18590-the-letters-of-cassiodorus-being-a:
Thomas Hodgkin prepared this condensed translation of the Variae Epistolae of Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator. Hodgkin was fellow of University College, London, and author of Italy and Her Invaders. Henry Frowde published it in London in 1886. The volume offers an abstract of Cassiodorus for historical students.

Hodgkin likens his work to Max Müller's Chips from a German Workshop, gathering letters that show the government, law, and daily business of Ostrogothic Italy. Through Cassiodorus, readers meet kings, officials, and subjects of a kingdom between Rome and the new order, in letters that served as state papers.
18607-the-mano-bos-of-mindana-o-memoirs-:
John M. Garvan wrote this long study for the National Academy of Sciences, printed at Washington in 1931. It describes the Manobo people of eastern Mindanao in the Philippines, with notes on nearby groups such as the Mandaya, Mamanwa, and Moro peoples. Maps of where each group lived open the work, followed by notes on build, dress, and looks.

Later chapters cover houses, food, tools, weapons, marriage, sickness, law, war, and religious ideas in plain detail. Garvan drew on field work in the Agusan Valley and along the Pacific coast. The memoir stands as a full early record of Manobo life before later change.
19143-correggio-a-collection-of-fifteen-:
Estelle M. Hurll wrote this 1901 art book on Correggio, with fifteen pictures and a supposed portrait of the painter. It opens with his character as an artist, a list of books, a directory of the pictures, and a table of his life and contemporaries. Each picture then gets an introduction and reading.

The Holy Night detail shows Mary leaning over the child in a manger, lit by dazzling light while shepherds gather round. Hurll reads the tender pose, the swaddling cloth, and the soft pillow of her arm. Readers get a gentle, accessible guide to a Renaissance master for home study.
19153-a-new-system-or-an-analysis-of-ant:
Jacob Bryant wrote this eighteenth-century study of ancient mythology, here in its third edition in six volumes. Volume one sets out his aim: to strip fable from tradition and reduce old tales to what he holds to be original truth. A portrait, plates, and a full index support the text.

Bryant reads Greek myths as dim memories of real peoples and events, and his later work pushed the same method to Troy, denying Homer's war and city. Learned readers of his day debated him fiercely. Readers get a landmark of early myth scholarship, bold, learned, and now chiefly of historical interest.
19230-the-story-of-paul-boyton-voyages-o:
Paul Boyton told this story of his voyages on all the great rivers of the world, paddling over twenty-five thousand miles in a rubber dress. He dedicates the book to his wife, whose patience helped him present his life. Chapters run from the Allegheny and college days to the Navy, wrecking, and life saving service.

As a boy Paul dodged Constable Sam by swimming to a bridge pier with his clothes piled on his head, while his studious brother Michael learned to love the water. Later he crossed channels, faced sharks, and met Queen Victoria. Readers get a thrilling true tale of a Victorian waterman and showman.
19319-a-description-of-the-bar-and-frame:
W. Augustus Munn invented the bar-and-frame hive described in this book, with an abstract of Wildman's guide for managing bees through the year. Published in London, it quotes Virgil on narrow hive entrances that guard honey from cold and heat. The aim is a hive a keeper can inspect with ease.

Each bar frame with bees and comb draws out alone, without harm to other frames or loss of a single bee, and without smoke, which harms bees and brood. Poplar wood, loose in grain, guards against heat and wet. Readers get a practical Victorian beekeeping manual on a hive built for inspection and honey harvest.
19331-ceremonial-of-hasjelti-dailjis-and:
James Stevenson recorded this nine-day Navajo healing rite, known as Hasjelti Dailjis, in careful day-by-day order. The account covers the building of the medicine lodge, the sweat houses, the masks, the prayer sticks, and the great sand paintings made of colored meal on the lodge floor.

Each day brings its own rites, songs, and prayers, and the book closes with Navajo myths, including the creation of the sun and the tale of Hasjelti. It is one of the fullest early records of a living rite, written while its singers and painters could still be watched at work.
19396-on-the-spanish-main-or-some-englis:
John Masefield wrote this 1906 history, On the Spanish Main, on English raids on the Isthmus of Darien. Buccaneers and old-time ships and sailors fill its pages. Twenty-two pictures and a map support the text, dedicated to Jack B. Yeats. Drake, Dampier, and other sea dogs fill the chapters.

Drake returns to a harbour a year after clearing paths, to find creepers and grasses spread across them, and spies smoke too big for an Indian fire. A lead plate from John Garret's Plymouth ship, nailed to a great tree, marks a recent visit. Readers get a rousing sea history of daring, hardship, and the Spanish Main.
19570-van-dyck-a-collection-of-fifteen-p:
Estelle M. Hurll wrote this study of Van Dyck, published in Boston and New York in the early nineteen hundreds with fifteen pictures and a portrait of the painter. An opening essay treats his character as an artist, followed by a directory of pictures and a table of his life.

One story tells of a star seen at noon when a king drew near St. Paul's Cross, hailed as a sign of a prince born in the west. Hurll's plain interpretations brought Old Master art to American homes, and the book remains a gentle introduction to Van Dyck.
19584-a-new-system-or-an-analysis-of-ant:
Jacob Bryant wrote this second volume of his great analysis of ancient mythology, in a third edition printed in London with plates and a full index. Bryant tries to strip fable from tradition and reduce old tales to what he takes as their first, pure truth.

His key claim is that deeds ascribed to many heroes of the first ages belong at bottom to one people or family, retold in varied forms. A long section on Osiris tests the method. Later scholars set much of Bryant aside, but the work remains a landmark of early myth study.
19602-rembrandt-a-collection-of-fifteen-:
Estelle M. Hurll wrote this study of Rembrandt, published in Boston and New York in the late eighteen hundreds with fifteen pictures and a portrait of the painter by himself. An opening essay treats his character as an artist, followed by a directory of the pictures and a table of his life.

One plate shows aged Simeon in the temple, kneeling with the child in his arms while Mary kneels beside him in wonder. Hurll's plain interpretations made great art open to American homes, and the book remains a gentle introduction to Rembrandt.
19777-aids-to-the-study-of-the-maya-codi:
Only a handful of Maya codices, painted folding books, survived the Spanish conquest. Aids to the Study of the Maya Codices appeared in the Sixth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology. Its author, Cyrus Thomas, offers finds not in his earlier papers. He calls the field American paleography, the reading of native manuscripts. Every glyph read was hard won.

Thomas worked when Maya writing was still mostly unread. His aids recorded signs, calendars, and picture sequences for other scholars. Some of his readings later proved wrong, as pioneers' work does. The report still marks a step toward decipherment. It shows federal science funding deep-time American studies. Students of the Maya can watch the field learning to see.
19827-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for June 1864 is volume 13, number 80. The Civil War was entering its fourth summer as this issue appeared. One piece turns on the flattery of fishing guides. The writer confesses his affections were caught in a net of silken flattery. Your good guide, your dear guide, he jokes, knows the sport of praise. Such light essays shared pages with war news.

Boston's Atlantic served the Union's educated readers. It printed Holmes, Lowell, and the era's best pens. A monthly number balances grave and gay on purpose. June 1864 readers needed both registers badly. The magazine's mix is itself a historical record. It shows a literary culture holding together under war strain.
20527-the-sherwood-foresters-in-the-grea:
The Sherwood Foresters in the Great War is the history of the regiment's 1/8th Battalion in the First World War. The battalion came from Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire. Its war is traced through maps and plans of the Western Front.

The maps list tells the battalion's road. There are plans of the Gorre Brewery and the Clock Tower at Béthune, and of the St. Quentin Canal at Bellenglise. Other sheets cover Kemmel, Hooge, the Hohenzollern Redoubt, Gommecourt, and Lens. Unit histories like this one kept faith with the men who served and fell.
20624-ballads-of-scottish-tradition-and-:
Ballads of Scottish Tradition and Romance gathers Scotland's old popular ballads: border raids, true loves, and tragedies in verse. It belongs to the same series as the English ballad volumes, with texts chosen and edited with care. Reviewers praised the work warmly.

There can be nothing but praise, said the Academy, for the selection, editing, and notes, which are all excellent and adequate. It is, in fine, a valuable volume of what bids fair to be a very valuable series. The ballads themselves — of Tam Lin, the border reivers, and drowned lovers — carry the old music of Scotland.
20839-the-mountain-chant-a-navajo-ceremo:
Branches, darkness, and a great fence of pinon limbs close the Mountain Chant's last night. Washington Matthews names the rite ilnasjingo qacal, the chant in the dark circle of branches. A corral of boughs takes in guests and singers after sunset.

Matthews, an army surgeon, recorded this Navajo ceremony with rare care. Chants, sand paintings, dances, and myths fill the fifth annual report study. He learned the Navajo tongue and won the singers' trust. The work stays a key record of a healing rite, kept in detail that later scholars still mine today.
21071-the-rover-s-secret-a-tale-of-the-p:
Pirates haunt the cays and lagoons of Cuba in Harry Collingwood's tale of the Rover's secret. The Rover himself is a pirate who appears through the story without the word rover ever being used in the main text. Wounded to death, he saves his secret for the final chapter.

That deathbed telling explains several puzzles the reader has met along the way. Around it Collingwood builds a Caribbean tale of lagoons, hiding places, and old piracy in his usual flowing style. The prose is ornate and long-winded at times, as his fans expected, but the delayed secret holds the plot together.
21204-the-recent-revolution-in-organ-bui:
George Laing Miller, a Fellow of the Royal College of Organists, surveyed the rapid changes in organ building here. The book first appeared in 1909 and was reissued in a second edition in 1913. Miller had played organs in England and America, including Christ Church, Pelham Manor, New York. His frontispiece shows the great Willis organ in St George's Hall, Liverpool.

The opening chapter, As It Was, sets the old organ against the new machinery: pneumatic levers, wind chests, and modern actions. Miller explains the new parts with photographs and diagrams. For organists of the time, it was a guide to instruments that were changing under their hands.
21274-the-american-cyclops-the-hero-of-n:
Pasquino, a pen name borrowed from Rome's talking statue, published this satire at Baltimore in 1868. Its target is General Benjamin Butler, the American Cyclops of the title. Butler had ruled occupied New Orleans, where his order on silver spoons and his treatment of the city's women made him hated across the South. The pamphlet dubs him spoiler of silver spoons.

Its introduction retells Ulysses and Polyphemus, with the modern Cyclops bottled up, the saucy rebel Beauregard keeping him sealed. Verses picture a pot-house soldier, bold by day and drunk by night. Illustrated and bitter, it is a piece of post-Civil War political abuse in classical dress.
21341-practical-english-composition-book:
Book Two of this school composition course serves the second year of English study, and its directions begin before any theme is written. When a corrected theme comes back, the student must number each correction and circle it heavily. On a fresh sheet the student states the error, corrects it, and gives the reason. Word misuse, repetition, and weak ideas each get named.

Lessons then build themes step by step, with a poem on metrical feet helping students hear rhythm in prose and verse. The method is strict: answer the critic's questions, follow suggestions, and hand the correction sheet in proper form. It preserves the drill-based composition teaching of its era in full working order.
21461-fred-markham-in-russia-or-the-boy-:
Fred Markham and his brother tour Russia with Cousin Giles in W. H. G. Kingston's Fred Markham in Russia. Giles, a naval officer hurt out of service, invites them in 1856. Their mother is glad the trip stays closer than the far side of the world.

After a rough sea crossing, the boys see Saint Petersburg and travel wider. New friends tell long tales of their own lives under the Czars. Through those tales Kingston teaches much about Russian customs, rule, and hardship. The boys find thrills of their own as well, and the book mixes travel fact with story in Kingston's known way.
21814-the-trial-and-death-of-jesus-chris:
James Stalker, a Scottish minister and writer on the life of Jesus, walks slowly through the Passion in this devotional history of 1894. The study begins where Jesus falls into the hands of justice, at the gate of Gethsemane at midnight. Chapters follow the arrest, the church trial, Peter's denial, and the civil trial before Pilate.

Stalker prints the Gospel texts at each chapter head, drawing on all four evangelists. Herod, the crown of thorns, Judas, and the way of the cross each get their own close study. The closing chapters rest at Calvary and the words from the cross. He writes for believers who want the story told in order, with feeling and care. It is devotion built on the text itself.
21902-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for May 1866, the hundred-and-third number of America's leading literary magazine, opens with The Harmonists. Its narrator measures himself against his brother Josiah, a successful attorney in a manufacturing town. Josiah belongs to the ruling class of slow eyes and bull-dog jaws. The narrator watches him, and the great market, from an odd little corner. Price-marks, he fears, are stamped on all things now.

The issue carries the magazine's usual mix of literature, science, art, and politics. Ticknor and Fields published it in Boston in the first spring after the Civil War. The Atlantic was then the voice of America's literary establishment. One monthly number preserves its tone exactly: reflective essays and stories from the pens that shaped the nation's reading.
22915-the-new-land-stories-of-jews-who-h:
Elma Ehrlich Levinger's The New Land, published in 1920, tells stories of Jews who helped make America. Her preface notes what the histories leave out. Peter Stuyvesant's hostility to Jews is well documented, she writes. Yet no history mentions the Jewish boy who hoped to play with the governor's young niece. A Jewish soldier who saved a Tory from a mob also went unrecorded.

Levinger fills those gaps with tales for young readers, from colonial days forward. Gallant young Franks, friend of George Washington, stands among her heroes. The book argues, story by story, that Jewish Americans belong in the national tale from its start. It remains a warm piece of educational storytelling with a clear purpose.
23041-the-works-of-william-shakespeare-c:
Scholarship explains itself in the first volume of the Cambridge edition of Shakespeare's Works. The editors promise the full results of their comparisons in footnotes. Proposed corrections from themselves and their correspondents appear there too. The reader thus gets, in compact form, a complete view of the materials from which the text has been constructed.

That promise made the Cambridge Shakespeare a landmark of Victorian editing when it appeared in the 1860s. Volume one opens the comedies with texts built by comparing the earliest printings line by line. The notes let any reader watch the editors choose between readings. For students of how Shakespeare reached modern pages, this apparatus is the story, as gripping as the plays it serves.
23819-la-chanson-de-roland-translated-fr:
Léonce Rabillon translated La Chanson de Roland from the seventh edition of Léon Gautier, professor at the Ecole des Chartes in Paris, and Henry Holt published it in New York in 1885. Rabillon, a French lecturer at Johns Hopkins, dedicated his version to Daniel C. Gilman, the university's president.

He followed as literally as possible the text of the Oxford manuscript, as revised by Gautier, keeping the ancient forms of names and their prosodic accent, with an index appended. Parts in parentheses are Gautier's interpolations. The poem itself is nine centuries old, and Rabillon hopes readers will forgive the quaint coloring of an ancient epic rendered in modern English.
24085-earl-hubert-s-daughter-the-polishi:
Emily Sarah Holt set this historical novel in the early years of the thirteenth century, among the high-born ladies of a royal court. Its subtitle, The Polishing of the Pearl, points to the slow shaping of character at the story's heart. Holt, known for careful historical fiction, builds the tale around court life and its tangled ties of kinship.

An old Jewish pedlar named Abraham brings rich wares to the court, and his young daughter Belasez is hired to embroider a scarf, on terms that protect her own customs. As Belasez, her mother Licorice, and her brother Delecresse are drawn deeper into court affairs, a hidden story from the past comes to light. The novel blends romance, faith, and family secrets with a close picture of medieval life.
24504-the-greville-memoirs-part-2-of-3-v:
Charles Greville kept this journal of the reign of Queen Victoria, published by Longmans, Green in 1885 as the first volume of the memoirs' second part. An earlier part, published in 1874, had covered his diary from 1818 to Victoria's accession in 1837. This continuation carries the record into her reign.

Greville, Clerk of the Council, knew ministers, courtiers, and society, and he wrote down what he saw and heard with unusual frankness. His journal mixes politics, gossip, and character sketches of the great. Historians still quote it as a firsthand record of Victorian public life, told by an insider who missed very little.
24777-celebrated-travels-and-travellers-:
Jules Verne wrote this history of world discovery, translated from the French by Dora Leigh and published in London in 1882. Part One covers the early age of exploration: ancient maps, Marco Polo, Prince Henry the Navigator, and the first voyages to Africa, Asia, and the Americas. It is the first of three volumes on great travelers.

Verne draws on old maps and drawings, many copied in the book, to show how the known world grew piece by piece. Columbus appears late in the volume, warning a governor against a storm that then wrecks a treasure fleet. Readers get both adventure and a clear sense of how geography itself was learned, voyage by voyage.
2511-the-history-of-henry-esmond-esq-a-c:
William Makepeace Thackeray tells this novel as the memoir of Henry Esmond, a soldier and gentleman who serves under Queen Anne in the early 1700s. Esmond grows up in the Castlewood household, split between England and the family's Virginia estate, and his fortunes rise and fall with wars, courts, and Jacobite plots.

Thackeray copies the manners and speech of Queen Anne's age with care, down to dedications to a patron. Battles under Marlborough, love for the Castlewood women, and loyalty to a lost cause all shape Esmond's life. The book reads as both a rich period piece and a wry study of honor, ambition, and the cost of serving princes.
2537-the-pocket-r-l-s-being-favourite-pa:
Robert Louis Stevenson did not assemble this little book himself; it gathers favorite passages from his works into a pocket sized companion. The selections open with a claim that reading Stevenson leaves a memory of the man, as if one had shaken a loyal hand and looked into brave eyes.

Short bits on youth, travel, courage, and the love of virtue follow, each chosen to stand alone. Readers can dip in for a paragraph at a time, or read straight through for a portrait of his mind. The volume suits anyone who wants Stevenson's voice in brief, without taking on a whole novel.
25442-aunt-friendly-s-picture-book-conta:
Aunt Friendly's Picture Book offers thirty-six pages of coloured pictures with letter-press descriptions. Frederick Warne published it in London, with Scribner, Welford and Armstrong in New York, and Kronheim printed the colours. Its preface promises old nursery favourites for young friends, with one new companion from over the sea.

The contents list a Nursery Alphabet, Sing-a-Song of Sixpence, The Frog Who Would a Wooing Go, The Three Little Pigs, Puss in Boots, and The Ugly Duckling. Alphabet rhymes pair each letter with a picture, from corn in the stack to a donkey with a cross on its back. The Ugly Duckling chapters follow the outcast bird from moor to cottage and beyond.
25532-the-detection-of-forgery-a-practic:
Douglas Blackburn, late expert to the Natal Criminal Investigation Department, and Captain Waithman Caddell write this 1909 handbook for bankers, solicitors, magistrates' clerks, and all who handle suspected documents. Forgery detection here is a practical trade, not a theory.

The book teaches readers to test handwriting, ink, paper, and the small habits that betray a forger, with tables, terminology, and alphabet variants to aid comparison. An erratum corrects averages printed from incomplete manuscript, a reminder that close checking matters in this work. Blackburn's Natal and Transvaal service gives the handbook its practical authority.
25700-the-greville-memoirs-part-1-of-3-v:
Charles Greville's memoirs appear here in part one of three, volume one of three. They form a journal of the reigns of King George IV and King William IV. Entries carry dates and sidenotes. Transcribers kept original spellings and punctuation. Monetary pounds appear in modern pound form for clarity.

Even pages in the original carried page, volume, and chapter headers. Odd pages carried the year of entry and a subject phrase. Those phrases now appear as sidenotes. The journal gives an insider's view of court, politics, and society in early nineteenth-century Britain, written by a clerk of the council close to power.
26065-hugh-bishop-of-lincoln-a-short-sto:
Charles L. Marson's short life of Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, follows him from boyhood through the monastery to the bishop's seat. Chapters trace Hugh as brother and prior, then as bishop elect and consecrated, at work in his diocese, in troubles and disputes, and as a builder of churches.

Marson shows a bishop willing to rebuke a king, charging him with unfaithfulness in marriage, with meddling in church appointments, and with selling rule over souls for money or favor. The rebuke, delivered as careful admonition, frames Hugh as a maker of medieval England: firm with rulers, active in his see, and steady under pressure.
26321-life-and-matter-a-criticism-of-pro:
Sir Oliver Lodge's Life and Matter, second edition of 1905, criticizes Professor Haeckel's Riddle of the Universe. The book expands a presidential address to the Birmingham and Midland Institute, and it quotes D. G. Ritchie to frame its case. Materialistic monism, Lodge allows, works well as a hypothesis for science in every field.

It turns false, he argues, only when offered as a complete philosophy, since it leaves out the conditions of human knowledge itself. Haeckel's law of substance, the eternal persistence of matter and force, draws special fire for its sweeping claims. Lodge writes as a physicist who respects science yet insists that mind, meaning, and knowledge need a place no laboratory balance can weigh.
26481-the-romance-of-mathematics-being-t:
P. Hampson, of Oriel College, Oxford, published this 1886 satire as the original researches of a lady professor of Girtham College in polemical science. The lectures and essays, supposedly found in a well-worn desk, treat the social properties of a conic, equations to brain waves, social forces, and the laws of political motion. Hampson, who will not say how the desk reached him, presents them as profound treasures.

The mock scholarship praises true patriotic loyalty in verse, urging subjects to watch, fight, bleed, and die for a loved and loving monarch under just and equal laws. Those preaching sedition, the professor argues, lack the judicial mathematical training of Girtham. The joke lands through deadpan learning applied to politics, society, and the mind.
26901-a-history-of-the-nineteenth-centur:
Edwin Emerson wrote this year-by-year history of the nineteenth century, with an introduction by Georg Gottfried Gervinus, published by P. F. Collier and Son of New York in 1902. Volume two carries sixteen colored plates, thirty-two full-page half-tone cuts, and two maps, among them the first steam railway, Balaklava, Solferino, and the last moments of Maximilian. Emerson belonged to the American Historical Association.

Volume two opens in 1816, an era of peace and reconstruction after a generation of war. France begins parliamentary government under the Duc de Richelieu, Napoleon and his relatives go into perpetual exile under the amnesty act, and Marshal St. Cyr rebuilds the army on a footing of military equality. Guizot speaks for the Doctrinaires, Chateaubriand offends the king, and Béranger leads the lyric poets. Later years reach Goethe at Weimar, where Werther's romantic suicide was aped by susceptible youth.
28052-john-brown-a-retrospect-read-befor:
Alfred S. Roe read John Brown: A Retrospect before the Worcester Society of Antiquity on December 2, 1884, privately printed at Worcester in 1885. The pamphlet opens with a previously unpublished letter from John Brown, written from Springfield, Massachusetts, on April 16, 1857, to Eli Thayer.

Brown writes that a United States hound is on his track, asks for sample Navy revolvers by express, and orders rifles and pistols packed for Cleveland. Roe's retrospect then places Brown in history, and the letter gives the pamphlet documentary value. Roe prints the letter as it was written.
28108-the-pennyles-pilgrimage-or-the-mon:
John Taylor, the King's water-poet, wrote The Pennyles Pilgrimage in 1618 about walking from London to Edinburgh with no money at all. Taylor swore to neither beg, borrow, nor ask for meat, drink, or lodging, and to live on the kindness of hosts he met. He printed the tale himself in London, dedicating it to the Marquis of Buckingham.

Along the road he reports inns, hunts in the Brae of Mar and Badenoch, and the folk who fed and housed him. His spelling and jokes keep the flavour of Jacobean England and Scotland. The book charms readers as a true, merry record of travel on foot and on trust.
28359-applied-psychology-making-your-own:
Warren Hilton's Applied Psychology: Making Your Own World is the second of twelve volumes applying psychology to personal and business efficiency, issued in 1920 under the Society of Applied Psychology. Hilton builds on his earlier book, Psychology and Achievement, and its claim that all achievement runs through bodily action directed by the mind.

Chapters explain sensation and perception, the unreliability of the senses, illusions used in business, and tests for attention and credibility. The book then turns to self-mastery: choosing what fills the mind, avoiding worry, and gaining balance and self-possession. It reads as a practical early self-help manual grounded in laboratory psychology.
28479-hymns-from-the-east-being-centos-a:
John Brownlie's Hymns from the East, published in Paisley in 1907, gathers centos and suggestions from the service books of the Holy Eastern Church. Brownlie, author of Hymns of the Greek Church and Hymns from the Greek Office Books, shapes Eastern liturgical material into English hymns for Western use.

The index of first lines groups hymns by season and theme: morning, evening, Christmas, Easter, Pentecost, communion, judgment, and aspirations. Titles include Now, God of Light, the morn appears, Crown the Lord of glory, and Even as Thou saidst, the Spirit came. The book offers English readers a doorway into Eastern Orthodox worship in verse.
28655-ralph-on-the-overland-express-or-t:
Allen Chapman's Ralph on the Overland Express, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1910, is the fourth book of the Railroad Series. Ralph Fairbanks, the youngest engineer in the Great Northern service, takes crack locomotive No. 999 on a trial run. A new car at the rear, blazoned China and Japan Mail, must reach the Overland Express, two hundred miles off at Bridgeport.

Beating timetable routine by half an hour is the test, and Stanley Junction turns out to cheer him. Chapters add a special passenger, four medals, Dave Bissell the train boy, fire, the Black Hand, Zeph Dallas, and an avalanche. Readers get a boys' railroad tale of duty, danger, and promotion.
2925-the-conditions-of-existence-as-affe:
Thomas Henry Huxley's fifth lecture to working men examines how the conditions of existence affect the perpetuation of living beings. He recalls proving in the last lecture that organisms tend to reproduce their kind while also tending constantly to vary, sometimes by a marked leap with no gradations. Such variation, arising from causes we do not understand, he calls spontaneous.

Huxley piles up evidence of variation in humans and animals, noting differences in limb proportions among men and the wide range of foxes across Europe, Asia, and America. Large foxes live in the north, smaller ones farther south. The lecture builds the case that variation is everywhere, the raw material on which selection, natural or human, can work.
30028-the-award-of-justice-or-told-in-th:
A. Maynard Barbour, author of That Mainwaring Affair, published The Award of Justice, or Told in the Rockies, in Chicago and New York in 1897, with Rand, McNally and Company. A second copyright is dated 1901. Barbour dedicates the book to W. James Barbour, her co-worker in the pleasant task, at whose suggestion it was undertaken and by whose inspiration it was guided. An Ecclesiastes motto fronts it: better is the end of a thing than the beginning.

Chapter one opens with the Pacific Express due at Valley City at 1:45 in the afternoon. A spring-board wagon drawn by bronchos appears at the dingy depot, with two young men aboard. Tom, a prosperous young ranchman, holds the restive ponies. Ned, in a tweed traveling suit, fetches their traps: two grips, a rifle case, fishing rods, and a large square case handled with great care.
30549-the-twentieth-century-american-bei:
H. Perry Robinson writes The Twentieth Century American, a comparative study of the peoples of the two great Anglo-Saxon nations. It draws on his earlier Men Born Equal and The Autobiography of a Black Bear. Transcriber notes keep original spelling and hyphenation, correct some printer errors, and mark italics with underscores.

Robinson compares Americans and Britons as cousins across an ocean, weighing character, institutions, manners, and public life. His study aims at fair, firsthand comparison rather than praise or blame alone. The book suits readers interested in Anglo-American ties, national character, and the early twentieth-century world.
30590-the-greville-memoirs-part-1-of-3-v:
The Greville Memoirs, part one of three, volume two of three, presents a journal of court and society, reproduced with original spelling and punctuation except for obvious typos corrected without comment. Monetary pounds, shown in the original as an italic l after the number, appear here in the more conventional pound form for clarity.

Even-numbered pages in the original set carried the page number, volume title, and chapter number. Odd pages gave the diary year, a topic line, and the page number. In this set, the year joins the date as in the original volumes. Greville's diary gives an insider's view of politics, personalities, and daily life at the top of British society.
30591-the-greville-memoirs-part-1-of-3-v:
The Greville Memoirs, part one of three, volume three of three, continues the journal of court and society with the same editorial care as volume two. Spellings and punctuation follow the original except for obvious typos corrected without comment, and monetary pounds appear in conventional pound form rather than italic l.

Even pages in the original set carried page number, volume title, and chapter number. Odd pages gave the diary year, a topic line, and the page number, with the year joined to the date in this set. Greville's third volume extends his insider record of politics, personalities, and daily life at the top of British society, for historians and general readers alike.
30862-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-15-no-:
This May 1865 number, volume fifteen, number ninety-one, of The Atlantic Monthly came from Ticknor and Fields of Boston, a magazine of literature, art, and politics. The issue opens with With the Birds, a piece that celebrates field and forest singers not in the mere spirit of exact science. It does so with the deep freedom of love and old acquaintance. Its writer listens through rain to robin, wood-thrush, flycatcher, cat-bird, wren, king-bird, and chimney-swallows.

That opening sets the tone for a monthly that mixed essays, stories, poems, and political writing for educated American readers. In May 1865, as the Civil War ended, The Atlantic offered both nature writing and serious public thought in one parcel. Modern readers will enjoy its clear prose, its bird lore, and its window on how thoughtful Americans read and talked in the spring of 1865.
31051-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-15-no-:
Volume fifteen, number ninety-two of The Atlantic Monthly, dated June 1865 and published by Ticknor and Fields, gathers literature, art, and politics in a single monthly issue. It opens with a letter about England, musing on the sea, the coast, and the salt air. It then moves through essays, poems, and stories including A Prose Henriade, Harpocrates, Needle and Garden, and Doctor Johns.

Later pieces take up Richard Cobden, the national debt, intolerance, a jaguar hunt, and, most tellingly, late scenes in Richmond. Those chapters tell how the city became the Confederate capital and how it was taken. The issue thus captures a magazine turning from war news toward peacetime letters.
31268-civilization-the-primal-need-of-th:
Alexander Crummell's 1898 volume, number three in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, prints two of the Academy's founding addresses. The first, his inaugural address of March 5, 1897, argues that civilization is the primal need of the race. It welcomes an assemblage drawn together by lofty aims and the desire for concerted Black thought and action.

The second, his first annual address of December 28, 1897, takes up the attitude of the American mind toward the Negro intellect. Sold at fifteen cents from Washington, the pamphlet is a primary record of the Academy's birth and of Crummell's program for Black scholarship and self-definition.
31329-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Drawn from the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, this long entry covers the University of Chicago, described as one of the great educational institutions of the United States. It was established under Baptist auspices in Chicago and opened in 1892. Though its president and two-thirds of its trustees were always Baptists, the university itself was non-sectarian except for its divinity school.

The entry goes on to survey the institution's growth, its ambition, and the organizing work of its first president. As a reference piece, it gives the facts a contemporary reader would want: founding terms, governance, and standing among American universities. It remains useful today as a snapshot of how the university looked to informed observers in the early twentieth century.
31454-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-16-no-:
Volume sixteen of The Atlantic Monthly, published at Boston by Ticknor and Fields in 1865, presents the magazine as one of literature, science, art, and politics. Its contents range widely: an article on assassination, J. T. Trowbridge on the field of Gettysburg, Mrs. H. B. Stowe's Chimney-Corner papers, a serial called Doctor Johns by Donald G. Mitchell, and pieces on the electric telegraph and books for children.

The volume belongs to the last year of the Civil War, and its pages carry that moment: war, politics, and the return to ordinary life sit side by side. For readers today, it is a record of what serious American readers were reading month by month. The mix of fiction, essay, and report shows a magazine speaking to a nation in transition.
31483-the-first-little-pet-book-with-ten:
The First Little Pet Book, with ten short tales in words of three and four letters, is by Aunt Fanny, author of Night Caps and Mittens. It was published in New York by James O'Kane in 1867, entered for copyright in 1863. Dedicated to Charlotte, Mary, and Willie, it carries as its motto a line credited to Richter: "I love God and little children." The book is made for the very youngest readers, who are just learning to read.

Each tale uses only short words, so a child can sound out a whole story alone. The pet theme keeps the reading gentle and familiar. For readers of children's literature, the book is a charming survival of early reading instruction, when a first book had to be both easy and kind. Its ten tales still suit a beginner's first shelf.
31838-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-14-no-:
This volume of The Atlantic Monthly, volume fourteen, published at Boston by Ticknor and Fields in 1864, is a magazine of literature, art, and politics from the Civil War years. Its contents list pieces on beer-drinking, a new school of biography, Cadmean madness, the Columbia River, and communication, among many others.

The volume's fiction includes a closing scene at sea. They also include where a boat cuts through tide-waves and spray, a woman named Éloise faces a maniacal man, and a horseman stands against the sky on a cliff above. Readers get a full year of a leading American magazine, with essays, stories, and poems from the summer of 1864.
32050-the-plants-of-michigan-simple-keys:
Henry Allan Gleason's 1918 book The Plants of Michigan, Simple Keys for the Identification of the Native Seed Plants of the State was published in Ann Arbor by George Wahr. It was written by the associate professor of botany and director of the Botanical Gardens and Arboretum at the University of Michigan. Its key to groups begins by separating woody plants, whose stems last from year to year, from herbaceous plants, whose stems live above ground only a single season.

Further keys distinguish plants with unusual habits or structures, including leafless, colorless, submerged, floating, parasitic, or hollow-leaved plants, from ordinary terrestrial or swamp plants. They also distinguish monocotyledons with parallel-veined leaves and flower parts in threes or sixes. Readers get a working field key for identifying Michigan's native seed plants.
32073-the-regular-brigade-of-the-fourtee:
Frederick Phisterer, late adjutant of the 2nd Battalion of the 18th United States Infantry, wrote this record of the Regular Brigade in the Battle of Stone River, or Murfreesboro, Tennessee. The brigade belonged to the Fourteenth Army Corps of the Army of the Cumberland. It fought from December 31, 1862, to January 3, 1863, both dates included. Phisterer dedicated the account in July 1883 to his comrades, the survivors of the brigade.

The narrative explains how General Rosecrans gathered five battalions of regular infantry from two divisions, added a regular battery, and formed them into one brigade. The 15th, 16th, and 19th regiments were already at Nashville. The two battalions of the 18th marched from near Gallatin to join them. Readers get a unit history written by a participant, aimed at placing on record exactly what the brigade did in the battle.
3241-corporal-cameron-of-the-north-west-:
Ralph Connor follows a young Scot to the Canadian West in this tale of the Macleod Trail. The quitter opens book one, with the glen of the cup of gold and the family solicitor. A question of honour, a lady and the law, and the waster's refuge follow, before a farewell to Cuagh Oir and the question of whether he will come back.

Book two cries ho for the open, and sets Cameron to a man's job, a day's work, and a rainy day in the force. The North West Mounted Police gives the story its spine: law carried on horseback across wide country. Connor writes with a minister's eye for character and a frontiersman's eye for weather, work, and the price of starting over.
33093-the-path-way-to-knowledg-containin:
Robert Recorde's Path-way to Knowledg, containing the first principles of geometry, is a Tudor textbook that taught English readers the science of shape and measure in their own tongue. Its preface declares briefly the commodities of geometry and its necessity, arguing that a reader who knows lines, parallels, squares, and angles gains a tool for building, surveying, and thinking clearly. The book's old spellings, right line for straight line and gemow for parallel, show its age.

Recorde writes as a teacher, moving step by step from first definitions to the properties of figures, with Greek terms explained and diagrams implied by the text. His aim was to make Euclid's wisdom accessible beyond Latin schools. As a landmark in English mathematics, the Path-way remains a fascinating read, both for its geometry and for the Tudor English in which a new science first spoke to ordinary readers.
33107-junius-unmasked-or-thomas-paine-th:
Junius Unmasked, published in Washington in 1872 and entered for copyright in 1871, argues a bold literary claim: that Thomas Paine wrote both the Letters of Junius and the Declaration of Independence. Its first part sets out method, mystery, and statement. It then works through a letter to the printer of the Public Advertiser, comments, Burke's estimate of Junius, and social position. The case is that Junius was not a partisan but a revolutionist. It ends by reviewing Junius, Common Sense, style, and characteristics.

A second part examines the Declaration itself, comparing its language and ideas with Paine's known work and with Junius, in side-by-side passages. The book's thesis is presented as proof, but modern scholarship does not accept it, and readers should treat it as a claimed identification, not a settled fact. As a document of nineteenth-century authorship hunting, it remains a fascinating, dogged piece of detective reading.
33124-hunted-down-or-five-days-in-the-fo:
Hunted Down, or Five Days in the Fog, is a thrilling narrative of the escape of young Granice from a drunken, infuriated mob. It was published in San Francisco in 1875, written by himself while in jail and dedicated to Mr. Nicholas Breen. Granice writes from the Modesto jail, awaiting trial for shooting the defamer of his mother's name in 1874, having given himself up to the sheriff.

The narrative that follows covers five days in fog, pursuit, and hiding. It tells of a young man who acted to defend his mother's name and flees a mob that wants its own justice. Granice's voice is urgent and personal, and the pamphlet preserves a California story of honor, violence, and law on a raw frontier. For readers of true crime and western history, it is a gripping first-hand account, short, tense, and rooted in a real jail cell.
33166-landseer-a-collection-of-fifteen-p:
Estelle M. Hurll's Landseer collects fifteen pictures and a portrait of the painter, with introduction and interpretation by Hurll. It is in the Riverside Art Series and was published in Boston and New York in 1901. A frontispiece from an engraving by Frank Cousins shows The Connoisseurs, property of King Edward VII. The volume opens with essays on Landseer's character as an artist, books of reference, a historical directory of the pictures, an outline of his life, and his contemporaries.

The pictures that follow include King Charles Spaniels and other famous animal paintings, reproduced from photographs and engravings. Hurll writes for general readers who wanted to look closely and understand what they saw, not merely admire it. The book remains a charming introduction to Landseer, the Victorian painter of dogs, deer, and Highland life, whose animals carried human feeling in every eye and paw.
3352-letters-to-his-son-1748-on-the-fine:
The Earl of Chesterfield writes to his son from the year 1748 in this volume. Letter twenty-four, dated 2 January, old style, finds the boy at Leipzig. Chesterfield praises the allotment of his time, employed from morning till night. A fool would say the boy had none left for himself, the earl writes, whereas a right use of time is having it all to oneself.

That praise sets the volume's theme: industry as the ground of the gentleman's art. Later letters press study, languages, and manners with the same insistence. Readers get Chesterfield the tutor at his most approving, before the sharper advice of later years. Industry first, manners always, and time used well: the 1748 letters set the curriculum for all that follow.
3353-letters-to-his-son-1749-on-the-fine:
A New Year's gift, thanked beyond its value, opens the 1749 letters: the thanks Chesterfield wants is the use his son makes of it. Letter sixty-two, dated 10 January, old style, answers a letter of 31 December, new style. The boy's thanks for a present, Chesterfield writes, exceed the value of the present itself. But the use the boy promises to make of it is the thanks the father desires to receive.

Due attention to the inside of books, the letter continues, matters more than their outsides, and the sentence gives the volume its temper. Chesterfield teaches reading as use, not display. Readers following the correspondence will find 1749 a year of steady schooling: gifts acknowledged, promises weighed, and a father's approval earned by application.
3354-letters-to-his-son-1750-on-the-fine:
A letter of 8 January 1750 shows Chesterfield at his most trusting: his son's reason, he says, needs no father's gloss on religion or morals. Letter one hundred, dated 8 January, old style, takes up a subject he has seldom touched. He has seldom or never written on religion and morality, he says, because the boy's own reason has given him true notions of both. They speak best for themselves, needing no father's gloss.

If they wanted assistance, Chesterfield adds, Mr Harte stands at hand, for precept and example both. The letter shows the earl trusting reason over sermon, and a tutor over a parent's lecture. Readers following the whole correspondence will find 1750 a gentler year: advice given with confidence that the son's judgment can now carry its own weight.
3355-letters-to-his-son-1751-on-the-fine:
