Paris in January 1751 gives the Chesterfield letters their most worldly season, as a son makes his debut in good company. Letter one hundred and twenty-six, dated 8 January, old style, reports a debut at Paris. By the boy's letter of 5 January, new style, Chesterfield finds the debut a good one. The boy has entered good company, and the father dares say he will not sink into bad.

Frequent the houses where you have been once invited, Chesterfield advises, and shed the shyness that makes most young men awkward. The letter shows the earl as social tutor, coaching a son through his first Paris season. Readers will find 1751 the correspondence at its most worldly: doors opening, company chosen, and a young man learning to belong.
3356-letters-to-his-son-1752-on-the-fine:
In January 1752 Chesterfield weighs two failures of learning against each other: the man who cannot be informed, and the man who will not. Letter one hundred and fifty-five, dated 2 January, old style, opens on an enemy to knowledge. Laziness of mind, or inattention, Chesterfield writes, harms learning as much as incapacity does. What difference is there, he asks, between a man who will not be informed and a man who cannot be?

This difference only, he answers: the former deserves blame, the latter pity. The distinction drives the volume's counsel on study and attention. Readers get Chesterfield the moralist in short, sharp form: no excuse for a wandering mind, and no pity wasted where will, not wit, is wanting.
33618-the-branding-needle-or-the-monaste:
Eugène Sue's The Branding Needle, or The Monastery of Charolles, translated by Daniel De Leon, is one volume in the great series The Mysteries of the People. That series is a history of a proletarian family across the ages. Neighboring volumes carry titles from the Gold Sickle and the Brass Bell to the Executioner's Knife and the Galley Slave's Ring, each marking an epoch through a family's story. This volume tells a tale of the first communal charter.

Its parts move from the valley of Charolles, with a signal, an annual celebration, and a watch at the river, to the castle of Brunhild, with a tower room. Sue writes popular historical fiction with a democratic argument: ordinary people, not kings alone, make history. Readers of sweeping nineteenth-century serial novels will enjoy its scale and its partisan energy.
33890-on-the-kentucky-frontier-a-story-o:
James Otis wrote this frontier tale for young readers, published in New York in 1900 with pictures by J. Watson Davis. Its preface tells of Simon Kenton, a pioneer wronged by lawsuits over his Kentucky lands. Kenton spent twelve months in prison on the ground of his 1775 cabin, and by 1802 he was landless.

Yet Kenton joined Kentucky troops under Shelby in 1813 and fought at the Thames, and in 1824, at seventy, he rode to Frankfort to seek relief. Otis builds his story of fighting pioneers around such lives. The book gives a stirring, plain account of the early West.
34056-remarks-on-some-fossil-impressions:
John C. Warren, president of the Boston Society of Natural History, wrote these remarks on fossil footprints in the sandstone rocks of the Connecticut River, published at Boston in 1854. Most of the remarks were first made at society meetings, with a portion printed in its proceedings. Warren aimed to give non-members a handy account of the impressions.

The papers also treat the Epyornis, or great bird of Madagascar, and its eggs, whose reported size in 1851 met wide disbelief. Warren links the great bird to the footprint record. The book offers an early American look at fossil tracks and giant birds.
34128-sir-james-young-simpson-and-chloro:
H. Laing Gordon's 1897 life of Sir James Young Simpson, in the Masters of Medicine series, follows the Scots doctor from birth in 1811 to death in 1870. Twelve chapters trace his boyhood at Bathgate, student years, early practice, and rise to professor and physician.

The heart of the book is chloroform: its discovery as a pain-killer, the fight to win it a place in surgery and medicine, and the quarrels that fight stirred. Gordon also notes Simpson's home life, his work in archaeology, and the honours that closed a busy career. Gordon's volume belongs to a series whose other lives include Harvey, Hunter, and Jenner.
34375-hocus-pocus-junior-the-anatomie-of:
Hocus Pocus Junior is an old book of conjuring tricks. Its full title runs The Anatomie of Legerdemain, or The Art of Juggling set forth in his proper colours. It claims to set out the art fully, plainly, and exactly. A person who knows nothing of the craft may learn its full mastery from the book, after a little practice, it holds. To each trick is added the figure, where needful for the teaching.

The text is the second edition, with many additions. It was printed in London in 1635 by T. H. for R. M. A note to the reader opens the book. Courteous reader, do you not wonder? it asks: to see so slight a pamphlet so quickly spent. The ebook was made from page pictures held by the Library of Congress. The work is a founding text of stage magic in English.
34771-the-scientific-basis-of-national-p:
George Gore argues for research in The Scientific Basis of National Progress, including that of morality, printed in London and Edinburgh in 1882. Williams and Norgate made the book. Gore had writ The Art of Scientific Discovery and works on electro deposition and electro metallurgy. A motto fronts the title: nations advance by new knowledge.

He gives the treatise to the Birmingham Philosophical Society. That young society had backed his long held views on the national importance of scientific investigation, he says. It set an intelligent example by establishing a fund for the endowment of original scientific research. Gore writes from his own Institute of Scientific Research at Birmingham. The small book makes the case that a nation's rise rests on the new knowledge its inquirers win.
35086-glimpses-of-king-william-iv-and-qu:
Glimpses of King William the Fourth and Queen Adelaide is a note book by Cecil White. Miss Clitherow notes of Boston House give the book its core in full. A London house brought it out in nineteen two in print form. Part one tells Boston House and the Clitherow kin of that place. The house stands off Boston Road near Brentford, built in sixteen twenty two.

Three gables, brick walls of three floors, and a stone porch mark its front. Part heads run through a St James meal of eighteen thirty in rank. Windsor week ends, plague at Brentford, and false queen tales fill next parts. Royal birth feasts, a Boston House meal for the crown pair, and Kew meals crowd mid parts. Death of the king in eighteen thirty seven closes the scheme.
35225-toronto-of-old-collections-and-rec:
Henry Scadding wrote Toronto of Old, collections and recollections of the early settlement and social life of the capital of Ontario. Adam, Stevenson and Company issued the book at Toronto in 1873. A portrait of Scadding stands at the front. The book is given to the Earl of Dufferin, governor general of British North America, praised as a keen sympathizer with the past as well as the present of his people.

Scadding's preface owns that the book grew by accident. A paper of early notices of Toronto, written for a local periodical a few years before, grew under his hand into a volume. He jokes that he meant it only as a spark in the shower of light literature of the age. The result is a store of memory of Toronto's infancy and early youth.
35226-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-11-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly, volume eleven, number sixty eight, is the June 1863 issue of a magazine of literature, art, and politics. Ticknor and Fields entered it under the copyright law that year in Massachusetts. The lead article takes up a grim medical subject: weak lungs, and how to make them strong.

The writer says the highest medical authorities charge tubercular disease with one third of the deaths among youth and adults in the civilized world. Genuine consumption, he argues, does not start from a cold but from tubercles, and the root cause is a tainted condition of the whole system. Prevention by wise hygiene, not local treatment of the lungs, is the article's plea.
35233-the-streets-of-ascalon-episodes-in:
Streets of Ascalon is a novel by Robert Chambers, published by Appleton at New York in 1912. Its subtitle calls it episodes in the unfinished career of Richard Quarren, Esquire. Charles Dana Gibson illustrated the volume for its author in this edition. A list of Chambers works at the front runs from The King in Yellow to The Common Law.

The list of illustrations names the world of the tale: suppers, dancers, and adorers in its plates. Westguard, colossal in his armour, gazes at a gorgeous spectacle in one plate caption.  The novel is a society tale of New York wealth and intrigue, drawn by Gibson in his famous manner. Chambers, who began with the horrors of the King in Yellow, ended as the laureate of the rich at play, and this is a prime specimen.
35386-the-children-s-story-of-the-war-vo:
Sir Edward Parrott wrote this fourth volume of The Children's Story of the War, printed at Toronto in 1916. Its subject is the story of the year 1915. Lines by Collins on how the brave sleep stand at the front. A picture shows the sinking of the Bluecher on January 24, 1915. The first chapters set the house in order and tell the loss of the Formidable.

The battle of the Dogger Bank and a Turkish descent upon Egypt follow. Winter warfare on the Western Front and stories from the battlefield fill the middle. The submarine blockade begins, the Lusitania sinks, and tales of submarines crowd in. The fall of Przemysl, the battle of Neuve Chapelle, and the Dardanelles come next. A poisonous cloud and the battle glory of Canada close the shown contents.
35492-dictionary-of-the-chinook-jargon-o:
The Dictionary of the Chinook Jargon, or Indian Trade Language of the North Pacific Coast, was published by Hibben at Victoria in 1889. The copyright was entered in Canada in 1877. Part one gives Chinook into English, letter by letter. Ah-ha is yes; ahn-kut-te is formerly, or long ago if the first syllable is drawn out, and al-kie means presently, hold on, not so fast. Amo-te is the strawberry, and ats a younger sister.

Bos-ton names an American, and Boston illahie the United States. Chickamin is iron or metal: white chickamin is silver, and red chickamin gold or copper. Chuck is water, a river, or the sea when salt; skookum chuck is a rapid. Examples in Chinook sentences accompany many entries, and the jargon served trade between settlers and the peoples of the coast.
35720-papers-relating-to-an-act-of-the-a:
Papers Relating to an Act of the Assembly of the Province of New York is a colonial pamphlet of state papers. The act encouraged the Indian trade and barred the selling of Indian goods to the French of Canada. Six documents make the book. First comes a petition of the merchants of London to the king against the act.

Then the king's order in council sends the petition to the lords of trade and plantations. Extracts of their minutes follow, with their report to the king on the merchants' claims. The council committee of New York answers the petition in its own report. Last stands a memorial on the fur trade of New York by Colden, the colonial thinker. The London merchants who sign include Samuel Baker, John Bayeux, and Joseph Paice.
35728-motor-boat-boys-on-the-st-lawrence:
Motor Boat Boys on the Saint Lawrence, or solving the mystery of the Thousand Islands, is a boys' adventure by Louis Arundel, copyrighted at Chicago in 1913. A pictured plea at the front asks a promise to read aloud the log of a past trip down the big river. The contents open after a game, with chums tried and true.

A chance clue, a blocked sly move, and a guardian of the fleet follow in the early chapters. A boat called the Flash, a boy who scents trouble, and a midnight watch fill the middle. A ghost of the island is hunted, a trail followed, and Yankee stubbornness tested. A daring venture by Jack, the secret out, and an escape close the list. The river of the title, with its maze of islands, gives the motor boat crew their stage.
36396-ruth-fielding-in-the-saddle-or-col:
Alice B Emerson wrote Ruth Fielding in the Saddle. Cupples and Leon issued the girls' book in 1917. Its full title adds College Girls in the Land of Gold. Emerson wrote the whole Ruth Fielding line. Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill began it. Twelve books stand listed on the series page.

Titles run from Briarwood Hall to Snow Camp. Lighthouse Point and Silver Ranch stand between. Gypsies, moving pictures, and Dixie fill later books. Ruth Fielding at College stands just before this one. A front plate shows a mad horse circling Ruth. She strikes at it again and again there. College friends ride into gold country in this entry. Series books like this gave girl readers a heroine who studied, traveled, and faced down danger term after term.
36461-the-female-soldier-or-the-surprisi:
Female Soldier is the life and adventures of Hannah Snell, told in an old chapbook account. Its title page gives her birth at Worcester and her alias James Gray for service. Deserted by her husband, she put on men clothes and travelled to Coventry for him. There she enlisted in Colonel Guise regiment of foot as a common soldier.

The regiment marched to Carlisle in the time of the Scottish rebellion of that age. What befell her in that city, and her desertion from the regiment, fill the tale. Later service at sea and wounds that hid her sex made her a public wonder. Readers get a famous case of a woman who lived years as a soldier.
36656-a-seasonable-warning-and-caution-a:
Daniel Defoe wrote A Seasonable Warning and Caution Against the Insinuations of Papists and Jacobites in Favour of the Pretender in 1712. J Baker printed the letter at the Black-Boy in Paternoster Row, London. The piece takes the form of a letter from an Englishman at the court of Hanover.

Defoe opens with a cry: how now, England, what evil spirit possesses thee? He praises England as a nation famous for defending liberty and pulling down tyrants. Footnotes name Edward the Second, Richard the Second, Richard the Third, and James the Second. He recalls the barons' wars and England's shelter of persecuted Protestants under Elizabeth. The tract warns readers against quiet Jacobite persuasion.
36691-conversations-on-natural-philosoph:
Conversations on Natural Philosophy appeared at Philadelphia from John Grigg in 1826, by the author of Conversations on Chemistry. Thomas Jones, professor of mechanics in the Franklin Institute of Pennsylvania, added corrections, fresh matter, questions, and a glossary. Plates illustrate the lessons throughout the volume. The preface laments that few school books truly fit their purpose.

Dialogue form carries the teaching, as its chemistry sister volume had done. Elements of the science are explained in familiar talk rather than dry rule. Jones aimed the American edition at schools and self taught readers alike. Students get physics broken into talk, test questions, and plain terms. The book shows how science reached young learners before the modern textbook age.
36734-the-browning-cyclop-dia-a-guide-to:
The Browning Cyclopaedia is a guide to the study of Robert Browning's works by Dr Berdoe. The edition here opens with pages of press opinions on the first edition. The Times calls the work conscientious and painstaking. The Pall Mall Gazette finds it in many ways very well done. The Speaker hopes it will be widely bought. The Scotsman praises its far-reaching research and careful industry.

Reviewers agree on the book's purpose. Berdoe tackles every allusion, every proper name, and every phase of thought in the poems. Dark and doubtful passages are cleared for the systematic reader. Notes and Queries calls it the most ambitious handbook of its class yet executed. The Bookman calls it a monument of industry and devotion. Vanity Fair notes that not a difficulty is shirked. The Daily Telegraph stresses the infinite labour behind it.
36802-the-romance-of-polar-exploration-i:
The Romance of Polar Exploration, by Firth Scott, was published in London in 1909. Twenty four pictures go with the text. Its subtitle promises accounts of Arctic and Antarctic adventure. The span runs from the earliest time to the voyage of the Discovery. A plate shows the Stella Polare nipped in the ice, with stores unloaded in haste. The publishers thank Lieutenant Shackleton of the Discovery for drawings and leave to use plates. Mill's Siege of the South Pole lends a picture too.

Scott had written From Franklin to Nansen in the same line. The Library of Romance aimed at accuracy with charm for readers of all ages. Ice, hunger, lost ships, and the race for the poles fill the pages. The book catches the heroic age of polar travel at its height.
36835-notes-and-queries-vol-iii-number-8:
Notes and Queries, Volume Three, Number 83, is a weekly number dated Saturday, May 31, 1851. The journal calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto is Captain Cuttle's saying: when found, make a note of. The price was threepence.

The contents open with the proposed record of existing monuments. Notes follow on Chaucer, on traditions passed through few links, and on Young's Narcissa. Minor notes take up a curious epitaph, the curse of Scotland, and pictorial antiquities. Queries ask after English poems by Constantine Huyghens and after the Reverend Gay. Minor queries run from a carved ceiling in Dorsetshire to publicans' signs and gloves. The number is the Victorian republic of letters talking to itself, question by question.
3689-letters-of-franz-liszt-volume-1-fro:
This first volume gathers the letters of Franz Liszt from his years as a traveling virtuoso, from Paris to Rome. The letters were collected by La Mara, the pen name of Marie Lipsius, and translated by Constance Bache. They cover Liszt's youth as a piano prodigy, his tours, his friendships, and his loves, in his own eager, confessional voice.

Readers meet Liszt among Paris salons, concert halls, and Italian journeys, writing to friends, patrons, and fellow musicians. The letters show a young artist becoming a legend, with all his charm and restlessness. The volume suits music lovers who want Liszt in his own words, before his later years as abbe and teacher.
37314-the-bradys-after-a-chinese-princes:
Number 658 of a weekly detective paper came out at New York on September 1 1911 for five cents. It sends Old and Young King Brady after a Chinese princess and the fiends of Frisco. The writer is billed only as a New York detective. The tale opens on a foggy night on the bay at San Francisco.

A motor boat with five men cruises close in to the wharves after two in the morning. Old King Brady, in a broad white hat, leads the party from the stern. Word has come that opium will be run in past the duty owed to the United States. The Bradys sailed on orders from the secret service bureau.
37432-short-stories-of-the-new-america-i:
Laselle, of the Newton high schools in Massachusetts, selected and edited this school anthology, Short Stories of the New America, printed at New York in 1919. Its subtitle states the aim: interpreting the America of this age to high school boys and girls. Ten stories by ten hands make the book.

A contents page sorts them. A Kansas tale by Canfield comes first, then survivors by Singmaster and a wildcat by Terhune. A citizen, an Indian of the reservation, a night attack, and a path of glory follow. A sergeant back from France, a coward by Empey, and a tale of Château-Thierry close the list. Notes on the authors follow. Canfield's story came from her book of France in the Great War, written while she worked for the relief of men blinded in the fighting.
37496-notes-and-queries-vol-iii-number-8:
Notes and Queries, a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, issued its eighty-sixth number on Saturday, June 21, 1851. The number is part of the third volume and sold at threepence, or fourpence stamped. Its motto, taken from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of. The contents open with notes on books, on Ireland and its freedom from serpents, and on the canons and articles of 1571.

Minor notes treat Lord Edward Fitzgerald's mother, Chaucer and Gray, the Shakespeare family, and an epitaph on Doctor Humphrey Tindall. Queries follow on Tennyson, on the old modes of hanging bells, on English Sapphics, statues on horseback, and plays in churches. The paper lived on this trade of questions and answers among readers, and it long stayed a chief storehouse of facts of English history and books.
37516-notes-and-queries-vol-iii-number-8:
Notes and Queries for Saturday, June 28, 1851, volume three, number 87, sold for threepence, or fourpence in the stamped edition. The weekly bills itself as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its lead piece urges that a record be made of existing monuments before they vanish. Around it sit notes, queries, and replies on Chaucer, on epigrams about Cromwell, on Lancashire folk lore, and on why a baker's dozen runs to thirteen.

The charm of the journal is this traffic in small facts. A reader asks, another answers from his own shelf or parish register, and a third corrects them both. Much of what passed as minor learning in Victorian England moved through these pages. Single numbers like this one preserve the questions a whole class of readers thought worth printing.
37568-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-89:
Notes and Queries, volume four, number eighty nine, a weekly journal dated Saturday, July 12, 1851, served as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, ran: when found, make a note of. Readers sent in notes, queries, and replies on points of history, literature, and word lore.

The notes in this number treat privately printed books, sardonic smiles, and the private amours of Oliver Cromwell. Professor De Morgan writes on spurious editions of Baily's Annuities. Queries ask after names, monuments, proverbs, and points of law. Replies take up the Princesses of Wales, the late William Hone, and Shakespeare's reputed small Latin. The number shows the journal at its work of shared inquiry.
37570-secret-history-of-the-court-of-eng:
Secret History of the Court of England, from the Accession of George the Third to the Death of George the Fourth, is here in volume one of two. A note explains a gap in the book. Pages one to twenty four were never printed, after an accusation of libel forced pages to be rewritten and reprinted.

Other asterisks in the text mark censored names. A thought break or a cut in a poetry quotation is shown by a row of asterisks. The preface tells the story of that libel trouble at length. Readers get a scandal history of two Georgian reigns. It claims to tell what open histories would not: court intrigue, favour, and ruin, with names sometimes hid for fear of the law. Even its missing opening is part of its story, and the text flags that loss plainly for the reader.
37571-secret-history-of-the-court-of-eng:
The hosted text is the second volume of a Secret History of the Court of England, from the coming of George the Third to the death of George the Fourth. It bears the name of Lady Anne Hamilton, sister of the Duke of Hamilton and Brandon. The title page promises full particulars of the mysterious death of the Princess Charlotte.

A verse motto at the front sets the tone. It bids the singer brand the crimes of lords and kings, and sing no more of meaner vice. The names of many persons in the tale are hidden behind rows of stars, as such scandal books of the day were printed. Court favour, court sin, and court revenge fill the pages. The first volume is also held by Project Gutenberg.
37593-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-90:
Notes and Queries, Volume IV, Number 90, came out on Saturday, July 19, 1851. The weekly called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. It cost threepence, or fourpence stamped. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, was to make a note of a thing when found.

Notes in this issue suggest a Caxton memorial, treat supposed witchcraft, and note the late Sir John Graham Dalyell. Queries ask about the origin of Fontainebleau, Shelley's children, and Baskerville the printer. Replies cover written sermons, salting the dead, and Jonah and the whale. A Caxton note says the Roxburghe Club bore the cost of a monument at Westminster. Small facts and open asks drive the whole issue.
37723-for-sceptre-and-crown-a-romance-of:
Gregor Samarow wrote this political romance, translated from the German and published by King in London in 1875. Advertisements for new novels fill the first pages before his title page appears. Volume one of two is this copy, of the English edition that year at Cornhill.

The success of the German original on the continent justified an English version, the translator says. Samarow, whose real name was Meding, had served the king of Hanover as a councillor, a note explains. Courts and camps of 1866, when Prussia crushed Austria and Hanover alike, fill a romance written by a man who watched thrones fall.
37724-for-sceptre-and-crown-a-romance-of:
For Sceptre and Crown, a romance of the present time, appears here in its second volume. Gregor Samarow is the pen name of Oskar Meding, as a note in the text states. Court and state intrigue in the Europe of its day form the ground of such a romance. Two volume sets of this kind were stocked by the circulating libraries of the era.

Front pages list other new novels at the libraries, in the custom of the time. Vanessa, Idolatry by Julian Hawthorne, and Woman a Riddle are praised there with press quotes. Such framing shows the market this volume aimed to serve in its day. Readers who took the first volume could follow the tale of crowns and courts to its end. Power, love, and duty at the top of society drive a romance with this title.
37778-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-91:
Notes and Queries, volume four, number 91, came out on Saturday, July 26, 1851, priced at sixpence. The journal called itself a means of contact for men of letters, artists, students of old things, and family historians. Its motto, taken from Captain Cuttle, urges readers to make a note of what they find.

The number opens with notes on Richard Rolle of Hampole, old verse scraps, and folk lore such as cures, charms, and school beliefs. Small notes touch on Chaucer, Gray, Burns, and Shakespeare in Sweden. A long list of queries follows, asking about words, arms, old books, Stonehenge, and much more, in hope that readers will reply.
37897-villages-of-the-algonquian-siouan-:
Villages of the Algonquian, Siouan, and Caddoan Tribes West of the Mississippi is a state study by Bushnell. It came out as a bulletin of the national house for first peoples lore. Its front plate shows a camp scene. Meat dries on racks in the sun in that scene.

Notes at the front tell how the text was set from page scans. Old spellings stand as they first stood. The study maps the old town sites of three great tongue stocks. Those stocks held the plains and woods west of the great river. It draws on trips, digs, and the tales of the tribes. From those it fixes where each folk lived and how their towns were built. It notes what marks of them still stand.
38212-the-making-of-william-edwards-or-t:
The Making of William Edwards, or The Story of the Bridge of Beauty, is a novel by Isabella Banks, published in London by Andrew Melrose in a second edition. Dewar illustrated the book. Banks had earlier written God's Providence House and The Manchester Man.

Twenty-four chapters follow a Welsh boy's making. A thunderstorm, paying the rent, a lost child, and a baffled agent mark the early story. Caerphilly Castle, grandfather's gold, and a blind instructor appear along the way. Bridge-building and Pont-y-Pridd close the list, pointing to the hero's engineering fate. The frontispiece shows the search for a missing farmer. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
38222-the-quest-of-the-golden-hope-a-sev:
The Quest of the Golden Hope is a boys' sea tale by Percy Westerman, set in the seventeenth century. Blackie published it in London and Glasgow, with pictures by Frank Wiles. Westerman's name fronts a long list of golden ship tales for boys. Thirty three chapters run from a fugitive of Sedgemoor to a safe port.

Captain Jeremy is wounded in the front plate, and a chart drives the plot. A cave in a lonely heath, a hold at sea, and Algerine pirates follow. The wreck of the Madre de Dios hides the treasure the boys hunt. Treasure Island, a stockade fight, and boarders repelled fill the middle chapters. Untold wealth, a mutiny of the Neptune, and a burning ship come near the end. A map of the island keys the stockade, paths, and shoals for readers.
38324-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-92:
Notes and Queries, volume four number ninety two, dated Saturday, August two, eighteen fifty one, is an issue of a literary weekly. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, is when found, make a note of. The price was threepence, or fourpence stamped. Its subtitle calls it a medium of intercommunication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists.

Contents split into notes, queries, and replies, as the title promises. Notes treat proverbial philosophy and a paraphrase of a psalm by Churchill. A note weighs the description of a famous statue in a poem of Byron. Queries ask about an old play, swearing on the horns at Highgate, and a proverb of a king. Minor queries range from Nostradamus to a salmon fishery in the Thames.
38337-notes-and-queries-vol-iv-number-93:
Notes and Queries served literary men, artists, antiquaries and genealogists as a medium of inter-communication. Volume four, number 93, appeared on Saturday, August 9, 1851, at threepence. Its motto from Captain Cuttle tells readers to make a note of things when found.

Lady Hopton leads the notes in this number's contents page at the front. Bealby writes on newspapers, taking The Times as his case in the notes. Devonshire superstitions supply the folk lore, and minor notes chase a curious inscription and the history of glass in windows, the small change of learning the journal traded in weekly.
38375-religion-in-the-heavens-or-mytholo:
Religion in the Heavens is a set of freethought lectures by Logan Mitchell. Mitchell signs himself a follower of nature. David Widger produced this edition from the 1881 printing. A stern quote from Mosheim heads the title page. It warns that impostors triumph when truth is dangerous.

The argument is stated at once. One universal myth lies at the basis of all religions. That myth has secret reference to the zodiac and the solar system. Priests turned the sun and the host of heaven into persons. They invented tales to subdue ignorant minds. Mitchell holds that the deception continues to this day. His preface attacks priestcraft and superstition in strong terms. He seeks to free his fellows from fear.
38866-the-evolution-of-photography-with-:
Evolution of Photography, by John Werge, records the growth of the photo art. Its full title promises a dated record of finds and inventions in the field. Front plates show Wedgwood, Niepce, Reade, Talbot, and Herschel as first period men. Their portraits come from casts, paintings, and early photo processes themselves.

Werge traces paper and asphaltum work and the first photo pioneers in order. The record aims to log contributions to photographic art as they arose. Readers get a chronicle of how the camera art grew step by step. Names, dates, and methods form the spine of the whole survey. The book serves as a reference shelf piece for photo history fans.
38966-the-manifestation-of-the-miraculou:
A brief book tells how the Miraculous Medal came to be and spread. The Association of the Miraculous Medal put it out at Perryville. Saint Mary's Seminary there was that group's home in Missouri. Church leave to print dates to June of 1918 in its front. The Archbishop of Saint Louis gave his seal on June 21.

Mary born with no sin, pray for us, is the medal's cry. The group's aim is to spread love for that call in all hearts. Its head in Saint Louis wrote in warm praise of the new work. Tales of the first sights and the medal's spread fill the book. Church folk get a short, sourced tale of a loved sign. Faith in that sign rules it.
39052-ecce-homo-or-a-critical-inquiry-in:
Ecce Homo is a critical inquiry into the history of Jesus of Nazareth by the Baron d'Holbach. The Gordon Press of New York reprinted it in 1977. That reprint follows the first American edition of 1827. Holbach's subtitle calls the work a rational analysis of the Gospels.

The introduction opens with a paradox meant to provoke the reader. The writings of the New Testament are in everyone's hands, it says. Yet few professors of Christianity know their founder's history at all. Fewer still have ventured to examine that history with serious care. Holbach, the French materialist who lived from 1723 to 1789, supplies the examination. The cross, it reads, was the banner under which madmen glutted the earth with blood.
39227-a-source-book-of-medi-val-history-:
A Source Book of Mediaeval History was edited by Frederic Austin Ogg, assistant in history at Harvard. The American Book Company published it in 1907 at New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago. The subtitle states the plan: documents illustrative of European life and institutions from the German invasions to the Renaissance.

An opening chapter treats the nature and use of historical sources. Ogg begins with a plain question: if one proposes to write a history of the times of Abraham Lincoln, how shall one begin, and how proceed? Books on Lincoln would fill shelf upon shelf, and a history drawn from them alone might read well and sell widely. Yet the first thing needed is information, accurate and trustworthy, drawn from the sources themselves. The documents that follow supply that material for the Middle Ages.
39578-the-broncho-rider-boys-on-the-wyom:
Frank Fowler wrote The Broncho Rider Boys on the Wyoming Trail, a western tale for boys. A L Burt Company issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred fourteen. Fowler had sent the boys to Arizona and Keystone Ranch before. Adrian, Billie, and Donald ride north in this round.

One more night out ends their gallop from the Arizona line, Adrian says. Billie owns that even good riding can pall in time. News of the Bar-S Ranch meets them on the trail. A night alarm and a wild stampede break their camp calm. Dead stock bears a plain bar and S brand in one plate. The boys trail cattle rustlers to a corral in Bittersweet Coulie. Treachery, a trap, and a timed wait crowd the last third. The sheriff rides in to close the case at the end.
39776-the-three-perils-of-man-or-war-wom:
James Hogg wrote The Three Perils of Man, or War, Women, and Witchcraft, a border romance published in London in 1822 in three volumes, this being the first. Hogg, the Ettrick Shepherd, also wrote Winter-Evening Tales and The Brownie of Bodsbeck. He inscribes the work to William Stewart Rose in memory of Yarrow.

An old song opens the first chapter, of a courteous king and his bonnie daughter in the halls of Binnorie. A warlock has undone the bravest knight that ever broke bread there. The narrator calls the days of the Stuart kings the days of chivalry and romance. Readers get a wild Scottish romance of siege, love, and sorcery.
39848-india-through-the-ages-a-popular-a:
India through the Ages is a popular history of Hindustan by Flora Annie Steel, published in London in a third edition in nineteen eleven. Steel was known for a novel of the Indian Mutiny named on the title page. Seven maps track India at set dates, from early times to the rise of British rule. The maps alone chart the book's sweep.

Steel writes history for general readers, with colour and scene rather than dry lists of kings. Hindu, Muslim, and British periods all fall within her story of the land. Her long life in India shaped the telling, for good and for period bias alike. The book stands as a readable Edwardian survey of a vast past.
39872-the-three-perils-of-man-or-war-wom:
Volume two of The Three Perils of Man, a Border romance by James Hogg, was issued at London in 1822. The three perils of the title are war, women, and witchcraft. Hogg had written Winter Evening Tales and The Queen’s Wake before this work. The novel ran to three volumes in its first form.

A line from Fletcher stands on the title page as a motto. The tale is set on the Scottish Border, in days of feud and raid. Its first chapter damns a base and cruel knight in ballad tones. Hogg mixes battle, love, and black arts in one wild plot. The middle volume drives the rivalries and spells toward their crisis. Readers get the Ettrick Shepherd at his most romantic and strange.
39959-the-three-perils-of-man-or-war-wom:
James Hogg wrote The Three Perils of Man, a Border romance in three volumes. Longman and partners published the set in London in 1822. This file holds the third volume. The perils of the title are war, women, and witchcraft. Hogg had already won readers with his Winter-Evening Tales and the Queen's Wake.

The volume opens mid-quarrel over a tale. A loud call at the gate halts the dispute about Tam's story. Passwords pass by moon and seven stars before the riders are known. The new arrivals are Warden's men sent from Northumberland to Aikwood. Dan Chisholm leads twenty-six chosen troopers to ask after the Warden's embassy. Charlie Scott greets his old companion with joy. The scene sets loyalty and border warfare at the heart of the tale.
40680-the-greville-memoirs-part-3-of-3-v:
The Greville Memoirs, third part, volume one, is Charles C F Greville's journal of the reign of Queen Victoria from 1852 to 1860. Longmans, Green, and Company of London published it in 1887, printed by Spottiswoode. Greville, clerk of the council, kept notes on the politics of his day for decades, and this third part appeared after his death.

The contents open on the fall of a government. Divisions of the Liberal party, hostility of the Radicals, Disraeli's budget, and the division on that budget fill the first chapter's summary. Lord Derby resigns, the Liberals negotiate, and Lord Aberdeen's government takes shape, with Lord Palmerston agreeing at last to join. Greville watched cabinets form from inside the council chamber, and his journal remains a chief source for the party politics of the 1850s.
40681-the-greville-memoirs-part-3-of-3-v:
Charles Greville keeps a court journal in The Greville Memoirs, third part, volume 2, a journal of the reign of Queen Victoria from 1852 to 1860. Longmans Green of London print the book in 1887. Greville was clerk of the Council. The third part runs to two volumes, of which this is the second.

Chapter eleven's contents show the diary's grain. France and Prussia lead, with the Emperor's speech and faint hopes of peace. A favourable view of the policy of Russia and the progress of the negotiations follow. Russia accepts the terms of peace, and the acceptance is explained. Popular feeling in favour of the war is weighed against it. Lord Stratford and General Williams, Disraeli's prospects, and the meeting of Parliament fill the run. State gossip and high policy mix on every page.
40777-autobiography-of-charles-clinton-n:
Autobiography of Charles Clinton Nourse was privately printed at Cedar Rapids, Iowa, in 1911. It was prepared for use of members of the family. It holds the incidents of more than fifty years' practice at the bar in the state of Iowa. Nourse writes it as a long letter to young Joseph Chamberlain, begun at Des Moines in May 1908.

He was born on April 1, 1829, in Sharpsburg, Maryland, near Antietam Creek. Twenty chapters follow his life from ancestry and early days in Iowa to the Des Moines river land titles. They treat the Brown impeachment case and a bank failure. They also treat temperance, freight tariffs, and cattle breeding. The book is a lawyer's life told for his own kin.
40781-the-art-of-cross-examination-with-:
Francis Wellman of the New York bar wrote the classic book on the questioning of witnesses. Macmillan published it in 1904. He gave the book to his two sons, who meant to enter the law themselves. An opening motto calls this art the rarest and hardest of the advocate's skills to gain.

Wellman holds that the fate of a case hangs on it. A speech seldom wins a cause, he says, but no contested cause escapes the mark of how its witnesses were handled. Chapters treat manner and matter, the false witness, and the expert. Golden rules for the work are set down near the end. Then come famed examples in full: the forger Pigott before the Parnell body, Russell Sage on the stand, and the Palmer case.
40804-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-123:
Notes and Queries, volume five, number 123, came out on March 6, 1852. Its price was fourpence, or fivepence for the stamped edition. The journal is a medium of inter-communication for literary men. Antiquaries, artists, and genealogists share its pages, the head says. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, urges making a note of finds.

Contents open with notes on South Sea playing cards by Sudlow. The birthplace of the Empress Josephine and notes on Homer follow. Folk lore treats an interment custom, pure rain water, and a cough cure. Sainted kings incorruptible and minor notes fill the section out. Queries ask seven questions, and plague stones take a query. Minor queries touch an old song, wild oats, and cross-legged effigies. Replies treat an old Scots march and the meaning of stickle. The number shows the journal's shared desk at full work.
40843-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-124:
Notes and Queries, volume five, number 124, is the weekly issue dated Saturday, March the thirteenth, 1852. The London journal called itself a medium of talk among literary men, artists, antiquaries, and family historians. Its motto came from Captain Cuttle: when found, make a note of. The price was fourpence, or fivepence stamped.

The contents sort matter into notes, queries, and replies. Notes treat Shakespeare readings and a charm that burning fern brings rain. Queries ask after snuff boxes, fasting deaths, and a place where pigs play the organ. Replies answer on Moravian hymns, ballad poetry, and Sterne in Paris. Readers wrote the journal as much as its editor did. Numbers like this built a storehouse of small facts still mined today.
40901-the-gentleman-and-lady-s-book-of-p:
The Gentleman and Lady Book of Politeness and Propriety of Deportment, by Madame Celnart, came to Boston readers in 1833. It was translated from the sixth Paris edition, enlarged and improved. The book is dedicated to the youth of both sexes in its title. Allen and Ticknor with Carter, Hendee and Company issued the translation.

A preface notes that the work had wide circulation in France. France is held up there as the genial soil of politeness in the world. Foreign visitors had told Americans freely what not to do in company. The publishers offer this book as sound word on what polished society in Europe does do. Young readers could thus learn how to act and how to avoid just censure in company.
40910-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-125:
Notes and Queries for Saturday, March 20, 1852 is volume V, number 125 of the weekly that called itself a medium of inter-communication. It served literary men, artists, antiquaries and genealogists, and its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: When found, make a note of. The price was fourpence.

The notes open with Bolton Corney on the Caxton Coffer, and continue with John Tradescant the younger and Cowley and his monument. Folk lore and London street characters follow, with minor notes on Dean Swift, Joe Miller and hints to book-buyers. Queries ask after Cromwell's skull, the meaning of the word elvan and clergymen first styled Reverend, and the replies take up the age of trees and the Tilford Oak.
40987-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-126:
Number 126 of a famous literary weekly dates to Saturday, March 27, 1852. The paper sells for fourpence. Its motto comes from Captain Cuttle: when found, make a note of.

Readers send in short notes on odd points of learning. This number treats pilgrimages to the Holy Land, surnames, and a malt license of 1596. One note asks where Lollard was buried, and what became of his bones. Dean Swift's library gets a note too. Folk lore covers churching of women and wassailing orchards in Sussex. Queries ask after Cromwell's skull, town halls, and the Knights Templars. Answers pile up on Welsh pedigrees and heraldry. The journal built a web of learned readers trading facts by post.
41091-the-price-of-power-being-chapters-:
William Le Queux wrote a novel drawn, its subtitle claims, from the secret history of the imperial court of Russia, in an edition dated 1913. Colin Trewinnard narrates. Captain Stoyanovitch, an equerry in the white uniform of the Imperial Guard, hands him a letter sealed with the imperial cipher. The Emperor commands Trewinnard to a private audience that day.

Trewinnard wonders whether the blow has fallen. The captain describes the Emperor's long tour: reviews at Orel and Saratov, a Volga trip to Astrakhan, and Crimea rest. They all hate the armoured train, he says. Le Queux builds court intrigue around an Englishman close to the throne.
41138-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-127:
Notes and Queries called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and family historians. Volume five, number 127, came out on Saturday, April 3, 1852, at fourpence. The motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs 'When found, make a note of.'

Lord Braybrooke writes on Bonaparte and Lord Whitworth, and a note treats Archbishop Laud on Prynne's Breviate. Readers ask about Algernon Sidney, old Irish tales, and print pamphlets. Small queries cover Chaucer notes, Cheke's clock, and the Ruthven family. Replies take up the old Countess of Desmond, English surnames, and maps of Africa. The issue shows how the journal traded facts week by week.
41171-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-128:
Notes and Queries of April 10, 1852 is an issue of a weekly journal for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. The number is 128 of volume five. It sold for fourpence, with a stamped edition at fivepence. The motto, from Captain Cuttle, bids the reader make a note of anything found.

The contents show the journal's method. Notes treat an unpublished song by Thomas Otway, a Shakespeare passage, Cowley's prose, and Coleridge's Christabel. Folk lore items cover game feathers and the Isle of Man. Queries ask about Dutch porcelain manufactories, salmon fisheries, and the birthplace of Saint Patrick. Replies to earlier queries close the number. Readers built knowledge by exchange. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
41205-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-129:
Notes and Queries, volume five, number 129, for Saturday, April 17, 1852, is a medium of inter communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle, is: when found, make a note of. The issue costs fourpence and divides into notes, queries, replies, and miscellaneous matter.

The leading note, by Thomas Gill, presents an epitaph in the church of Saint Giles, Cripplegate, possibly by Milton, whose dust that church possesses. Other notes treat popular stories of the English peasantry and points of folk lore, from giving cheese at a birth to a spectral coach and horses. Queries ask about the Danes in England and whether a clergyman can marry himself. Replies handle Saint Christopher, plague stones, rhymes on places, and a passage in Hamlet, with books wanted and notices to correspondents at the back.
41254-notes-and-queries-vol-v-number-130:
Notes and Queries for Saturday, April 24, 1852 is number 130 of volume five. The weekly journal billed itself as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Captain Cuttle's advice, when found, make a note of, stands as its motto. The stamped edition cost fivepence.

The notes in this number conclude a piece on the Tradescants and Elias Ashmole. Other notes treat inedited poetry, a point in Virgil, and the printing bills for the King's Book. Minor notes range from book-keepers to waistcoats worn by women. Folk lore covers the frog, an oath in court, and two saints' days. The queries ask after Speaker Lenthall, suffragan bishops, poison, gipsies, and Stonehenge. The number is a fair sample of the correspondence college that Victorian scholarship built for itself.
41258-memoirs-of-the-life-and-labours-of:
Memoirs of the Life and Labours of the Rev Samuel Marsden tells of the senior chaplain of New South Wales. The Religious Tract Society published it in London. The Rev J B Marsden edited the volume. He stresses that he was no relation, despite the shared name. Marsden of Paramatta also links to the missions of New Zealand and Tahiti.

The editor drew on rich unpublished sources. The Church Missionary and London Missionary Societies opened Marsden's correspondence. J S Nicholas, who accompanied Marsden's first New Zealand visit, lent a manuscript. A life by Lieutenant Sadleir of Paramatta supplied extracts. The contents trace the career. Early life and the voyage out come first. The colony's moral state on his arrival follows. His magistracy, his farming, and the charge of secularity get a chapter. His care of the Polynesian mission and his 1807 return to England continue the story.
42078-the-letters-of-jane-austen-selecte:
The Letters of Jane Austen gathers letters by the famed English novelist, drawn from the set put out by her great nephew Edward, Lord Brabourne. Sarah Chauncey Woolsey picked and shaped this smaller book. The first copyright dates to 1892, and the Boston printing shown here is from 1908.

A short preface notes the fresh fame of Austen and the new printings of her novels in the past ten years. The letters show Austen in her own voice, writing on daily life in a quieter, slower England. Woolsey frames them for readers who know Sense and Sensibility and Pride and Prejudice and want the woman behind them. The book helps readers hear Austen speak plainly, with wit, outside her fiction.
42129-her-majesty-s-mails-an-historical-:
William Lewins traces the growth of the British Post Office from its early days to the system of his own time. Writing in 1864, he covers the carriage of letters by road and rail, the rise of the penny post, and the reforms that made cheap postage a settled part of British life. He writes as a man who knew the office from inside. He backs his account with figures, dates, and stories from the mails.

The book moves from the first royal posts through the coaching era to the railway age, when trains reshaped how fast letters could travel. Lewins explains how rates were charged, how the penny rate changed who could write to whom, and how the office handled a volume of mail that kept growing year by year.
42218-maori-religion-and-mythology-illus:
Edward Shortland wrote Maori Religion and Mythology, issued at London in 1882 by Longmans, Green, and Company. Shortland was late Native Secretary in New Zealand. He had writ Traditions and Superstitions of the New Zealanders. The book holds English texts of traditions and karakia, or prayers. Notes on Maori tenure of land are added.

Shortland says the Maori manuscripts were gathered many years past. The men who gave them are now dead, save one. All were men of good birth and sound knowledge, he says. One who could write sent his lore in his own hand. He drew it from the tohunga, or wise men of his family. Others told their tales by mouth. Shortland bade them tell each tale as if to their own folk in a sacred house. The book is given to the memory of Sir William Martin.
42544-soyer-s-culinary-campaign-being-hi:
Soyer, chef of the Reform Club, published his culinary campaign with Routledge at London in 1857. The book is a memoir of the war in the Crimea and a cookery manual. Its title promises the plain art of cookery for army, navy, and civil institutions. He dedicates it to Lord Panmure, who had sent him east. His object, the preface says, is to record his work improving the dieting of the hospitals in the East and the soldiers' rations before Sebastopol.

The contents march: a supper at the Albion and its consequences, a summons to Stafford House, off to the war. A tour round the kitchens and first operations follow. The Scutari mission accomplished, he sails for the Crimea and a new enemy, disease in the pots. Soyer cooked for an army that had been fed like a mob, and wrote the receipt book of his generalship.
42709-poisons-their-effects-and-detectio:
Poisons, Their Effects and Detection is a work manual on the lore of dire drugs. Its front pages carry the lists of the hands past works on food craft, held in high praise by the press of the craft. One sheet says that food book will be used by each man of the test craft. A next calls it with no peer for full fact.

The manual serves men who test goods and men of the law of heals in cases of death by craft. Its scope, past its name, is the signs each dire drug leaves in the frame and the tests that find it there. Tables and drawn plates of the gear of tests stand in the hands past works of the same school. The book is a desk mate for the test room and the court in its age.
42747-the-shinto-cult-a-christian-study-:
Milton Terry, a teacher of comparative religion at Garrett Biblical Institute, wrote The Shinto Cult, a Christian study of the ancient religion of Japan, issued in 1910. The book grew from a course of lectures he had given for years to his classes. Terry trimmed and shaped the lectures into a small manual that pulls facts from many sources not easy for common students to reach.

Early chapters ask what Shinto is, what the word means, and where word of it comes from. Later ones take up Japanese tales of the world's making, the gods, shrines, rites, and the link of the cult to the state. Terry also hoped the book would help Christian missionaries meet the Japanese people with more knowledge.
43114-the-gold-kloof:
The Gold Kloof, by H A Bryden, was published in nineteen oh seven by Thomas Nelson and Sons. Bryden was a hunter and writer who knew South Africa well. The story is a boys' adventure that begins at school in England and ends at a gold-bearing gorge.

The first chapter stages a school boat race on the Severn at Tewkesbury. From school days the action moves to Bamborough Farm and up-country life. The boys find a gold spoor, trek into the elephant country, and cross the thirst-land. A lion camp, a missing Guy, shadowers tracking the party, and the last of Karl Engelbrecht fill the middle chapters. At the kloof they gather gold before turning homeward bound.
43497-trans-himalaya-discoveries-and-adv:
Sven Hedin wrote Trans-Himalaya, volume one, printed in nineteen nine, an account of travel and finds in Tibet. The book holds hundreds of photos, sketches, and maps by the author. Hedin gave the work to the Earl of Minto, viceroy of India, with thanks. The trip begins at Simla and moves through Srinagar to Leh.

From Leh the party crosses the Karakorum range and enters the high tableland. Chapters tell of storms on lakes, wild yak country, first meetings with nomads, and a cold Christmas in the wilds. Hedin pushes on through a closed land to Shigatse. There he meets the Tashi Lama and walks the great shrine town, its monks, graves, and feasts.
43549-trans-himalaya-discoveries-and-adv:
Trans-Himalaya: Discoveries and Adventures in Tibet, volume two, is Sven Hedin's narrative of his expedition. Macmillan of London published it in 1910; the first edition was 1909. The volume holds 388 illustrations from photographs, sketches, and drawings by the author, and ten maps.

Chapters open among immured monks and cross the Chang-La-Pod-La. Hedin searches for the sources of the Brahmaputra, the Sutlej, and the Indus. He spends a night on Manasarowar and rides out a storm on the lake. A pilgrimage round Kang-Rinpoche and the mantra Om Mani Padme Hum fill chapters. Chapters reach the heights of Dapsang and the roof of the world. Forty degrees below zero, thirty days of storm, and the death of the last veteran close the volume's march.
43939-the-scandinavian-element-in-the-un:
The Scandinavian Element in the United States is a study by Kendric Charles Babcock. The University of Illinois published it at Urbana in September 1914. Babcock was dean of its college of liberal arts and sciences.

The chapters follow the three peoples of the title in turn. Swedes, Norwegians, and Danes are first set side by side for the reader. Early Norwegian immigration and its rising stream take two chapters. Swedish settlement before 1850 and the smaller Danish stream follow. A half century of expansion and spread, from 1850 to 1900, is then mapped. Economic forces at work in the movement receive a long chapter of their own. The religious and intellectual standpoint of the settlers closes the main argument.
44201-the-military-adventures-of-johnny-:
The Military Adventures of Johnny Newcome gives an account of his campaign on the Peninsula and in Pall Mall, with notes by an officer. Fifteen coloured sketches by Rowlandson illustrate it. This new edition was published in London in 1904, founded on the original of 1816.

A dedication is addressed to the subalterns of the British Army. The author trusts he will be acquitted of any servile view. A motto heads the title: he jests at scars who never felt a wound. The plates list Johnny progress: starting to join his regiment, going to lay in stock, getting into his billet, and taking his breakfast. The verse tale follows a young cornet through war and London society. Readers get a Regency comic poem of army life, with Rowlandson plates.
44414-the-mormon-prophet-and-his-harem-o:
The Mormon Prophet and His Harem is a hostile history of Brigham Young by Waite, printed at Cambridge in 1867. Its full title promises an authentic history of Young, his numerous wives and children. A fourth edition, revised and enlarged, is the form preserved here. Waite quotes Richard the Third over her title page.

Her preface offers no apology for the book. She calls hers the only authentic account of Young and his polygamous family. Mormonism, she argues, refuses the spirit of progress and the laws alike. It draws converts from abroad, she says, and threatens national trouble. The book shows how anti-Mormon writers made their case in the years after the Civil War.
44469-the-sheepfold-and-the-common-or-wi:
Volume one of The Sheepfold and the Common, or Within and Without, was printed by Blackie and Son in eighteen sixty-one. The work first ran more than thirty years before, under the name of the Evangelical Rambler. In that form it sold, by careful count, from sixty thousand to a hundred thousand copies in England, with a like spread in America. The new name was chosen to fit its aim more closely.

The preface says the aim is to teach and please through simple tales of daily life. Truth forms the base of each tale, though some scenes are shaped by fancy. The author chose the dramatic form over dry statements of faith, as more apt to catch the young. Two lines of Scripture head the volume, on the sheep who hear the shepherd's voice and on those who are without.
44746-household-stories-from-the-land-of:
Household Stories from the Land of Hofer gathers the popular myths of Tirol, printed in London by Griffith and Farran in 1871. The author is named only as the writer of an earlier book of Spanish stories. Illustrations by Green appear through the volume, and the title piece is the Rose-Garden of King Lareyn.

The contents group the tales by region. Norg myths open the book, with eggshells, a reckoning day, and a magic cap. Myths of north and south Tirol follow, with a wild hunter, three black dogs, and Saint Peter's three loaves. Tales from the Italian-speaking valleys and from Vorarlberg close the set. The introduction praises peoples of whom history is silent. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
44769-the-sheepfold-and-the-common-or-wi:
Volume two of this religious village tale appeared in 1861 from Blackie and Son in Glasgow, Edinburgh and London. Its title takes two lines from the Gospels about sheep who hear a voice and those who are without. The chapters follow folk in and around a parish, in scenes named for places, visits and turns of faith.

Old Rachel, a blind woman, opens the volume. Later parts deal with doubt, a sceptic's visit, theatre as a pastime, a farm-house kitchen and a party at the Elms. Marriages, deaths, a wanderer's return and a rector's funeral close the long arc, all told to teach Christian lessons.
44837-thirty-years-view-vol-2-of-2-or-a-:
Thirty Years' View, volume two, is a history of the working of the American government from 1820 to 1850. Its author signs himself a senator of thirty years: Thomas Hart Benton, whose speeches and view of men and affairs fill the book. D Appleton and Company of New York published this edition in 1883, from copy entered in 1856.

The matter comes chiefly from the Congress debates, the private papers of General Jackson, and Benton's own speeches. Volume two opens with Van Buren's inauguration and the great money crisis: banks suspending specie payments, business in disorder, and Congress called. The divorce of bank and state, the independent treasury, and hard money payments follow, with Benton's speeches at length. The Florida Indian War, resumption of payments, and the fight over Clay's resolutions carry the story on.
44907-an-interesting-account-of-several-:
Orson Pratt, a minister of the gospel, published this account of several remarkable visions and of the late discovery of ancient American records. The third American edition appeared in New York in 1842. Pratt wrote for readers who had heard of Joseph Smith and wanted the facts of his story set down plainly.

Pratt begins with Smith's life. Smith was born in Sharon, Vermont, on December 23, 1805, and moved with his family to Palmyra, New York, at the age of ten. He worked the land and had little schooling, reading with some difficulty and writing an imperfect hand. From that plain start Pratt builds his case: a boy of small learning could not have invented the records he brought forth. The visions and the discovery of the ancient records follow, making the pamphlet a founding text of the new church.
45011-the-logs-of-the-serapis-alliance-a:
The Naval History Society issued The Logs of the Serapis, Alliance, and Ariel in 1911 at New York in three hundred copies. John S Barnes edited the book. The ships sailed under John Paul Jones in 1779 and 1780. Prints of rare art and extracts from state papers and letters fill the book.

Copy Number 175 is the copy shown here. Front pages list the heads of the society for 1910 and 1911. Captain John S Barnes was its head. Rear Admiral F E Chadwick stood as vice head. A portrait of Jones heads the work. The logs give a day by day sea record of Jones and his ships in war time. Scholars and sea fans are the chief readers.
45128-the-works-of-william-shakespeare-c:
The Works of William Shakespeare, Cambridge edition volume two, was published in 1863. William George Clark and William Aldis Wright edited the set at Cambridge. Both men were fellows of Trinity College in that university town. Macmillan issued the volume at Cambridge and London in the same year.

Much Ado About Nothing opens the contents at page three of the volume. Notes to that comedy follow before the next play begins in the book. Love Labour Lost comes next, with its own notes after the text. A Midsummer Night Dream holds the middle place in the volume order. The Merchant of Venice follows in the list of plays printed here. The Cambridge Shakespeare set a scholarly standard for editing the plays in its day.
45130-charles-bradlaugh-a-record-of-his-:
Charles Bradlaugh, A Record of His Life and Work, Volume One, is a life of a famed free mind man of the past age. Its hand is his own daugh ter, Hypatia Bradlaugh Bonner. Robertson, a man of the state house, wrote its count of the man's fight in that house, his state craft, and his teach. The host print is the seventh form, of nineteen eight. A plate gives the man's birth and death days.

The hand's first words tell how the book came to be. I wish you would tell me things, she said to her sire one night, and let me write the tale of your life. That talk came six weeks past his death, she says. Per haps I will, some day, he said back.
45131-charles-bradlaugh-a-record-of-his-:
Hypatia Bradlaugh Bonner continues her father's biography in Charles Bradlaugh: A Record of His Life and Work, volume two, in a seventh edition from T Fisher Unwin, 1908. John M Robertson contributes the account of Bradlaugh's parliamentary struggle, politics and teachings. A portrait caption dates Bradlaugh's birth September 26, 1833 and his death January 30, 1891.

The volume opens with a third American lecturing tour, then turns to Mrs Besant and the Knowlton pamphlet. Long chapters detail the prosecution of Bradlaugh and Besant, the Westminster trial, the quashed indictment, and a run of debates and later lectures. Portraits and appendices close the record of a public life.
45887-homes-and-haunts-of-the-most-emine:
Homes and Haunts of the Most Eminent British Poets, volume two, is a literary tour. William Howitt wrote it, with engravings by Hewet for the plates. Harper and Brothers published it in New York in the year 1847. A quote hails the stamp that great men leave on their abodes. Contents list Crabbe at Belvoir Castle as the first poet's home.

Hogg, Coleridge, and Mrs Hemans at Rhyllon follow in the contents. A poet known by initials stands at Cape Coast Castle in the list. Scott fills the giant's share, from Abbotsford to his tomb at Dryburgh. That Scott section runs from page 167 to page 536 in bulk. Pilgrims of poetry could plan real visits from Howitt's warm pages.
46050-the-relations-between-the-laws-of-:
C H W Johns gave the Schweich Lectures of nineteen hundred twelve on law in Babylonia and among the Hebrew peoples. Humphrey Milford printed the talks for the British Academy in nineteen hundred fourteen. Johns led Saint Catharine’s College at Cambridge. The first talk centers on a famed stone law text.

French diggers found the Code of Hammurabi at Susa in late nineteen hundred one. Three chunks of black stone fit into one tall pillar. A carved scene shows the king taking law from the sun god Shamash. Johns counts the columns of script and notes lines cut away by a later king. He then sets that code beside Hebrew law. Scholars of old law get a clear side by side view.
46097-trooper-bluegum-at-the-dardanelles:
Trooper Bluegum at the Dardanelles is a war narrative by Oliver Hogue. Hogue served in the Second Light Horse Brigade. Andrew Melrose issued the second edition in London in 1916. The book is dedicated to all the braves of the war. Its chapters tell of the Gallipoli campaign. A list of plates shows Anzac Cove and its officers.

The tale begins with a soldier of the king. Sailing away and the first fight follow. Heroes of the twenty-fifth of April get a chapter. Anzac itself is treated at length. Stories of bombs, aeroplanes, and padres fill the middle. Lone Pine and Shell Green name hard-fought spots. The Anzac VCs are honoured near the close. Hogue wrote as a trooper among troopers. His book keeps the light-hearted face the men showed.
46309-the-greville-memoirs-part-2-of-3-v:
Greville Memoirs, second part, volume two, is a journal of the reign of Queen Victoria. Charles Greville, clerk of the council, kept the journal day by day. The span of this part runs from 1837 to the year 1852. Longmans, Green, and Company published it in London in 1885. Edward notes and author notes stand apart by marks in the text.

Contents run through the fall of governments and the talk of courts. Dissolution of Parliament, want of confidence votes, and Ascot races all appear. Peer and minister, lady of the bedchamber and race horse fill the pages. Readers meet high politics as one insider saw and heard them. The tone is frank, close, and full of names and dates.
46310-the-greville-memoirs-part-2-of-3-v:
Charles Greville, clerk of the council, kept a journal of the reign of Queen Victoria from 1837 to 1852. It was published at London in 1885, and this is the third volume of its second part. The contents are diplomatic history at first hand. Chapter twenty-three takes up the confidential correspondence on the Spanish marriage.

Greville records French overtures to England, Palmerston's hostility to France, a visit to Paris, and conversations with Guizot and Thiers, each man's version of the transaction set against the others. Princess Lieven's account and Lord Cowley's opinion are both entered. A dinner at Thiers's table and a ball at the Hôtel de Ville fill out the Parisian record. The Normanby quarrel carries the next chapter. Court and embassy gossip, minuted daily, is the memoir.
46342-ancient-armour-and-weapons-in-euro:
Ancient Armour and Weapons in Europe was written by John Hewitt, a member of the Archaeological Institute of Great Britain. The book traces arms and armour from the Iron Period of the northern nations to the end of the thirteenth century. John Henry and James Parker published the work at Oxford and London in 1855. Its evidence comes from contemporary monuments, which the book illustrates throughout.

The frontispiece shows the great seals of King Richard the First, and the description of the engravings reads them closely. On the seals the king wears a hauberk of chain mail with a continuous coif over a long tunic, mail chausses on his legs, and a rounded helmet strengthened by bands. His bowed shield carries a lion. Hewitt's method is to let seals, effigies and other period images testify to what warriors actually wore and carried.
46516-bird-guide-water-birds-game-birds-:
Chester Reed wrote this Bird Guide to water birds, game birds, and birds of prey for Doubleday, Page. The Garden City printing of 1921 rests on copyrights of 1906 and 1910. Reed had written North American Birds' Eggs and served as curator at Worcester. A ruffed grouse fronts the guide as its first plate.

Reed sorts birds by order and family with field marks stated plainly. Diving birds come first, grebes, loons, auks, murres, and puffins in their turn. Long winged swimmers, tube nosed swimmers, and totipalmate swimmers follow in neat order. Bills, feet, tails, and flight habits tell each group apart at a glance. A diagram names every part of a bird up front. Pocket science for shooters and watchers alike fills the pages.
46647-true-tales-of-the-weird-a-record-o:
True Tales of the Weird records claimed first hand meetings with the supernatural, written by Sidney Dickinson. Duffield published the book at New York in 1920. A professor of psychology at Oberlin supplies the opening essay. An officer of the American Society for Psychical Research adds a note of praise.

Dickinson insists in his preface that the stories are not founded on fact but are fact. The society kept a copy of his papers in its files, its officer writes. Tales treat a mystery of two continents and a midnight horseman. One long story, The Haunted Bungalow, runs to twelve chapters of crime and haunting. A spectral burglary and kitchen goblins fill later pages. The book is a period piece of psychical research in story form.
46658-sterminator-vesevo-vesuvius-the-gr:
Sterminator Vesevo is a diary of the Vesuvius eruption of April 1906 by Matilde Serao. Its subtitle calls the mountain Vesuvius the great exterminator in plain dread words. Perrella of Naples issued the diary in 1907, close on the disaster itself. The translator note pleads to keep the warm local colour of Serao Italian untouched.

No polish of English phrasing, the note says, should cost the book its southern fire. Tender pathos and bold strokes of colour mark the pages the note commends. Serao writes day by day as ash, lava, and terror work on Naples. Readers gain an eyewitness diary by Italy foremost woman writer of her age.
4667-seven-wives-and-seven-prisons-or-ex:
L. A. Abbott published Seven Wives and Seven Prisons in 1870, as the true story of a matrimonial maniac, written by himself. The first chapter calls his first wife the first and worst, tracing early history, a first marriage, leaving home to prospect, sending for his wife, her mysterious journey, and a final separation. A trial for forgery and a private marriage follow, with summary separation.

Later chapters bring miseries from a second marriage, arrest for bigamy, trial at Northampton, a stunning sentence, and state prison, where he learns the brush business and sharpens picks. The Scheimer sensation, a widow, two milliners, and further prisons follow. Readers get a strange, candid Victorian confession, sensational and moral by turns, about marriage, crime, and a life that kept repeating its worst mistake.
47109-gospel-doctrine-selections-from-th:
Gospel Doctrine gathers selections from the sermons and writings of Joseph F. Smith, sixth president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The Deseret News published it at Salt Lake City in 1919. The first chapter makes truth the foundation of everything, with man saved by truth and righteousness sure to prevail. Chapters follow on the eternal nature of the church, the priesthood, and man himself.

Revelation, free agency, and the nature of God and man take up the next parts. A later chapter defines the purpose and mission of the church: the kingdom of God, the plan of life restored, and a mission to save. The headings under each chapter break the teaching into short heads, so the book serves as a handbook of doctrine as much as a volume of sermons.
47111-letters-from-a-farmer-in-pennsylva:
John Dickinson wrote these famous letters as a farmer in Pennsylvania, reissued in New York in 1903. Halsey supplies a historical introduction to the Outlook Company edition. A front plate calls Dickinson the patriotic American farmer, a barrister who asserted the liberties of the British colonies with spirit.

Verse under the plate praises stemming taxation's rage in bold terms. Life in bondage, the lines say, is a worthless thing, while happiness and joy spring from freedom. Dickinson argues in calm, legal prose against British taxes on the colonies, urging united resistance short of revolt in letters that stirred America.
47704-masters-in-art-part-79-volume-7-ju:
Masters in Art, part seventy-nine, is the July print of a month sheet of drawn lives for nineteen six. It treats the French paint hand Ingres. Ten plates of his work lead the print. They run from a sphinx scene to a spring scene and a great chant of a bard of old.

Parts give the life of Ingres and the art of Ingres past the words of three named men of note. The works come next, with tales of the plates and a list of his paints. A list of books on the man closes the print. A self plate of the hand, from a great hall in Florence, stands in the rows. The sheet ran month by month, each print a life of one great hand.
47715-the-works-of-william-shakespeare-c:
William George Clark and William Aldis Wright edited this seventh volume of the Cambridge Shakespeare, published by Macmillan in 1865. Both editors were fellows of Trinity College, Cambridge. The volume holds four plays: Romeo and Juliet, Timon of Athens, Julius Caesar, and Macbeth. Notes follow each play. The Cambridge edition was the first to give Shakespeare's text with a full record of the early editions' readings.

The preface explains a special feature. Romeo and Juliet first appeared in a quarto of 1597 whose text differs so widely from later editions that notes could not hold the differences. The editors therefore reprint that early quarto whole, after the play itself. It may preserve the play much as first written, some critics held. This apparatus made the Cambridge Shakespeare the working text of scholars for generations. Volume seven, with Macbeth and Julius Caesar among its plays, remains a monument of Victorian editing.
47767-the-propaganda-for-reform-in-propr:
The Propaganda for Reform in Proprietary Medicines, volume two, was issued by the American Medical Association in nineteen twenty two. Its four parts gather reports, laboratory work, and journal pieces on patent medicines. Part one presents the reports of the Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry. That part sets out the rules by which the council tests medicaments for sale.

Part two gives contributions from the association's own laboratory on such products. Parts three and four reprint journal pieces, first on proprietary products by name. The last part is a miscellany of journal contributions on kindred themes. The whole volume backs a campaign against secret and hyped remedies of the day. It aims to guide doctors in what drugs they can trust for patients.
48126-ancient-landscapes-of-the-grand-ca:
Ancient Landscapes of the Grand Canyon Region explains the geology of five parklands. Edwin McKee wrote the guide. He was assistant director of the Museum of Northern Arizona. The author published it himself in 1931. Sketches and charts came from park naturalists. The edition here is the thirteenth, from 1952.

Five chapters follow the earth's eras in order. The oldest rocks of the canyon open the story. Granite and tilted strata succeed. The age of fishes and the Redwall limestone follow. Tracks in the Supai sandstone witness vanished life. The middle era brings the Petrified Forest and dinosaur tracks. The last era cuts the canyon itself. Bryce, Zion, and the Painted Desert share the explanation.
48151-a-history-of-inventions-discoverie:
John Beckmann wrote this reference work, A History of Inventions, Discoveries, and Origins, rendered from the German by Johnston and printed at London in 1846; the hosted text is the first volume. Beckmann was a professor at the University of Göttingen. This fourth edition was revised and enlarged by Francis, a journal editor, and Griffith, a physician.

An epigraph from Herschel praises the taste for reading as a shield against life's ills. Contents then run in short articles from Italian book-keeping to stamped paper. An odometer, a machine for noting down music, the refining of gold and silver ore, tulips, the canary bird, and magnetic cures come early. Coaches, water-clocks, the speaking-trumpet, the pine-apple, secret ink, the diving-bell, coloured glass, sealing-wax, corn-mills, saffron, alum, and falconry follow.
48152-a-history-of-inventions-discoverie:
John Beckmann, a professor at Göttingen, wrote this history of inventions, translated by Johnston. Francis and Griffith revised and enlarged the fourth edition, published by Bohn in London in 1846. Volume two of two opens with a portrait of James Watt at its front.

The steam engine and Watt's discoveries fill a preliminary essay in the contents. Lending and pawnbroking, chemical names of metals, zinc and carp follow in the list. Mirrors, glass cutting, soap, madder, jugglers and automata show Beckmann's range, for he traced who first made or found nearly everything in daily life around him.
48342-outlines-of-zun-i-creation-myths-t:
