Outlines of Zuni Creation Myths is a study by Frank Hamilton Cushing, printed as part of a report on the peoples of the Southwest. Cushing first sets out the survival of early Zuni traits and a sketch of Spanish and Zuni dealings. He then turns to the old order of Zuni life and the plan of its priestly groups.

The myths tell how the worlds began, how men and beasts were formed, and how they came up into daylight. Tales cover the birth of corn, the naming of clans and kinds, and the long search for the Middle of the world. The book keeps a people's own account of its start, told with care for detail.
48499-jaundice-its-pathology-and-treatme:
Jaundice, its pathology and treatment, by George Harley, came out in London in 1863. Harley taught the law side of physic at University College, London, and served its hospital. A plate shows blocked bile and pancreas ducts. He gives the book to his friend William Sharpey, a deep thinker and sound reasoner.

Harley vows to waste no time, for time is money to the trade man and the doctor alike. He skips old views and the past books on his theme. His core claim is that new body chemistry aids the spotting and cure of liver and pancreas ills. A table sums up his views on the ill at one glance. A full part treats the chemistry of what the body casts off. Doctors get a short, bold brief for a new lab path in their work.
48582-my-life-at-sea-being-a-yarn-loosel:
My Life at Sea is a sailor's memoir by Commander Crutchley, printed at London in 1912 with twelve pictures. Its full title calls it a yarn loosely spun to hold together memories of the change from sail to steam in the British merchant service, from 1863 to 1894. Earl Brassey wrote the preface, and a photograph of Cape Horn from the Ruapehu stands at the front.

Crutchley served as a younger brother of Trinity House and as secretary of the Navy League. His twelve chapters span thirty years of work afloat. Pictures show the clipper ship Essex, steamers of the New Zealand line, and the handy mainsail at work. The book keeps a vanished world of sail in plain, hearty telling.
48709-information-for-the-guidance-of-fi:
The Bureau of Biological Survey issued this handbook in April 1931 as Miscellaneous Publication number 115 of the Department of Agriculture. It was prepared under Paul Redington, chief of the Bureau, in the division led by Stanley Young. Its purpose is stated in the title: guidance for field men and cooperators who control injurious rodents and predatory animals.

The contents lay out the legal basis for the work, the animals on the control program, and the rules of the field. Warnings on handling poisons stand beside the methods for rodent and predator work. The opening pages tell why Washington took up the fight. Settlers saw their stock ranges raided by wolves, coyotes, mountain lions, and bobcats. Their fields suffered from prairie dogs, ground squirrels, pocket gophers, and jack rabbits. Government hunters got their orders and their ethics in one pamphlet.
48796-index-expurgatorius-anglicanus-or-:
Index Expurgatorius Anglicanus is a catalogue of suppressed books by Hart. Burt Franklin reprinted it in New York in 1969. The first edition ran in parts from 1872 to 1878. Its full title lists the books it covers. They are works printed in England that were suppressed. Some were burnt by the common hangman. Others were censured, or their makers prosecuted. Five parts fill one volume of 290 pages.

The title mocks the Roman index of banned books. England had no such single list, Hart implies. His catalogue gathers the scattered record instead. Authors, printers, and publishers all stand in its net. Such a list serves students of press freedom. It shows what the state feared in print across centuries. Bibliography here becomes a kind of history of dissent. The work remains a standard tool for the subject.
49007-the-works-of-william-shakespeare-c:
Volume six of the Cambridge Shakespeare, edited by William George Clark and William Aldis Wright, was published by Macmillan in 1865. Both editors were fellows of Trinity College, Cambridge. The volume holds four plays, each followed by its notes: King Henry the Eighth, Troilus and Cressida, Coriolanus, and Titus Andronicus. A preface treats the early printings of the plays. Henry the Eighth, it notes, was first printed in the Folio of 1623.

On Troilus and Cressida the preface is fullest. The quarto of 1609 appeared in two issues from the same type, one carrying a publisher's preface to an ever reader. The editors argue from the running title that the copies without that preface came first. Their case rests on close comparison of the sheets, part by part. The Cambridge edition set the scholarly standard for Shakespeare in its century.
49204-buffalo-bill-from-prairie-to-palac:
John Burke compiled an authentic history of the Wild West with sketches and anecdotes of Buffalo Bill, hero of the plains, printed at Chicago and New York in 1893. It was made with the authority of General Cody, Buffalo Bill himself. Burke, known as Arizona John, signs the note. He thanks General Dodge's Thirty Years Among the Indians for a few facts used here.

The book is given to those pioneers of progress who led the advance of civilization into savage lands, defying danger and suffering every hardship, and to the army of the United States. So quickly was the history of the central West recorded, it begins, as to make the Great American Desert of our childhood seem a geographical mirage. Cody's life, scout, hunter, and showman, is told by his own manager.
49297-the-works-of-william-shakespeare-c:
Clark and Wright edited this fifth volume of Shakespeare works at Cambridge. Macmillan printed it at Cambridge and London in 1864. Contents hold the three parts of King Henry the Sixth. King Richard the Third closes the volume with full notes.

Early quarto texts, The Contention and The True Tragedie, stand between. The preface notes Henry Six first printed in the Folio of 1623. The second part grew from a quarto of 1594, it says. Each play gets notes at its end by the two editors. The good Duke Humphrey death stands in the second part title as the preface quotes it.
49569-bleeding-armenia-its-history-and-h:
Williams, a Chicago clergyman, and Gabriel, president of an Armenian patriotic alliance in New York, wrote this appeal, Bleeding Armenia, its history and horrors under Islam, printed in 1896 with many pictures. Williams had studied mission work in the East for twenty years. The book also carries the views of Gladstone on the Turkish atrocities, of Salisbury on England's stance, and of a historian on the Eastern Question.

A preface sets the aim. The writer does not seek, he says, merely to harrow readers with outrages, nor to argue the tangled Eastern Question at length. He seeks to wake interest in the history and fate of a people he calls the martyr nation of the world. Fifty or sixty thousand helpless people, he reports, had already died in the present persecution, and behind it lay a thousand years of the same bitter story.
49585-proceedings-of-a-board-of-general-:
Washington ordered a board of general officers to sit on the case of Major John Andre, adjutant general to the British army, and the board met on September 29, 1780. These proceedings, first printed by Francis Bailey at Philadelphia in 1780 and privately reprinted at New York in 1867, give the record of that hearing. Appended are the letters that passed to and from New York on the occasion.

The papers open with Washington's letter to Congress of September 26, 1780, written from Robinson's House in the Highlands. He tells how Arnold fled to the Vulture on hearing Andre was taken, seized as John Anderson with papers in Arnold's hand about West Point. The board's question was whether he had come as a spy. The letters let the reader follow the case as the command itself saw it.
49791-miscellanea-curiosa-vol-1-containi:
Printed in London in 1708, this second edition gathers discourses read to the Royal Society. Volume one of three promises accounts of great natural phenomena, set out by leading thinkers of the age. Curious travels, voyages, antiquities and natural histories of countries, also laid before the Society, fill out the set.

The editor tells readers that fine discoveries sat hidden in the Society's large journals. Few inquiring gentlemen, he says, had even heard of them among so much lesser matter. A discourse by Mead on the sun and moon acting on human bodies is added, along with Fontenelle's preface on the use of mathematical learning.
49819-worlds-within-worlds-the-story-of-:
Worlds Within Worlds: The Story of Nuclear Energy, volume 1, is Isaac Asimov's account of what matter is made of. The United States Atomic Energy Commission issued the set in 1972. This first volume carries Library of Congress number 75-189477. It lays the groundwork with atomic weights and electricity. It then reaches the first hints that atoms have parts.

Asimov follows the trail through radioactivity and isotopes. Each discovery forced a new picture of the atom. The writing is plain and patient, built for readers with no training in physics. By the close of the volume the atom has been opened. The stage is set for fission and nuclear power in the volumes that follow. The set was a public education project of the atomic age. It aimed to give citizens the science behind the headlines.
49820-worlds-within-worlds-the-story-of-:
Isaac Asimov wrote Worlds Within Worlds, a story of nuclear energy in three volumes. This second volume treats mass and energy, the neutron, and the nucleus. A United States energy agency published the booklet in 1972. The series was made for general readers.

Asimov opens with a bold claim for the atom. Steam, railroads, cars, planes, radio, and television changed the world in two centuries. None seemed so fantastic as what man has done with the atom since 1939. He sees almost no limits ahead, only widening knowledge. A sketch of the author notes his post as a teacher of biochemistry at Boston University. It counts more than 150 books from his pen in twenty years. About twenty of them are science fiction stories.
49821-worlds-within-worlds-the-story-of-:
Worlds Within Worlds is the third volume of a history of nuclear energy by Isaac Asimov, issued by the United States Atomic Energy Commission in 1972. Its three parts treat nuclear fission, nuclear fusion, and what may lie beyond fusion. The Commission's Office of Information Services sponsored the series for general readers.

Asimov argues that nothing in human history opened eyes like atomic power. Steam, railroads, automobiles, airplanes, radio, and television all seemed less fantastic. What man has done with the atom since 1939 outruns them all, he writes. Ahead he sees almost no limits: inexhaustible energy, new worlds, ever widening knowledge. The volume explains reactors and fusion research in Asimov's clear popular style. It is government science writing at its most optimistic, from the agency that both promoted and regulated the atom.
4987-the-outdoor-girls-at-rainbow-lake-o:
Laura Lee Hope's Outdoor Girls at Rainbow Lake opens with a grand surprise, missing papers, and a runaway, before the girls are ready for a cruise. Stowaways, hints of ghosts, and a regatta follow, with chapters at Rainbow Lake, on Elm Island, and in camp, where crackers and olives fuel the fun.

Fighting fire, a storm, a queer disturbance, and a ghost that must be caught keep the trip lively, along with a missing saddle and Mollie's discovery. Hope keeps the tone cheerful and the friendships central. Readers get a girls' adventure of boating, camping, and mild mystery, ideal for young readers who like their heroines outdoors.
49951-wawenock-myth-texts-from-maine-for:
Wawenock Myth Texts from Maine presents native tales with translations, by Frank G Speck. The texts were published with leave of a Canadian museum's anthropology division, a note says. They appeared in a bureau of ethnology annual report. A plate shows Francois Neptune, called the last speaker of the Wawenock dialect in nineteen twelve. Contents open with an introduction and a note on sounds.

Tales of Gluskabe the transformer fill the main part. He creates himself and competes with the creator in the first. A turtle insults the chief of the birds in another, and mountains are created. Gluskabe grows angry with the birch tree and marks it for life in a third. Free translations follow each text. The origin and use of wampum and a drinking song close the set.
50095-the-works-of-william-shakespeare-c:
The Works of William Shakespeare, volume four, is part of the Cambridge edition of the plays. William George Clark and William Aldis Wright edited the volume. Macmillan published it at Cambridge and London in 1864. This volume gathers five history plays in order. King John opens the book, with notes after the text. King Richard the Second follows in the same form.

The two parts of King Henry the Fourth come next in sequence. King Henry the Fifth closes the set of plays. Each play is followed by its own section of notes. An old Chronicle Historie of Henry the Fifth is appended. The preface treats the sources of King John in detail. It notes the play was first printed in the Folio of 1623. Shakespeare drew plot and characters from an earlier play of 1591.
50124-frederick-william-maitland-downing:
Fisher's Frederick William Maitland, a biographical sketch of the Downing Professor of the Laws of England, was printed at the University Press, Cambridge, in 1910. A photogravure frontispiece by Annan and Sons shows Maitland, with his signature beneath. Fisher's prefatory note is frank about his limits: he was schooled neither at Eton nor Cambridge nor Lincoln's Inn, and is no lawyer.

He met Maitland only in the man's thirty-seventh year, he owns, and never had a formal schooling in law. Before printing, the sheets were read by Mrs Maitland and Mrs Reynell. Dr Henry Jackson, Dr Verrall, and Professor Vinogradoff also read them, and Fisher credits their close knowledge and weighty counsel for what merit the memoir has. The sketch follows, of the legal historian's life and work.
50421-historical-record-of-the-third-or-:
Richard Cannon compiled the Historical Record of the Third, or the King’s Own Regiment of Light Dragoons. Parker, Furnivall, and Parker issued the book in London in eighteen hundred forty seven. Cannon worked at the Adjutant General’s office at Horse Guards. Plates show the dress and arms of the corps.

The record traces the corps from its raising in sixteen hundred eighty five. It runs through service up to eighteen hundred forty six. Army orders printed at the front set the plan for such books. They call for stations, battles, and sieges. They also call for lists of the killed and wounded. Honors and badges get their own full account.
50559-the-works-of-william-shakespeare-c:
Volume three of the Cambridge edition of William Shakespeare's works appeared in 1863 from Macmillan and Company. William George Clark and William Aldis Wright, both of Trinity College, Cambridge, edited the text. The volume gathers four plays that first appeared in the Folio of 1623.

Inside are The Taming of the Shrew, All's Well That Ends Well, Twelfth Night, and The Winter's Tale, each followed by its own notes. The preface compares the early Quarto of the Shrew with the Folio text and argues the Quarto was printed from the Folio. Readers get the plays in a careful scholarly edition with the editors' reasoning laid out before the text.
51439-taxidermy-without-a-teacher-compri:
Walter P Manton wrote a manual of taxidermy for learners without a teacher. Lee and Shepard issued the second, enlarged form at Boston, rights from 1882. The book sells at fifty cents in his Practical Helps in Natural History set. A front chart names the parts of a bird from beak to tarsus.

Chapters treat skinning and mounting birds, mammals, fishes, and reptiles in turn. Eggs, nests, skeletons, hunting, and health fill the later parts. Manton asks the reader to stand in his workshop in mind as he works. Beginners gain cheap, sure teaching in a once-common cabinet art.
51557-the-colloquies-of-edward-osborne-c:
The Colloquies of Edward Osborne, citizen and clothworker of London, was published by Nimmo in London in 1900, with ten illustrations by John Jellicoe. The title page names no author, only the writer of Mary Powell and The Household of Sir Thomas More. Chapters are headed in archaic style, beginning with A Country Lad Cometh to Town.

Edward walks to London Bridge with his mother, past stalls and droves of oxen, and shudders at the traitors' heads on the gateway. He is bound apprentice in Master Hewet's house, and later chapters give the disposition of that house, the defence of the bridge and Osborne out of his time. A snake among the flowers and Master Hewet ordering things discretely close the contents.
51646-the-war-book-of-the-german-general:
The War Book of the German General Staff gives the German usages of war on land in English. Morgan, a law professor at University College, London, translated and introduced it. McBride, Nast published the New York edition in March nineteen fifteen. The German text was the staff's own manual for the teaching of its officers.

Morgan's note calls his version literal and whole, footnotes and headlines included. The Hague rules, he charges, are treated in it as scraps of paper. Its only laws are the usages of the staff, resting on cold self interest. His long introduction traces the book's descent from Prussian military custom. Clausewitz, Bismarck, Treitschke, and Bernhardi are named as its line of fathers. In the German mind, he argues, peace is only war held in check.
51754-the-road-to-en-dor-being-an-accoun:
The Road to En Dor tells how two prisoners of war at Yozgad in Turkey won their way to freedom. Jones, a lieutenant, wrote it, and Hill, a fellow officer, drew the illustrations. John Lane printed it in London and New York in 1920, and this is the third edition. A Kipling poem about the road to En Dor supplies the epigraph.

The contents give away the scheme: how spooking began in Yozgad, how the camp turned spiritualist, and how the mediums were tested. A spook finds a revolver, writes a magic letter, and arranges the authors' arrest. The pair are tried and convicted for telepathy, put on parole by their colonel, and sent to prison, all as steps in a worked out escape.
52022-the-cricket-field-or-the-history-a:
Cricket Field, or the History and Science of Cricket, is a handbook. Longman issued this second edition in London in the year 1854. Its author had written The Principles of Scientific Batting before it. A plate shows William Clarke, slow bowler of the All England Eleven. Clarke served as secretary to that famed eleven as well.

Two Latin tags from Horace front the book as learned mottoes. One says joy dwells in the sunny grass of the open field. A verse of boys bounding out of school opens the early pages. History of the game joins the science of batting and bowling. Players of 1854 got rules, lore, and craft in one volume.
52070-a-virginia-girl-in-the-civil-war-1:
Myrta Lockett Avary collected and edited the record of a Virginia girl in the Civil War, published at New York in 1903. Its full title promises the actual experiences of the wife of a Confederate officer. The opening chapter looks back on home life in a Southern harbor, Norfolk before the war.

Her harbor, she says, was covered with shipping flying the flags of all nations, and her society was the society of the world. Chapters follow her meeting with Dan Grey, the first days of the Confederacy, and a sight of Belle Boyd. A run through the blockade, a flag of truce, and capture by the enemy fill the middle. The last days of the Confederacy close the record.
52175-italian-prisons-st-angelo-the-piom:
Italian Prisons is a volume in the History and Romance of Crime series, issued by the Grolier Society in a limited edition. Its author, Major Arthur Griffiths, had been an inspector of prisons in Great Britain. He wrote also on the mysteries of police and crime. A front picture shows Machiavelli in talk with Pope Alexander the Sixth, in whose reign Rome saw every wickedness done in public.

The contents begin with the castle of Saint Angelo, then the Leonine City. Other chapters treat the Piombi under the leads of Venice, the Vicaria of Naples, and the prisons of the Roman Inquisition. The Saint Angelo chapter traces the castle from Hadrian's mausoleum, through the barbarian struggles, to its life as fortress and prison. Griffiths mixes history, famous prisoners, and escapes into a rich survey. The book preserves the grim romance of Italy's old prisons for armchair travellers.
52260-the-visitor-s-hand-book-for-holyhe:
The Visitor's Hand-Book for Holyhead, by Thomas Jackson, was published in London in eighteen fifty-three by Smith and Sons, just after the Chester and Holyhead Railway opened. Jackson wrote for the new crowds of tourists arriving at the far western point of Wales.

The guide covers the town and church, the pier, the triumphal arch, the mountain with its Roman watch tower, and the wonders of South Stack with its lighthouse and sea birds. Later sections describe the gigantic new harbour, the steam packets to Ireland, hotels, sea trips, and distances and postal facts. Jackson's preface says visitors kept asking what was worth seeing, and the small book answers them in the order a short stay allows.
52977-the-alumni-journal-of-the-college-:
The Alumni Journal of the College of Pharmacy of the City of New York, for February 1895, is the second number of its second volume. The alumni association of the college published the monthly. Its contents open with a paper on the rise and progress of photography. Professor Elliott, a chemist of the college, wrote that lead piece.

An editorial on the ability of construction follows the photography paper. New literature and the most recent work in pharmacy get their pages. Notes here and there, alumni matter, and college notes fill the middle. Senior class notes and junior notes stand near the end. A section on medicine and pharmacy, and a note on spelling, close the number. The journal is a window on drug trade schooling in the nineties.
53624-art-studies-from-nature-as-applied:
Art Studies from Nature, as Applied to Design is a set of four papers for architects, designers, and manufacturers, printed at London in 1872. The papers, by Hulme, Glaisher, Mackie, and Hunt, were reprinted from the Art-Journal and carry many wood pictures. The book teaches makers to draw their patterns from the living world rather than from habit.

The preface argues that nature is open to all who seek, and that the artist may find in her the richest hints of form and colour. The lichen on the rock and the fungus by the path, it says, hold as much beauty as grander sights. A verse quoted in the preface calls even the meanest flower of the vale a gate to paradise for such a student.
53964-the-sins-of-the-cities-of-the-plai:
Privately printed in London in 1881, this two volume work holds frank recollections. Just two hundred fifty copies were printed, the title page states. Volume one opens with the recollections of a narrator in Leicester Square. Jack Saul recollections then carry the main text of both volumes.

Volume two adds further recollections and a tale called The Same Old Story. Short essays on the title themes close the second volume at length. The book is a rare period document of London underworld life. Its plain, first person voice records a world polite print shunned.
54217-the-farmer-s-own-book-a-treatise-o:
The Farmer's Own Book is a treatise on the numerous diseases of the horse, with a treatise on the disease of horned cattle. Koogle prints it at Middletown, Maryland, in 1858. Rights were held from 1857. The title page promises symptoms and the course of treatment for each ill.

His preface states the aim. A farmer who has the care of horses should be able to spot a disease in its first stages. Then it is an easy case to cure, he says. Other works fail, he argues, since they do not point out the symptoms with care. Their treatment is badly set out and hard to grasp. This book's edge is plainness, he claims.
54337-reminiscences-of-joseph-the-prophe:
Reminiscences of Joseph, the Prophet, and the Coming Forth of the Book of Mormon, by Elder Edward Stevenson, was published by the author at Salt Lake City in 1893. Stevenson was born at Gibraltar in 1820. The book grew out of illustrated lectures he had given more than two hundred times in tabernacles and halls across the Territory.

Stevenson knew Joseph Smith in person and stood with him in many trying hours. He offers the book as his testimony to the truth of the work Smith began. The lectures had done much good, he was told, and hearers pressed him to print them with their engravings. He who judges without investigation, he warns, is unwise. The first chapter gives a brief record of the Prophet's life of heroism, persecution, imprisonment, and martyrdom.
55295-historical-record-of-the-second-or:
An official account of the Second Regiment of Foot, the Queen's Royal, makes up this volume in the Historical Records of the British Army. The series was prepared for publication under the direction of the Adjutant-General and printed in London by William Clowes and Sons. A general order from the Horse Guards, dated January 1, 1836, stands at the front and sets the rules for every volume.

By the King's command, each record must give the regiment's formation, its stations, and the battles and sieges in which it served. It must name officers, and count the non-commissioned officers and privates, killed or wounded in each action. Honours, badges, and devices granted to the regiment, and the reasons for them, are also required.
55390-triumphs-and-wonders-of-the-19th-c:
Triumphs and Wonders of the Nineteenth Century, by James Boyd with thirty two fellow authors, was issued at Philadelphia by the Holman company with copyrights of 1899 and 1901. Its frontispiece shows Industry crowned by Fame, with electricity, railroads, machinery, and art gathered round. The subtitle calls the book the true mirror of a phenomenal era.

The opening argues that the nineteenth century, heir of all before it, outdid every past age in invention and progress. Chapters then march through the domains of human activity with many pictures. It is the century congratulating itself, in the heavy gilt style of the subscription book trade.
55403-the-petrol-engine-a-text-book-deal:
Francis John Kean wrote this textbook on the petrol engine, published in London in 1915 with seventy-one illustrations. Kean headed the motor car engineering department at the Polytechnic in Regent Street and had lectured at McGill University.

The title page promises the principles of design and construction, with a special chapter on the two-stroke engine. The publisher's list around it shows the young trade's library: books on electrical ignition, dynamo lighting, motorcycle repair, and motor body building. Students and working engineers of the early motor age get a clear, grounded course in the engine that was changing the roads.
55976-the-trial-of-an-ox-for-killing-a-m:
The Trial of an Ox is a penny tale book from Rusher of Banbury. Its full name adds the quiz of those who saw the deed in full. An ox gored his driver to death in Smithfield Mart in the tale. Dogs seized the ox and bore him to trial at Quadruped Court. Judge Lion sat on the bench at Beast Park for the case.

The dogs gave them selves as proof men, but the judge barred them. They were thief takers with a stake in the case, he ruled. Rusher list of penny books crowds the front leaf of the print. Cake tales, Gilpin rides, and cat tales fill that cheap list. Cuts of a camel, a quill pig, and the ox dress the front leaves.
56118-general-anatomy-applied-to-physiol:
Volume one of General Anatomy, Applied to Physiology and Medicine is a medical work by Xavier Bichat of Paris. It was turned from the French by George Hayward and published at Boston in 1822. Bichat was physician of the great hospital of Paris and a professor of anatomy. A portrait of him stands at the front. Hayward began the rendering while he studied medicine in Paris in the winter of 1813. News of a London version made him lay the work aside for years.

Bichat's fame rests on his doctrine of the tissues. The body, he taught, is built of a small set of simple webs or membranes. Each tissue has its own life, its own diseases, and its own way of dying. The book works that scheme through the whole frame. It is a root text of modern medicine, here in an early American dress.
56147-general-anatomy-applied-to-physiol:
The second volume of a medical treatise by Xavier Bichat. George Hayward translated it from the French. Richardson and Lord published it at Boston in 1822. Bichat was physician to the great hospital of humanity at Paris. He also taught anatomy and physiology there. Three volumes divide his general anatomy.

This volume opens with the capillary systems. Two great vascular systems meet in the capillaries, Bichat writes. Red blood changes to black in the body's general system. The lungs' confined system reverses that change. Bichat founded the science of tissues before microscopes matured. He died at thirty, leaving anatomy reorganised around membranes and textures. Hayward's translation carried his system to American medical schools. The copyright deposit text fills the front pages here.
56157-nether-lochaber-the-natural-histor:
Alexander Stewart gathers a parish's lore in Nether Lochaber, the natural history, legends, and folk lore of the West Highlands, printed at Edinburgh in 1883. Paterson made the book. Stewart was minister of the parish of Ballachulish and Ardgour. He inscribes the volume to a doctor of the place, in pleasant recollection of happy hours and midsummer rambles.

A prefatory note tells the papers' first life. They appeared as a series from Nether Lochaber in the Inverness Courier, a well known northern journal. They drew a kindly greeting, fortnight by fortnight, he records. At one time he meant to rewrite and rearrange them all. On second thoughts, backed by literary and scientific friends, he let them keep the form in which they first won attention.
56211-recollections-of-rifleman-harris-o:
Recollections of Rifleman Harris is the life story of a private soldier of the 95th Rifles in the wars against Napoleon. It was edited by Henry Curling and published in London in 1848. The full title promises tales of his officers and his comrades as well.

The editor vouches for the truth of the tale. He argues that such plain records show the stern facts of war more closely than grand histories do. Harris served through the most famed years of the British army, in the Peninsula. His pages bring out wrongs and hardships that busy campaigns pass by. The book is dedicated to the Marquess of Londonderry, in praise of his bearing in the battles of the Peninsula.
56328-general-anatomy-applied-to-physiol:
Xavier Bichat, physician of the great hospital at Paris and professor of anatomy and physiology, wrote a general anatomy applied to physiology and medicine. George Hayward translated it from the French for a Boston edition of 1822, in three volumes. This is volume three. The copyright was entered in Massachusetts on April 17, 1822.

The volume treats the muscular system of organic life. Bichat notes that this system is less spread through the body than the one before it. It is centered in the thorax, where the heart and gullet belong to it. In the abdomen it helps form the stomach and intestines, and in the pelvis the bladder and womb.
56597-the-legends-and-myths-of-hawaii-th:
The Legends and Myths of Hawaii is a book of Hawaiian folk lore by King Kalakaua. Its subtitle calls the Hawaiians a strange people in the idiom of its day. Daggett, a former United States minister to the islands, edited it. He also wrote an introduction for the volume. Charles Webster and Company published it in New York in 1888. A preface thanks many helpers for material in the legends. 

Fornander, author of a work on the Polynesian race, is thanked specially. The preface explains the order of the legends in the book. Those tied to great political events may be read as in a measure historic. The legends run up to the tale of the destruction of the temples. Later tales were chosen as the most striking of the remaining folk lore. The king presents his people's old stories to English readers.
56700-mormon-doctrine-plain-and-simple-o:
Mormon Doctrine Plain and Simple, or leaves from the tree of life, is a teaching booklet by Charles Penrose, issued at Salt Lake City in 1888. Its introduction opens with a plain claim. There is no subject of common talk on which there is so little sound knowledge, it says, as that called Mormonism. This little work means to explain, in a simple way, the leading points of that doctrine.

The very names Mormon and Mormonism are not strictly correct as commonly used, Penrose warns. They are drawn, a little wrongly, from the Book of Mormon. That book, he states, holds the history of the first peoples of the American land, written by many hands. A prophet named Mormon gathered it, and it was cut on metal plates and hidden in the earth. It came forth in the latter days, he holds, as a witness to Jesus.
56805-gleanings-from-the-harvest-fields-:
Bombaugh culled bright bits from all books for the keen and the odd. Gleanings from the Harvest-Fields of Literature is its full name. A Ruth verse on hand culls in a field heads the fat book. A Montaigne line calls it a bunch of culls tied by his string. The book came out in Philadelphia in 1890 in this form.

Its first rights were filed in 1874 by a Hartford house. A nose gay of culled blooms, the Montaigne line in sum says. Naught of mine but the tie string, that line goes on to own. Wit, lore, verse, and grave thought mix in no stiff rank. Each bit is short and stands on its own for a spare hour. Browsers get a rich store.
56985-the-boy-travellers-in-the-far-east:
Thomas Knox wrote The Boy Travellers in the Far East, adventures of two youths in a journey to Japan and China, published at New York in 1880. Knox also wrote Camp-Fire and Cotton-Field and Overland through Asia. His preface addresses his young friends directly.

Not many years ago, he says, China and Japan were counted barbarous nations, and the world knew little of their peoples. Today they hold close relations with America and Europe, and young readers want to know them. The two boy travellers are fictitious, but the scenes they pass through are drawn from fact. Readers get the first volume of the era's favourite travel series for boys, part story and part geography lesson.
5708-stray-pearls-memoirs-of-margaret-de:
Charlotte Yonge's Stray Pearls presents the memoirs of Margaret de Ribaumont, Viscountess of Bellaise, set against the wars and courts of seventeenth-century France. Chapters move from Whitehall before the cobwebs through salons, garrisons, victories dearly bought, widowhood, and exile, with narratives shared between Margaret and her friend Annora. Cavaliers, queens, barricades, and court appointments fill the long story.

The novel blends invented memoirs with historical incident, letting two women's voices carry war, faith, and family honor across decades. Readers meet the Fronde, Paris under siege, and the Hague, all seen from inside households rather than from thrones. Yonge's careful, moral storytelling suits readers who enjoy historical fiction told at leisure, with loyalty and endurance as its steady themes.
57330-the-opening-heavens-or-a-connected:
Joseph Bates wrote this work on prophecy, the heavens, and the New Jerusalem. The Press of Benjamin Lindsey printed it in New Bedford in 1846. Bates sets prophet and apostle testimony beside star observations. He asks where the Paradise of God now stands and will stand.

Front quotes praise a vast mass of bright matter in the sky. News of Lord Rosse great telescope feeds the opening argument. Rumors claimed Regulus was a disc, not a sphere, Bates notes. The book blends Bible reading with the star science of its day.
57370-the-mysteries-of-heron-dyke-a-nove:
Volume two of a three-volume sensation novel continues the tale of a great house by the sea. Richard Bentley and Son issued it at London in 1880. The author hides behind earlier titles, In the Dead of Night among them.

The contents promise winter at Heron Dyke, then Dr Downes' snuff-box. A chapter named Patchwork and the twenty-fourth of April follow. Mr Charles Plackett calls upon the squire. Sudden tidings and the mistress of Heron Dyke raise the stakes. Dorothy spies something in the shrubbery. The tale goes aboard the Seamew for a rescue. Hubert Stone returns near the close. Winter opens the volume: fishing boats lost, bodies washed ashore, and the Easterby lifeboat standing ready in the gale.
57415-the-mysteries-of-heron-dyke-a-nove:
The Mysteries of Heron Dyke is a tale of strange turns in three parts, by the hand of two past night tales. The host text is the third part of the set. It was put out at London in eighteen eighty. The press of the book was the press in chief to the queen of the realm. Its list of parts runs to three teen.

Who did it heads the run. What a maid of the tale had to tell comes next. A green stone and gold, and a man of the tale in a maze, stand past them. A fruit less trip, talk taken with a man of law, and a strange guest at an inn fill the mid run. To geth er at last, in the dusk of eve, and the truth at last stand past them.
57511-index-for-works-of-ruth-ogden-hype:
Index for Works of Ruth Ogden, compiled by David Widger, gathers the tales of one author. Tattine, Courage, and His Little Royal Highness head the contents of the index. A Loyal Little Red-Coat, A Little Queen of Hearts, and Little Homespun follow in the list. Tables of contents of each volume are given in full for the reader.

Tattine chapter one is called Trouble Number One in its own contents. A maple wax morning and a set of setters fill the next heads of that tale. Courage, a story of 1891 with pictures by Gordon, gets the same treatment here. Named at Last and On the Watch open the chapter list of Courage. Such indexes let readers find every chapter of an author works in one place.
57524-index-for-works-of-mary-gaunt-hype:
Index for Works of Mary Gaunt is a guide book made by David Widger. It lists the works of Mary Gaunt held in a great free store. The works are set in a plain roll at the front. Past that roll the book gives the list of parts of each work in full. The whole is a find tool, not a tale.

Five works stand in the first roll. A tale of a move touch heads it. A lone trip past a dark main, a maid in a far east land, and a broke trip stand past it. A work on where the two worlds meet closes the roll. Then the parts of the tale book are set out: a trot horse, a feast eve at a far farm, a lost man, and the loss of a ship.
57755-the-mysteries-of-heron-dyke-a-nove:
The Mysteries of Heron Dyke, volume one of three, is a novel of incident by the author of In the Dead of Night. Bentley printed it in London in 1880. The contents open with Gilbert Denison's will, then introduce Heron Dyke and its inmates across twelve chapters.

Chapter one sets its scene just after Waterloo, when the First Gentleman in Europe sat on the throne. Gilbert Denison of Heron Dyke, Norfolk, a man of sixty, lies dying in lodgings in Bloomsbury Square. Days before, his horse slipped as he rode into town from Enfield and rolled heavily over him. By the bed sits his favourite nephew and heir, also named Gilbert, a resolute young man of three or four and twenty.
57898-useful-knowledge-volume-1-minerals:
Useful Knowledge, or a familiar account of the productions of nature, by William Bingley, fills three volumes, the first on minerals. Bingley, late of Peterhouse, Cambridge, also wrote Animal Biography. This fourth edition was printed in London in 1825. A front plate compares the heights of mountains, cities, and lakes across the British Islands, Europe, Asia, and America.

The preface scolds the old way of teaching such subjects. Small catechism books, in question and answer form, may suit children, Bingley says. They cannot serve readers in search of extended knowledge. His plan treats each mineral, plant, and animal that men chiefly use, with figures for reference. The set was built as a household work of instruction, meant to sit between the schoolbook and the full treatise.
58031-report-of-the-president-s-commissi:
The Report of the President’s Commission on the Assassination of President Kennedy is the Warren Commission report. St Martin’s Press issued the book in New York. John Fitzgerald Kennedy, thirty fifth president, lived from May twenty ninth, nineteen hundred seventeen, to November twenty second, nineteen hundred sixty three.

Chief Justice Earl Warren chaired the group of seven men. Senators Russell and Cooper and Congressmen Boggs and Ford sat with him. Allen W Dulles and John J McCloy filled the last seats. J Lee Rankin led the legal staff as general counsel. Still frames from the Zapruder film mark the key Dallas pages. Staff names fill page on page of front matter here. The book stands as the state’s full account of that Dallas day.
58062-the-preacher-s-complete-homiletic-:
The Preachers Complete Homiletic Commentary is a verse by verse aid for priests, here on the first part of the book of Isaiah. A note at its front tells its use: to help priests in the prep of their talks. Much of its thought is drawn, in brief form, from talks in print.

That note is plain about its cast. The book is a store of mans views on the word of God, it says. The man who set the print form owns he does not hold with each view in it. Church takes the place of the old land, and mans work sways Gods pace of times to come: both stand in his list of points he would not back. The note flags too its hard words on the church of Rome.
58076-caliban-by-the-yellow-sands-a-comm:
A community masque by Percy MacKaye, published at New York in 1916. Doubleday, Page issued the volume for the Shakespeare tercentenary. MacKaye built the piece on Caliban from the Tempest. Joseph Urban sketched the design for Setebos, Caliban's god. The Drama League of America endorsed the enterprise. A special notice guards performance rights strictly.

New York staged the masque at the City College Stadium in May 1916. Five performances ran on consecutive nights. Thousands of amateur citizens took part in such productions. MacKaye had already filled Saint Louis with a civic masque of seven thousand performers. Print adds interludes and directions for smaller towns to follow. The work belongs to the pageant movement that swept American towns. Shakespeare's monster becomes a symbol of art awakening in the crowd.
5817-the-clockmaker-or-the-sayings-and-d:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton introduces Samuel Slick of Slickville in The Clockmaker, published at Halifax in 1836. An epigraph from Horace sets the tone, followed by verses praising a cheerful sage who conceals moral counsel in a tale when solemn dictates fail. Slick, a Yankee clock peddler, travels, talks, and trades, offering shrewd sayings on people, politics, and profit.

Readers meet early Canadian humor through an American voice, as Slick's Yankee wit needles Nova Scotian slowness and pride. The book's sketches favor dialogue and anecdote over plot, letting each saying land like a proverb. It suits readers of humor, Canadian literature, and the tall-talking tradition that later fed American comic writing.
58175-the-boy-travellers-in-the-far-east:
Thomas Knox wrote The Boy Travellers in the Far East, Part Second, for Harper and Brothers in 1882, sending two youths on a tour of Siam and Java. The tour also takes in Cochin-China, Cambodia, Sumatra, and the Malay Archipelago, and the book is thick with pictures.

The party sails from Hong Kong to Saigon, walks the ruins of Angkor, and rides up the Menam from Bangkok to Ayuthia. Later chapters present the travellers to the king of Siam, show them the white elephant, and carry them to Singapore, Sumatra, and Batavia. Malay pirates, a tea plantation, and the Dutch culture system in Java all get their turns. Knox mixes story with steady teaching about the lands visited.
58531-history-of-the-second-massachusett:
Caroline Whitcomb compiled this history of the Second Massachusetts Battery, known as Nims' Battery, a light artillery unit of the Civil War years 1861 to 1865. The Rumford Press of Concord, New Hampshire, printed it in 1912. Her sources, named on the title page, were the official records of the war, reports, diaries, and rosters.

The contents run from the battery's own story to the work of its veterans' group. A life of Colonel Ormand Nims, the unit's captain in war time, takes a full section. A roster of the men closes the book. The picture list shows camps, landings, and the batteries at Baton Rouge. Families and students of the war get names, dates, and first-hand records in one place.
58608-the-boy-travellers-in-the-far-east:
Thomas Knox sent his two youths on to Ceylon and India in this third part of the Boy Travellers series. Harper printed it at New York in 1882. Borneo, the Philippine Islands, and Burmah stand in its subtitle beside the main road.

Knox was a famed travel writer, author of Overland through Asia and Camp-Fire and Cotton-Field. His plan was fixed and strong: two boys, a wise guide, and a whole region opened port by port. Departure fills chapter one, and the road runs east by sea. Temples, tea lands, elephants, and bazaars pass in talks sized for young readers. The series taught geography as an adventure, and this volume covers the richest ground of the set.
58767-the-preacher-s-complete-homiletic-:
The Preacher's Complete Homiletic Commentary on the Books of the Bible, volume thirteen, covers the book of Proverbs. Harris, author of the commentary on Samuel, wrote this volume. Funk and Wagnalls published the series in New York: the Old Testament fills volumes one to twenty one, the New Testament volumes twenty two to thirty two.

Each chapter of Proverbs gets critical notes and a run of homiletic heads, verse by verse. Chapter one treats the author, his method, and his object. The characteristics of a wise man follow. The root of true knowledge, enticement to sin, and the cry of wisdom close the chapter. Later heads take up human understanding and divine knowledge, and God as a giver with man as receiver. Transcriber's notes warn that the commentary prints men's opinions on Proverbs and does not include the scripture text itself.
58837-the-boy-travellers-in-the-far-east:
The Boy Travellers in the Far East, part fourth, by Thomas Knox, takes two youths to Egypt and the Holy Land. Harper and Brothers published it at New York in 1883. Knox also wrote The Young Nimrods and Overland Through Asia, the title page lists. A preface grants that Egypt and the Holy Land are old themes for authors.

Herodotus and Strabo wrote on those lands long ago, he notes with respect. Many books have treated them since those ancient days, he adds for his readers. He could not expect to say much that is new in such a field. Yet press and public kindness to the earlier parts excused this fourth journey. Two boys learn history and custom on the Nile and in Palestine in these pages.
59021-the-boy-travellers-in-the-far-east:
The Boy Travellers in the Far East, part fifth, by Thomas Knox, recounts the adventures of two youths on a trip through Africa. Harper and Brothers published it in New York in 1884. With this volume the wanderings of the Boy Travellers end.

Frank Bassett and Fred Bronson come home in company with their companion and mentor, Doctor Bronson. The preface states the aim: a story of travel that would interest and instruct their school mates and friends. Knox is frank about his sources. He had visited several parts of Africa, but never the equatorial regions. The central African experiences of Frank and Fred were not his own. He drew incidents from many books of African travel and exploration. Fiction, he says, was kept to the narrowest bounds. The four earlier parts took the boys to Japan and China, Siam and Java, Ceylon and India, and Egypt and Palestine.
59075-the-life-and-work-of-james-a-garfi:
John Clark Ridpath wrote The Life and Work of James A Garfield, twentieth President of the United States, in a memorial edition from 1881. The book covers Garfield's boyhood, the struggles of his youth, and his early manhood. It treats his valor as a soldier and his career as a statesman. His election to the presidency and the tragic story of his death close the arc.

The preface warns that sudden death tends to glorify a great man. Ridpath sets Garfield beside the Prince of Orange and Lincoln, both cut down by killers. He grants that fervor will fade and cool judgment will follow. Still, he claims a residuum of greatness in Garfield that time cannot wear away. Many pictures fill the volume.
59101-the-printer-in-eighteenth-century-:
Colonial Williamsburg's account of the printer in eighteenth-century Williamsburg opens with a word about the typography of the period. Its first pages are set in Caslon, cut by William Caslon, the greatest of English letter founders.

The note explains the long s, borrowed from German hand script, and the ligatures formed where letters overlapped. Caslon also designed type flowers, ornaments excavated at the printing office site on Duke of Gloucester Street and reproduced here. Printers capitalized all nouns and expressions of emphasis, a style the modern reader may find odd. The booklet tells of the printer's life, times, and craft.
59325-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
An index of the Project Gutenberg works of Margaret, Queen of Navarre, guides readers to her tales. David Widger compiled the index for the Gutenberg set of her works. The Heptameron tales fill five volumes in that online edition of hers. Clicking a mark by a title opens that volume's contents list. Clicking the title itself opens the plain file of the volume.

Volume one opens with a preface and notes on the queen's life. Peter Boaistuau's dedication and preface stand before the tales begin. The prologue sets ten tellers at their story game across seven days. Tale heads name a muleteer's wife, a queen of Naples, and more. The boatwoman of Coulon outwits the friars in one famed tale here. A wife's ruse saves her lover in another of the first day. The index lets a reader jump straight to any one tale.
59340-the-motor-boys-on-thunder-mountain:
Motor Boys on Thunder Mountain is a boys' adventure by Clarence Young. Its subtitle names the treasure chest of Blue Rock as the prize. Cupples and Leon of New York published the Motor Boys series. A front plate shows the boys riding in front of a cave. A long series list fronts the volume for eager young readers.

Motor Boys, Motor Boys Overland, and Motor Boys in Mexico head it. Across the plains, afloat, and on the Atlantic fill the next lines. In strange waters, on the Pacific, and in the clouds ensue there. Over the Rockies, over the ocean, and on the wing follow fast. Cars, boats, planes, a ranch, and the army vary the boys' travels.
59399-the-ayenbite-of-inwyt-remorse-of-c:
The Ayenbite of Inwyt, or Remorse of Conscience, appears here in a partial translation into modern English by Wyatt. A J Wyatt was a tutor of the University Correspondence College, and the book belongs to its tutorial series. It was issued in London by the Clive firm for students reading early English texts.

The medieval work teaches how a sinner should confess and seek mercy. Its prologue begins with the ten commandments given to Moses on Sinai. Whoever breaks one must repent, be shriven, and pray for God's mercy to be saved. The book was written, the prologue says, for Englishmen to know how to shrive themselves. Wyatt's rendering makes a hard Kentish text usable by correspondence students, sentence by plain sentence.
59698-observations-on-antimony-read-befo:
Observations on Antimony is a medical paper by John Millar, a London doctor. Millar read it before the Medical Society of London in seventeen seventy four. Johnson in Saint Paul Churchyard printed it at the Society request then. Some members had feared free censure of popular views would breed resentment.

Millar prints anyway, softening objections with their friendly cautions in mind. An account of the earlier chymists opens the medical history of antimony. Their exaggerated praises misled and abused mankind, he charges in plain words. He grants he has not himself assayed the ores or run the processes. Assay by others and clinical use ground his caution on the drug.
60078-the-white-heart-of-mojave-an-adven:
The White Heart of Mojave is Edna Brush Perkins's adventure with the outdoors of the desert. Boni and Liveright published it in New York in 1922. Perkins dedicates it to Charlotte Hannahs Jordan, who shared the adventure in the wind and sun of big spaces. The first chapter is called The Feel of the Outdoors.

Two women drive into the Mojave and on into Death Valley. Chapters tell of the outfit, the strangest farm in the world, and the burning sands. A dry camp, a mountain spring, and high white peaks follow, then snowstorm and sandstorm together. Pictures show burros at Silver Lake and a pack train crossing a dry lake. The book is a noted early desert travel tale by a woman.
60101-large-fees-and-how-to-get-them-a-b:
Large Fees and How to Get Them is a trade craft book for doctors by Albert Harmon. Its leaf marks it for the sole use of men of the cure craft. A Chicago house brought it out in nineteen eleven with a front part by Lydston. The first part calls cure work a trade flop on the purse side. Doctors blame their own slack ways for that flop, the part says.

Free wards and cure shops sap the pay of paid craft men, it claims. Parts name the marks of the man who wins high fees in the trade. Fast bill take, clean garb, and mind craft all count in that win. A part on trade rules scorns them as a bugbear used to scare the young. Press tricks of famed men fill tales of how note is won.
60197-the-attack-in-trench-warfare-impre:
Capt André Laffargue of the one hundred fifty third Infantry, French Army, wrote The Attack in Trench Warfare, impressions and reflections of a company commander. An officer of infantry rendered the study into English for the Infantry Journal. The United States Infantry Association at Washington issued the book in nineteen sixteen. General Joffre had the study issued to the French Army before general publication.

An intro says no book on a military topic since the war began had stirred so much interest in European military circles. Laffargue treats the tactics of attack in trench war in general and in detail. Training of infantry units and careful preparation stand at the heart of his case. He contrasts two regiments of very different quality in battle. One shows real infantry, and the other mere cannon fodder. Officers got a famed, field tested guide.
60318-star-land-being-talks-with-young-p:
Robert Stawell Ball, professor of astronomy at Cambridge, wrote Star-Land, talks with young people about the wonders of the heavens. This new and revised edition was published by Ginn and Company in 1899. Ball based the book on his Christmas lectures at the Royal Institution in 1881 and 1887, courses given to young audiences.

He dedicated the little book to the young friends who attended those lectures. The first lecture treats the Sun: its heat, size, spots, and the seasons its light brings. The second takes up the Moon. Ball explains how astronomers measure the distances of the heavenly bodies, in words a child can follow. Star-Land remains a model of clear popular science, written by a working astronomer.
60575-the-seventy-s-course-in-theology-t:
The Seventy's Course in Theology, Third Year, is a study manual on the doctrine of Deity for the Seventies of the Mormon church. Roberts, of the First Council of the Seventy, compiled and edited it at Salt Lake City in 1910. The lessons were meant for quorum classes, with home reading, scripture citations and discussion built into the plan.

Roberts adapts the method to small classes. The men should sit round a table, read the lesson together, and discuss the notes. The subject needs no apology. The manual quotes Jesus, that eternal life is to know the only true God, and Joseph Smith, that knowing God's character for a certainty is the first principle of the gospel. The year's lessons build that knowledge systematically.
60667-molly-o-rigge-sit-ye-awhile-and-ti:
Molly O'Rigge is a Scots chapbook of comic songs, printed at Glasgow for the booksellers. Its title piece bids the reader sit awhile and tipple a bit. The contents join Molly O'Rigge and Tom Treacle with The Delights of Wine, Caledonia Native Land, The Warrior Bard, and Beadle of the Parish.

The first song opens at Cork, where Miss Molly O'Rigge lived with a nose like the snout of a pig. Cornelius O'Whack gave her heart such a smack that the pair capered a jig to church. Yet what a false-hearted Molly she proves. The verse is broad, sung Scots-Irish fun of the street market kind. Chapbooks like this one carried songs, jokes, and tales to readers who bought print by the penny at fairs and doors.
60677-the-grenadier-guards-in-the-great-:
Volume one of The Grenadier Guards in the Great War of 1914 to 1918 is the regimental history of a famed British foot regiment. It was writ by Sir Frederick Ponsonby, late of the regiment, and published by Macmillan of London in 1920. The Earl of Cavan wrote the introduction. Maps by Emery Walker go with the text. The book is dedicated, by leave, to the King, the regiment's colonel in chief. A portrait of the King stands at the front.

The first chapter sets the scene before the war. Then the Second Battalion lands in France. The retreat from Mons, the battle of the Marne, and the passage of the Aisne follow in order. The First Battalion joins for the first battle of Ypres. The three volumes trace the guards through the whole war, battalion by battalion.
61216-the-grenadier-guards-in-the-great-:
Frederick Ponsonby, a late Grenadier Guards officer, wrote this regimental history, published by Macmillan in 1920. Volume two of three carries the war from January 1916 onward in its contents. A Sargent portrait shows the Duke of Connaught, colonel of the regiment, at the front.

Cavan, a lieutenant general, supplies an introduction, and Walker drew the maps. Chapter eighteen runs from January to September 1916 for the third and fourth battalions. The battle of the Somme follows for all four battalions in chapter nineteen, in the Guards' own record of the Great War's middle years.
61533-the-american-electro-magnetic-tele:
A technical treatise by Alfred Vail, published at Philadelphia in 1845. Lea and Blanchard issued the book. Vail was Samuel Morse's assistant and a builder of the first line. Eighty-one wood engravings illustrate the apparatus. A verse from Job heads the title page. It asks whether man can send lightnings that answer back.

The contents describe the whole American system. Battery, wire, electromagnet, and register get chapters in turn. The telegraphic alphabet and specimen messages follow. Keys, circuits, and secret correspondence receive detailed treatment. Reports of Congress fill the later pages. Vail also surveys every known electric telegraph abroad. The book appeared one year after the Washington to Baltimore line opened. It is the founding manual of American telegraphy.
62148-the-preacher-s-complete-homiletic-:
George Barlow wrote this preacher commentary volume on Paul epistles here. Funk and Wagnalls printed volume twenty nine in New York. It treats Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians in one volume. First and Second Thessalonians complete the six epistles covered here.

The full set runs thirty two volumes on the whole Bible text. Critical and explanatory notes join sermon outlines for the preacher. An introduction sketches the Galatians as Celtic folk of old. A Gaulish invasion swept them into Asia Minor, it recounts. Barlow also wrote on Kings, Psalms, Ezekiel, and Timothy in the same preacher series set.
62240-a-history-of-chester-cathedral-wit:
History of Chester Cathedral is a guide and history by an unnamed author. He was a member of the Chester Archaeological Society, the title says. Prichard published it at Chester in the year 1852 for visitors. Notices of the bishops and deans join the building's story inside. A quote from Coleridge on entering a cathedral fronts the work.

Coleridge felt devotion and awe there, lost to all that surrounded him. His whole being expanded into the infinite in that hushed space. The publisher dedicates the history to the dean of Chester by permission. A Visit to the Cathedral forms the opening descriptive chapter here. Stone, glass, tombs, and the long line of bishops fill its pages.
62327-historical-and-descriptive-sketche:
Historical and Descriptive Sketches of the Town and Soke of Horncastle is a town past by George Weir. This is its next form, out in eighteen twenty-two, with plates. The first form sold out while calls for it still came, Weir says. He put in such fresh facts as he could get and a new view of a monks wreck. To cut the price he left out the old and new plans and the back grants of the first form.

Parts treat the towns seat, its days past two old realms, its manor, and its part in the wars of a past king. Its old finds, its church, its school, and its stream and cut take heads. The towns of its soke and past a score of spots near it fill the book, with a part on its rocks and wild life at the close.
62603-how-to-enamel-being-a-treatise-on-:
Howard Chapin wrote a how to book on the enameling of jewelry with hard enamels, first printed in 1911 at New York and London. Nine chapters and a set of views make up the small work book. Views show an agate mortar and pestle, a spatula, firing gear, and a pickle pot among the tools of the trade.

Chapter one treats the making ready of the enamel, bought in hard chunks from acorn size to dinner plate size. Makers pour it into a mold where it hardens as a slab a foot or more across, Chapin says. Wrapped in cloth and struck with a hammer, chunks break to pea size and are washed clean for use.
63081-love-s-coming-of-age-a-series-of-p:
Love's Coming-of-Age, a series of papers on the relations of the sexes by Edward Carpenter, author of Towards Democracy, was published in Chicago in 1902 by Stockham. A head note gives the book's figure: the little god of Love is generally pictured as a child, and rightly, given his erratic ways. Signs of a new order, Carpenter says, are appearing in the relations of the sexes.

Contents run from The Sex-Passion through Man, the Ungrown, Woman: the Serf, and Woman in Freedom. Marriage gets a retrospect and a forecast, then The Free Society. Notes treat primitive group marriage, jealousy, the family, and checks to population. The first paper owns the subject's difficulty: a natural reticence, much prudery, and words too few and weak for a passion that fills so much of human thought. Carpenter argues for freer, more equal unions.
63111-the-grenadier-guards-in-the-great-:
The Grenadier Guards in the Great War is a unit history in three volumes. Colonel Ponsonby, a late guards man, wrote the long war record. The hosted text holds the third volume of the three. Maps by a famed map hand aid the text of the fights.

This book covers the last year of the war, month by hard month. Four corps of the guard take turns in the line of fire and rest. A front print shows the Prince of Wales in his guard dress. The last push from spring to the truce day fills the bulk here. Names, dates, and ground won form the stuff of the stout record.
6322-personal-narrative-of-travels-to-th:
Alexander von Humboldt and Aime Bonpland travel the equinoctial regions of America from 1799 to 1804, in a narrative translated from Humboldt's French and edited by Thomasina Ross. This first volume, in a three volume set, opens with preparations, instruments, departure from Spain, and a landing in the Canary Islands. Tenerife follows, with a journey to Orotava and an excursion to the peak of Teyde.

From Tenerife the travellers cross to South America, reach Tobago and Cumana, and explore the Manzanares banks, the Araya peninsula, and the missions of the Chayma people. Humboldt notes harbours silting, rivers, mountains, and the cavern of the Guacharo with its nocturnal birds. The book is a scientist's log, measuring, naming, and wondering, as a new continent opens chapter by chapter.
63379-from-monkey-to-man-or-society-in-t:
Austin Bierbower's From Monkey to Man, or Society in the Tertiary Age, was published at Chicago in 1906 by the Ingersoll Beacon Company, with illustrations by Heaton. The frontispiece is the battle in the swamp. A publisher's preface, announcing a new and revised edition at a reduced price, calls the book the first attempt at a prehistoric novel.

The scenes lie in the Tertiary Age, when, on the Darwinian theory, men were emerging from the ape. The subtitle promises the first steps in industry, commerce, government, religion, and the arts, with the great expedition from Cocoanut Hill and the wars in Alligator Swamp. Origins crowd the story: of arms, building, religion, and government, the first use of fire and clothing. Bierbower aimed, the preface says, to be scientifically accurate, with no more liberty than historic fiction allows.
63584-the-nuclear-ship-savannah-first-at:
The United States Department of Commerce, the Maritime Administration, and the Atomic Energy Commission issued this booklet on the nuclear ship Savannah. The subtitle calls her the first atomic merchant ship and one of the world's safest ships. A cutaway labels her pressurized water reactor, boron steel control rods, fuel elements, and thermal shield. The Savannah is named as the first nuclear-powered cargo-passenger ship.

Every fit safety device, the booklet says, was sought at the design stage. Her building was inspected and tested more closely than that of any other merchant ship ever built. The Merchant Marine Act of 1936 charges the Maritime Administration with keeping the safest fleet for trade and defense. The Atomic Energy Act of 1954 guides the peaceful use of the atom.
63610-speeches-at-the-constitutional-con:
Speeches at the Constitutional Convention is a pamphlet of the speeches of General Robert Smalls. It was put together by Miss Sarah V. Smalls and printed in Charleston, South Carolina, in 1896. With the speeches goes the right of suffrage as passed by that convention. The opening essay states the stakes of the hour in plain terms.

Months before the convention met, Conservatives and Reformers had said in public that they meant to take the vote from the Negro in South Carolina. For the pamphlet, the parts of the new constitution that touch the colored people have been picked out. With them stand the speeches of Robert Smalls on those parts. Pieces from lead newspapers and a few of the many letters sent to him are added, as the opening states.
63710-a-manual-of-photographic-chemistry:
A Manual of Photographic Chemistry is a practical handbook by Frederick Hardwich. Its full title adds the practice of the collodion process. Hardwich lectured on photography at King's College, London. He had earlier demonstrated chemistry there.

The copy at hand is the fourth edition, issued by John Churchill in 1857. In the preface to the third edition the author marvels at the pace of demand. Less than fourteen months after first publication, a third edition was called for. He took that call as proof of the art's rapid advance in Britain. His rule in revising was to keep only what served practice as well as science. Most photographers, he notes, come to the art for pleasure as much as learning. The printing chapters were wholly rewritten later.
64182-historical-and-descriptive-sketche:
George Weir wrote this local history of Horncastle in Lincolnshire, printed for the author in London in 1820 and sold in Horncastle by Weir and Son. Engravings dress the book. Weir says a love of place-history led him to spend his spare hours, over years, on the early past of the town and its soke. Health and local troubles held the work back five years.

He calls the result mere sketches, the fruit of an untrodden path. Friends fed him facts: Edmund Turnor of Stoke Rochford sent useful notices, and Richard Hill helped arrange the whole. The geology chapter draws on a sketch of the Lincolnshire Wolds. The book is one man's mite toward a long-neglected record.
64252-only-an-ensign-a-tale-of-the-retre:
James Grant wrote Only an Ensign, a tale of the retreat from Cabul, in three volumes, of which this file holds the first, issued at London by Tinsley Brothers in 1871. Grant had written The Romance of War and other military tales. His preface owns that he has not entered fully into the fighting before the retreat, since that would not suit his story's purpose, and he sends readers to history for it.

He anchors the fiction in fact: an officer of the Queen's 44th wrapped the regimental colour round him and so escaped death in the Khyber Pass. Like incidents, he says, befell a havildar of the Shah's Ghoorka regiment after its destruction. Captain Waller's adventures carry the tale in volume one.
64253-only-an-ensign-a-tale-of-the-retre:
Volume two of Only an Ensign, by James Grant, turns to the retreat from Cabul. Tinsley Brothers issued the book in London in eighteen hundred seventy one. Grant had written The Romance of War on his name. A Macbeth line on time and the hour fronts this part.

Far from Cornwall’s Tintagel, the scene shifts past the Indus. A British army under General Elphinstone camps before Cabul. Denzil Devereaux, the young ensign, takes his turn at the front. Captain Bob Waller and Jack Polwhele share his small fort. Fur trimmed coats and brandy pawnee warm their November post. A dozen such forts dot the plain to the Black Rocks. Tiffin with the Trecarrels and a mosque visit fill calm days. Christmas at Cabul, then the retreat’s grim morning, ends the calm.
64254-only-an-ensign-a-tale-of-the-retre:
James Grant wrote Only an Ensign, here in volume three. A tale of the retreat from Cabul is its subtitle. Tinsley at London put out the third volume in 1871. Grant had written the Romance of War before this tale. A pair of noble brothers heads the contents of the volume.

Downie's reflections follow in the list. Hope of the dead takes the next chapter. At Jellalabad stands in the middle heads. A famous brigade fills the later contents. To Toorkistan, a governor, and an alarm crowd the same list. The hostages close the tale's march. A durbar stands near its conclusion. Swallow this tale of a tub, a voice opens it. The thing was invented for monetary extortion, he charges hotly. Grant gives the Kabul retreat a third volume of wounds.
64378-the-smoky-valley-reproductions-of-:
Birger Sandzen made The Smoky Valley, copies of a series of his stone prints of the Smoky Valley in Kansas, printed at Kansas City in 1922. Powell wrote an introduction. The introduction opens on the artist's sight. When Sandzen looks into the seamed face of a pioneer farmer of Kansas, he sees the winning through of a spirit.

The Smoky Hill River is not much wider than a creek, and the early homesteader prized it for water for land and stock. Then came Sandzen, who settled near the stream at Lindsborg. A deep fondness sprang up at once between artist and river. Used to a land of many streams, he haunted the banks of the river that seemed to speak to him of home. By sunlight and moonlight he studied it, and learned to love the Kansas landscape through it.
64419-tales-of-an-old-sea-port-a-general:
Tales of an Old Sea Port, by Wilfred Harold Munro of Brown University, sketches the history of Bristol, Rhode Island, for Princeton University Press in 1917. Three parts carry the tales: Simeon Potter and the Prince Charles of Lorraine, Norwest John and the voyage of the Juno, and James de Wolf and the privateer Yankee.

Munro also treats the voyages of the Norsemen so far as they may touch Narragansett Bay. Personal narratives of notable voyages by sailors from the Mount Hope lands fill out the sketch. A letter of Father Fauque appears among the papers in the first part.
64822-the-alhambra-being-a-brief-record-:
Albert Calvert wrote a brief record of the Alhambra, printed at London in 1907 and given to King Alfonso the Thirteenth of Spain. A Spanish rhyme at the head says that who has not seen Seville has not seen a great marvel. Calvert signs the gift page from his house at Hampstead in 1904.

The book tells of the Arab conquest of the land, then of Muslim building and ornament in the great palace at Granada. Lists of plates name panels, writings in stone, tile work, frets, cornices and capitals. Views show Granada, the palace from San Nicolas, and the hills of the Sierra Nevada behind it.
64900-toledo-an-historical-and-descripti:
Toledo, an account of the City of Generations, is by Albert Calvert. John Lane of London and New York brought the book out in 1907. Over five hundred illustrations stand through the Spanish Series volume. Calvert edited the whole Spanish Series of city and painter books. The book is given to the Infanta Maria Teresa of Spain.

Contents run from the childhood of the city to El Greco's chapter. Toledo under the Visigoths and under the Moor fill the early parts. Toledo as capital of Castile and its buildings follow in order. The cathedral gets a full chapter in the heart of the book. The decline of the city closes the historical account given here. Plates show the Tagus river, the Alcantara bridge, and Zocodover plaza. Streets of Toledo stand pictured again and again in the plate list.
65411-report-on-the-migration-of-birds-i:
Three naturalists drew up a report on the travels of birds in the spring and autumn of 1880. Sonnenschein and Allen of London published it in 1881 at two shillings. Harvie Brown took the Scottish returns. Cordeaux took the east coast of England, and Kermode the west.

The plan was a net of watchers at set stations, sending in dated notes on each kind of bird. Forms and letters went out through the Scottish weather society to Iceland and Faroe. Two stations lay in Iceland, at Stykkisholm and Reykjavik, and one in Faroe. A fourth, on Fair Isle, was won for the next year. The report works by coasts, kind by kind. Spring and autumn passages are set side by side. Watchers wrote in of swans, crows, puffins, and lapwings.
65414-travels-into-turkey-containing-the:
Busbequius, a Fleming who served as ambassador from the Emperor Ferdinand to Solyman the Great, wrote these travels into Turkey. They were turned from his Latin into English and printed in London in 1744, with memoirs of his life at the front. The title page promises the most accurate account of the Turks and their neighbors.

The life sketch tells how he learned near ten languages, went to Constantinople, and traveled on to Amasia when the Sultan was not to be found. He gathered old manuscripts and coins, hunted rare plants, and studied the Turkish state at close range. The travels treat manners, customs, religion, policy, riches, and coinage. Readers get the Ottoman court seen by one of the sharpest eyes of the 1500s.
65458-the-primrose-path-a-chapter-in-the:
Mrs Oliphant sets a Scottish tale in the kingdom of Fife in a novel issued by Harper and Brothers at New York in 1878. The title page quotes Ophelia's warning on the primrose path of dalliance, from Hamlet.

Oliphant calls the book a chapter in the annals of Fife. Her name fronts a long Harper list of her novels. Agnes, Miss Marjoribanks, and the Chronicles of Carlingford stand among them. The primrose path of the title hints the plot's bent: pleasure first, and the reckoning after. Oliphant wrote at a pace few could match. She supported a large family by her pen for fifty years. Her Scottish tales draw on close knowledge of manse, town, and farm life north of the Forth.
65471-report-on-the-migration-of-birds-i:
Report on the Migration of Birds in the Spring and Autumn of 1881 was printed by West, Newman and Company in London in 1882. Five authors sign the title page: Harvie Brown, Cordeaux, Kermode, Barrington, and More.

A preface tells the origin. A committee of the British Association, appointed at York in 1881, was charged to gather observations on bird migration at lighthouses and lightships. The Trinity House, the Northern Lights commissioners, and the Irish Lights commissioners consented. Cordeaux served as secretary. The returns are arranged by coast: the east coast of Scotland and of England, both west coasts, and the Irish coast. Schedules went even to Iceland and the Faroe islands. The Scottish section opens with stray records: a wheatear seen from a ship east of Orkney, a night heron killed in Faroe, turtle doves in autumn.
65515-report-on-the-migration-of-birds-i:
Report on the Migration of Birds in the Spring and Autumn of 1882 is the fourth such count of a board of bird men. It came out at London in eighteen eighty-three at the price of a few coins. Four named hands sign the work. A board of a great lore guild, named the past year, set the task.

A wish heads the work, that the keepers of the light towers past the shore would note the seals, whales, birds, and fish they see. Such notes would add true new facts to the store of lore, the quote holds. Parts give the counts shore by shore, each led by a verse on birds in flight. Light men past the isles sent in the bulk of the notes that fill the count.
65585-a-brief-history-of-printing-part-i:
A Brief History of Printing, part two, treats the money side of the printing trade from 1450 to 1789. Hamilton, who wrote it, was teaching director of the printers' association that issued the book in 1918. Its full title names the ground: government rules, censorship, the inside state of the trade, and the ties between masters and men.

The contents run from rules and monopolies to censorship, then to the growth of the idea of copyright. Trade guilds and the coming of the new industry follow. How the old time printers worked, and how their shops were ordered within, fill the middle chapters. The last treats the ties between employer and employed. Review questions and a list for further reading close the school book.
65609-report-on-the-migration-of-birds-i:
The fifth Report on the Migration of Birds in the Spring and Autumn of 1883 was printed in London in 1884. A committee of the British Association for the Advancement of Science prepared it. Harvie Brown, Cordeaux, Barrington and More signed the report. The committee worked under Professor Newton, with the lighthouse boards of England, Scotland and Ireland.

Keepers at lighthouses and lightships recorded the birds that struck, rested or passed, and the returns are arranged by coast. They cover the east coast of Scotland, the east coast of England and the west coast of Scotland. The coasts of Ireland close the volume. No return came from the west coast of England and the Isle of Man, a gap the preface states plainly.
65670-speech-of-the-right-honourable-wil:
Speech of William Pitt is a pamphlet printing of Pitt great Commons speech of 1799. Pitt spoke on January thirty first 1799, offering resolutions as the basis of a union.
