The union proposed was between Great Britain and Ireland, then in rebel shadow. Wright of Piccadilly sold this fifth edition at one shilling and sixpence in London.

The speech opens with the king message read by the Speaker to the House. Enemies, the message says, design the separation of Ireland from this kingdom by unremitting industry. Pitt answers with the union resolutions that made the Act of Union follow. Political history keeps the speech as a founding document of the United Kingdom.
65700-report-on-the-migration-of-birds-i:
Five naturalists share the title page of this report on the migration of birds in the spring and autumn of 1884, printed in London in 1885. It is the sixth report of a committee of the British Association, reappointed at Montreal in 1884 under Professor Newton, with Cordeaux as secretary. The committee's task was to gather sightings of bird migration at lighthouses and lightships.

Leave to collect the sightings came from Trinity House and from the lighthouse boards of Scotland and Ireland. The returns were arranged by coast: Scotland by Harvie Brown, the east coast of England by Cordeaux, the west coast by Eagle Clarke, and Ireland by Barrington, More, and Clarke. A new sketch-map in this report marks all the stations in red.
65710-a-synopsis-of-the-british-mosses-c:
Charles P Hobkirk wrote A Synopsis of the British Mosses, a handbook of mosses in Great Britain and Ireland. L Reeve and Company issued the book in London in eighteen hundred seventy three. Hobkirk led the Huddersfield Naturalists’ Society. Wilson’s Bryologia Britannica and Schimper guided his plan.

Each moss here was checked under the microscope before its notes were set. That care sets the book past a mere copying task. Plain keys sort the kinds so new hands can name finds. Rare kinds get the spots where they grow. Bruch, Schimper, Mueller, and Braithwaite all fed the work. Linnean Society papers and French journals join that source list. Hobkirk begs the book be read as a field aid, not a grand work. It suits both the working moss man and the novice.
65780-memoirs-of-sarah-duchess-of-marlbo:
Memoirs of Sarah, Duchess of Marlborough, and of the Court of Queen Anne, by Thomson, fills two volumes, the first printed in London in 1839 by Colburn. Thomson also wrote memoirs of the court of Henry the Eighth and a life of Raleigh. Her introduction marvels at the gap she means to fill: ninety-six years after the duchess's death, no full account of her career had appeared.

Had Sarah lived in the present day, Thomson writes, the press would have unveiled every peculiarity of her resolute and singular character. Both duke and duchess, she notes, won as much fame as any British subjects of their age. Yet they risked passing without any connected, adequate record. The memoirs draw on the duchess's own papers to show the favorite who rose, quarreled, and fell at Anne's court.
65781-memoirs-of-sarah-duchess-of-marlbo:
Memoirs of Sarah, Duchess of Marlborough, and of the Court of Queen Anne, volume two, is a biography of 1839. Thomson, author of memoirs of the court of Henry the Eighth, wrote the work. Henry Colburn published the set in London from Great Marlborough Street that year. Contents of the second volume open with characters of the great men of the court.

Chapter one treats the character of Lord Peterborough and of Lord Montague in its heads. The violence of party spirit at this era is a head of the same chapter in the list. The conduct of the duchess in politics and her dislike to Lord Rochester come after in turn. Sarah Churchill, the queen favourite and enemy, left letters by the thousand. Thomson life, built from them, fixed the portrait of the imperious duchess for the Victorian reader of court history.
65823-the-journal-lancet-vol-xxxv-no-5-m:
The Journal-Lancet, the journal of the Minnesota State Medical Association, came out twice a month from Minneapolis. This issue is volume thirty-five, number five, dated March 1, 1915. Its lead paper, on feeding the healthy infant, was read to the Hennepin County Medical Society the past November.

Huenekens, who taught the care of children at the University of Minnesota, argues that feeding rules had swung too far. He backs the longer gap between feeds, yet notes that some young infants take more milk on a three hour plan. Mother's milk, he insists, is by far the best food for a healthy child. Doctors of the day got firm, plain guidance.
65840-report-on-the-migration-of-birds-i:
Report on the Migration of Birds in Spring and Autumn of 1885 is a science report. It is the seventh report of a British Association committee on bird movement. Lighthouse and lightship keepers across the British Isles sent in the observations. Trinity House and the lighthouse boards of Scotland and Ireland granted access.

Harvie-Brown arranged the Scottish returns; Cordeaux took the east coast of England. Eagle Clarke handled the west coast; Barrington and More covered Ireland in turn. Sections treat Heligoland and each coast in order, with a station map. Unst, Sumburgh Head, Flamborough, and Spurn Point are among the watch points named.
66032-report-on-the-migration-of-birds-i:
This eighth report on the migration of birds covers spring and autumn 1886 and was printed at Edinburgh in 1887 for two shillings. Five ornithologists compiled it: Harvie-Brown, Cordeaux, Barrington, More, and Eagle Clarke. A British Association committee directed the work.

The preface explains that the committee gathered observations on bird migration at lighthouses and lightships, by consent of the lighthouse authorities. Returns for Scotland were arranged by Harvie-Brown, the east coast of England by Cordeaux, and the west coast by another hand. Keepers' logs of birds striking lanterns became data. Readers get Victorian citizen science in print, the raw record behind the first migration maps.
66119-little-miss-dorothy-the-story-of-t:
Martha James wrote a tale for children called Little Miss Dorothy, issued in New York in 1901 with many art cuts by Watson Davis. Dorothy May is a bright eyed girl who loves her Cousin Ray, a dimpled boy who lives near by. A verse at the front sends them off in fairy boats to dreamland with Captain Snore.

Twenty parts bring a funny pudding, a boy in a teapot, a bronze woman, and a fairy bell. Dolls have a paradise, a horse is enchanted, and a chair learns to talk. A trip to Toy Land, a store kept by a queer little man, and a pair of old shoes fill the last half. The fun is soft and dream like.
66152-report-on-the-migration-of-birds-i:
Five bird men wrote a report on bird migration in spring and autumn of 1887. McFarlane and Erskine printed the ninth report at Edinburgh in 1889. J A Harvie-Brown, J Cordeaux, R M Barrington, A G More, and W Eagle Clarke share the byline. A British Association group had been re-formed at Manchester in 1887 for the task.

Keepers at lighthouses and lightships logged birds as they passed each coast. Harvie-Brown sorted the Scots returns, and Cordeaux took the east coast of England. Clarke took the west coast, and Barrington and More took Ireland. Bird students gain a rich, dated map of flight lines round Britain.
66172-textile-fabrics-a-descriptive-cata:
Daniel Rock, a priest, made a full list of the cloth treasures held at the South Kensington Museum. Chapman and Hall published the book in 1870 for the Science and Art Department. It covers church vestments, dresses, silk stuffs, needlework, and tapestries. A hood of a cope, wrought by hand in silks and gold with the Adoration of the Magi, stands near the front.

A long opening essay sorts the whole field. It treats the lands that gave wool, cotton, flax, and silk. It names the old kinds of silk, samit, cendal, taffeta, and velvet among them. It maps the towns that wove, from Sicily and Lucca to Flanders and Cologne. Later parts treat stitch work of many lands and the hanging art of tapestry. Rock also shows what the set can teach the student of history, of the church, of art, and of trade.
66252-the-black-watch-at-ticonderoga-and:
Frederick B Richards wrote The Black Watch at Ticonderoga and Major Duncan Campbell of Inverawe. Richards served as secretary of the New York State Historical Association at Glens Falls. His book joins a battle tale with a family legend.

The Black Watch was the famed Highland regiment of the British army. Ticonderoga, the French fort on Lake Champlain, saw hard fighting in the old French war. Major Duncan Campbell of Inverawe fell in that campaign. Tales of a ghost and a sworn warning cling to his name. Richards sifts records, notes and family trees to weigh the tale. Family trees at the end trace the Campbells of Inverawe.
66541-facts-and-fancies-for-the-curious-:
Facts and Fancies for the Curious is a grab bag book by Charles Bombaugh, a doctor of arts and cure. A Lippincott house brought it out in nineteen oh five at two ports. Its full name calls it a mix of cuts from the yield fields of books. Cuts are grouped by kind in a long scheme of heads. Americana opens the field with the Norse reach of the new world.

That first cut weighs which shores Bjarne saw in the year nine eighty six. Nantucket, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland are the lands it names in turn. Leif Erikson bought that same ship and sailed west in the year one thousand. Heads run on through first things, puns, slips, and famed fair women. Toasts, word riddles, and graveyard lines fill the late heads of the book.
66858-history-of-the-cape-mounted-riflem:
The History of the Cape Mounted Riflemen belongs to the Historical Records of the British Army, an official series directed by Richard Cannon at the Adjutant-General's Office. The records were printed by authority in London in 1837, by command of King William the Fourth and under the patronage of Queen Victoria.

General orders from Horse Guards, dated the first of January 1836, explain the scheme. The King commanded that an account of the services of every regiment in the British Army be published, to do justice to regiments and to men who had shown bravery in action. Each record was to give the regiment's original formation, its stations, its services against the enemy, and the colours and trophies it had captured. Names of officers and men killed or wounded were to be listed. This volume applies that scheme to a South African corps.
66945-memoirs-and-services-of-the-eighty:
Memoirs and Services of the Eighty-third Regiment, published at London in 1908, traces the County of Dublin regiment from 1793 to 1907. Hugh Rees printed the history. The title page lists the battle honours: Cape of Good Hope, Talavera, Busaco, Fuentes d'Onor, Ciudad Rodrigo, Badajos, Salamanca, Vittoria, Nivelle, Orthes, Toulouse, Peninsula and Central India.

Major William Fitch raised the regiment in September 1793. It embodied at Dublin and lodged two months in the old Custom House at Essex Bridge. Its first strength stood at 72 sergeants, 26 drummers and 1200 rank and file. Seven parts carry the battalions through the West Indies, Africa, the Peninsula, Ceylon, Canada and India, the Mutiny included.
67117-history-of-iridotomy-knife-needle-:
Ziegler, an eye surgeon at the Wills Eye Hospital in Philadelphia, read this history of iridotomy to the ophthalmology section of the American Medical Association at Chicago in June 1908. His subject is the operation that cuts an artificial pupil in the eye.

He gives the honour of origin to Cheselden, whose report appeared in the Philosophical Transactions for 1728. For a century and a half after, the making of an artificial pupil ranked second only to cataract in surgical interest, filling monographs and chapters everywhere. Ziegler blames the many blocked pupils of that age on crude surgery, poor technique, and the want of asepsis. He then sets the older methods out in order and describes his own V-shaped method, weighing the knife-needle against scissors.
67321-the-co-opolitan-a-story-of-the-co-:
The Co-opolitan is a story of the co-operative commonwealth of Idaho, by Zebina Forbush, issued at Chicago in 1898. Charles Kerr published the tale in his Library of Progress. A motto from Gerald Massey promises a brighter world coming. The preface offers the book without other excuse than that it was written.

If it is read, Forbush says, it may do some good in the world. If it is not read, the hour that knew it will pass with it. Utopian tales of co-operation filled the socialist press of that decade. Idaho here holds a commonwealth run for all, not for profit. Forbush writes fiction as argument for a new order of work. The book is a curio of the great co-operative dream in America.
67474-the-experienced-angler-or-angling-:
Colonel Robert Venables wrote The Experienced Angler, or Angling Improved, and Septimus Prowett issued this edition at London in 1825. The title promises the aptest ways and choicest experiments for taking most sorts of fish in pond or river. Isaac Walton praised the work in words set on the title page.

Six chapters cover tools and their making, sorts of angling, and the artificial fly first. Ground angling, baits for each kind of fish, and the keeping of baits follow. A letter to the author from a thirty-year practitioner thanks him for raising his skill. Walton calls the book an epitome of angling, high in judgment and reason. Plain practice, not sport talk, fills the pages.
67821-life-of-emanuel-swedenborg-togethe:
William White wrote this life, Life of Emanuel Swedenborg, together with a brief synopsis of his writings, both philosophical and theological, printed at Philadelphia in 1880. A long preface surveys the lives of Swedenborg already in print, and places this one among them.

Tafel of Tubingen, White says, gathered the testimony of Swedenborg's friends, his letters, and scattered documents into one book of documents in 1839, and every later life draws on it. Hobart of Boston shaped those documents into a connected life that ran to three editions. Rich printed a sketch in London in 1849 that sold out in months. Wilkinson's life of the same year White praises above all, for art, originality, and poetic beauty.
67987-h-m-i-some-passages-in-the-life-of:
Sneyd-Kynnersley, formerly an inspector of schools in the North-West Division, published his recollections in 1913, first issued in 1908. The title's initials stand for one of Her Majesty's Inspectors of Schools. He dedicates the records to the chief inspector and his late colleagues, by whose desire they were put together.

His first acquaintance with the office dates to 1854, when he was twelve and the Reverend Henry Sandford came visiting. Inspectors, he was told, travel about and examine children in the National Schools, and he wished wistfully to be one. Chapters follow him through Anglesey and Cheshire to the Isle of Man, with school boards, managers, singing, and needlework on the way.
68130-a-handbook-of-library-appliances-t:
A Handbook of Library Appliances, the Library Association's guide to the technical equipment of libraries, opens with the Association itself. It was founded on October 5, 1877, at the close of the International Conference of Librarians in London, under Winter Jones, principal librarian of the British Museum. Its objects: to help found new libraries, to win better laws for rate-supported libraries, and to unite all who work in them.

Its own museum of appliances, at the Clerkenwell Public Library, shows apparatus, catalogues, and forms to visitors. Then come the appliances themselves. First comes Cotgreave's library indicator, in use in some two hundred public libraries, thirty in London and suburbs. It shows at a glance which books are in or out. It tells who has a book out, and how long he has had it. It also names every borrower who has had a book since it was added.
68765-twenty-five-years-in-the-secret-se:
Twenty-Five Years in the Secret Service, subtitled The Recollections of a Spy, is a memoir by Major Henri Le Caron. The edition shown is the third, printed in London by William Heinemann in 1892, with portraits and facsimiles. An epigraph from Aristotle sets the tone: no citizen belongs to himself alone, but all belong to the state.

In his introduction Le Caron says that many people urged him to set down the story of his eventful life in a lasting form. He calls the task a daring one. The front matter shows a signed portrait of the author. The book promises a first-hand account of a life spent in secret work for the state, told by the man who lived it, at the close of that career.
68989-catalogue-of-a-collection-of-early:
An exhibition catalogue printed for the Burlington Fine Arts Club in 1920. The Chiswick Press produced it at London. The show gathered early drawings and pictures of London. Some contemporary furniture joined the pictures. A committee of collectors and museum men organised it. Campbell Dodgson and Emery Walker served among them.

The lender list reads like a roll of Edwardian wealth. His Majesty the King lent works. So did livery companies, the Bank of England, and great collectors. A transcriber's note flags the catalogue's small puzzles. One plate is Canaletto in the index, Samuel Scott in the text. Such slips make the volume human as well as useful. It records how London pictured itself across three centuries.
69002-the-village-labourer-1760-1832-a-s:
The Village Labourer 1760-1832, a study in the government of England before the Reform Bill, was written by Hammond and Barbara Hammond. A second impression was printed in London, New York, Bombay, and Calcutta in 1912. The book is dedicated to Gilbert and Mary Murray. A long quote from Lord Acton on wages and political power heads the title page.

Chapter one maps how the English aristocracy held Parliament and local rule through justices and family settlements. Later chapters show the village before enclosure, the enclosure acts in Parliament, and the village after, with small farmers, cottagers, and squatters losing common rights. The Hammonds write with documents and anger, a landmark plea for the rural poor.
69152-a-journal-containing-an-accurate-a:
Elias Darnell wrote this journal of the Kentucky volunteers and regulars under General Winchester in the years 1812 and 1813, printed by Lippincott, Grambo, and Company of Philadelphia in 1854. The title promises hardships, sufferings, battles, defeat, and captivity. Two added tales come from men wounded on the River Raisin and taken captive by the Indians.

Darnell says he wrote the journal for his own pleasure, then showed it to friends who urged print. He was an eye and ear witness to much of it, and reports the rest from testimony he trusts. He owns that honest witnesses differ on details, as in courts of law. The men behind the tales are vouched for: Davenport as truthful, Mallary left to his neighbours' judgement.
69581-sacred-and-legendary-art-volume-1-:
Jameson wrote Sacred and Legendary Art, here volume one. Legends of the saints and martyrs make this first series. Their stories are told as the fine arts represent them. A fifth edition carries nineteen etchings in two volumes. One hundred eighty-seven woodcuts stand with those etchings in it.

Legends of the monastic orders make the second series listed. Legends of the Madonna make the third in the front pages. A history of our Lord in works of art closes the roll. That history was finished with another writer's aid, it notes. Draughts to quench the thirst for knowledge are praised in it. Wells are dug and fountains made to flow in time's desert. Such praise from reviewers stands quoted in the front pages. Jameson gives Christian art its story book for English homes.
69710-the-neutral-merchant-in-relation-t:
The Neutral Merchant defends Britain's sea measures of 1915, written by Francis Piggott, late chief justice of Hong Kong. The University of London Press issued the essays that year. They first ran in a monthly review in the spring and summer. The subject is the Order in Council of the eleventh of March 1915.

That order answered the German submarine campaign with reprisals on enemy trade. It reached wider than any contraband list, Piggott grants. Neutral merchants cried out that it struck their lawful business. The United States protested that it broke the limits of the law of nations. Piggott answers that a belligerent may press its foe by such means. The pamphlet is a lawyer's brief for sea power in total war.
7014-personal-narrative-of-travels-to-th:
Alexander von Humboldt and Aime Bonpland's personal narrative of travels to the equinoctial regions of America, 1799 to 1804, appears here in its second volume. Translated from Humboldt's French and edited by Thomasina Ross, the Bohn's Scientific Library edition runs to three volumes, this one printed in London in 1907. Tables of old measures open the book, from the tablon and legal acre to the torta and the cubic foot.

The second volume's contents turn to the lake of Tacarigua and the hot springs of Mariara, among other chapters of South American travel. Only this volume's matter is described here, as Humboldt measures, notes, and wonders across a continent. The narrative joins science, landscape, and daily travel in one great record.
70591-elizabeth-montagu-the-queen-of-the:
Emily Climenson's Elizabeth Montagu, the Queen of the Blue-Stockings prints her great-great-aunt's correspondence from 1720 to 1761, in volume one of two. John Murray published it at London in 1906. Climenson's preface tells how her cousins gave her the whole manuscript hoard in October 1899: sixty-eight cases holding a hundred to a hundred and fifty letters each. Her grandfather, the fourth Baron Rokeby, Montagu's nephew and adopted son, had published four volumes in 1810 and 1813.

He had gathered the letters back from her friends: the Duchess of Portland's daughter returned the earliest, and Elizabeth Carter's nephew returned those to the translator of Epictetus. Many letters are lost, including Walpole's and much of Reynolds's, destroyed by a caretaker at Denton Hall. The frontispiece is a miniature portrait of Montagu, born Elizabeth Robinson. The letters open the bluestocking circle from inside.
70592-elizabeth-montagu-the-queen-of-the:
Elizabeth Montagu, the Queen of the Blue-Stockings, volume two, came out in London in 1906. Emily Climenson, her great great niece, edited Montagu's letters. The letters span 1720 to 1761. A portrait of Mrs Montagu, engraved after Frances Reynolds, fronts the volume. Chapter notes list a dense world of kin, friends, and news. Deaths, marriages, lawsuits, and book talk fill the heads.

Readers meet Pitt, Garrick, David Hume, and Admiral Byng in passing. The Lisbon earthquake and fears of French invasion appear. Sarah Scott's daily life gets close attention. The famous blue stocking assemblies take their place near the end of chapter two. The volume shows a letter writer at the hub of taste, family duty, and public talk.
70889-travels-of-an-arab-merchant-in-sou:
Bayle St John shortened and rendered a French version of an Arabic travel account, published in London in 1854. Sheikh Mohammed of Tunis wrote of his journey to two kingdoms of central Africa. Doctor Perron made the French version, edited by M Jomard of the Institute. St John says that version was too long to win many English readers.

The two parts treat Darfur and Wadaï in turn. St John had written on village life in Egypt and on Paris. His abridgment keeps the merchant's own route and observations. The book gave British readers a rare inside account of regions then little known to them.
72438-principles-and-practice-of-agricul:
Principles and Practice of Agricultural Analysis is a manual for judging soils, fertilizers, and farm products. Volume two, on fertilizers, is hosted here. Harvey Wiley, chemist of the United States Department of Agriculture, wrote it. The Chemical Publishing Company issued it at Easton, Pennsylvania, in 1895, for analysts, teachers, and students of farm chemistry.

In his preface Wiley says he treats fertilizers and their materials as the first volume treated soils. He sets out the general rules of making and using them, so far as they shed light on sound methods of testing. He regrets that the volume again grew beyond all expectation. Cutting it further, he holds, would have broken its purpose and its completeness. Such manuals made farm science exact: a farmer could learn what a bag of fertilizer truly held. Wiley later won fame as a pure food crusader, and this work shows his laboratory roots.
7254-personal-narrative-of-travels-to-th:
Alexander von Humboldt and Aime Bonpland's Personal Narrative reaches its third volume in this text. Thomasina Ross translated it from the French, covering travels to the equinoctial regions of America during 1799 to 1804. Notes on measures open the volume, with longitudes reckoned from the Paris observatory, the real valued near sixpence halfpenny, and the caballeria counted in cordels and varas.

Such care with measures suits Humboldt's method: a traveller who counts, maps, and names as he goes, turning a journey into science. The narrative joins river, forest, and town in one long act of attention, and Ross's English keeps its steady, learned pace. This volume carries the great South American journey onward.
73280-the-journal-of-elizabeth-lady-holl:
The Earl of Ilchester edited the Journal of Elizabeth, Lady Holland for Longmans, Green in 1908. Two volumes span the years 1791 to 1811 in her own hand. Volume two covers 1799 to 1811, with portraits of Lord Holland and others. The front plate shows Henry Richard, third Lord Holland, in 1796.

Entries resume on July 26, 1799, with a tour into Wales and the west. Cavalry watering on Ascot Heath strikes her eye for colour against brown turf. At Warwick Castle the family hides in towers and shuns the visitors coldly. Lady Holland laughs at the escape while her husband smarts at the slight. Kenilworth, Birmingham, the Leasowes, and Hagley follow by carriage in order. A sharp, social eye records travel.
73302-principles-and-practice-of-agricul:
Harvey Wiley, chemist for the United States farm office in Washington, wrote a manual on farm testing, and volume one came out in 1894. The full set was meant to cover soils, plant food mixes, and farm goods. Wiley wrote for testers, teachers, and students of farm chemistry, and he signed his preface in January 1895.

Volume one deals with soils alone. Early pages define terms, trace how soil forms, and list the parts found in soil and in rocks. Wiley thanks men such as Hilgard and Whitney for help with soil make up and with ways to sort soil by grain and weight in the lab.
73359-the-botanist-s-repository-for-new-:
Volume five of The Botanist's Repository, by Andrews, gives coloured plates of new and rare plants. Each plant gets a botanical account in Latin and English. The system used is that of Linnaeus. Plate 289 shows Protea cordata, the heart leaved protea. Its class and order, its blossom parts, and its seed are set out in fixed form. A guide explains each part shown on the plate.

The protea came to Britain in 1792 from the Cape of Good Hope. Lee and Kennedy raised it at their nursery. It first flowered in this country in March 1803. Andrews notes where it grows wild, how to keep it in a greenhouse, and how to raise it from cuttings. Later plates follow the same strict plan.
73363-the-botanist-s-repository-for-new-:
Volume six of The Botanist's Repository, by H. Andrews, gathers coloured engravings of new and rare plants with accounts of each in Latin and English. Andrews was a botanical painter and engraver, and the work follows the plant naming system of Linnaeus.

Each plate gives the plant's class and order, its shared family marks, and the marks that set the species apart. A full account in Latin is followed by notes in English on where the plant came from and where it was grown. The volume opens with plate 361, a flesh-coloured Sanseviera brought from China in 1792 and still rare. The notes name the gardens and growers from which the drawn plants came, making the book a record of prized plants in British hands.
73371-the-botanist-s-repository-for-new-:
Botanist Repository for New and Rare Plants, volume seven, is a plate book by Andrews. Andrews served as botanical painter and engraver for the coloured plates in the set. Each plant gets a description in Latin and English after the Linnaean system. Plate four hundred and thirty three opens this volume with Agave americana.

The great American aloe is set out by class, order, and generic character in form. Blossom, chives, seed bud, shaft, capsule, and seeds are named part by part. Specific marks note the stemless growth and toothed, spiny leaves of the plant. Growers and botanists of the age gained new and rare plants in picture and word.
73396-the-botanist-s-repository-for-new-:
Botanist Repository, volume eight, gives coloured plates of new and rare plants. Henry Andrews, botanical painter and engraver, made the set after Linnaeus. Each plant gets Latin and English descriptions under the Linnaean system here. Plate four hundred ninety three shows Bignonia grandiflora, the large flowered sort.

Class fourteen, order two, heads the Bignonia entry in the old scheme. Two chives longer and seeds covered mark that class and order pair. Empalement five cleft and cup shaped, blossom bell shaped, define the genus. Scarlet bell blossoms hang in a panicle on the upright climbing stem. Leaflets oblong, lance shaped, and sawed edge the winged leaves there.
7343-the-church-and-the-empire-being-an-:
D. J. Medley's Church and the Empire, volume four of The Church Universal, outlines the history of the Christian church in its dealings with empire. The series, edited by W. H. Hutton, promises eight brief histories of the church's continuous life from the beginning to the present day, with volumes on the apostles and other ages beside this one.

Medley, professor of history in the university, writes a compact, scholarly outline rather than a devotional chronicle, tracing how church and imperial power shaped each other. The series praise quoted in the front matter calls an earlier volume far better than a mere textbook, well proportioned and scholarly. This volume keeps that standard for a wide, difficult subject.
73661-maxims-and-counsels-of-st-francis-:
Maxims and Counsels of Saint Francis de Sales gives a word for each day. Ella McMahon turned the French sayings into plain English speech. M H Gill and Son issued this second form at Dublin in eighteen eighty four. Cardinal McCloskey of New York blessed the book in eighteen eighty two.

Cardinal MacCabe of Dublin set his own seal on this new form. Francis, the gentle bishop of Geneva, speaks through the whole year. Saint Jane Chantal and Saint Vincent de Paul praised his mild way. Love for souls is his great passion, the front talk owns. Falls and discouragement meet cures as gentle as they are strong. Keep in God’s presence; shun hurry and dread, the first day bids. Cast your heart gently into the Saviour’s wounds, the second counsels. Finish the path step before you before dreaming of the last, runs three.
74280-rambles-in-germany-and-italy-in-18:
Mrs Shelley's Rambles in Germany and Italy in 1840, 1842, and 1843 was published by Edward Moxon of London in 1844, in two volumes. She gives the book to Samuel Rogers, author of Italy, in respect and thanks. Volume one is kept here.

Her preface says the volumes grew from letters written on the road, the way a traveller keeps the books of earlier travellers in the carriage. For Germany she claims no more than a fellow traveller's fresh eye. Italy changed her scope: of Florence and Rome she could add little, so she chose touches she had not seen told elsewhere. The people, above all in their politics, drew her most, and she owns a warm liking for the Italians.
74301-rambles-in-germany-and-italy-in-18:
Mrs Shelley wrote this set of travel notes in the form of letters home. Volume two came out in London in 1844. It covers trips made in 1842 and 1843. The road runs from Prague south through rich old towns.

Letters tell of Salzburg, the Brenner Pass, and Lake Garda in turn. Long stays in Venice and Florence fill much of the book. Shelley notes art, churches, palaces, and the life of the streets. She ends with notes on books, song, and stage life in Italy in that day and age. Edward Moxon printed the two volumes in London.
74978-the-botanist-s-repository-for-new-:
Andrews paints new plants in The Botanist's Repository, volume 9, a set of coloured engravings of new and rare plants only. Descriptions run in Latin and in English, after the Linnaean system. Andrews signs himself botanical painter and engraver.

Plate 553 treats Lobelia assurgens, the assurgent lobelia. Its class and order are given first, with the generic character in both tongues. The specific character follows: leaves lance shaped and serrate, toothed towards the base, running down the stem. The plate is keyed in parts: a blossom spread open, the chives spread open, and the seed bud. The plant is a native of high mountains in Jamaica, the text says, where it grows to five or six feet. No figure of it had been published before, it adds.
74999-observations-on-m-laennec-s-method:
Charles Scudamore weighs a new French method in Observations on Laennec's Method of Forming a Diagnosis, printed in London in 1826. The method tests diseases of the chest by the stethoscope and by percussion, or tapping. Some points of the French practice of medicine follow.

Scudamore gives the book to Henry Halford, president of the College of Physicians and physician to the king. His letter owns deep respect for Halford in public and private life. Scudamore held posts in London and Dublin societies and served the Prince Leopold of Saxe Coburg. Doctors of the day get a grave test of a tool that would change their art.
75389-principles-and-practice-of-agricul:
Principles and Practice of Agricultural Analysis, volume three, treats agricultural products. The whole work is a manual for the examination of soils, fertilizers, and agricultural products. It is for the use of analysts, teachers, and students of agricultural chemistry.

Harvey Wiley, chemist of the United States Department of Agriculture, wrote it. This concluding volume was published at Easton, Pennsylvania, in 1897, copyright that year. A preface says the volume was written in harmony with the plan adopted at the start of volume one. An effort has been made to place the analyst or student in possession of the methods needed. Corrections listed at the end of the book have been applied to this text. Readers get the standard American laboratory manual of farm chemistry at its third volume, covering foods, feeds, and farm products for analysis.
75863-memoirs-of-the-right-rev-daniel-co:
Memoirs of the Right Rev. Daniel Corrie is a life of the first Bishop of Madras. It was put together chiefly from his own letters and journals by his brothers. The book came out in London in 1847 from Seeley, Burnside, and Seeley of Fleet Street. A portrait of Corrie stands at its front, with the date of January 1847.

The preface states the plan and the hope of the makers. Since the great part of the memoirs comes from the papers of Corrie himself, the risk of a false picture of the man has been in great measure dodged, they hold. In the use of such matter as they held, they chose to give full detail, as the preface goes on to state. The book is a life in the man's own words, set in order by his kin.
76018-hope-leslie-or-early-times-in-the-:
Catharine Maria Sedgwick wrote Hope Leslie, or Early Times in the Massachusetts, and this book is the second of two volumes. Harper and Brothers printed it in New York in 1842. Sedgwick had written The Linwoods, Poor Rich Man, and Redwood before it. Fourteen chapters and notes make up the volume, under a verse epigraph on the fallen Indian chieftain.

Chapter One picks up Hope after a talk with Everell, in which she showed less art than zeal for her friend. Passing through the hall, she meets an Indian woman selling fine moccasins. The stranger's sweet voice and grave grace strike Hope at once. A look of inborn royalty shows through the plain blanket the woman wears.
76028-hope-leslie-or-early-times-in-the-:
Hope Leslie; or, Early Times in the Massachusetts is a novel by Catharine Maria Sedgwick, the author of The Linwoods and Redwood. Harper and Brothers of New York published this edition in 1842, in two volumes, of which this is the first. An epigraph in verse mourns the Indian chieftain whose fires have gone out and whose sun has set.

The first chapter opens with William Fletcher, under a motto from Milton's Comus about virtue assailed but never hurt. Sedgwick sets her tale among the Puritan settlers of Massachusetts Bay and the Native peoples they displaced. The contents run to thirteen chapters plus notes. As one of the earliest American historical novels by a woman, Hope Leslie gives its heroine an independence, and its Native characters a dignity, that set it apart from its contemporaries.
76155-timmy-whoof:
Timmy Whoof is a children's story of a little pet bear, by Kate Innes, published at Boston in 1917. Its full title calls it a story of a little pet bear. Chapter one brings the cub on stage. Timmy is a fat bear cub, not unlike a big kitten. His fur is yellowish and thick, his head broad, his small brown eyes bright. In time he will be a cinnamon bear, of the light brown hue of the spice. Just now he is not yet two months old.

He has no name yet, and may never have had one. His father before him was plain Mr Cinnamon Bear. The tale tells of his greed for honey in later days. Bees sting his nose till it swells to twice its size, and shut his small eyes with their stings. Innes writes for young children, in a warm and simple voice.
76316-travels-and-discoveries-in-north-a:
Henry Barth, a German scholar backed by the British state, crossed North and Central Africa from 1849 to 1855. Longman printed his journal at London in 1857, in five volumes. This first volume opens one of the great travel works of its age.

Barth gave the set to the Earl of Clarendon, the foreign chief under whose wing he rode. A plate of Auderas, drawn from Barth's own sketch, dates to November 2, 1850. Barth was a fellow of the Royal Geographical and Asiatic bodies, and his notes on lands, tongues, and trade ran deep. Few men of his time saw so much of the Sudan and the Sahara at first hand.
76317-travels-and-discoveries-in-north-a:
Henry Barth tells his travels in North and Central Africa in volume two. Longman printed the five volume journal in London in 1857. The trip ran from 1849 to 1855 under British government backing. A plate shows the meeting of the Benue and Faro rivers.

Chapter twenty two opens with the travelers parting on border districts. Tasawa town, its chief, markets, and dye pits get close notes. Richardson health fails as roads to Kano divide the party. Chapter twenty three treats Gazawa and a stay in Katsena. Markets, wells, horsemen, and camp scenes fill the daily journal with life.
76318-travels-and-discoveries-in-north-a:
Travels and Discoveries in North and Central Africa, volume three, is the journal of Henry Barth expedition of 1849 to 1855. Longman and partners published the volume in London in 1857. The expedition was undertaken under the auspices of the British government, as the title page states. A frontispiece shows a Musgu chief, drawn from a sketch by Barth himself.

Contents of this volume open with chapter thirty eight, the rainy season in Kukawa. Its heads treat supplies, herbage, tropical rains, and the winged ant in that season. Various kinds of cultivation and a statement by Vogel, a fellow traveller, follow in the chapter. An intended excursion to Kanem is named among its plans for the party. Barth volumes remain a chief source for the states and peoples of the Sudan belt in the 1850s, written by a scholar who travelled with notebooks, vocabularies, and a map maker patience.
76319-travels-and-discoveries-in-north-a:
Travels and Discoveries in North and Central Africa, volume 4 of 5, is Henry Barth's journal of his 1849 to 1855 expedition. Longman and partners published it in London in 1858. The British government sponsored the journey. A view of Timbuktu from the traveler's terrace fronts the volume.

Barth writes in the shadow of his companion's death. Mr Overweg is gone, and Barth's pecuniary circumstances press him. Tawárek raiders threaten the northwestern provinces of Bornu. He takes leave of the Sheikh and crosses the Komadugu country. Manga warriors, immense anthills, and a daring theft mark the road. The mountainous territory of Muniyo fills the next chapter. Its natron lakes, palmgroves, and slave-hunting governor receive close notice. Zinder's ground plan and importance follow. Chapter fifty-five returns to Katsena for a second stay. Highway robbers, Barth remarks, are less to be feared than rapacious governors.
76320-travels-and-discoveries-in-north-a:
Travels and Discoveries in North and Central Africa is the record of an expedition of eighteen forty nine to eighteen fifty five. Henry Barth, its leader, wrote the journal. The hosted text is volume five, issued at London in eighteen fifty eight. A picture of Gao, drawn from Barth's sketch, stands at its front. The work ran to five volumes in all.

Contents of this volume open at chapter seventy, with the start of a new year. Heads treat the rising of the Niger and the trade of Timbuktu. Talk of religious dispute, a loan, and Moroccan merchants' plots all appear. Barth notes the town's manufactures as limited, with leather work chief among them. Rainy days in January and a put off departure fill out the chapter's list.
77517-the-life-and-times-of-selina-count:
The Life and Times of Selina, Countess of Huntingdon, volume one, was written by a member of the houses of Shirley and Hastings and printed in London in 1844. The book had reached its sixth thousand. A portrait of the countess stands at the front.

The preface says Lady Huntingdon wished her memory to rest for some years after her death. Her kin held back her letters till now, when a cadet of her family had spent long years on her papers. He alone could reach those records with ease. The memoir praises her talents, her ample means, and a head and heart set on the glory of God and peace on earth. Church readers get the life of a great Methodist patron in full.
79194-the-proof:
W C Tuttle's The Proof is billed as a moving little story of a wanderer who came home. Wanderin' Jones sits in a saloon on Christmas Eve, a tall, lean-jawed man of forty who looks sixty or seventy, in a faded mackinaw, sheepskin chaps, and a smoke-stained old Stetson. He was a good cow hand who never stayed long in one place and never told his story.

The bartender, stoking the stove, tells him of Archie Bell, who has just left drunk. Archie thinks his brother Buck has cut him out with a girl in town, and his trigger finger itches. Wanderin' listens with narrowed eyes, his jaws bulging, as the church bell sounds far away.
79200-how-to-read-and-correct-proof:
Lloyd Smith's How to Read and Correct Proof appeared in 1929 as Little Blue Book number 1431, edited by Haldeman-Julius and printed at Girard, Kansas. The booklet starts with a plain question: what is a proof? A proof, it says, is a print of type that shows how the matter will look when done.

Proof is pulled so it can be read for slips, gaps, and faults of type or style, and the reader marks each fault so the printer can follow fast. Smith splits the trade in two: the steady proofreader of a publishing house, and the author who gets proof later. Proofreader's marks get their own chapter, with points to remember at the end.
79358-the-botanist-s-repository-for-new-:
Volume ten of The Botanists Repository holds hue plates of new and rare plants. Andrews, a plant painter and plate man, made the work in Latin and English. Each plate gives the class and rank of the plant in the Linnaeus scheme. Plate six hundred nine shows the Bergamot lemon with its parts laid out. Cup, five leaves, and near twenty threads make its kind marks by rule.

The plant came to England in seventeen eighty five from Nice by a Mrs Evelyn hand. Its fruit yields the prized scent oil made in Italy in that age. The plate notes break each bloom part down for the reader eye. Andrews doubts the lump of all citrus kinds under one or two names. More kinds stand in the works of late plant men, he points out.
79531-inscriptions-from-dante-s-divina-c:
Ida Riedisser wrote this guide to the Dante inscriptions in the streets of Florence, printed in 1913 by Alfieri and Lacroix of Milan and Seeber of Florence. The Commune of Florence had set verses from the Divina Commedia on the places Dante names in the poem. Houses of the families he mentions bear them too.

Riedisser grants that many verses mean little to a reader who does not know every line of the poem. Her small book explains them, strung not by street but by time, as a short history of Florence up to Dante's age. The aim is to show what remains of the city Dante knew, and to call his life there back to mind in the Florence of today.
852-democracy-and-education-an-introduct:
John Dewey wrote this landmark work on the philosophy of education, linking school to democracy itself. He argues that education is not mere preparation for life, but life itself, and that schools should train citizens to think, to share, and to grow. Growth, experience, and social life are his key terms.

Dewey writes for teachers and thinkers, not just scholars, and his prose is earnest and systematic. He rejects rote learning and fixed aims, urging schools that mirror a free society. The book shaped American education for a century, and it remains essential reading for anyone who asks what schools are for.
8903-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-0:
The Atlantic Monthly, volume two, number eight, June 1858, shows the young magazine in full stride, its contents a roll call of American letters. American Tract Society, Ann Potter's Lesson, Asirvadam the Brahmin, and the Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table. His landlady and his breakfast to the public, sit beside birds of garden, orchard, pasture, and forest, bulls and bears, and a bundle of Irish pennants. Catacombs of Rome, Chesuncook, Colin Clout and the Faery Queen, and Crawford and sculpture follow.

Daphnaides, Denslow Palace, a dot and line alphabet, eloquence, an evening with telegraph wires, farming life in New England, the German legend of Doctor Faustus. The gaucho continue the feast. The issue captures the Atlantic's ambition: literature, art, politics, science, and travel in one monthly volume. Readers browsing it meet Thoreau, Holmes, and their contemporaries at work, and see American magazine culture taking confident shape.
909-the-adventures-of-col-daniel-boon-co:
John Filson wrote this early narrative of Colonel Daniel Boone and the wars of Kentucky, from the discovery and settlement of that land. Boone, the hunter and pathfinder, leads families through the wilderness, fights Native peoples and British allies, and opens the road to the West.

Filson writes with the plain vigour of a frontier chronicler, and his Boone became the model frontiersman of American legend. The narrative, first printed in 1784, mixes fact with frontier tale, and it shaped how America imagined its own westward march. The book is a founding text of the Boone myth.
9196-the-clockmaker-or-the-sayings-and-d:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton created Sam Slick, the clockmaker of Slickville, in this book revived in an 1871 edition. Sam's name passed into popular use for a conventional Yankee, sharp and green at once, in curious proportions. The book had long been out of print, yet its shrewd observation, anecdotes, and racy adventure kept it alive.

No other work preserves so large a store of Yankee idiom, quaint speech, and keen mother wit. Sam Slick fixed the prevailing idea of the Yankee character for a generation. The book remains a classic of American humor, and a treasury of dialect.
9472-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-3:
The May 1860 issue of the Atlantic Monthly opens with an essay called Instinct, which starts from Falstaff's quip that instinct is a great matter. From that jest, the essay weighs what instinct means in beasts and in men. The same number prints a poem called Circumstance, a life of Mary Somerville, and a piece on General Miranda's expedition. A sketch of Nathaniel Hawthorne also appears.

Book reviews close the issue, rounding out a number rich in science, life writing, and history. The mix shows the magazine's range in 1860: mind, nature, fame, and revolt in one sitting. A reader gets a fine sample of mid-century American letters, where a Shakespeare joke could open a grave essay on the mind.
9486-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-3:
The June 1860 issue of the Atlantic Monthly leads with an essay on the future of American railways. It asks whether any rail line had yet paid its builders, or merely paid its users while wearing itself out. The same number prints chess notes on the Sicilian game, verse, and a piece called The Representative Art. Book reviews close the issue, as in past months.

The railway essay doubts rosy claims, noting that repair and renewal can eat gains that look large on paper. The chess and art pieces show the magazine's range, from pastime to high craft. A reader gets a sharp view of 1860 America weighing its great new network, its books, and its arts in a single sitting.
9493-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-5:
The July 1862 issue of the Atlantic Monthly came out in the second year of the Civil War. Its lead piece, Some Soldier-Poetry, asks why war has so seldom been sung well, from Homer down to the present day. The number mixes essays, verse, and fiction, as the magazine had done since 1857. Book reviews close the issue, giving readers fresh titles to chase.

War verse, the essay finds, often praises heroes yet misses the ideas that drive the fight. Political songs fare better, since great crises breed sharp satire and praise alike. A reader today gains a wartime view of art itself: what songs soldiers sang, and what critics hoped verse could do while guns fired.
9560-the-vaudois-teacher-and-other-poems:
John Greenleaf Whittier's Narrative and Legendary Poems opens, in this first part, with tales in verse of faith and brave deeds. The Vaudois Teacher leads, followed by The Female Martyr, The Funeral Tree of the Sokokis, and Cassandra Southwick. Whittier, a Quaker poet, drew on history and legend for moral tales that stirred his age. This edition was revised with his own notes on each poem's source.

Other poems in the part include The Bridal of Pennacook, Barclay of Ury, and Skipper Ireson's Ride, each a compact tale of conscience or fate. Whittier's verse stays plain and earnest, aimed at heart and duty. A reader gets a strong first taste of Whittier the storyteller, where verse carries history's hard lessons.
9561-the-bridal-of-pennacook-part-2-from:
Part two of Whittier's Narrative and Legendary Poems holds The Bridal of Pennacook, a tale in verse of a 1662 Indian wedding. Winnepurkit, sachem of Saugus, wed a daughter of Passaconaway, the great Pennacook chief, at Pennacook, now Concord, New Hampshire. Feasts, escorts, and tribal custom frame the marriage. Eight sections carry the tale from the Merrimac to the departure.

When the bride longs to visit her father's house, custom and pride tangle the return, and a messenger bears hard words. Whittier tells the tale with respect for native ways and a moral eye. A reader gets a vivid colonial legend in verse, and a window on native diplomacy in early New England.
9565-pennsylvania-pilgrim-and-other-poem:
Part six of Whittier's Narrative and Legendary Poems leads with The Pennsylvania Pilgrim, a tale of German settlers in America. Whittier traces German emigration to William Penn's 1677 visit to Pietist circles on the Continent. The Frankfort Land Company bought Penn's land near Philadelphia, and mystic settlers followed. The poem honors their quiet faith and toil.

Other poems in the part include King Volmer and Elsie, The Three Bells, John Underhill, and The Witch of Wenham. King Solomon and the Ants and Rabbi Ishmael add fable and legend. A reader gets Whittier's gift for turning history into verse, with pioneers, witches, and kings in one gathering.
9566-bay-of-seven-islands-and-other-poem:
Part seven of Whittier's Narrative and Legendary Poems opens with The Bay of Seven Islands, a poem of coast and memory. Whittier dedicated the book that held it to Edwin Percy Whipple, the critic who first urged his claim as a poet when abolitionists faced scorn. The part also prints The Wishing Bridge, How the Women Went from Dover, and St. Gregory's Guest. Birchbrook Mill, The Two Elizabeths, and The Homestead follow.

Later poems include Requital, How the Robin Came, and Banished from Massachusetts, each a short tale of faith, exile, or home. Whittier writes with plain grace and moral fire. A reader gets a rich late slice of his narrative verse, where New England history meets lyric feeling.
9572-religious-poems-part-1-part-5-from-:
Part five of volume two of Whittier's works holds his religious poems, verse of faith, prayer, and Bible scenes. The Star of Bethlehem opens, set where Shiraz sleeps in flowers and a poet's thoughts sow deeper blooms. The Crucifixion, Palestine, and hymns from Lamartine follow, with The Angel of Patience and Andrew Rykman's Prayer. Whittier, a Quaker, writes of God in plain, heartfelt lines.

Later poems ask questions of life, trust, and the soul's wish, and close with hope rather than fear. The verse favors simple speech over church pomp, true to Quaker ways. A reader gets a devout, gentle set of poems, fit for quiet reading and for grasping Whittier's faith at its source.
9573-religious-poems-part-2-part-6-from-:
Part six of volume two of Whittier's works continues his religious poems with The Answer, a plea to spare the speaker from reproof and let sunshine weave life's poor gray threads. The Eternal Goodness, Our Master, The Meeting, and The Clear Vision follow, with Divine Compassion and The Prayer-Seeker. The Prayer of Agassiz, A Christmas Carmen, and The Two Angels add prayer and wonder.

Later poems in the part include The Minister's Daughter, Hymn of the Dunkers, and Oriental Maxims, each plain and devout. Whittier's Quaker faith favors inward light over outward show. A reader gets a further set of his prayers in verse, gentle, hopeful, and fit for quiet hours.
9575-anti-slavery-poems-1-part-1-from-vo:
Part one of volume three of Whittier's works opens his anti-slavery poems with a salute to William Lloyd Garrison. Toussaint L'Ouverture, The Slave-Ships, and The Hunters of Men follow, with The Yankee Girl and Stanzas for the Times. Clerical Oppressors and The Pastoral Letter rebuke churches that blessed bondage. A Virginia slave mother's farewell adds grief to anger.

Later poems in the opening group include Pennsylvania Hall, The World's Convention, and Massachusetts to Virginia, with The Christian Slave beside. Whittier writes as a Quaker crusader, blunt and urgent. A reader gets the first blast of his abolitionist verse, where poetry served as a weapon for freedom.
9576-anti-slavery-poems-2-part-2-from-vo:
Part two of Whittier's anti-slavery poems takes up the fight over Texas and the spread of slave states. The opening poems voice New England's fierce alarm at annexation, which threatened six new slave states. Pieces include Voice of New England, To Faneuil Hall, and To Massachusetts, plus The Branded Hand and The Slaves of Martinique. Whittier, a Quaker abolitionist, wrote these as calls to act.

Later poems in the part name southern statesmen, lost statesmen, and the curse of charter-breakers, with a paean and a crisis cry. The verse is blunt, urgent, and meant to rouse citizens to stand by home and altar. A reader gets abolitionist poetry at white heat, and a record of how verse served a moral war.
9577-anti-slavery-poems-3-part-3-from-vo:
Part three of Whittier's anti-slavery poems turns to Kansas, Derne, and the Fugitive Slave era. Derne opens, recalling General Eaton's 1805 storming of the Moorish city with nine Americans and a motley host. A Sabbath Scene, Moloch in State Street, and Official Piety follow, with The Rendition and Arisen at Last. The Kansas Emigrants and a missionary's letter from Kansas press the slavery fight westward.

Later poems include Burial of Barber, To Pennsylvania, and a song for the Fremont clubs, with The Pass of the Sierra beside. Whittier's verse stays fierce and topical, naming deeds and men. A reader gets abolitionist poetry in the heat of the 1850s, when Kansas bled and the nation chose sides.
9612-the-botanic-garden-a-poem-in-two-pa:
Part one of Erasmus Darwin's Botanic Garden holds The Economy of Vegetation, a poem on plant life and the elements. Darwin's design enlists fancy in the service of science, leading readers from loose poetic images to strict philosophic thought. The poem teaches plant physiology and the work of air, water, earth, and fire in growth. Notes add the science behind the verse, with praise for Linnaeus.

Flora, attired by the elements, fronts the book, a sign of its blend of myth and botany. Darwin urges readers to study plants through verse, as a doorway to a delightful science. A reader gets a landmark of science poetry, where a poem teaches botany and a garden becomes a cosmos.
9935-woman-s-institute-library-of-cooker:
Volume one of the Woman's Institute cookery course lays the groundwork for all the volumes that follow. It opens with the problem of food: how to select it, what food substances are, what food is worth, and how the body digests and absorbs it.

Later sections teach cereals, from Indian corn to Italian pastes, and bread in all its forms, including hot breads, with the importance of bread as food explained. Written for correspondence students, the book mixes science with practice. Beginners get the principles that make later recipes make sense.
9965-an-enemy-to-the-king-from-the-recen:
Robert Neilson Stephens's 1897 romance claims to retell the recently discovered memoirs of the Sieur de la Tournoire, an enemy to the king in old France. It opens with two encounters by night, love-making at short acquaintance, and a strange request from Mademoiselle d'Arency.

La Tournoire is enlightened in the dark, escapes from Paris, flees southward, annoys Monsieur de la Chatre, and keeps his word at the Château of Maury. Stephens writes swashbuckling historical romance in the manner of Dumas. Readers get swordplay, honor, and a hero who stays loyal to his promise.
a-description-of-the-bar-and-frame-hive-: William Augustus Munn describes the bar and frame hive for beekeepers. The book adds an abstract of Wildman's complete guide to managing bees through the year. Beekeepers learn hive construction and seasonal care in plain terms. Munn's manual serves both beginners and experienced keepers of bees. New keepers will learn the craft step by step from this plain guide.
a-gunner-aboard-the-yankee-from-the-diar: Russell Doubleday, number five of the after port gun, tells his yarn as a gunner aboard the Yankee. Edited by H. H. Lewis, the diary follows the Yankee into commission, under way, and cruising for prizes. Orders south and a wild goose chase lead to the fights of the naval reserves in the Spanish American War. Doubleday writes a sailor's firsthand account of war at sea.
a-journey-to-katmandu-the-capital-of-nap: Laurence Oliphant journeys to Katmandu, capital of Nepal, with the camp of Jung Bahadoor. The journey begins with Jung Bahadoor's arrival in Ceylon and voyage to Calcutta. Rifle practice aboard the Atalanta, the Grand Trunk Road, and an explosion at Benares mark the road. Oliphant describes a romantic country and its independent court.
a-new-system-or-an-analysis-of-antient-m: Jacob Bryant attempts to strip ancient tradition of fable in this first volume of his six-volume analysis of ancient mythology, seeking to reduce its stories to their original purity. The volume opens with an account of his life and writings and a vindication of the Apamean medal. Observations on ancient history and forty-one engraved plates stand alongside them. Its argument treats myth as corrupted history, to be cleaned of fable until the truth underneath stands clear.

Jacob Bryant continues his analysis of ancient mythology in this second volume, carrying forward the attempt to divest tradition of fable and recover its original purity. The volume opens with the phoenix and the Phoenicians, a subject long clouded by uncertainty about the meaning and extent of those terms. It works through related legends and peoples in the same comparative manner, testing names and stories against one another for a shared historical root.
a-ramble-of-six-thousand-miles-through-t: Simon Ansley Ferrall recounts a six-thousand-mile ramble through the United States in letters first written for the amusement of his immediate acquaintances. Published in London in 1832, the sketches avoid repeating seaboard statistics already set before the public, preferring remarks on subjects other travellers passed over. A facsimile from the Cherokee Phoenix of July 1830 opens a young traveller's view of a republic still forming.
a-supplement-to-a-compilation-of-the-mes: William McKinley's time in office is rounded out in this add-on to the set of White House notes and papers, issued in 1904. The opening note says that late changes left McKinley's notes short, and the add-on pulls in those left out of volume ten plus his next in line Roosevelt's to date. Notes, calls, and White House orders set forth home affairs and show the steadiness of American rule and its bodies.
a-williams-anthology-a-collection-of-the: Edwin Partridge Lehman, with Julian Park, compiles a Williams anthology of verse and prose of Williams College from 1798 to 1910. The editors of the Literary Monthly open with The Mountains by Washington Gladden of the class of 1859. Its chorus greets mountains whose echoes mingle with anthems of winds and fountains. Winter snows, summer clouds, autumn's scarlet mantle, and spring's garniture dress the monarchs of the mountain land in a college songbook.
an-enemy-to-the-king-from-the-recently-d: Robert Neilson Stephens draws on the recently discovered memoirs of the Sieur de la Tournoire in An Enemy to the King. The romance opens with two encounters by night, love-making at short acquaintance, and a strange request from Mlle. d'Arency. Set in France, it mixes swordplay, intrigue, and romance in the Dumas manner.
anti-slavery-poems-1-part-1-from-volume-: John Greenleaf Whittier gathers anti-slavery poems in part one of volume three of his works, opening with songs of labour and reform and a poem to William Lloyd Garrison. The verses denounce slavery with Quaker fervour and plain speech. This part shows Whittier as the poet-voice of abolition.
anti-slavery-poems-2-part-2-from-volume-: John Greenleaf Whittier continues his anti-slavery poems in part two of volume three, with pieces on Texas and the voice of New England among songs of labour and reform. The poems protest annexation and slavery's spread, urging the North to stand firm. Whittier's verse here is public poetry with a cause.
anti-slavery-poems-3-part-3-from-volume-: John Greenleaf Whittier offers part three of his anti-slavery poems from volume three, including Derne and a Sabbath scene among songs of labour and reform. The poems mix protest with Sabbath quiet, history with present duty. This closing part rounds out Whittier's poetic campaign against slavery. Faith and protest join hands in these last poems.
bay-of-seven-islands-and-other-poems-par:
John Greenleaf Whittier's narrative and legendary poems continue in this seventh part of his works' first volume, headed by The Bay of Seven Islands. Whittier's own note recalls that the poem's original volume was dedicated to Edwin Percy Whipple, the critic who first urged his public recognition when championing a proscribed abolitionist took courage. The title poem tells a Maine coast legend of love and loss.

Companion pieces include The Wishing Bridge, How the Women Went from Dover, and St Gregory's Guest. Birchbrook Mill gives the sample mood: birches whisper, the song-sparrow sings, yet schoolgirl and farmer hurry past at nightfall, dreading the grind of shadowy stone on stone where no wheel now turns. Banished from Massachusetts and How the Robin Came round out a set steeped in New England folklore and Quaker memory.
britannica-1911-abercorn-james-hamilton-:
James Hamilton, first Earl of Abercorn, receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abercorn, eldest son of Claud Hamilton, Lord Paisley, was born about 1575. Sheriff of Linlithgow in 1600, he took large land grants in Scotland and Ireland.

Baron Abercorn in 1603, then earl in 1606 with Mount Castle and Kilpatrick titles, he was paid for service in the matter of the union, the entry states. Marion Boyd, a Lord Boyd's daughter, bore him five sons. The eldest, Lord Strabane, followed him in 1618. The Abercorn title heads the Hamilton family still, rising to marquessate in 1790 and dukedom in 1868. Its second duke, born 1838, chairs the British South Africa Company in the entry's present.
britannica-1911-aberdeen-george-hamilton:
George Hamilton Gordon, fourth Earl of Aberdeen, receives a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Aberdeen, born at Edinburgh in 1784 and orphaned young, named Pitt and Dundas his guardians at fourteen. Greek travel and a Troy review earned him Byron's gibe, the travell'd thane, Athenian Aberdeen.

Vienna in 1813 set his course: the Töplitz treaty, Leipzig, Châtillon, and Paris followed. Foreign secretary under Wellington in 1828, he won credit on Turkey, Greece, and Portugal. Peel gave him the seals again in 1841, and Queen Victoria's trust made those five years his most fruitful, the entry holds. Church patronage fights in Scotland mark the home record. His first wife's death in 1812 and a second Abercorn marriage thread the private story.
britannica-1911-agreda-maria-fernandez-c:
Maria Fernandez Coronel (1602-1665) was abbess of Agreda in Spain. In religion she was Sor Maria de Jesus. She was born at Agreda in April 1602. Her whole family shared Spain's ecstatic piety. At fifteen the family entered religion together. Her father and brothers joined the Franciscans at Nalda. Maria, her mother, and her sister founded a nunnery. Their own family house became that nunnery. At twenty-five she was made abbess, against her wish.

Visions and a king fill her fame. Franciscans claimed she flew miraculously to Mexico. Five hundred such journeys were alleged in one year. Her Mystic City of God praised the Virgin through visions. The Inquisition noticed her Quietist leanings without severity. Philip IV corresponded with her until her death. She wrote answers on his own folded sheets.
britannica-1911-agriculture-board-of:
Agriculture, Board of, tells how Britain set up its Board of Agriculture and Fisheries. The root of the board lies in the cattle plague of 1865. A small office for sick beasts was formed that year. It took a new name in 1883. The Board itself was set up by act in 1889. Its head does the work of a farm minister. The post is a party one and may sit in the cabinet. A staff of clerks and aides serves the board.

Wide tasks came to the board at its birth. Laws on sick farm beasts came from the privy council. Land work came with them in the same move. One branch gathers facts on farms and woods. Local men send in notes on crops and stock. The piece goes on to the farm office in the United States. It ends with the like boards of other lands.
britannica-1911-aix-la-chapelle-congress:
Three congresses were held at Aix la Chapelle, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry takes them in order. The congresses fell in the years 1668, 1748, and 1818. The first of them closed the War of Devolution. Its treaty was signed on the second of May 1668.

That treaty grew out of a pact made at St Germain a few weeks before. France there dealt with the envoys of the Triple Alliance powers. The peace left France all its gains in Flanders from the campaign of 1667. Those gains came with their appurtenances, dependencies, and annexes, in the words of the treaty. That vague clause later caused fresh trouble. After the peace of Nijmwegen, Louis the Fourteenth used it to seize towns claimed as dependents of his new lands.
britannica-1911-akaba-gulf-of:
Akaba, the Gulf of, is the eastern of the two arms into which the Red Sea splits near its northern end, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes it. The ancients called it the Sinus Aelaniticus. It cuts into Arabia Petraea running north-north-east for one hundred miles, with a breadth of twelve to seventeen miles. Islands narrow its entrance, and coral reefs crowd its waters.

Sudden squalls sweep down from the mountains beside it, many of which rise sheer to two thousand feet, making its navigation dangerous. The gulf is the southward run of the same great depression as the Jordan valley. Raised beaches on its coast show that the sea bed has lifted by a good amount. Its one well-sheltered harbour is Dahab on the western shore.
britannica-1911-albany-dukes-of:
Albany, Dukes of, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article tracing a Scottish title. The name Albany once covered the parts of Scotland north of the firths of Clyde and Forth. The title duke of Albany was first given in 1398 by King Robert the Third. He gave it to his brother Robert Stewart, earl of Fife, but it died out in 1425.

The dukedom was made again about 1458 for Alexander Stewart, the entry says. His son left no lawful heir, so that line ended too. Next the title went in 1565 to Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, from Mary, queen of Scots. From him it passed to his son James, king of Scotland and England. Later kings gave it anew to their sons, and in time to a brother of George the First.
britannica-1911-all-saints-festival-of:
All Saints is a feast of the Catholic Church kept on the first of November. It honours all the saints, known and unknown. It was formerly called All Hallows, or Hallowmas. In the Roman Catholic Church it ranks as a festival of the first class. It has a vigil and an octave, a full week of observance.

Shared commemorations of martyrs began in the fourth century. An early general celebration met at Antioch on the Sunday after Pentecost. The entry weighs two Roman threads. In 609 or 610, Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon to the Virgin and all martyrs. Gregory III later founded an oratory in St Peter's for relics of apostles, saints, and martyrs. Louis the Pious made the feast binding across the Frankish empire in 835. That decree fixed the November date.
britannica-1911-anglesey-arthur-annesley:
Arthur Annesley, first earl of Anglesey (1614–1686), was a British statesman born at Dublin on 10 July 1614, son of the first Viscount Valentia. Educated at Magdalen College, Oxford, and admitted to Lincoln's Inn in 1634, he made the grand tour before returning to Ireland. Employed by parliament on a mission to the duke of Ormonde, he concluded a treaty with him in June 1647 that saved Ireland from complete subjection to the rebels.

Annesley sat for Radnorshire in the Commons, supported the parliamentary against the army party, and suffered exclusion in 1648. Disgusted by the anarchy of the commonwealth's last months, he turned royalist and worked actively for the Restoration, then used his influence to moderate the measures that followed it. The entry follows his council presidency in 1660, his peerage, and his later writings, closing with a wide net of state papers, trials, and tracts as sources.
britannica-1911-anglesey-henry-william-p:
Henry William Paget, first marquess of Anglesey (1768–1854), was a British field-marshal born on 17 May 1768, eldest son of the first earl of Uxbridge. Educated at Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, he entered parliament in 1790 as member for Carnarvon. At the outbreak of the French Revolutionary wars he raised a regiment of Staffordshire volunteers on his father's estate, gaining temporary rank as lieutenant-colonel.

That corps became the 80th Foot and fought under Paget in the Flanders campaign of 1794, where he held a brigade command despite his youth. There he also gained his first experience of cavalry, the arm with which he stayed associated through transfers to the light dragoons and a colonelcy in 1796. The long entry pursues his cavalry career through the Peninsular and Waterloo era. Its tail even follows a namesake officer's Crimean service and published journals.
britannica-1911-angouleme-charles-de-val:
Malta was the planned path for Charles de Valois, duke of Angoulême (1573–1650). Meant for that order, he rose at sixteen to grand prior of France, among its highest ranks. Great estates then came to him from Catherine de' Medici; from one of them came his title, count of Auvergne.

Born at the castle of Fayet in Dauphiné on 28 April 1573, Charles was the natural son of Charles IX of France and Marie Touchet. His father died the next year, first charging his successor, Henry III, with the boy's care, and Henry kept that charge faithfully. Freed from his vows in 1591, Charles married a daughter of Marshal d'Amville and served Henry IV as colonel of horse. Angered by the king's tie to his half-sister, the marchioness of Verneuil, he joined the 1601 conspiracy led by Savoy, Biron, and Bouillon. His later career and writings follow.
britannica-1911-anhalt-dessau-leopold-i-:
Leopold I, prince of Anhalt-Dessau (1676–1747), was a Prussian field marshal. Soldiers called him the Old Dessauer. He was born at Dessau in July 1676. His father was John George II of Anhalt-Dessau. Leopold was the only surviving son. Arms absorbed him from earliest youth. He trained himself in body and mind. In 1693 he became a regimental colonel. His father's death that year made him prince.

His first campaign came in the Netherlands in 1695. He served at the siege of Namur. His mother managed the principality meanwhile. In 1698 he married Anna Luise Föse. She was an apothecary's daughter from Dessau. His mother opposed the match for years. The emperor later raised the wife to princess. Their marriage proved long and happy. She softened his stern nature throughout. The entry follows his dual career as sovereign and Prussian officer.
britannica-1911-antrim-randal-macdonnell:
Randal MacDonnell, first marquess of Antrim, lived from sixteen nine to sixteen eighty-three. He was the son of the first earl of that name and was raised in the old faith. He roamed abroad, then came to court and wed the rich widow of a great duke. He lived in great pomp on her wealth for years.

War in Scotland drew him to plot a host in Ireland to strike a foe and win back old lands. That plan failed past scorn from the kings man. He was seized twice by the foes of the king, fled twice, and rose to a new high rank.
britannica-1911-appointment-power-of:
Power of appointment is a term of English property law. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as a right kept back in a settlement. A donor places goods in trust to such uses as another shall name. That second person, the donee, may name anyone to take the goods. He may even name himself. Until he acts, a third person's share stands in place.

Such powers come in two kinds, general and limited. A general power can be used for any person at all. That breadth makes it near the same as ownership in law. Goods under a general power can be seized for the donee's debts. They are also taxed at his death, used or not. A limited power can serve only named persons or classes. Marriage settlements often grant one to be used among the children.
britannica-1911-arches-court-of:
Court of Arches is an English ecclesiastical appeal court. It serves the archbishop of Canterbury. Canterbury province's lower courts appeal to it. Consistory and commissary courts fall under it. Its name comes from its ancient seat. That seat was St Mary-le-Bow church in London. Bow translates the Latin Arcubus, meaning arches. Its steeple had stone pillars like a bow.

That parish was exempt from London's bishop. Thirteen such parishes existed locally. That exemption likely explains its selection. The judge's proper title is official principal. Custom styles him dean of the Arches instead. That title once belonged to a subordinate official. Peculiar jurisdictions numbered nearly 300 in England once. Popes introduced them to curtail bishops. Sittings are now rare, the entry notes. Lambeth Palace library hosts them when needed.
britannica-1911-arran-earls-of:
Arran, Earls of, is a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It traces a now extinct Scottish title held by famed men of the past. With two brief breaks, all the holders came from one great house. The first earl of the new line was born near fourteen seventy five.

The entry tells how that earl rose as a knight, a sheriff, and a royal councillor. He helped seal a royal marriage pact with England and led hosts to the isles. He also sailed in aid of a Danish king with a large force. A trip as envoy to France ended with his arrest in England. Peace talks and court posts fill the rest of his busy tale.
britannica-1911-arta-gulf-of:
The Gulf of Arta is an inlet of the Ionian Sea, and a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its shores. The gulf runs twenty five miles long and ten miles broad. Most of its northern shores belonged to Turkey at that time. The southern and eastern shores belonged to Greece. Its chief feeder streams flow in from the north.

The gulf abounds with mullets, soles, and eels, the entry notes. Ruins of ancient cities ring its shores in number. Actium stands at the entrance, where the famed battle was fought in 31 before Christ. Nicopolis, Argos, Limnaea, and Olpae are named among the ruins. Flourishing towns stand there too, such as Preveza and Arta. The river Arta is the chief river of Epirus. It was said to have been fit for boats in ancient times.
britannica-1911-arundel-earldom-of:
Earldom of Arundel is called the premier earldom of England in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Folk think it goes with the holding of Arundel Castle, but the text calls that view wrong. Norman earls were earls of counties, and this title was in truth that of Sussex. Its root was a grant by Henry the First to his second wife, in dower, of the honour of Arundel.

On the death of the king, his widow wed William de Albini, who held the castle by that marriage. He is styled earl of Sussex, of Chichester, or of Arundel from about 1141. Henry the Second gave him the castle and honour in fee, with a share of the court fees of Sussex. His male line died out in 1243 with Hugh de Albini, who left four sisters as joint heirs.
britannica-1911-aspern-essling-battle-of:
Aspern-Essling, a battle of May 1809 between the French under Napoleon and the Austrians under Archduke Charles, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Napoleon held Vienna, but the Danube bridges had been broken. The archduke's army stood on the left bank near Korneuburg. The first French task was to cross the river. They chose Lobau, an island among the channels, as their crossing point.

On the night of May 19 to 20, the French bridged the channels to Lobau and occupied the island. The last arm of the river was then bridged, and Masséna's corps crossed and drove off the Austrian outposts. By dawn on May 21, some 40,000 men stood on the Marchfeld plain.
