The archduke did not contest the crossing. His plan was to let a large force come over before striking.
britannica-1911-assumption-feast-of:
The Feast of the Assumption marks the taking up of the Blessed Virgin Mary into heaven. The Christian Church keeps the feast on 15 August. It marks the belief that the mother of Christ rose to heaven in a wondrous way. That belief rests on old tales that the Church has not held as true books of faith. Two such tales are named, one ascribed to the Apostle John and one to Melito of Sardis. The second was in fact written about A.D. 400.

Pope Gelasius I put both tales on his list of books to be barred in the years 492 to 496. Yet a writer of the 5th century took them as true, and so did Gregory of Tours. Gregory, in his work on the glory of the martyrs, gives this tale of the wonder.
britannica-1911-asylum-right-of:
Asylum, the right of, is a term of international law in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the right of a state to shelter fugitives from another country. That right rests on a simple ground in the article. Every independent state is sole master within its own boundaries.

Extradition treaties cut into the exercise of this right. States bind themselves there to give up refugees from justice. Yet their terms show how dearly nations hold the right itself. Weak or strong, each state guards it as part of its free action at home. The piece also treats asylum for fighting forces in war. A neutral state's right to shelter belligerent troops is now fixed by treaty. Articles of the Hague Convention of 1899 govern that case in detail. The short article is signed by the jurist Thomas Barclay.
britannica-1911-atacama-desert-of:
The desert of Atacama is a dry, bare, and salty region of western South America. It covers most of the Chilean provinces of Atacama and Antofagasta. It also takes in the Argentine land of Los Andes and the south-west corner of the Bolivian department of Potosí. Its high parts are known as the Puna de Atacama. That puna runs south from the great puna region of Peru and Bolivia.

The land is broken and hilly, volcanic in places and salty in others. It stands from 7,000 to 13,500 feet high as a rule. A rough line of peaks and dead volcanoes marks its high ridges. On the east side, some rain falls, and streams from the snowy peaks give a slight show of green. For the most part, though, the plains are dry and cold in winter. Great salt lagoons and dry salt basins also break the ground.
britannica-1911-augsburg-confession-of:
Confession of Augsburg is the subject of a faith article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Confession is the chief Protestant statement of belief drawn up at the Reformation. In 1530 the emperor called a diet and offered a fair hearing to all parties. Luther and his allies were asked to state the Saxon position. Their first articles told only why Saxony had ended certain church abuses.

The article tells how attacks from a Catholic writer forced a fuller statement. Melanchthon drafted the Confession, and Luther approved it in May. Its first twenty one articles argue that the reformers had changed teaching only to restore the pure old teaching. Its later articles defend the reform of named abuses. The Catholic reply was read in August. Melanchthon then wrote a defence of the Confession, printed with it in 1531.
britannica-1911-avoca-vale-of:
Avoca, or Ovoca, Vale of, is a mountain glen in county Wicklow, Ireland, formed where the Avonmore and Avonbeg rivers join to make the Ovoca river. Their united waters flow south and south-east to the Irish Sea at Arklow. The glen is narrow and densely wooded.

Fame came to the vale through Thomas Moore's Irish Melodies, which sang its praises and fixed the spelling Avoca, though locals write Ovoca. Lead and copper mines and the Dublin and South Eastern railway somewhat mar its beauty. Of its two meetings of the waters, the upper one near Castle Howard inspired Moore's song. At Avondale above it, Charles Stewart Parnell was born.
britannica-1911-aylesford-heneage-finch-:
Aylesford, Heneage Finch, 1st Earl of (c. 1640-1719), second son of the earl of Nottingham, was educated at Westminster and Christ Church, Oxford, and became a barrister of the Inner Temple in 1673. By 1679 he was solicitor-general, sitting in parliament for Oxford University and later Guildford.

As crown counsel Finch prosecuted Lord Russell and Algernon Sidney, arguing that Sidney's unpublished treatise was itself an overt act of treason. Yet in 1686 James II dismissed him for refusing to defend the royal dispensing power. Two years later he led for the seven bishops against that same power, boldly and well. After the Revolution he opposed the Orange settlement, held no office under William, and stayed a great opposer of the government.
britannica-1911-azov-sea-of:
Azov, Sea of, is an inland sea of southern Europe joined to the Black Sea by the Strait of Kerch, the ancient Cimmerian Bosporus. Romans knew it as Palus Maeotis, and its neighbours called it Temarenda, Mother of Waters. It stretches 230 miles long and up to 110 broad, over 14,515 square miles.

Shallowness rules it: near the Don's mouth the water runs three to ten feet deep, and nowhere passes forty-five. It freezes from November to mid-April, and fierce east winds stir varied currents. The water is mostly fresh, fish so plentiful that Turks call it Fish Sea, though the Sivash lagoons behind the Arabat spit are intensely salt. Taganrog, Berdyansk, and Mariupol serve its trade for Russia.
britannica-1911-bar-confederation-of:
The Confederation of Bar is the subject of a history article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a league of Polish nobles and gentry formed at the small fort of Bar in Podolia in 1768. Its aim was to guard the freedom of Poland, inside and out, against Russia. The men behind it were Adam Krasinski, bishop of Kamenets, Osip Pulawski and Michael Krasinski. King Stanislaus first hoped to make peace between the league and Russia. When that failed, he sent troops against them, and Bar was taken.

The confederates then asked for help abroad, and their move helped bring on a war between Russia and Turkey. In 1770 the league's council moved to Hungary. From there it dealt with France, Austria and Turkey to build a front against Russia. France sent Dumouriez to lead their troops, but he did them little good.
britannica-1911-basel-confession-of:
Confession of Basel is the name of a Reformation statement of faith treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was put out in 1534 and must not be confused with the First and Second Helvetic Confessions, the entry warns. Its author was Oswald Myconius, who built it on a shorter confession issued by Oecolampadius, his predecessor in the church at Basel. The town of Mühlhausen adopted it too, giving it a second name, the Confession of Mühlhausen.

Reaching for unity caused friction. The confession tried to bring into line with the reforming party both those still leaning toward the old faith and the Anabaptist section. Instead, publication stirred controversy, above all over its statements on the Eucharist. Strassburg accused Basel of celebrating a Christless supper. It was read from Basel pulpits yearly on the Wednesday of Passion week until 1826. A council resolution in 1872 practically annulled it.
britannica-1911-basel-council-of:
Council of Basel is the subject of a long historical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A decree of the Council of Constance had obliged popes to summon general councils at set intervals. Martin V therefore called this council to Basel for 1431 and named Cardinal Julian Cesarini to preside. Martin died before it opened, and the fathers from Italy, France, and Germany were slow to arrive, while Cesarini was busy with the war against the Hussites in Bohemia.

Conflict with the pope opens the story. Eugenius IV, Martin's successor, judged the council doomed and ordered the fathers in December 1431 to disperse and meet again at Bologna. The order brought an outcry at Basel and Cesarini's deep disapproval, since the Hussites might think the Church afraid to face them. The council stayed at Basel from 1431 to 1449, meeting publicly in the cathedral choir.
britannica-1911-bath-william-pulteney-ma:
William Pulteney, first earl of Bath (1684–1764), an English politician known by the name Pulteney, is the subject of a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Sent to Westminster school and Christ Church, Oxford, he gained deep classical learning and entered parliament in 1705 for Hedon in Yorkshire. He backed the Whigs under Queen Anne. He spoke up for his friend Walpole when the Tories sent Walpole to the Tower in 1712, and served as secretary at war from 1714 to 1717.

Rivalry with Walpole shaped the rest. Pulteney left office with Walpole in 1717, refused a peerage when Walpole rose again, and later led the attack on him in the Commons. When Walpole fell in 1742, Pulteney was set to form a government. He weakly handed the top post to Wilmington and took a peerage as earl of Bath. Public anger at that step broke his power at once, and his later years brought only brief, failed office.
britannica-1911-beaconsfield-benjamin-di:
Benjamin Disraeli, earl of Beaconsfield, was a British statesman and prime minister. He lived from eighteen o four to eighteen eighty one. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second child and eldest son of Isaac Disraeli.

Disraeli was born in Bedford Row, London, in December eighteen o four. His sister Sarah gave him wise and steady support in early days. All the children were born into the Jewish communion at first. His father left that faith with his household in eighteen sixteen. Benjamin was baptized at Saint Andrew church, Holborn, in eighteen seventeen.
britannica-1911-bedford-earls-and-dukes-:
Bedford, Earls and Dukes of, is a title article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It traces the holders of one of England's great noble titles. The present dukedom sits in the Russell family. John, Baron Russell, was made earl of Bedford in January 1550.

His descendant William, the fifth earl, became duke of Bedford in May 1694. The Russell line fills the later part of the article. Before the Russells, though, the title had other famous holders. The most notable was John Plantagenet, third son of King Henry the Fourth. Born in 1389, he received high dignities once his father took the throne. His career as regent of France lies ahead in the entry's telling. Readers get a title's full procession, from a Plantagenet prince to the Russells of later centuries.
britannica-1911-belesme-robert-of:
Robert of Belesme, active about 1100, was earl of Shrewsbury and a great marcher lord. The 1911 Britannica entry draws him as the model feudal noble of his hard age. From his mother he held Belesme, guarding Normandy against Maine to the south. From his father, a companion of the Conqueror, he held Shrewsbury against the Welsh.

That double border power made him proud, rich, and hard to curb by kings. The entry calls him shrewd, bold in battle, skilled in siege craft, and savagely cruel. He backed revolt in 1077 and joined the plot of 1088 against Rufus. At his peak he rose in revolt once more against royal rule.
britannica-1911-belle-isle-strait-of:
Belle Isle, Strait of, is the more northern of two channels joining the Gulf of St Lawrence with the Atlantic. It splits northern Newfoundland from Labrador and runs north-east to south-west for thirty-five miles, ten to fifteen miles wide. A steep granite island, 700 feet high, at its sea mouth gives it the name.

Lighthouses on that island are kept by Canada, with wireless links to the mainland. The strait is the shortest route from Europe to the St Lawrence, yet it opens only from June to late November, and ice and fog trouble it even then. Jacques Cartier sailed through it in 1534, while the year-round Cabot Strait was found later.
britannica-1911-bengal-bay-of:
Bengal, Bay of, is the part of the Indian Ocean lying between India and Burma, shaped roughly like a triangle. A line fifty miles wide runs from Ceylon and the Coromandel coast to the bay’s head, then south through the Andaman and Nicobar islands. Soundings mark the hundred-fathom line there, with five hundred fathoms fifty miles beyond.

Great rivers feed the bay: the Ganges and Brahmaputra from the north, the Irrawaddy from the east, and the Mahanadi, Godavari, Kistna and Cauvery from the west. Its west coast has no true harbour, Madras being an open roadstead, while the east holds good ports such as Akyab, Moulmein and Rangoon. Off Burma, mud volcanoes on the Cheduba group now and then throw up new islands.
britannica-1911-bergamot-oil-of:
Bergamot, oil of, is an essential oil pressed from the rind of the fruit of Citrus bergamia. The bergamot tree is small, with leaves and flowers like the bitter orange, and bears a round fruit near three inches across with a thin, smooth, lemon-yellow skin. Southern Calabria grows the whole world’s supply.

Machines mostly squeeze the oil from fruit picked in November and December. The clear greenish-yellow oil throws down a solid on standing, called bergamot camphor, and its strong, pleasant smell comes mainly from linalyl acetate, a compound chemists can also make in the laboratory. Perfumery takes nearly all the oil. The word itself seems to come from the Italian town of Bergamo.
britannica-1911-bergman-torbern-olof:
Torbern Olof Bergman (1735–1784) was a Swedish chemist and naturalist born at Katrineberg in Vestergötland. He entered Upsala at seventeen, torn between his father’s wish for law or divinity and his own love of mathematics and natural science. Overwork in trying to please both broke his health for a time.

Rest turned Bergman to field botany and insects, and he sent Linnaeus new specimens, even proving one supposed species a leech’s egg. Back at Upsala he taught mathematics and physics, writing on the rainbow, the aurora and tourmaline. In 1767 he won the chemistry and mineralogy chair with a memoir on making alum. His collected works, on minerals, crystals and the earth’s frame, fill six volumes.
britannica-1911-berwick-james-fitzjames-:
James FitzJames, Duke of Berwick (1670–1734), was a marshal of France. He was the natural son of James, Duke of York, later James II of England. His mother was Arabella Churchill, sister of the great Duke of Marlborough. He was born at Moulins in August 1670. Jesuits educated him in France. At fifteen he went to learn soldiering under Charles of Lorraine in Hungary.

He was made Duke of Berwick in 1687 and fought at Mohacz. The revolution drove him to France for good. He served James II in Ireland and stood at the Boyne. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his long French career to its end. A cannon shot killed him at the siege of Philipsburg in June 1734. Cool, cautious, and strict, he typified the 18th-century general.
britannica-1911-bessborough-earls-of:
Bessborough, Earls of, traces the Ponsonby family in Irish and English public life. The line starts with Sir John Ponsonby, a Commonwealth soldier who died in 1678. He gained land grants in Ireland. His son William became Baron Bessborough in 1721 and Viscount Duncannon in 1723. William's son Brabazon rose to the earldom itself in 1739. The article then runs down the earls in order.

The 2nd Earl was a noted Whig who held state offices. The 4th Earl served as lord-lieutenant of Ireland in 1846. The 6th Earl was a famous cricketer in his day. He chaired the 1881 commission on the Irish land system. His brother the 7th Earl died in 1906. The line passes to the 8th Earl at the article's close.
britannica-1911-bidpai-fables-of:
Bidpai, or Pilpay, is the medieval name for a famous set of Hindu animal fables. The name comes from the Sanskrit Vidya-pati, meaning chief scholar. The stories rest on the Pancha Tantra, the Five Sections of early fables. A second collection, the Hitopadesa, built on the first and became better known in Europe. A Persian court physician turned many tales into Pahlavi in the 6th century AD.

That Persian version is lost, but its Arabic child survives. Abdallah ibn Mokaffa's Arabic Book of Kalilah and Dimna took its name from two jackals in the first tale. The 1911 Britannica article traces the fables through Greek, Hebrew, and Latin versions. Each translation carried the tales further across Europe. Sir Thomas North's English version stands among the editions listed. The article is a history of transmission, not a retelling of the tales.
britannica-1911-bienne-lake-of:
Bienne, Lake of, also called the Bielersee, is a Swiss lake south-west of the town of Bienne. It runs along the southern foot of the Jura range. The lake measures seven and a half miles long and two and a half miles broad. Its depth is 249 feet, and its surface is 1,424 feet above sea level. Its area is 16 square miles. The island of St Pierre sits in its waters.

Rousseau stayed a short time on that island in 1765, the 1911 Britannica entry notes. Many traces of old lake-dwellings have been found on the shores. The river Suze enters at the north-east end. The Hagneck canal brings Aar water in, and the Nidau canal leads it out. At the south-west end the Thièle flows in from Lake Neuchâtel. The entry is a compact gazetteer note, signed by the Alpine writer Coolidge.
britannica-1911-biscay-bay-of:
Biscay, Bay of, is a great inlet of the Atlantic Ocean between France and Spain. France bounds it east and north-east as far as the island of Ushant. Spain bounds it south as far as Cape Ortegal. The Romans called it the Sinus Aquitanicus or the Cantabrian Ocean. Its modern English name is a worn form of the Spanish Vizcaya. In French it is the Golfe de Gascogne, and in Spanish the Golfo de Vizcaya.

The bay forms a fairly regular curve along its shores. The Loire, Garonne, and Adour mouths break the French coast. The Spanish coast is rugged, cut by fjord-like inlets in the west, where navigation can be dangerous. The bay's open position and mixed currents have made it notorious for storms, the 1911 Britannica entry warns. The note is short, focused on bounds, names, and weather.
britannica-1911-bolton-dukes-of:
Bolton, Dukes of, traces a title held by the Powlett family from 1689 to 1794. Charles Powlett, the first duke, became sixth marquess of Winchester in 1675. He had sat in parliament for Winchester and Hampshire. He backed William and Mary in 1688. He was made duke in April 1689.

The first duke is drawn as an eccentric. He was at odds with Halifax and later Marlborough. He is said to have toured in 1687 with four coaches and 100 horsemen. He slept by day and feasted by night. His son Charles, the second duke, was lord-lieutenant of Hampshire and Dorset. He helped arrange the union with Scotland. He served twice as a lord justice, and held the lord chamberlain's post. The entry then follows the later dukes to the title's end in 1794.
britannica-1911-bridgewater-francis-eger:
Francis Egerton, 3rd Duke of Bridgewater (1736–1803), is named the originator of British inland navigation. Born on 21 May 1736, the younger son of the 1st duke, he succeeded at twelve when his brother, the 2nd duke, died. As a boy he was sickly and so slow at learning that cutting him off from the estates was once weighed in earnest.

A broken engagement changed his course: after the duchess of Hamilton refused to drop her sister Lady Coventry, he broke up his London house and withdrew to Worsley to build canals. His canal from Worsley to Manchester, cut to carry coal from his own pits, was, apart from the Sankey canal, the first great work of its kind in modern Britain. The entry traces his Egerton lineage back through earls of Bridgewater to Sir Thomas Egerton, lord keeper under Elizabeth.
britannica-1911-bridgewater-francis-henr:
Francis Henry Egerton, 8th Earl of Bridgewater (1756–1829), was a scholar, naturalist and antiquarian who spent his last years in Paris. Schooled at Eton and Christ Church, Oxford, he became a fellow of All Souls in 1780 and of the Royal Society in 1781. He held church livings at Middle and Whitchurch in Shropshire, though a proxy did the duties, and succeeded his brother in the earldom in 1823.

When he died in February 1829 the earldom died with him. His will left the British Museum the prized Egerton manuscripts on French and Italian letters, plus 12,000 pounds. A further 8000 pounds went to the president of the Royal Society to pay writers for a treatise on the power, wisdom and goodness of God shown in creation. Eight men were picked, each to take one branch and receive 1000 pounds, producing the famed Bridgewater Treatises.
britannica-1911-brienz-lake-of:
Lake of Brienz lies in the Swiss canton of Bern and is the first lake into which the river Aar spreads. It fills a deep hollow between the village of Brienz at its east end and Bonigen at the west, close to Interlaken. The lake runs about 9 miles long and 1 and a half miles wide.

Its greatest depth is 856 feet, its surface covers 11 and a half square miles, and it sits 1857 feet above the sea. On the south shore stand the Giessbach Falls and the hamlet of Iseltwald, while a few small villages dot the north shore. The mood is gloomy next to nearby Lake Thun. Brienz village, with 2580 people, is the chief centre of Swiss wood-carving, the main stream feeding the lake is the Lutschine, and the first steamer crossed in 1839.
britannica-1911-brissac-dukes-of:
Brissac dukes take their title from a fief in Anjou bought late in the 15th century by the Cosse family, nobles of that same province. Rene de Cosse married into the then-powerful Gouffier family and became chief pantler to Louis XII. Two of his sons rose to be marshals of France, setting the family's pattern of high military office.

Brissac became a countship in 1560 for Charles, the eldest son, grandmaster of artillery and governor of Piedmont and Picardy. His brother Artus held great household and finance posts and fought in the religious wars. Charles II de Cosse fought for the League, yet as governor of Paris opened the city gates to Henry IV, who made him a marshal in 1594. The title rose to a duchy in the peerage of France in 1611. The last holder named, Louis Hercule Timoleon, was killed at Versailles on 9 September 1792 for loyalty to Louis XVI.
britannica-1911-bristol-earls-and-marque:
Bristol, Earls and Marquesses of, is a title held by the Hervey family since 1714, though an earlier Digby earldom of Bristol came first. The Herveys appear in the 13th century seated in Bedfordshire, then in Suffolk, where they have held Ickworth since the 15th century. Two Digby holders get separate lives elsewhere in the encyclopaedia; this entry walks the Hervey line.

John Hervey (1616–1679) held high place in the household of Catherine, wife of Charles II, and sat for Hythe in Parliament for years. Left no children, so his estates passed to his brother Sir Thomas, who died in 1694. Sir Thomas was followed by his son John (1665–1751), educated at Clare Hall, Cambridge. John sat for Bury St Edmunds from March 1694. He was made Baron Hervey of Ickworth in March 1703 and earl of Bristol in October 1714. The long family history unrolls from that founding earl.
britannica-1911-bristol-george-digby-2nd:
George Digby, 2nd Earl of Bristol (1612–1677), was the eldest son of the 1st earl and a courtier of striking gifts. Born in October 1612, he pleaded at the bar of the House of Commons at age twelve for his father, then held in the Tower. His youth, grace and well-delivered speech made a great impression.

Admitted to Magdalen College, Oxford, in August 1626, he became a favourite pupil of Peter Heylin and took his master's degree in 1636, then spent years in study and travel. Clarendon called him the most accomplished person of the nation. Letters with Sir Kenelm Digby from 1638-1639 attacked Roman Catholicism, a spell in the Fleet prison in 1634 soured him on the court. In 1640 he sat for Dorsetshire in both the Short and Long Parliaments, working with Pym and Hampden against Charles.
britannica-1911-bristol-john-digby-1st-e:
John Digby, 1st Earl of Bristol (1580–1653), was an English diplomatist, son of Sir George Digby of Coleshill in Warwickshire. Born in 1580, he entered Magdalen College, Oxford, in 1595 and the Inner Temple in 1598. In 1605 he carried James I word of the princess Elizabeth's safety at the time of the Gunpowder Plot, won royal favour, and was knighted in 1607.

Spain shaped his career. Sent as ambassador in 1611, he worked for a match between Prince Henry and the infanta Anne, won strong concessions for English merchants, placed consuls at Lisbon and Seville. Uncovered a secret list of English pensioners paid by the Spanish court, news he brought home in 1613. He went again in 1614 to pursue a match between the infanta Maria and Charles, though he himself favoured a Protestant marriage and a political rather than a bridal treaty.
britannica-1911-brunswick-karl-wilhelm-f:
Karl Wilhelm Ferdinand, Duke of Brunswick (1735–1806), was a German general born on 9 October 1735 at Wolfenbuttel. He received an unusually wide and thorough education and travelled in his youth in Holland, France and various parts of Germany. His first military experience came in the North German campaign of 1757, under the duke of Cumberland.

At Hastenbeck he won great renown by a gallant charge at the head of an infantry brigade. After the capitulation of Kloster Zeven his uncle Ferdinand, who succeeded Cumberland, easily persuaded him to stay in the war as a general officer. The hereditary prince's exploits soon made him an acknowledged master of irregular warfare, and in pitched battles, above all at Minden and Warburg, he proved an excellent subordinate. After the Seven Years' War he visited England with his bride, daughter of Frederick, prince of Wales.
britannica-1911-buccleuch-dukes-of:
The dukes of Buccleuch head a Scottish ducal house. The family name is Scott. This 1911 Britannica article traces the line. Its rise began with land grants from James II. He rewarded Sir Walter Scott of Buccleuch after the fall of Douglas in 1452. The family traced itself back further, to a Sir Richard le Scott. He lived in the 13th century.

A lordship came in 1606 and an earldom in 1619. The first duke was created through a marriage. Anne, countess in her own right, wed the duke of Monmouth in 1663. The line then passed down to the 6th duke. In 1810 the 3rd duke added the Queensberry dukedom. The 5th duke built the harbour at Granton, near Edinburgh. It cost over £500,000. The 6th duke sat as a Conservative member for Midlothian. The article lists each duke in turn, with dates and offices.
britannica-1911-buchan-earls-of:
The earls of Buchan held one of the old Scottish earldoms. This 1911 Britannica article traces the title through several families. Mar and Buchan began as one earldom. It was one of seven original Scottish earldoms. Later the two were split apart. Early earls included Alexander Comyn and John Comyn. Both men served as constables of Scotland.

John Comyn's wife Isabel crowned Robert the Bruce at Scone in 1306. She was then imprisoned at Berwick. About 1382 the earldom passed to the Stewarts. One holder was Alexander Stewart, the “wolf of Badenoch.” Another was John Stewart, constable of France. He died at the battle of Verneuil in 1424. In 1617 the earldom came to the Erskine family. The article gives the later line in detail. It dwells on the eccentric 11th earl, David Steuart Erskine. He founded the Scottish Society of Antiquaries in 1780.
britannica-1911-buckingham-and-normanby-:
John Sheffield (1648–1721) was an English statesman and poet. He became the first duke of Buckingham and Normanby. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his career at court. He was born on 7 April 1648. His father was the earl of Mulgrave, and he inherited that title in 1658. At eighteen he joined the fleet for the Dutch war. He fought at Southwold Bay in 1672. He later commanded a ship and served under Turenne.

Sheffield backed the duke of York at court. He helped bring about Monmouth's disgrace. James II made him lord chamberlain. He stayed with James during the king's flight. Yet he accepted the Revolution that followed. In 1694 he became marquess of Normanby. Queen Anne made him lord privy seal. In 1703 she created him duke of Buckingham and Normanby. He later served as lord steward and lord president. He died on 24 February 1721.
britannica-1911-buckingham-earls-marques:
Buckingham is a title borne by several English noble lines. This 1911 Britannica article traces the earldom, marquessate and dukedom. The origin of the earldom is obscure. Charter evidence may place it under William Rufus. Walter Giffard is usually counted the first earl. He held forty-eight lordships in the county. He died in 1102.

The title passed through the de Clare family. It lapsed with Richard de Clare in 1176. In 1377 Thomas of Woodstock became earl of Buckingham. His line led to Humphrey Stafford. Humphrey was made the first Stafford duke in 1444. That dukedom ended with Edward Stafford's fall in 1521. In 1617 James I created George Villiers an earl. He became marquess in 1618 and duke in 1623. The Villiers dukedom died out in 1687. A side line later claimed the earldom. The claim rested on the patent's special remainder.
britannica-1911-buckingham-henry-staffor:
Henry Stafford (1454–1483) was the second duke of Buckingham. This 1911 Britannica entry tells of his rise and fall. His father died at the first battle of St Albans in 1455. His grandfather, the first duke, died at Northampton in 1460. Both men fought for Lancaster. Henry had royal blood on both sides. His vast lands made him a power in the land. Edward IV gave him the hand of Catherine Woodville, the queen's sister.

At first Henry held small place at court. Then Edward IV died, in 1483. Henry helped Richard of Gloucester seize the young king. Richard rewarded him with great Welsh offices. He became constable of England as well. In June 1483 he urged London to accept Richard as king. Soon after, he withdrew to Brecon. He rose in revolt against Richard that autumn. A servant betrayed him for a reward. Richard had him executed at Salisbury on 2 November 1483.
britannica-1911-buckinghamshire-earls-of:
The earls of Buckinghamshire were a branch of the Hobart family. This 1911 Britannica article traces their line. It warns readers not to confuse them with the earls of Buckingham. The first earl was John Hobart, born about 1694. He descended from Sir Henry Hobart, a judge under James I. In 1728 he became Baron Hobart of Blickling. In 1746 he became earl of Buckinghamshire.

The second earl served as ambassador to Russia. He was lord-lieutenant of Ireland from 1776 to 1780. The entry says he was hardly equal to that post. His half-brother George followed as third earl. Robert Hobart, the fourth earl, came next. He was chief secretary for Ireland from 1789 to 1793. He worked to block concessions to Roman Catholics. The article follows the later earls in turn. It gives their seats, marriages and offices.
britannica-1911-bute-john-stuart-3rd-ear:
John Stuart, third Earl of Bute (1713–1792), was an English prime minister, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens in his quiet years. He was born on the twenty fifth of May 1713. He was the son of James, the second earl, and of Lady Jane Campbell. His mother was a daughter of the first duke of Argyll.

Bute was educated at Eton and succeeded to the earldom in 1723. The earldom was a Scottish peerage, created in 1703 for his grandfather. In 1737 he was elected a representative peer for Scotland. He was not returned in the parliaments that followed. He seems never to have spoken in debate in that role. In 1738 he was made a knight of the Thistle. For years he lived in retirement in Bute, at farming and botany.
britannica-1911-cardigan-james-thomas-br:
James Thomas Brudenell (1797–1868) was the seventh earl of Cardigan. He was an English lieutenant-general of cavalry. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his stormy career. He was born at Hambleden, in Bucks, on 16 October 1797. He studied at Christ Church, Oxford, for several terms. In 1818 he entered parliament, and in 1824 the army. Within eight years he bought his way to lieutenant-colonel.

Cardigan commanded the 15th Hussars with great harshness. In two years he held 105 courts-martial in the regiment. He made over 700 arrests among only 350 men. Personal quarrels drove him from that command in 1834. In 1836 he took command of the 11th Hussars instead. He spent large sums on that regiment's equipment. Wellington praised its discipline and its turnout highly. Cardigan succeeded his father as earl in 1837. In 1840 he fought a duel with one of his own officers.
britannica-1911-carli-rubbi-giovanni-rin:
Giovanni Rinaldo Carli-Rubbi (1720–1795) was an Italian economist and antiquarian. He was a count, born at Capo d'Istria in 1720. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. At twenty-four the Venetian senate appointed him to a new chair. It was the professorship of astronomy and navigation at Padua. He also superintended the Venetian marine for the senate. After seven years he resigned both offices in good credit.

Carli then devoted himself to antiquities and political economy. His book on coinage treats the mints of Italy. In 1759 he argued against the balance-of-trade doctrine. Both nations may gain by trade between them, he held. In 1771 he wrote on free trade in grain. He argued that such freedom is not always advisable. Leopold of Tuscany made him head of the council of public economy. He also led the board of public instruction from 1765. He died at Milan in February 1795.
britannica-1911-carlisle-earls-of:
The earls of Carlisle form an English title of two families. This 1911 Britannica article traces both lines of holders. James Hay was created the first earl in 1622. The title died in his line with his son in 1660. In 1661 it was given to Charles Howard instead. It descends in the Howard family to the present day.

James Hay was a Scotsman of the Erroll kin. James VI knighted him and made him a prime favourite. He came to England with the king in 1603. He became a gentleman of the bedchamber at court. In 1604 he went on a mission to France. There he pleaded for the Huguenots, to Henry IV's annoyance. The king's present to the envoy was sharply cut. In 1606 Hay got a barony for life by patent. It gave precedence but no seat in parliament. The article follows the Hay and Howard earls in turn.
britannica-1911-carnarvon-earldom-of:
Earldom of Carnarvon is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry tracing a British peerage title and the statesman who held it in the nineteenth century. The title was created in 1628 for Robert Dormer, Baron Dormer of Wyng, who was killed at the first battle of Newbury while fighting for Charles I. It became extinct in 1709, was later held by the Brydges family, and was created again in 1793 for Henry Herbert, Baron Porchester.

Most of the entry follows Henry Howard Molyneux Herbert, the 4th earl (1831–1890), who entered the House of Lords in 1849. As colonial secretary he introduced the 1867 bill for the federation of the British North American provinces, then resigned over Disraeli's Reform Bill. He later served as lord-lieutenant of Ireland, where a dispute with Parnell over Home Rule talks ended his time in office.
britannica-1911-carpentaria-gulf-of:
Gulf of Carpentaria is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a wide arm of the sea cutting into the north coast of Australia. The gulf runs 480 miles long and 420 miles across at its widest, bounded east by Cape York Peninsula and west by the Northern Territory. The Wellesley islands sit near its southern end, and the Sir Edward Pellew islands and Groote Eylandt lie toward the western side.

Many rivers reach the gulf, and the entry names the chief ones shore by shore. The Mitchell flows in from the east, the Gilbert, Norman, Flinders, Leichhardt, and Gregory at the south-east, and the Roper from the west. The name came from Pieter Carpentier, governor-general of the Dutch East Indies, whose name Jan Carstensz gave to a small river in 1623. After Tasman's second voyage in 1644, charts carried the gulf under its present name.
britannica-1911-carthage-synods-of:
Synods of Carthage is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the many church councils held at Carthage in Africa during the third, fourth, and fifth centuries. Only the most important synods are treated. The first, in May 251 under Cyprian, took up the lapsi, Christians who had fallen away under persecution. It excommunicated Felicissimus and five Novatian bishops and ruled that the lapsed be handled by each person's guilt, not with blanket severity.

A Rome synod confirmed those rulings the same autumn, and further synods on the lapsed met in 252 and 254. Two synods in 255 and 256 under Cyprian then declared heretical baptism invalid, defying Stephen, bishop of Rome. A third synod in September 256 restated the position without a dissenting voice. Stephen broke with the African church, and his claim to be “bishop of bishops” drew sharp resentment. Numbered sections and source references work through each council in turn.
britannica-1911-chalcedon-council-of:
Council of Chalcedon is a church history article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The council was the fourth general council of the Catholic Church, held in the year 451. Its cause was the Eutychian heresy and the scandal of the Robber Synod. Protests against that synod rose in both East and West.

The emperor Theodosius the Second ignored calls for a new council. His successor Marcian granted the demand at once. Five to six hundred bishops gathered at Chalcedon in October 451. Nearly all were Eastern, apart from the Roman legates and two Africans. Rome's legates claimed the right to preside over the meeting. The first session was stormy, with party feeling running high. The acts of the Robber Synod were examined for fraud and force. The entry gives readers the opening of a council that shaped Christian teaching.
britannica-1911-champeaux-william-of:
William of Champeaux, a French thinker and churchman who lived from about 1070 to 1121, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The hosted text opens with the tail of the Champaran district entry, then gives his own article in full. Born near Melun, he learned under Anselm of Laon and Roscellinus and taught at Notre Dame in Paris.

Among his pupils was Abelard, a fact that still draws readers to his name. In 1108 he withdrew to the abbey of Saint Victor and taught there, and he later served as bishop of Châlons sur Marne. Few of his works were printed. The entry names a piece on the Eucharist and works on morals and on the soul, in which he held that a soul is made new for each child. Scraps of his writing on God are also noted.
britannica-1911-chandos-barons-and-dukes:
Chandos, barons and dukes of, is an English title, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces it through the Brydges family. The title began as a barony in 1554 and rose to a dukedom in 1719, lasting until 1789. In 1822 the dukedom was revived in connection with that of Buckingham. The first baron was John Brydges (about 1490 to 1557), a son of Sir Giles Brydges.

John Brydges stood high at court under Henry the Eighth, Edward the Sixth, and Mary. He helped put down the rebellion of Sir Thomas Wyatt in 1554. As lieutenant of the Tower of London he held in his charge Lady Jane Grey and Wyatt, and for a short time the princess Elizabeth herself. He was made Baron Chandos of Sudeley in 1554 and died in 1557.
britannica-1911-chatham-william-pitt-1st:
William Pitt, 1st Earl of Chatham (1708–1778), is the subject of a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English statesman born at Westminster. He was the younger son of Robert Pitt of Boconnoc in Cornwall. His grandfather was Thomas Pitt, governor of Madras, called “Diamond” Pitt. That name came from his sale of a huge diamond to the regent Orleans for about £135,000. The sale raised the family to wealth and influence.

Pitt was educated at Eton and entered Trinity College, Oxford, in January 1727. He read the classics widely, and Demosthenes was his favourite author. He trained his expression by translating and retranslating. Hereditary gout forced him to leave Oxford without a degree. On his return he chose the army, as a younger son must choose a profession. Friends procured him a cornet's commission in the dragoons. His military career was destined to be short.
britannica-1911-chicago-university-of:
Chicago, University of, is one of the great educational institutions of the United States, established under Baptist auspices in Chicago and opened in 1892. Its president and two thirds of its trustees are always Baptists, yet the entry calls it non-sectarian apart from its divinity school. First president William R Harper gave it immense ambition and rapid growth. Grounds cover about 140 acres by the Midway Plaisance.

Students rose from 698 in the first college year to 5,038 in 1907–1908, of whom 2,186 were women. Faculties cover arts, literature, science, divinity, medicine, law, education and commerce. Grey limestone Gothic buildings stand in quadrangles, and the Yerkes Observatory holds the largest refracting telescope in the world. A library of 450,000 volumes, a strong press, extension teaching and a full summer quarter are all stressed.
britannica-1911-chronicles-books-of:
Chronicles, Books of, is a Bible article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It treats the two Old Testament books called Chronicles. Their Hebrew title means Events of the Times. Jerome suggested the name Chronicon, from which the English name derives.

The entry explains how the books stand in the Bible. The Greek translators split one long book into two parts. They titled it Things Omitted, meaning matter left out of the other histories. Chronicles begins with Adam and breaks off in the middle of Cyrus's decree. That decree appears in full at the start of Ezra. The article argues that Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah once formed a single work. Readers get a clear account of the books' name, place, and tangled growth.
britannica-1911-clanricarde-ulick-de-bur:
Clanricarde, Ulick de Burgh, 1st Earl of (d. 1544), styled MacWilliam and called of the Heads, was son of Richard de Burgh, lord of Clanricarde. He succeeded to the headship of his clan and held vast estates in county Galway, including Loughry, Dunkellin, Kiltartan and Athenry. His family had abjured English law for generations after the earldom of Ulster merged in the crown. He exercised a quasi-royal authority over his people.

In March 1541 he wrote to Henry VIII lamenting his family's fall into Irish and disobedient rule, and placed himself and his estates in the king's hands. That same year he was present at Dublin when the act making Henry king of Ireland was passed. Submission thus replaced generations of independence for the de Burghs of Clanricarde. His grim nickname came from a mount of heads of men slain in battle, covered with earth.
britannica-1911-clare-john-fitzgibbon-1s:
Clare, John Fitzgibbon, 1st Earl of (1749–1802) was lord chancellor of Ireland, second son of John Fitzgibbon, who had left the Catholic faith to pursue a legal career. Educated at Trinity College, Dublin, as a distinguished classical scholar, and at Christ Church, Oxford, he was called to the Irish bar in 1772. A lucrative practice and an inherited fortune followed quickly. In 1778 he entered the Irish House of Commons for Dublin University.

At first he generally supported Grattan's popular party, yet he opposed removing Catholic disabilities from the start and tried to impede the Relief Bill of 1778. He distrusted priests deeply and held for life that a conscientious Catholic ecclesiastic could never be a well attached subject of a Protestant state. From 1780 he broke with the national party over Irish parliamentary independence. His mind inclined naturally to authority over democratic liberty, the entry argues.
britannica-1911-clarence-dukes-of:
Dukes of Clarence form the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on an old English title. The name comes from Clare, and the first duke was Lionel of Antwerp, third son of Edward the Third. He was made duke in 1362, and the title died with him in 1368. It was brought back in 1412 and again in 1461 for new holders.

George, the third holder, was charged by his brother the king and killed in 1478, and his lands were lost. No new duke was made until 1789, when William, son of George the Third, took the title. The entry then gives a full life of Lionel and his work in Ireland.
britannica-1911-clarendon-henry-hyde-2nd:
Henry Hyde, second earl of Clarendon, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in sixteen thirty eight, he was the eldest son of the first earl. He went into exile with his parents and served his father as secretary. The family came back to England in sixteen sixty.

The entry traces his posts and his shifts in politics. He sat in Parliament for Wiltshire and rose to lord chamberlain to the queen. After his father's fall he turned into a sharp critic of the court. He defended his father and attacked Buckingham and Arlington. In sixteen seventy four he became earl on his father's death.
britannica-1911-clerfayt-francois-sebast:
Clerfayt, François Sebastien Charles Joseph de Croix, Count of (1733–1798) was an Austrian field marshal who entered the Austrian army in 1753. In the Seven Years' War he distinguished himself greatly, earning rapid promotion and the order of Maria Theresa. Still under thirty at the peace, he was already a colonel. As a Walloon he resisted pressure in 1787 to abandon Joseph II, and in the Turkish war he beat the Turks at Mehadia and Calafat.

In 1792 he commanded the Austrian contingent in Brunswick's army and checked the French at Croix-sous-Bois, then won at Aldenhoven and Neerwinden in 1793. Wattignies and West Flanders reversed his fortune in 1794, and he recrossed the Rhine in supreme command. In 1795, now field marshal, he beat Jourdan at Höchst and relieved Mainz brilliantly. An armistice he concluded was disapproved by Thugut, and he resigned his command in consequence.
britannica-1911-clergy-benefit-of:
Clergy, Benefit of, was an obsolete but once very important feature of English criminal law, sparing convicted clerks the death penalty. It began with the 12th century claim that every clericus should answer to spiritual courts alone, exempt from temporal courts. Compromise followed, where common law courts dropped the death punishment for a clericus and the church accepted a secondary punishment. Clerk always covered many in minor orders, and in 1350 the privilege reached secular clerks too.

Reading the opening words of Psalm 51, the neck-verse, became the test of clerkship, until even that requirement was abolished in 1705. Laymen convicted of a clergyable felony were branded on the thumb from 1487 and barred from claiming the benefit twice. Peers gained it in 1547 even if they could not read, and women gained it fully in 1692. Atrocious crimes stayed unclergyable, and the device became a means of softening the criminal law's severity.
britannica-1911-cleveland-barbara-villie:
Cleveland, Barbara Villiers, Duchess of (1641–1709) was the mistress of the English king Charles II, daughter of William Villiers, 2nd Viscount Grandison. In April 1659 she married Roger Palmer, created earl of Castlemaine two years later, and her intimacy with Charles began soon after. The king probably fathered her first child, Anne, born in February 1661. Queen Catherine disliked her, yet at the king's insistence she became a lady of the bedchamber and entered court intrigue.

Her house became a rendezvous for enemies of Clarendon, whose fall in 1667 delighted her, by Pepys's account. In August 1670 she was created countess of Southampton and duchess of Cleveland, with great gifts and a post office income of 4,700 pounds a year. Extravagance and gaming losses still forced her to sell household contents. About 1670 her influence over Charles began to decline, the account continues.
britannica-1911-cockaigne-land-of:
The Land of Cockaigne is an imaginary country from medieval tales. Life there was one long round of rich food and idle ease. The name links to a word for cake. In plain terms it means the land of cakes. French and Italian forms of the word point the same way.

In that land the rivers ran with wine. Houses were built of cake and barley sugar. Streets were paved with pastry, and shops gave goods for nothing. Roast geese walked about and asked to be eaten. Buttered larks fell from the sky like manna. A French tale of the 1200s told of the place. An English poem of the same age used it to mock monks. London later took the name in jest.
britannica-1911-common-order-book-of:
The Book of Common Order, also called the Order of Geneva or Knox's Liturgy, is covered in a 1911 Britannica article. It was a guide for public worship in the Reformed Church in Scotland. John Knox and other church men drew up a first form among exiles at Frankfort. Knox then printed it at Geneva in 1556.

The book reached Scotland and gained ground after Knox came home in 1559. In 1562 the General Assembly ordered its use for sacraments, weddings, and burials. A larger print run came out at Edinburgh in 1564. Each church reader then had to own a copy and use it in prayer too.
britannica-1911-common-pleas-court-of:
Court of Common Pleas is the subject of a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The court was once one of the three common law courts at Westminster. The other two were the king's bench and the exchequer. The court grew out of the king's council. Before Magna Carta, the part of the council that handled court business followed the king's person.

The article explains the hardship that caused for private suitors. They had to follow the king from place to place or lose their chance of a trial. Magna Carta therefore ordered that suits between subject and subject be heard in a fixed place. That place was set at Westminster. A chief judge and four lesser judges presided over the court. In 1873 its powers passed to a division of the High Court of Justice.
britannica-1911-como-lake-of:
Lake Como, in Lombardy in northern Italy, is surveyed in a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. The Romans called it Lacus Larius, a name still in use as Lario. The Adda river flows through the Valtelline into its north end and out at the south-east, on its way to the Po. The lake runs about 43 miles end to end and up to two and a half miles broad.

Its surface stands 653 feet above the sea, and its great depth is 1,365 feet. The lake fills a deep cut through limestone ranges. At Bellagio a headland splits it into two arms, one ending at Lecco and one a shut bay at Como. A morning wind blows from the north and an afternoon wind from the south. Grand villas line the shores, and Bellagio is called the loveliest spot of all.
britannica-1911-conde-louis-de-bourbon-p:
Louis de Bourbon, prince of Condé (1530–1569), was the fifth son of Charles de Bourbon, duke of Vendôme. He was the younger brother of Antoine, king of Navarre. He first bore the famous name of Condé. After his father's death in 1537 he was raised in the reformed faith. Brave though deformed, and gay but poor for his rank, he chose the sword.

He fought with honour in Piedmont under Marshal de Brissac. In 1552 he forced his way into Metz while Charles V besieged it. He led bold sallies from that town. In 1554 he led the light horse on the Meuse. At Saint Quentin in 1557 he did more good service. Yet the court distrusted his house and passed his deeds by. That slight fed his turn to the Huguenot cause. At Jarnac he charged the whole Catholic army with 400 horsemen. Worn out with fighting, he fell there.
britannica-1911-conde-louis-ii-de-bourbo:
Louis II de Bourbon, prince of Condé (1621–1686), called the Great Condé, was born at Paris on 8 September 1621. His father was Henry, prince of Condé, and his mother came from the Montmorency house. He studied with care at the Jesuits' College at Bourges. At seventeen he governed Burgundy in his father's absence. Campaigns in north France marked him out before he was twenty.

Richelieu ruled France in his youth, and princes bent to the cardinal. Condé's father sought that favour like the rest. The young prince loved Marthe du Vigean with a deep return of love. Yet at twenty he was forced to wed Richelieu's niece, a child of thirteen. The long entry follows his wars in full. Its middle turns to July 1652, when his army met Turenne near Paris. Only the city gates, opened by the duke of Orleans's daughter, saved his force.
britannica-1911-conde-princes-of:
The princes of Condé formed a branch of the house of Bourbon. Their title came from the old town of Condé-sur-l'Escaut. The first to take it was Louis de Bourbon, the Huguenot leader and fifth son of the duke of Vendôme. His son Henry (1552–1588) held to the Huguenot party as well. He fled to Germany and raised a small army there.

Henry died of poison, men of his time believed, at his wife's hand. Doubt then fell on his heir's birth, though King Henry IV let the matter rest. That heir wed Charlotte de Montmorency in 1609. He soon had to flee with her to Spain and Italy to save her from the king's pursuit. The line runs on through the 1600s in the entry. Its last named prince, Louis Joseph (1736–1818), won note in the Seven Years' War. A victory at Johannisberg heads his deeds.
britannica-1911-connaught-arthur-william:
Arthur, duke of Connaught, was the third son and seventh child of Queen Victoria. He was born at Buckingham Palace on the first of May eighteen fifty. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was set for the army and entered Woolwich academy in eighteen sixty six.

Arthur rose through the Royal Engineers, Royal Artillery, and Rifle Brigade posts. He fought in Egypt in eighteen eighty two and led the Guards at Tel el Kebir. He was praised three times in reports and thanked by parliament then. From eighteen eighty six he led the Bombay army in India for four years. He later led the Aldershot command and the forces in Ireland.
britannica-1911-constance-council-of:
The Council of Constance, a great church meeting of the 1400s, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. Emperor Sigismund pushed for it, and Pope John the Twenty Third called it. Its aims were to end the Great Schism of the West and to reform the church. It opened on November 5, 1414, and closed on April 22, 1418.

At the time three popes split the Christian world. John hoped the council would name him the sole true pope. That hope soon failed, since the Pisa rulings were still in dispute. All three claims had to be weighed anew on fair terms. John faced calls to step down and fled the city with help from the duke of Austria.
britannica-1911-constance-lake-of:
Lake Constance is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article on a great lake in the Alps. The Romans called it Lacus Brigantinus, the lake of Bregenz. In German it is now called the Bodensee, or the Swabian Sea. The text calls it the largest sheet of water in the Alpine region after Lake Geneva.

The lake lies on the north-east edge of Switzerland and is formed by the Rhine. Its shape is long, and at its north-west end it splits into two arms. One arm is the Untersee, and the other is the Überlingersee. The article gives its length, height above the sea, width, depth, and area in plain figures. Readers get a clear map in words of a lake shared by the lands around it.
britannica-1911-cork-and-orrery-mary-cou:
Mary, Countess of Cork and Orrery, lived from 1746 to 1840 and loved books and talk. She was born Mary Monckton, a viscount's daughter, in May 1746. The 1911 Britannica life stresses her keen love of letters from youth. Through her, her mother's London house drew the great minds of the day. Doctor Johnson came often and talked with her at great ease.

Sheridan, Reynolds, Burke, and Walpole were among her steady guests. Her closest friend was the actress Mrs Siddons, the entry says. In 1786 she wed the seventh earl of Cork and Orrery. As Lady Cork her hunt for famed guests grew yet more bold. Statesmen and poets from Byron to Scott filled her rooms.
britannica-1911-cork-richard-boyle-1st-e:
Richard Boyle, first earl of Cork, an Irish statesman who lived from 1566 to 1643, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born at Canterbury on October 3, 1566. He was schooled at the King's School and at Cambridge, then read law in London. Work as a clerk offered him little scope to rise.

Boyle sailed for Ireland in June 1588 with just twenty seven pounds in his purse. He rose fast as a deputy in the land office there. A marriage in 1595 brought him an estate worth five hundred pounds a year. Envious foes charged him with fraud and had him jailed more than once. A revolt in Munster in 1598 cut him back to poverty.
britannica-1911-corpus-christi-feast-of:
Corpus Christi is a feast of the Roman Catholic Church for the sacrament. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its Latin sense as festival of the Body of Christ. It falls on the first Thursday after Trinity Sunday each year. Its root lies in a church ruling on the sacrament in 1215.

A vision by Julienne of Liège sparked the feast at local level first. Bishop Robert set it for his diocese in 1246 on her prompting. Pope Urban IV made it binding on the whole church in 1264. Thomas Aquinas wrote a new office for the feast at that time. Grand processions later became its chief public mark across Europe.
britannica-1911-coutances-walter-of:
Walter of Coutances (died 1207) was bishop of Lincoln and then archbishop of Rouen. He began his career in the chancery of Henry II. In 1182 he was elected bishop of Lincoln. In 1184, with the king's help, he gained the see of Rouen. Church and state work of a high order filled the rest of his life.

He set out with Richard I for the Third Crusade. Richard sent him back from Messina on a hard task. He was to probe the charges laid by barons and officials against the chancellor, William Longchamp. No love was lost between the two churchmen. Men saw them as rivals for the see of Canterbury. Walter sided with the barons and John and backed Longchamp's fall. The Great Council then named him chief justiciar. He headed the government until 1193. He also did good service in the talks for Richard's release.
britannica-1911-craven-william-craven-ea:
William Craven, Earl of Craven (1608–1697), was the eldest son of Sir William Craven, lord mayor of London. His mother was a daughter of Alderman William Whitmore. He was born in June 1608 and inherited his father's vast fortune on his death in 1618. He matriculated at Trinity College, Oxford, in 1623. A year later he joined the Middle Temple.

Before he came of age he had won note in the service of the princes of Orange. Back home he was knighted and made Baron Craven in 1627. Zeal for the king and queen of Bohemia marked his early manhood. In 1632 he joined Frederick on a march to win back the Palatinate. At the storm of Kreuznach he was first, though wounded, to mount the breach. Gustavus Adolphus praised him for that deed on the spot. Craven came home when the elector was denied a command of his own.
britannica-1911-crawford-earls-of:
The earls of Crawford head the house of Lindsay, one of the great families of Scotland. That house traces its line back to the barons of Crawford of the 1100s. Its men have played leading parts in Scottish history age after age. One claim in the entry sets its rank in bold terms. No Scottish family, it says, can match the Lindsays in genealogical weight.

Their forebears stood as barons at the dawn of parliament in Scotland. They were never enrolled in the modern sense, the claim runs. They stood among the pares of the realm from the first records. The earldom itself formed a petty principality, a state within the state. Its earls kept a council of their great vassals for high affairs. With that council's advice they acted on great occasions. The long entry, past 16,000 bytes, then walks the line earl by earl.
britannica-1911-crewe-robert-offley-ashb:
Robert Offley Ashburton Crewe-Milnes, first Earl of Crewe, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born on the twelfth of January 1858, he was the son of Lord Houghton. He was schooled at Harrow and at Trinity College, Cambridge. Like his father, he had a taste for books, and he printed a book of verses in 1890.

A Liberal in politics, Crewe served as private secretary to Lord Granville in the early 1880s. In the Liberal government of 1892 to 1895 he was lord lieutenant for Ireland. He was made first earl of Crewe in 1895, after he came into his grandfather's estate. In 1905 he joined the cabinet as lord president of the council. In 1908 he became secretary of state for the colonies under Asquith.
britannica-1911-cromarty-george-mackenzi:
George Mackenzie, 1st earl of Cromarty (1630–1714), was a Scottish statesman, eldest son of Sir John Mackenzie of Tarbat. He joined the rising for Charles II in 1654 and spent six years in exile. After the Restoration he became a lord of session as Lord Tarbat in 1661. Dismissed in 1664 for a plot against Lauderdale, he returned as lord justice general in 1678. From 1682 to 1688 he was chief minister in Scotland for Charles II and James II.

In 1688 Mackenzie left James and made his peace with William III. Anne created him earl of Cromarty in 1703, and he backed the union of England and Scotland in print. He died on 17 August 1714. The entry follows his line to his grandson George, the 3rd earl, who joined the Jacobites in 1745, was condemned to death, and won a conditional pardon with his peerage forfeited. Later pages trace the title to the countess created in 1895.
britannica-1911-cumberland-dukes-and-ear:
The earldom of Cumberland was held by the Clifford family from 1525 to 1643, when it died out with Henry, the 5th earl. Henry, 11th Lord Clifford, was made 1st earl by Henry VIII in 1525 and stayed loyal in the northern rising of 1536. His son Henry, the 2nd earl, was a scholar rather than a soldier. His daughter Margaret was thought by many in 1557 to be the rightful heir to the English throne.

George, the 3rd earl, turned from youthful waste to the sea, fighting the Armada and leading plundering voyages that won rich booty. His daughter Anne claimed the barony, while his brother Francis took the earldom, and a long lawsuit over the estates ran until 1617. The entry then follows the later dukedom. It was given in 1799 to Ernest Augustus, who became king of Hanover in 1837. His line kept the title of duke of Cumberland even after Prussia annexed Hanover in 1866.
britannica-1911-cumberland-william-augus:
William Augustus, duke of Cumberland (1721–1765), was a son of George II and Queen Caroline, born on 15 April 1721 and made duke at five years old. Meant first for the navy, he soon left it for the army. Made major-general in 1742, he first fought in Germany the next year. At Dettingen he was wounded, and his energy there founded his military fame. In 1745 he led the allied armies in Flanders.

At Fontenoy that May, Cumberland led the bold column that pierced the French centre, and his cool retreat saved his army. His men bore harsh discipline yet held a strong loyalty to him. That trust marked him out to crush the rising of Prince Charles Edward in 1745 and 1746. The entry faults his want of sagacity and tact beside his courage. In later life public favour swung back to him, and Pitt's return was sought through him. He died on 31 October 1765.
britannica-1911-cutch-runn-of:
The Runn of Cutch, a vast salt marsh on the west coast of India, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It lies in the native state of Cutch. From May to October it fills with salt water. At its widest it joins the Gulf of Cutch to the Gulf of Cambay. It varies in breadth from five to eighty miles. In the rains it is nearly impassable for horsemen.

The whole marsh is put at about 8,000 square miles. Rivers such as the Luni and Banas feed it in the monsoon. By December it is quite dry and mostly hard. In places it stays moist and muddy. The soil is soaked with salt. The Runn is a key source of salt supply. Its making is still a matter of dispute. Wild asses are common on its borders. They are seen in herds of sixty or seventy.
britannica-1911-cyprus-church-of:
Church of Cyprus is an Orthodox church that rules itself, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It is in communion and in full accord of teaching with the other Orthodox churches of the East. Yet it is subject to no patriarch, a stand it has always claimed. Its freedom by ancient custom was upheld at the council of Ephesus in 431, against the claims of the patriarch of Antioch.

An edict of the emperor Zeno and the Trullan Council of 692 backed that freedom in turn. Later bids by the patriarchs of Antioch to claim rule over Cyprus all came to nothing. Save for the years when Lusignan and Venetian lords held the island, from 1193 to 1571, the church never lost its self rule. It still took its holy ointment from abroad, a point of courtesy and not of rule, the text notes.
britannica-1911-dartmouth-earl-of:
Dartmouth, Earl of, is an English rank held by the Legge family, and its rise is traced in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The line runs from William Legge, born about sixteen hundred and nine. He was the eldest son of a lead man in Munster. He won skill at war on the mainland of Europe.

He came home to aid Charles the First in his war with the Scots. He was of great use in the months before the Civil War broke out. His bid to seize Hull for the king failed in January of sixteen forty two. In the war he stood out at two great fights. In sixteen forty five he was made head of Oxford for the king. He lost that post in months, caught in the fall of Prince Rupert.
britannica-1911-derby-earls-of:
Derby, Earls of, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article tracing the holders of an English earldom. The first earl was likely Robert de Ferrers, who died in 1139. King Stephen is said to have made him an earl after the battle of the Standard in 1138. His line held the earldom until 1266.

The entry tells how the last Ferrers earl joined the barons' rising against Henry the Third and lost his lands and title. Those estates went that same year to the king's son Edmund, earl of Lancaster. In 1337 Edmund's grandson Henry was created earl of Derby anew. The title later passed to John of Gaunt, who had married Henry's daughter Blanche, and the article follows that line onward.
britannica-1911-dort-synod-of:
The Synod of Dort was an assembly of the Reformed Dutch Church, with deputies from Switzerland, the Palatinate, Scotland, England and other lands, held at Dordrecht in 1618 and 1619. It was called to settle the quarrel between the Arminians, or Remonstrants, and the strict Calvinists led in Arminius's lifetime by Francis Gomar of Leiden. The five points of Arminianism, set out in a remonstrance of 1610, denied irresistible grace and held that Christ died for all men.

Conferences at the Hague and Delft failed to reconcile the parties, and a toleration edict of 1614 only fanned the fight. The dispute tangled with politics: the house of Orange backed strict Calvinism, while Oldenbarnevelt and Grotius stood with the Arminians. Prince Maurice imprisoned both men in 1617 and called the synod to crush their party.
britannica-1911-elgin-and-kincardine-ear:
Earls of Elgin and Kincardine are traced in a 1911 Britannica entry that starts with Thomas Bruce, the seventh earl. He was born in 1766, went to Harrow and Westminster, and then studied law and war abroad. He rose in the army but gave most of his care to state service abroad. Posts took him to Brussels, Berlin, and then to the Porte.

While at Constantinople he formed the plan to take the famed Greek carvings now called the Elgin Marbles. The move drew sharp blame, and he set out his case in print in 1810. The state bought the set in 1816 for the British Museum. The entry then turns to his son James, the eighth earl.
britannica-1911-ellenborough-edward-law-:
Ellenborough, Edward Law, Earl of (1790–1871), was the eldest son of the 1st Lord Ellenborough, born on 8 September 1790. He was educated at Eton and at St John's College, Cambridge. He sat in the Commons for St Michael's, Cornwall, until his father's death in 1818 gave him a seat in the Lords. Under Wellington in 1828 he became lord privy seal, then president of the board of control.

At the board of control Ellenborough took a close interest in Indian policy, holding that India's government should pass directly to the crown. He sent Burnes to explore central Asia, watching for a Russian advance. Made governor-general of India, he held that post for only two and a half years, and his term was filled with war. The entry weighs his Afghan policy, his conquest of Sind, and his campaign in Gwalior. He died near Cheltenham on 22 December 1871, and the earldom became extinct.
britannica-1911-ellesmere-francis-egerto:
Ellesmere, Francis Egerton, 1st Earl of (1800–1857), was born in London on 1 January 1800, the second son of the 1st duke of Sutherland. He was known as Lord Francis Leveson Gower until 1833, when he took the surname Egerton alone on inheriting Bridgewater estates. Educated at Eton and at Christ Church, Oxford, he entered parliament soon after coming of age.

In politics Ellesmere was a moderate Conservative of independent views, backing a university of London and free trade long before Peel gave way. He was chief secretary for Ireland from 1828 to July 1830. His lasting fame rests on his service to letters and the fine arts. Before he was twenty he printed a volume of poems, and he later published an early English rendering of Goethe's Faust. He also built a gallery for his pictures that the public could enter free. He died on 18 February 1857.
britannica-1911-elvira-synod-of:
Elvira, Synod of, was a church synod held in Spain whose date cannot be fixed with exactness. Some argue for 300 to 303, before the Diocletian persecution, and others for dates after it. The entry judges 305 or 306 the closest guess the evidence allows. The meeting place, Elvira, stood near the modern Granada, if it was not Granada itself.

There nineteen bishops and twenty-four presbyters from all parts of Spain, chiefly the south, met to restore order and discipline in the church. The eighty-one canons they adopted mirror the life of the Spanish Church in the 4th century. Canons bar marriage and dealings with Jews, pagans, and heretics, and shut Christians out of pagan festivals and games. The entry singles out canon 33, the oldest canon ordering celibacy for clerics, and canon 36, which forbids pictures in churches. Canon 38 allows lay baptism in set cases.
britannica-1911-enoch-book-of:
Book of Enoch is an old Jewish work that stands outside the Bible as it is now fixed. The 1911 Britannica article calls it the most weighty of all such lost or fringe books for the tale of faith. It is not the work of one hand. Parts that once ran under the names of Enoch, Noah, and Methuselah were joined in one mass. The Ethiopic book is set apart from a Slavonic book of the same broad kind.

The book was written in the second and first centuries BC. Writers of the New Testament knew it well. The Epistle of Jude quotes it by name as true work of Enoch. Early church fathers held it near in rank to the canon. By the fourth century it fell under the ban of the church and was lost. In 1773 Bruce found the Ethiopic text in Abyssinia and brought it back.
britannica-1911-ephesus-council-of:
Ephesus, Council of, was a church council called together in 431 to take binding action on the doctrine of the person of Christ. Nicaea and Constantinople had asserted Christ's full divinity and real humanity without defining how the two were joined. The attempts to solve that puzzle produced first Apollinarianism, which set the divine Logos in place of Christ's human mind.

Cyril of Alexandria led the side holding the perfect union of two complete natures in one person, with “God-bearer” as the watchword for Mary. A Roman synod of 430 found Nestorius heretical, and the emperor then summoned the council, which met at Ephesus on 22 June 431. Nestorius, present with an armed escort, refused to attend, since the patriarch of Antioch had not arrived. The council still declared him excommunicate and deposed. The emperor at last banished Nestorius, dissolved the council, and ruled for the orthodox side.
britannica-1911-epiphany-feast-of:
Epiphany, Feast of, takes its name from a Greek word for the appearing of a divine being. The word was used in singular or plural, as one appearing or several joined in one feast were in view. In the East, early on, the feast of Christ's Baptism gathered to itself the birth and the Star of the Magi. It also gathered the miracles of Cana and the feeding of the five thousand. 

Clement of Alexandria first names it, writing about 194 that the Basilidians feasted the day of the Baptism, keeping the night before in scripture readings. The great church had not then taken up the feast, but by about A.D. 300 it was widely kept. By the Nicene age the primate of Alexandria had to announce Easter's date to the churches in a Festal Letter sent at every Epiphany.
britannica-1911-essex-earls-of:
Essex, Earls of, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a line of English earls. The first earl was most likely Geoffrey de Mandeville. He gained the title about 1139, and his two sons held it after him. The line lapsed when the younger son died in 1189. In 1199 Geoffrey Fitzpeter took the title. He was linked to the Mandevilles through his wife.

When that line ended in 1227, the title went back to the crown. It then passed by marriage to the Bohun family. The Bohuns were earls of Hereford as well as Essex. Both titles died out with them in 1373. The Essex title next went to Thomas of Woodstock. He was a son of Edward the Third and wed a Bohun heir.
britannica-1911-essex-kingdom-of:
Essex, Kingdom of, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on one of the kingdoms of Anglo Saxon Britain. Properly it was the land of the East Saxons. Of its origin and early history no record survives, the entry says, beyond Bede's note that its settlers were of the Old Saxon race. Its ruling house claimed descent from Seaxneat, not from Woden.

The article notes the bounds of the later kingdom, the rivers Stour and Thames. Its first limits are quite uncertain, though it likely held most of Hertfordshire and all of Middlesex. Bede first names the kingdom in 604, when its bishop was set over London. Essex then stood close under Kent, ruled by a nephew of the Kentish king. Under him the East Saxons took the Christian faith.
britannica-1911-essex-robert-devereux-2n:
Robert Devereux, second earl of Essex, who lived from 1566 to 1601, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Herefordshire and took a degree at Cambridge in 1581. In 1585 he rode with his stepfather Leicester on a campaign in Holland. He showed great dash at the battle of Zutphen.

At court his good looks won the warm favor of Queen Elizabeth. That favor set him at odds with Raleigh and shaped all his later life. The entry calls his place as chief favorite a harm that led at last to his ruin. Court life galled him, and he longed for deeds abroad. In 1589 he slipped away to join a sea raid on Spain without leave. The queen called him home at his utter peril.
britannica-1911-este-house-of:
Este is one of the oldest of the former reigning houses of Italy, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It is in all probability of Lombard origin in its roots. It is traced, on the word of Muratori, to princes who governed in Tuscany in Carolingian times. The lordship of the town of Este was first won by Alberto Azzo the Second.

Alberto Azzo also bore the title of marquis of Italy and died about 1097. He married Kunitza, sister of Welf the Third, duke of Carinthia, in that age. Through her son Welf the Fourth the house became connected with the houses of Brunswick and Hanover. The Italian titles and estates were inherited by Folco the First, son of Alberto Azzo by his second wife.
britannica-1911-ferrara-florence-council:
The Council of Ferrara Florence, held from 1438 onward, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The entry calls it the peak of a run of failed medieval bids to reunite the Greek and Roman churches. The emperor John had been warned by his father to avoid such talks. Past bids had only bred more bitterness, his father held.

Yet John felt forced to seek union, since the Turks were fast tearing his empire apart. The state of the western church tangled the matter further. Pope Eugenius the Fourth was locked in strife with the council of Basel. Both sides sent envoys to the emperor, since eastern support could decide their own fight. The Greeks at first leaned toward the council party, fearing rule by the papacy.
britannica-1911-floridablanca-don-jose-m:
Don Jose Moñino y Redondo, Count of Floridablanca (1728-1808), was a Spanish statesman from Murcia. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his study of law at Salamanca. He won fame as a lawyer before state work opened to him. As envoy to the pope he handled a hard mission well.

Charles III then made him chief minister in Spain. His rule reformed police, built canals, and backed farming and learning groups. Trade revived, and a long dispute with Portugal was settled. Fear of the French Revolution turned him toward harsh rule later. Dismissed in 1792, he returned in 1808 to head the central junta.
britannica-1911-fonseca-bay-of:
The Bay of Fonseca, also called Amapala or Conchagua, is an inlet of the Pacific Ocean. It lies in the volcanic region between Honduras, Salvador and Nicaragua. In extent and security it is unsurpassed, the entry says, by any other harbour on that Pacific coast. It measures upwards of 50 miles in greatest length and about 30 miles in average width. Its entrance from the sea is about 18 miles wide, set between the great volcanoes of Conchagua and Coseguina.

Two lofty islands and a cluster of rocks called Los Farellones divide the entrance into four channels, each deep enough for the largest vessels. A channel named El Estero Real runs 50 miles inland toward Lake Managua. The entry lists the bay's islands and their owners, Honduras and Salvador. Tigre, the most important, rises in a cone to 2,500 feet, with black lava cliffs on its southern and eastern shores.
britannica-1911-fools-feast-of:
The Feast of Fools, in Latin festum stultorum, is the name for burlesque, half-religious festivals of the middle ages. They were the church's counterpart to the secular revels of the Lord of Misrule. The entry traces them straight to the pagan Saturnalia of ancient Rome. In spite of the empire's conversion and the denunciations of bishops and councils, the people kept the Kalends of January with all their old licence, year after year.

The custom spread with the barbarian peoples who took Rome's lands: Goths in Spain, Franks in Gaul, Alemanni in Germany and Anglo-Saxons in Britain all kept it. As late as the eleventh century Bishop Burchard of Worms thundered against its excesses.
