The long article follows the feast into the medieval church itself, where lesser clergy played at bishops and fools. It shows how an ancient festival of licence survived inside the Christian year for centuries.
britannica-1911-galilee-sea-of:
Galilee, Sea of, is a lake in Palestine, an expansion of the Jordan, 13 miles long and 8 broad, its 64 square miles of water lying 680 feet below the Mediterranean. It is pear-shaped, narrowing southward, and reaches 150 feet in depth. Scripture calls it the Sea of Chinnereth; Josephus and Maccabees name it Gennesar. The Gospels usually call it the Sea of Galilee, twice the Sea of Tiberias, and the Arabic name is Bahr Tubariya. Like the Dead Sea it is a rift lake in the Jordan fault.

The lake sits deep among hills rising 2000 feet on the east, and sudden storms, like those in the Gospels, spring from the differences of level and temperature. Its water, slightly brackish, is drunk. Hot springs abound, the baths south of Tiberias reaching 137° F. The plain of Gennesareth on the west, now almost uncultivated, was praised by Josephus, and the springs of Tabighah feed the basin.
britannica-1911-gersoppa-falls-of:
Falls of Gersoppa is the subject of a falls article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The falls form a cataract on a river in the Bombay district of India. They are counted the finest falls in India. The river drops in four separate cascades. Their names are the Raja or Horseshoe, the Roarer, the Rocket, and the Dame Blanche. The cliff over which the river plunges stands over eight hundred feet high.

The article says the pool at the base of the Raja fall is over a hundred feet deep. Near a village stand wide ruins of an old capital. The finest ruin is a cross shaped temple of the Jain chiefs of Gersoppa. Their family rose to power in 1409 under greater kings. The lordship was held at times by women and fell in 1608.
britannica-1911-glencairn-earls-of:
Glencairn, Earls of, is a family history in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a line of Scottish nobles. The first earl was Alexander Cunningham, made earl in 1488. Weeks later he died at the battle of Sauchieburn, fighting for King James the Third.

The article walks through each heir in turn. Robert lost the title under James the Fourth, and his son Cuthbert won it back. William, the fourth earl, backed the new faith early and often worked for English pay. He fought at Solway Moss in 1542 and was taken there. Alexander, the fifth earl, was a close friend of John Knox. He helped call Knox back to Scotland and took up arms against the regent.
britannica-1911-glendalough-vale-of:
Glendalough is a mountain glen in County Wicklow, Ireland. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica praises both its scenery and its church ruins. No railway reaches the glen, which keeps its look. Cars run to it from Rathdrum station. The Glenealo stream threads the glen and swells into two small lakes. Steep heights wall the upper lake. Lower down the glen widens, and ruins dot the ground.

Those ruins are known as the Seven Churches. A hermit, Saint Kevin, founded the settlement long ago. He is said to have died in the year 618. The place grew into a famed seat of learning. Danes and Normans sacked it more than once. A round tower, among the finest in Ireland, stands 110 feet high. Saint Kevin's church has a steep stone roof and a round bell spire. The entry calls it the earliest of its type.
britannica-1911-gloucester-earls-and-duk:
Earls and dukes of Gloucester held one of the great English titles across many centuries. The 1911 Britannica article lists its holders in turn. The earldom was held by men of the royal house, among them Robert, a son of Henry the First, and John, who later became king. In 1218 Gilbert de Clare was confirmed as earl, and his house kept the title until 1314. That year an Earl Gilbert fell at Bannockburn.

Claims and new grants fill the rest of the entry. Kin of the Clares pressed claims, and Thomas le Despenser gained the earldom in 1397, then lost it and his life soon after. The dukedom began in 1385 with Thomas of Woodstock. Later dukes include Humphrey, son of Henry the Fourth, and Richard, who became King Richard the Third.
britannica-1911-gloucester-gilbert-de-cl:
Gilbert de Clare, earl of Gloucester, lived from 1243 to 1295. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Christchurch in Hampshire. He wed a half sister of Henry the Third. On his father's death in 1262 he took the earldoms of Gloucester and Clare. He joined the barons' party of Simon de Montfort at once. At Lewes in 1264 the king surrendered to him in person.

Gloucester soon quarrelled with Leicester and changed sides. He met Prince Edward after that prince's escape at Ludlow. His skill helped win the battle of Evesham in 1265. The alliance proved as brief as the first. In 1267 he seized London to press the barons' demands. Peace followed fast, and he helped seat Edward the First in 1272. In 1291 a violent feud with the earl of Hereford brought him a fine and prison.
britannica-1911-gloucester-humphrey-duke:
Humphrey, duke of Gloucester, is weighed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1391, he was the fourth son of Henry the Fourth. He was knighted at his father's crowning in 1399. Henry the Fifth made him duke of Gloucester in 1414. He fought in France and was hurt at Agincourt the next year. His brother's valour saved his life on that famed field.

Humphrey took the Cotentin and the port of Cherbourg in 1418. At home he stood as regent while his brother campaigned abroad. Henry's will left him mere deputy to Bedford in England. He claimed full rule and was held to a lesser post. His rash marriage to Jacqueline of Holland stirred fresh strife.
britannica-1911-gloucester-richard-de-cl:
Richard de Clare, Earl of Gloucester, born in twelve twenty two, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was son of Gilbert de Clare, and he gained his father's earldoms at age eight. His first wife was a daughter of Hubert de Burgh. After her death he wed a daughter of the Earl of Lincoln.

His early years went to tourneys and pilgrimages, and his part in politics was minor and shifting. He refused to aid King Henry the Third on a French campaign in twelve fifty. Later he was with the king at Paris and ran errands to Scotland and Germany. About twelve fifty eight he took his place as a leader of the barons against the king. He quarrelled with Simon de Montfort, then made peace with him again.
britannica-1911-gloucester-robert-earl-o:
Robert, Earl of Gloucester, who died in 1147, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Henry the First of England, born at Caen in Normandy. Through his wife Mabel, a rich heir, he gained the lordships of Gloucester and Glamorgan. The earldom of Gloucester was made for him about 1121.

The life then traces his part in the fight for the throne after his father died. He first backed King Stephen, then broke with him and raised revolt in the west in 1138. His win at Lincoln in 1141, where Stephen was caught, made good the claim of his half sister Matilda. The entry shows why his lands and rank made him a key power in the realm.
britannica-1911-gloucester-thomas-of-woo:
Thomas of Woodstock, duke of Gloucester, lived from 1355 to 1397. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica shows him checking his nephew king. He was the seventh and youngest son of Edward the Third. He was born at Woodstock in January 1355.

Marriage to a Bohun heiress brought him the constable office. His nephew Richard made him earl of Buckingham in 1377. He fought French and Castilian raids, then led an army in France. A failed siege of Nantes marred that campaign abroad. Home strife over his wife sister marriage strained his house ties. He helped crush the peasants rising of 1381 in Essex. In 1385 the king made him duke of Gloucester. He soon led the party that hated the royal favorites. That party forced out the chief minister in 1386.
britannica-1911-godolphin-sidney-godolph:
Sidney Godolphin, Earl of Godolphin (about 1645-1712), is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came of an ancient family of Cornwall. At the Restoration he was brought into the royal household by Charles the Second, whose favour he had won before. At the same time he entered the House of Commons as member for Helston.

The article notes a strange kind of rise. He seldom spoke in the House, and then only in the fewest words. Yet he slowly won a name as its chief, if not its only, master of finance. In 1679 he joined the privy council and was raised, with two others, to the top management of affairs. Though he voted for the bill to bar the king's brother from the throne, he kept his place. In 1684 he was made a baron and put at the head of the treasury.
britannica-1911-gondomar-diego-sarmiento:
Diego Sarmiento de Acuna, count of Gondomar, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Galicia in Spain in fifteen sixty seven, he was the eldest son of a royal official. His mother was an heiress of the Acuna family. He inherited wide estates in Galicia and in Old Castile.

In fifteen eighty three King Philip the Second gave him command of the frontier with Portugal. That post covered the sea coast of Galicia as well. He is said to have taken an active part in beating back an English raid on the coast. The entry follows his rise toward his famed role as a Spanish envoy.
britannica-1911-goose-game-of:
Goose is an old French board game said to come from Greek roots. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls it very popular at the close of the middle ages. Play used a card with a curling track called the goose garden. Sixty three spaces bore signs such as dice, an inn, and a bridge.

A goose marked the first and last spaces and each ninth space between. Two dice set how far a counter moved on each turn. Landing on the inn forced a wait while rivals played twice. Landing on the death head sent a player back to the start. Stakes and fines for set spaces raised the risk in play.
britannica-1911-gowrie-john-ruthven-3rd-:
John Ruthven, third earl of Gowrie, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a Scottish conspirator. He lived from about 1577 to 1600. He was the second son of the first earl of Gowrie. His mother was Dorothea, daughter of Lord Methven. The Ruthven family was of ancient Scottish stock. It held large estates as far back as William the Lion. Its peerage dated from the year 1488.

The men of the house had a dark record in plots. His grandfather and father both had a part in Rizzio's murder. Both men also sided with the Kirk in faction fights. The first earl held Mary, queen of Scots, at Loch Leven. He led the raid that seized young King James the Sixth. That raid is known as the raid of Ruthven. The entry sets the son against this charged family past.
britannica-1911-grafton-dukes-of:
Grafton is an English dukedom traced through its holders in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The dukes descend from Henry Fitzroy, a natural son of Charles the Second by Barbara Villiers. In 1675 the boy was made duke of Grafton.

The first duke was raised a sailor and served at the siege of Luxemburg. In the Monmouth rebellion he led royal troops in Somerset. Yet he later joined William of Orange against King James. His grandson, the third duke, became a leading politician of his age. In 1766 he stood first lord of the treasury under Chatham. When illness felled Chatham, he led in fact. Attacks in print drove him to resign in 1770.
britannica-1911-granby-john-manners-marq:
John Manners, Marquess of Granby, a British soldier who lived from 1721 to 1770, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was the eldest son of the third duke of Rutland. He was schooled at Eton and at Trinity College, Cambridge. In 1741 he was returned to parliament for Grantham.

Four years later he was made colonel of a regiment raised by the Rutland interest. It was meant to help put down the Highland revolt of 1745. The corps never got past Newcastle. Granby went to the front as a volunteer on the duke of Cumberland's staff. He saw active service in the last stages of the rising. His regiment was soon disbanded. He kept his seat in parliament and joined it with army duties. In 1747 he made the campaign of Flanders. The piece follows a soldier-statesman at the start of his rise.
britannica-1911-haddington-earl-of:
The earldom of Haddington is a Scottish title created in 1627. Thomas Hamilton, earl of Melrose, received it. He lived from 1563 to 1637. He was a lawyer from the great Hamilton family. In 1592 he became a lord of session as Lord Drumcairn. James VI trusted his legal talents greatly. Hamilton was one of the eight Octavians of 1596. They managed Scotland's finances for the king.

He became king's advocate in 1596 as well. When James moved to London in 1603, Hamilton carried much of Scotland's government. He became secretary of state in 1612. The earldom of Melrose came in 1619. He exchanged it for Haddington in 1627. Under Charles I he served as lord privy seal. He left a large and valuable library at his death. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the earl of Haddington entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-halifax-charles-montague:
Charles Montague, earl of Halifax, lived from 1661 to 1715 and served the state. The 1911 Britannica life adds that he was also a poet of note. He was born at Horton in Northamptonshire in April 1661. At age fourteen he went to Westminster school as a king's scholar. There he shone at quick verse made on set themes for tests.

In 1679 he entered Trinity College at Cambridge as a youth. He built a firm grasp of the classics while there at school. In logic and in ethics he beat all his peers of that age. Later he turned from Descartes to the work of Isaac Newton. He joined the small band who helped Newton form a learned society.
britannica-1911-halifax-george-montagu-d:
George Montagu Dunk, second earl of Halifax, who lived from 1716 to 1771, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He became earl on his father's death in 1739, after Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge. His wife brought him a great fortune and the name Dunk. In 1748 he became president of the Board of Trade.

In that post he helped found Halifax, the capital of Nova Scotia, which bears his name. He gave good service to trade, most of all with North America. In 1761 he went as lord lieutenant to Ireland, and in 1762 he became secretary of state. He signed the general warrant under which Wilkes was seized in 1763, for which courts later fined him. He left office in 1765, came back in 1770, and died in 1771, his titles dying with him.
britannica-1911-halifax-george-savile-1s:
George Savile, first Marquess of Halifax, an English statesman and writer who lived from 1633 to 1695, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of Sir William Savile, who stood out in the civil war for the royalists and died in 1644. His mother was a daughter of Lord Keeper Coventry.

Savile was thus nephew to Sir William Coventry, who is said to have shaped his political opinions, and to Lord Shaftesbury, afterwards his most bitter opponent. By marriage he became brother in law to Lord Sunderland. He entered public life with all the advantages of lineage, political connections, great wealth and estates, and uncommon abilities. In 1660 he was elected to the Convention parliament for Pontefract, his only appearance in the Lower House. A peerage sought for him in 1665 was blocked by Clarendon.
britannica-1911-halsbury-hardinge-stanle:
Hardinge Stanley Giffard, 1st earl of Halsbury (1825– ), was an English lord chancellor. He was born in London on 3 September 1825. His father was Stanley Lees Giffard. Merton College, Oxford, educated him. The Inner Temple called him to the bar in 1850. He built a large practice at the central criminal court. The Overend and Gurney and Tichborne trials engaged him.

He became queen's counsel in 1865. Twice he contested Cardiff without success. Disraeli made him solicitor-general in 1875, with a knighthood. Launceston returned him to Parliament in 1877. In 1885 he rose to the peerage as Baron Halsbury. He took the woolsack that year, a rare feat for a criminal lawyer. He held it until 1892 and again from 1895 to 1905. No chancellor since Eldon had served so long. The earldom came in 1898.
britannica-1911-hamilton-james-hamilton-:
James Hamilton, 1st duke of Hamilton (1606–1649), was a Scottish nobleman. He was born on 19 June 1606. After James VI's descendants he stood heir to Scotland's throne. He married at fourteen; his bride was seven. Oxford's Exeter College educated him. He succeeded his father as marquess in 1625. In 1631 he led 6,000 men to help Gustavus Adolphus. Disease and starvation destroyed that army in Germany.

He returned to England in 1634 as Charles I's chief Scottish adviser. The Prayer-Book revolt made him commissioner for Scotland in 1638. Covenanting leaders intimidated him easily, contemporaries charged. He urged Charles to give way instead of fighting. Suspicion grew that he courted the Scots' favour for himself. The long narrative follows his missions back and forth. His end on the scaffold in 1649 closes it. His supposed treachery is weighed from the Thomason Tracts.
britannica-1911-hardwicke-philip-yorke-1:
Philip Yorke, first Earl of Hardwicke, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Dover on the first of December 1690, he was an English lord chancellor. His father was an attorney, and the boy entered an attorney's office in London at the age of fourteen.

The article traces a swift rise in the law. His powers caught the eye of the chief justice of the day, who brought him to the Middle Temple. Called to the bar in 1715, he moved to the court of chancery and won quick fame. A case for the Walpole family in 1719 fixed his name as a master of equity law. He entered parliament that year and rose to solicitor general in 1720. High treason trials added to his fame as a speaker.
britannica-1911-harrowby-dudley-ryder-1s:
Dudley Ryder, first earl of Harrowby, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London in December seventeen sixty two, he was the eldest son of Nathaniel Ryder, first Baron Harrowby. His grandfather Sir Dudley Ryder had risen in the law. That rise owed much to the favour of Sir Robert Walpole.

The grandfather became solicitor general, then attorney general, and was knighted. In seventeen fifty four he was made lord chief justice and a privy councillor. A peerage patent for him was signed but never passed, since he died first. Against that family record the entry turns to the earl's own public career.
britannica-1911-hastings-francis-rawdon-:
Hastings, Francis Rawdon-Hastings, first Marquess of, is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a British soldier and ruler of India. He was born on the ninth of December 1754 and died in 1826. His father was an Irish peer, Baron Rawdon of Moira. His mother was a daughter of the earl of Huntingdon.

Lord Rawdon was schooled at Harrow and Oxford and joined the army in 1771. The article splits his life into four parts. From 1775 to 1782 he served with honour in the American war. From 1783 to 1813 he held high posts at home and sat in the Lords. From 1813 to 1823 came his great years of work in India. His last post, from 1824, was governor of Malta. In America he fought at Bunker Hill.
britannica-1911-hertford-earls-and-marqu:
Earls and Marquesses of Hertford are traced in a 1911 Britannica entry that spans five centuries of one title. The Clare family held the earldom from about 1138 until an earl fell at Bannockburn in 1314. In 1537 Edward Seymour, brother of Queen Jane Seymour, was made earl. Ten years later he rose to duke of Somerset and protector of England.

His son Edward lost the title when his father was attainted, then regained it in 1559. A secret marriage to Lady Catherine Grey angered Queen Elizabeth and sent both spouses to prison. The entry follows their son and grandson William, who became marquess in 1640. It gives a clear line of descent through plots, falls, and returns to favour.
britannica-1911-hildebrand-lay-of:
The Lay of Hildebrand (Das Hildebrandslied) is a unique survival of Old German alliterative poetry. Two monks of Fulda wrote it about the year 800 on the flyleaves of a theological manuscript. The fragment runs to sixty-eight lines, and the ending is lost. Its mixed Low and High German forms point to a Low German original.

Hildebrand, home after thirty years among the Huns, is challenged by a young warrior. Asking his name, he finds his own son Hadubrand, left behind as an infant when he followed Theodoric eastward. He tries to stop the fight, but the son takes his words for cowardice. Spears fall, swords hew the white shields to pieces, and there the fragment breaks off, the issue untold.
britannica-1911-hippolytus-the-canons-of:
The Canons of Hippolytus is the subject of a church book article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The book stands at the head of a series of church orders. Those orders give rules for choosing and ordaining ministers. They also cover widows and virgins, the taking in of converts, and baptism. Rules for the shared meal, fasting, daily prayer, and first fruits follow.

The article sets out its plan in three parts. First it describes the book as we now have it. Next it states how the book relates to kindred documents. Last it treats evidence for its date and author. The canons survive only in an Arabic version made from a Coptic one. The Greek original is lost. The book is split into thirty eight canons with short headings. Early canons govern the choice of bishops, priests, and deacons.
britannica-1911-hof:
Hof is a town of Germany, in the Bavarian province of Upper Franconia, set on the Saale at the north-eastern spurs of the Fichtelgebirge, 103 m. S.W. of Leipzig. Its people numbered 36,348 in 1905. It has one Roman Catholic and three Protestant churches, a town hall of 1563, a gymnasium with a large library, and a hospital founded in 1262.

Hof is a seat of busy industry: woollen, cotton and jute spinning and weaving, dye-works, flour-mills, breweries, iron-works, and makers of machinery, chemicals and sugar. Marble quarries and iron mines lie near. First called Regnitzhof and built about 1080, it was sold in 1373 to the burgraves of Nuremberg. It passed to Prussia in 1792, to France in 1806, and to Bavaria in 1810. A fire destroyed most of the town in 1823.
britannica-1911-holdernesse-earl-of:
Holdernesse is an English earldom borne first by Sir John Ramsay and later by the Darcy family. Ramsay, a Scot of the Dalhousie house, was knighted for helping rescue James VI from the earl of Gowrie in 1600. James made him Viscount Haddington in 1606 and earl of Holdernesse in 1621. He died without surviving issue in 1626, and the titles died with him.

Charles I created Prince Rupert earl of Holdernesse in 1644, but the title lapsed again at his death in 1682. Days later Conyers Darcy received it, and it passed to his son and grandson. Robert Darcy, the 4th earl (1718–1778), was ambassador at Venice and the Hague, then a secretary of state from 1751 to 1761. Dismissed by George III, he later governed two of the king's sons. He left no sons, and the earldom ended, though the old barony of Conyers passed to his daughter Amelia.
britannica-1911-holland-henry-rich-1st-e:
Henry Rich, 1st Earl of Holland (1590–1649), was the second son of Robert, earl of Warwick, and of Penelope, Sir Philip Sidney's Stella. Baptized in 1590, he was educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, knighted in 1610, and sat in parliament for Leicester. James I showered favours on him: gentleman of the bedchamber to Prince Charles, captain of the yeomen of the guard, and in 1623 Baron Kensington.

In 1624 Rich went to Paris to negotiate Charles's marriage to Henrietta Maria, and that September he was created earl of Holland. He later commanded the troops sent to aid Buckingham at Rhé, but started late and met only the beaten men returning. He became master of the horse in 1628 and a proprietor of Newfoundland in 1637. As chief-justice-in-eyre he revived the hated forest laws. At court he intrigued against Portland and Strafford, who held him in open contempt.
britannica-1911-home-earls-of:
The earls of Home head an old and famous Scottish border family. An early member, Sir Alexander Home, fell at Verneuil in 1424. His son, another Sir Alexander, was warden of the marches and founder of the family's fortunes. His son was made Lord Home in 1473 and stood among the nobles who beat James III at Sauchieburn in 1488. The 3rd Lord Home was chamberlain to James IV and fought at Flodden.

That 3rd lord quarrelled with the regent Albany in James V's minority, intrigued with England, and was beheaded for treason in 1516; his brother George regained the title in 1522. Alexander, the 5th lord, fought Mary, queen of Scots, at Carberry Hill and Langside, then became her stalwart supporter. He was taken defending Edinburgh castle for her in 1573. His son became 6th Lord Home in 1575 and 1st earl of Home.
britannica-1911-huntingdon-selina-hastin:
Selina Hastings, countess of Huntingdon, an English religious leader who lived from 1707 to 1791, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. She founded a body of Calvinistic Methodists known by her name. Born in Leicestershire, she was the daughter of an earl. At twenty one she married the ninth earl of Huntingdon.

In 1739 she joined the first Methodist society in London, the entry says. On her husband's death in 1746 she cast her lot with Wesley and Whitefield in the great revival. In 1748 she made Whitefield her chaplain, and he often preached in her London house. Hearers there included lords and wits of the day. At her Bath chapel, bishops sat hidden in a curtained corner to hear him. She spent her ample means building chapels in many places.
britannica-1911-huntly-earls-and-marques:
Huntly is the subject of a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Huntly title, held by the Gordon family in Scotland, dates as an earldom from 1449. As a marquessate it dates from 1599 and ranks first in Scotland. The first earl was Alexander de Seton, lord of Gordon. His son married a daughter of King James the First of Scotland.

The article follows the third earl, who made his house supreme in the north. He led the Scottish front line at Flodden. The fourth earl played a leading part in the troubles of his time. He revolted against Queen Mary and was killed in battle in 1562. His son was restored to the lost earldom and backed Mary for some years. The first marquess, born in 1562, was schooled in France as a Catholic and joined plots at court.
britannica-1911-inchiquin-murrough-o-bri:
Murrough O'Brien, 1st Earl of Inchiquin (c. 1614–1674), was an Irish soldier and statesman. He was the son of Dermod O'Brien, 5th Baron Inchiquin, and his family traced its line back to Brian Boroimhe, king of Ireland. He became 6th baron in 1624, gained army experience in Italy, and in 1640 was made vice-president of Munster.

He took a leading part in putting down the great Irish rising that broke out the next year. Parliament made him president of Munster, but early in 1648 he declared for Charles I and upheld the royal cause in Ireland for about two years. Charles II made him an earl in 1654. His last years were spent partly in France and Spain, and he died in Ireland on the 9th of September 1674. His son William, the 2nd earl, governed Tangier and then Jamaica. The earldom died out in 1855, while the barony passed to a kinsman.
britannica-1911-inebriety-law-of:
The law of inebriety covers the legal ties that drunkenness gives rise to in daily life. Those ties are partly civil and partly criminal in their kind. On civil capacity, English law treats the drunkard much as it treats the mentally ill. The two fields have passed through much the same stages of growth. A man may still wed or make a valid will while drunk.

He may also bind himself by contract while in that state, under set limits. He must be sober enough to know what he is doing at the time. No unfair advantage may be taken of his state by the other party. The law is the same in Scotland and in Ireland on this point. A sale law of eighteen ninety three adds a rule on goods sold. If goods that are necessaries are sold to a drunk man, he must pay a fair price.
britannica-1911-inkerman-battle-of:
Battle of Inkerman was fought on the fifth of November 1854 in the Crimean War. A 1911 Britannica entry places Allied English and French troops against a Russian army under Menshikov. The name comes from a ruin by the Tchernaya river near its mouth. The fight itself fell on a nameless ridge between river and ravine.

Home Ridge on that ground was held by British troops at the start. French troops under Bosquet guarded the rear toward the Balaklava battlefield side. Russian plans joined two forces, of sixteen and nineteen thousand men in all. Their aim was to strike the ridge and break the siege of Sevastopol.
britannica-1911-james-epistle-of:
Epistle of James is a book of the New Testament, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its opening line ascribes it to James, a pillar of the first church at Jerusalem. He is shown as fit to address a general letter to the twelve tribes of the dispersion. The text argues that phrase is a figure for the whole new people of God.

That reading rests on the context of the letter and on its links with other early writings. The tribes are not a literal blood line in this view of the piece. They are a people begotten in spirit by the word received in faith, as Paul described the Israel of God. The text then sets that view against a literal reading of the phrase. The piece is dense and learned, with close weighing of Greek terms and of cross references throughout.
britannica-1911-jashar-book-of:
Jashar, Book of, is the subject of a Bible entry in the 1911 Britannica. The Hebrew name for it is given in the entry. It is named as a well known work in two Bible texts. Those texts lie in Joshua and in Samuel. From them it seems to have been a book of songs. Those songs dealt with great events of the folk. No early set of that kind now survives at all. Nothing more is known of the book itself.

Guesses on the name take up much of the entry. One guess ties it to a word for the upright. That would mean Israel or its famed men. One guess makes it a twist of a word for song. One guess reads its first word as sing in command form. Since it held a lament of David, it postdates him.
britannica-1911-jeremy-epistle-of:
Epistle of Jeremy is an apocryphal book of the Old Testament in letter form. Its book entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The letter claims to be by Jeremiah to exiles bound for Babylon. Scholars hold the true author was a Hellenistic Jew, likely of Alexandria.

The writer warns exiles they will stay in thrall for seven generations. He urges them to shun the idol worship they will see there. Idols, he says, are mere hand work with no speech or hearing. They cannot bless their followers even in the smallest life concerns. With sharp irony he likens an idol to a scarecrow in a field.
britannica-1911-jersey-earls-of:
Jersey, Earls of, is the head under which the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica traces a noble line. It starts with Sir Edward Villiers, born about sixteen fifty six. He was made baron and viscount in sixteen ninety one. Six years later he was made earl of Jersey.

His grandfather held high posts at the mint and in Munster. That elder was half brother to the first duke of Buckingham. The new earl held posts in the royal house in turn. He served two rulers as a chief of their house staff. He spoke for his land at a great peace meet and as an envoy at The Hague and in Paris. In time he held a chief state post as well. His sister was a close friend of the king and a countess in her own right.
britannica-1911-jubilee-year-of:
The Year of Jubilee, in the Bible, is the name given in Leviticus chapter twenty five to the keeping of every fiftieth year. In that year the land was to rest in full: no sowing, and not even the natural growth of field and vine was to be gathered.

At the start of the year, the freeing of all Israelite slaves and the return of family lands were to be proclaimed. The name itself, from the Hebrew yōbēl, is taken to mean a ram or a ram's horn. The year thus means the year opened by the blowing of the ram's horn. By the text, the trumpet was to sound through the land on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement. Liberty was then proclaimed, each man returning to his land and family.
britannica-1911-jubilees-book-of:
The Book of Jubilees is an apocryphal work of the Old Testament. It retells the history of the world from the creation to the giving of the Law on Sinai, rewritten from the Pharisaic standpoint of its time. It stands as the oldest commentary on Genesis and part of Exodus, filling gaps in the Bible story.

The book takes its main name from its scheme of time, which splits the history into jubilee spans of forty nine years each. It is also known as The Little Genesis, from its fuller handling of small details. Other names attach to it, among them The Apocalypse of Moses. Its aim was to defend Judaism as the Pharisees of the 2nd century B.C. held it, against the pull of Greek thought. The long article works through its titles, its aim, and its place among the writings of its age.
britannica-1911-kent-earls-and-dukes-of:
Kent, Earls and Dukes of, is a family article tracing the holders of the Kentish earldom. The first holder was probably Odo, bishop of Bayeux, and the second a certain William de Ypres, who died in 1162. The regent Hubert de Burgh gained the honour in 1227, and in 1321 it passed to Edmund Plantagenet, the youngest brother of Edward II.

Edmund (1301–1330) was born at Woodstock on the 5th of August 1301. He had many marks of favour from his brother the king, whom he backed steadily until the last act of Edward's reign opened in 1326. He fought in Scotland and in France, and sat on the council of Edward III. Soon at odds with Queen Isabella and Roger Mortimer, Edmund was drawn into a plot to restore Edward II. He was arrested and beheaded on the 19th of March 1330, condemned as a traitor.
britannica-1911-kimberley-john-wodehouse:
John Wodehouse, first Earl of Kimberley, an English statesman who lived from 1826 to 1902, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in January 1826, eldest son of a Wodehouse heir. He succeeded his grandfather as Baron Wodehouse in 1846. Eton and Oxford gave him a first class in classics.

A Liberal by inheritance, Kimberley entered office young under Aberdeen and Palmerston. He also went as envoy to Russia for two years. A mission to Copenhagen in 1863 sought peace in a Danish quarrel and failed. In 1864 he became Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland at a hard hour. There he grappled with the first Fenian risings. His vigour in that post won him his earldom in 1866. Under Gladstone he later held the colonial office. The great diamond town of Kimberley in South Africa bears his name.
britannica-1911-kings-first-and-second-b:
The First and Second Books of Kings are two books of the Bible, the last of the old histories called the Former Prophets. The 1911 Britannica entry notes they were once counted as a single book. Greek texts split them in two and called them the third and fourth books of Kingdoms, the books of Samuel being the first two.

The entry warns that the split is not a neat one. No single author wrote Kings or Samuel, it says. Editors shaped the tale from older sources, adding a time frame and notes to stress the moral sense of the past. Beneath that frame, readers can still see the seams of the mixed source texts the editors drew on and cut to fit.
britannica-1911-kingston-elizabeth-duche:
Elizabeth, Duchess of Kingston, who lived from 1720 to 1788, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Colonel Thomas Chudleigh and was also at times called Countess of Bristol. In 1743 she became a maid of honour to Augusta, Princess of Wales. The entry notes her beauty and names two men who sought her hand, a duke and a naval officer.

She wed the naval officer, Augustus John Hervey, in secret in August 1744. Both were poor, so the marriage stayed hidden to let her keep her post at court. Hervey went back to his ship, and the pair soon lived apart in an unhappy match. Trouble grew when Hervey looked set to become Earl of Bristol. The hidden marriage then turned into a public problem with real legal weight.
britannica-1911-la-hogue-battle-of:
The battle of La Hogue is the name now given to a run of sea fights from the 19th to the 23rd of May 1692. They were fought between an allied British and Dutch fleet and a French force, off the Cotentin in Normandy. French troops and Jacobite exiles had gathered in the Cotentin, and Louis XIV had prepared a fleet to cover their crossing of the Channel.

The count of Tourville thus sailed with only 45 or 47 ships of the line. Against him the British fleet of 63 sail under Edward Russell was joined at St Helens on the 15th of May by 36 Dutch ships under van Allemonde. Tourville's boldness is explained by a belief that many British captains, discontented after the Revolution of 1688, would cross over to James II. The first clash took place off Cape Barfleur, by which name the battle was once often called.
britannica-1911-lading-bill-of: A bill of lading is the document a ship's master gives to the consignor of goods as a receipt. It stands as a guarantee that the goods will be delivered safely to the consignee. The word lading comes from "to lade," the Old English hladan, to put cargo on board, and is kin to load. The law behind the document is treated under affreightment.
britannica-1911-lancaster-henry-earl-of:
Henry, earl of Lancaster, who lived from about 1281 to 1345, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the second son of Edmund, earl of Lancaster, and so a grandson of Henry the Third. In early life he campaigned in Flanders, Scotland, and Wales. Yet he stayed in the shadow of his elder brother Thomas.

The entry turns on the fall of that brother, who lost his life in 1322 for opposing the king. Henry was made earl of Leicester in 1324 but could not gain the Lancaster titles and lands that were his by right. When Queen Isabella rose against her husband in 1326, Henry joined her at once. He helped in the moves against the king and kept Edward as a prisoner at Kenilworth.
britannica-1911-lancaster-house-of:
The House of Lancaster names the line of English kings sprung from John of Gaunt, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the house to its root. John of Gaunt was the fourth son of Edward the Third. The history of the family and title reaches back to Henry the Third. That king made his second son Edmund earl of Lancaster in 1267.

Edmund gained the surname Crouchback in his own day. The entry corrects a later guess about that name. It did not come from a bent back or deformity. It came from the cross he wore on his back, in token of a crusading vow. Edmund matters little in history in himself. A strange theory about his birth, raised in a later age, gives him his weight. His son Thomas inherited the title and led the nobles of his time.
britannica-1911-lancaster-john-of-gaunt-:
John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster (1340-1399), is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the fourth son of Edward the Third and Queen Philippa, born at Ghent in March 1340, whence his name of Gaunt. He was made Earl of Richmond as a child in 1342, and knighted in 1355.

The article says his marriage in 1359 to Blanche, heiress of the Duke of Lancaster, made him the greatest lord in England. Through her he took the earldom in 1361 and a dukedom the next year. In 1366 he joined his eldest brother in Aquitaine, and the next year led a force into Spain to back Pedro the Cruel, fighting in the front rank at Najera.
britannica-1911-lauderdale-john-maitland:
John Maitland, duke of Lauderdale, gets a close life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1616, he was the eldest son to live of the earl of Lauderdale. He began public life as a strong friend of the Presbyterian cause. He took the covenant and sat as an elder at St Andrews in 1643. That year he went to England as a help for the covenant.

Lauderdale sat on the joint board of both kingdoms in 1644. He pressed King Charles to accept Presbyterian rule at Uxbridge talks. Then he swung round to the king and worked for his return. At Carisbrooke in 1647 he won from Charles a pledge called the Engagement.
britannica-1911-laymen-houses-of:
Houses of Laymen are assemblies of the laity of the Church of England, one for Canterbury and one for York, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives them a short church entry. The Canterbury house was formed in 1886, and the York house shortly afterwards. They are merely consultative bodies, and their first purpose was to join the laity to the work of convocation. They have no legal status.

Members are elected by the diocesan conferences, which are in turn elected by the laity of the parishes or rural deaneries. London sends ten members, four named dioceses send six each, and the rest send four each. The president of each house may appoint up to ten more laymen at his discretion. The entry is brief, but it fixes how the lay voice was organized in the Church of England of that day.
britannica-1911-lazarus-st-order-of:
Saint Lazarus, Order of, a religious and military order, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was founded in Jerusalem about the middle of the twelfth century. Its first aim was the care of the sick, above all lepers. Lazarus was regarded as the patron of lepers, and the order took his name.

From the thirteenth century the order spread to Sicily, lower Italy, Germany, and above all France. In 1253 Louis the Ninth gave its members lands at Boigny and a building at the gates of Paris. They turned that building into a lazar house for the lepers of the city. A papal confirmation came from Alexander the Fourth in 1255. The knights, one hundred in number, could marry and hold pensions. As leprosy faded, the order grew more secular over time, and branches merged with other orders.
britannica-1911-leicester-earls-of:
Leicester is an English earldom traced through its holders in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The first family to hold it was that of Beaumont. Robert de Beaumont, who died in 1118, is often said to have gained it from Henry the First. That claim, the article says, is an error.

His son Robert was without doubt earl of Leicester by 1131. The third Beaumont earl joined the stewardship of England to the title. That dignity stayed with the earldom until 1399, when it merged in the crown. The line failed in 1204, and King John confirmed a Montfort heir in the earldom. His son, the famed Simon de Montfort, lost it by attainder and death at Evesham. The title then passed down the Lancaster line to John of Gaunt. Elizabeth revived it in 1564 for her favourite, Robert Dudley.
britannica-1911-leicester-robert-dudley-:
Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He lived from about 1531 to 1588. He was the favourite of Queen Elizabeth. He came of an ambitious family. They were not the mere upstarts their enemies loved to call them.

His grandfather was the notorious Edmund Dudley. Edmund was one of the chief tools of the extortions of Henry the Seventh. Yet he descended from a younger branch of the barons of Dudley. The love of power was a passion in the family. It seems to have grown with each generation. The grandfather was beheaded by Henry the Eighth. His service to the prior reign had been too devoted. The father grew strong enough, in the days of Edward the Sixth, to trouble the succession. That father was John Dudley, duke of Northumberland. The article opens a life lived one step from the throne.
britannica-1911-leicester-robert-sidney-:
Robert Sidney, earl of Leicester, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1563, he was the second son of Sir Henry Sidney. He learned at Christ Church, Oxford, then spent years seeing Europe. In 1585 he sat in parliament for Glamorganshire. That year he sailed to the Netherlands to fight Spain.

Sidney stood by his elder brother Philip when Philip was fatally hurt. He served as governor of Flushing and fought on in the Dutch war. James the First made him Baron Sidney, then Viscount Lisle. In 1618 he became earl of Leicester. At his seat, Penshurst, he backed writers and lived in high style.
britannica-1911-leicester-thomas-william:
Thomas William Coke is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English land improver known as Coke of Norfolk. Born in seventeen fifty four, he came into great estates in Norfolk as a young man. He sat in parliament for the county for most of his long life.

The entry says his true fame rests on his farms, not on his votes. His land at Holkham was poor and worn when he took it in hand. He brought in new methods and the best advice he could find. Wheat grew where it had failed, and herds and flocks grew strong. The rent from the estate rose more than nine fold in his time.
britannica-1911-lepanto-battle-of:
Lepanto was a sea fight of 7 October 1571. Turkish seizure of Cyprus scared the sea states into a holy league. Pope Pius V drove the league. Venice and Philip II of Spain gave most of its force. Chief command went to Don John of Austria, Philip's half-brother.

Two hundred galleys and eight galeasses made the allied fleet. Most ships came from Venice. Genoa, the pope, Sicily, and Naples sent the rest. Eight thousand Spanish troops sailed with it. The Turkish fleet held 273 lighter galleys. Bows still served its men more than guns. The fleets met near Cape Scropha in set line. Loss fell at 20,000 Turks and 8,000 Christians. Turkish sea power took a blow it never shook off.
britannica-1911-lerma-francisco-de-sando:
Francisco de Sandoval y Rojas, duke of Lerma (1552-1625), ruled Spain in all but name for twenty years. Page at court from age thirteen, he won the favour of the prince who became Philip III in 1598. A dukedom came in 1599. The king let him sign royal papers in the royal name.

Power served him ill and served Spain worse. A near-bankrupt state was pushed to spend more. His own fortune was put at forty-four million ducats. The Moriscoes were cast out in 1610 on his drive. War with England dragged to 1604. Fleet and army shrank while funds failed. His own son plotted his fall with the king's confessor. Out he went on 4 October 1618. A cardinal's hat, won that same year, shielded his last years.
britannica-1911-leven-and-melville-earls:
Leven and Melville are two Scottish earldoms held by one family, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the line from its root. The Melvilles descend from Sir John Melville of Raith in Fifeshire. Sir John belonged to the reforming party in Scotland. He was put to death for high treason on the thirteenth of December 1548.

His son Robert lived from 1527 to 1621 and rose high in service. Robert had been a stout partisan of Mary, queen of Scots, and spoke for her at the English court. He held key offices in Scotland under her son, James the Sixth. In 1616 he was made a lord of parliament as Lord Melville of Monymaill. The fourth holder of that lordship was George, born about 1634. The entry follows the line as the two earldoms came together in one house.
britannica-1911-lights-ceremonial-use-of:
Lights in church rites form the subject here. Two roots are proposed. One is plain meaning: light stands for joy and life, dark for death. The other is taking up of older Jewish and pagan rites, with new Christian sense laid on them.

Fire held a sacred place in many faiths. Parsis honour it as the seen form of their god of light. Brahmans treat it as divine. The Hindu feast of Dewali fills homes and temples with lamps each November. In the Jewish temple a branched lampstand burned without pause. Synagogues keep a lamp that never goes out. Lamps by the thousand light the Ka'ba at Mecca. Greek torch races and Roman sacred fire get their place before the Christian use is traced.
britannica-1911-limitation-statutes-of:
Statutes of limitation are acts that cap the time to sue in the United Kingdom. A set term runs from the act that gives cause to sue. When the term lapses, the claim dies for good. The plan uses time to close old fights. Law holds that the state gains when suits reach an end.

Two tools work to that end. Prescription backs long use as a sound title. Limitation counts the years a claimant sat out of use. Land suits came first in English law. Early acts set a fixed start date. Richard I's first year became the line of legal memory. Fixed dates wore out in time. Counting back set years took their place. The act of 1623 set the frame for most claims in person. Land acts of 1833 and 1874 cut the land term from twenty years to twelve.
britannica-1911-lincoln-earls-of:
Earls of Lincoln form a line traced name by name here. William de Roumare, made earl about 1140, stands first in all likelihood. A grandson of the same name is at times called earl, but no grant backs the claim. King Stephen gave the title to Gilbert de Gand about 1148.

Death left the title asleep for near sixty years. A second Gilbert took it in 1216. Ranulf of Chester then claimed it, and through his sister Hawise it passed to the Lacy house. John de Lacy became earl in 1232. Henry, third Lacy earl, serves the long middle of the tale. He fought for Edward I in Wales, France, and Scotland. Gascony command came in 1296 and Falkirk field in 1298. Talks with two popes and with Philip IV fill his last years. He joined the ordainers of 1310.
britannica-1911-linlithgow-john-adrian-l:
John Adrian Louis Hope, first marquess of Linlithgow (1860-1908), was a British administrator, and this 1911 Britannica entry opens with his family's long story. He was the son of the sixth earl of Hopetoun. The Hopes traced their line to John de Hope, who came from France to Scotland in 1537 in the train of Queen Madeleine. One branch gave Scotland its lord advocates and the earls of Hopetoun.

Another branch settled in Amsterdam and founded the famous Dutch banking house of Hope. The fourth earl was a noted soldier of the Peninsular War and was made Baron Niddry in 1814. The marquessate itself was granted to the seventh earl in 1902. The award marked his success as the first governor of the new Australian federation, a post he held from 1900. The entry goes on from the family record into his own service.
britannica-1911-londonderry-charles-will:
Charles William Stewart, 3rd Marquess of Londonderry (1778-1854), was a British soldier and diplomat, and his career is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of the 1st marquess by a second marriage, he entered the army and fought in the Netherlands, on the Rhine and Danube, and in the Irish rebellion. By 1807 he was under secretary for war.

The entry praises his cavalry service in the Peninsula under Wellington, where he served as adjutant-general and was at the taking of Ciudad Rodrigo. Sent to Berlin in 1813, he backed his half-brother Castlereagh's diplomacy, then served as ambassador at Vienna in 1814. He became 3rd marquess on his brother's death in 1822.
britannica-1911-lonsdale-earls-of:
Lonsdale is an English earldom held by the Lowther family, traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The line runs back to Sir Hugh Lowther, of the days of Edward the First. One of his kin took in Mary, queen of Scots, on her flight into England in 1568. That same man then worked to free her from her prison.

Later Lowthers built the trade of Whitehaven and rose in state. John Lowther was made viscount Lonsdale in 1696 and held the treasury and the privy seal. His line died out with his son in 1751. James Lowther then drew the wealth of three branches of the house into his own hands. As first earl of Lonsdale he held sway over votes in the north for years. The entry follows the house from march wardens to great land lords.
britannica-1911-lothian-earls-and-marque:
Lothian is the subject of a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Mark Kerr, first earl of Lothian, died in 1609. He was the eldest son of an abbot of Newbattle. He came from the famed border family of Ker of Cessford. That family spells its name Ker in one branch and Kerr in the Lothian branch. Like his father, Mark served as a high law officer under King James the Sixth.

The article says he became Lord Newbattle in 1587 and earl of Lothian in 1606. Report credits him with thirty one children. His son Robert, the second earl, died without sons in 1624. A royal charter let his daughter Anne inherit if she married into the Ker kin. She wed William Ker in 1631, and he became third earl that year. He signed the Scottish national covenant in 1638 and marched with the Scots into England.
britannica-1911-loyola-st-ignatius-of:
Ignatius of Loyola, who lived from the late fourteen hundreds into the next age, founded the Society of Jesus. The 1911 Britannica entry opens with his birth at the castle of Loyola in Spain, as the youngest of thirteen children. He served first as a page at court, then as a soldier under a duke, and showed skill, nerve, and care in that life.

The head of the entry follows him to the siege of Pampeluna, where a French force held the town. In the last attack a cannon ball broke one of his legs and hurt the other badly. The French treated him with care and sent him home in a litter, where his leg had to be broken and set anew, a pain he bore in silence.
britannica-1911-lugano-lake-of:
Lake Lugano, also called Ceresio, is a small lake in Lombardy, northern Italy. Its lake entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies between Lake Maggiore to the west and Lake Como to the east. Its shape is bent, with arms cut by the Monte Salvatore peak.

The lake runs about twenty two miles long and two miles wide at most. Its depth reaches nine hundred forty five feet in the deep parts. A stone dam at Melide bears the Saint Gotthard rail line and road. Towns round the shore link by rail to Bellinzona, Como, and Varese. Part of the lake lies in the Swiss canton of Ticino, the rest in Italy.
britannica-1911-macclesfield-charles-ger:
Charles Gerard, first Earl of Macclesfield, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He lived from about 1618 to 1694. He was the eldest son of Sir Charles Gerard. His family was an old Lancashire one. His great-grandfather was a noted judge of the reign of Elizabeth.

His mother was Penelope Fitton of Gawsworth, in Cheshire. Gerard was educated abroad. In the Low Countries he learned soldiering. When the Civil War broke out in England, he raised a troop of horse for the king. He commanded a brigade with distinction at Edgehill. He won further honours at the first battle of Newbury and at Newark in 1644. For that service he was appointed to a chief command. The article follows a Cavalier whose sword carried him from county rank to an earldom. War and loyalty made the family's fortune in one hard generation.
britannica-1911-maelduin-voyage-of:
The Voyage of Maelduin is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an early Irish romance. The tale is also known by its Irish name, Imram Maeleduin. It survives in a version from the eleventh century. That version is credited to Aed the Fair, called chief sage of Ireland. Signs in the text point to a tale from the eighth century.

The romance belongs to a group of Irish sea tales called Navigations. Maelduin learns as a grown man who his father was. His father, Ailill, had been slain by a raider from Leix. Maelduin sails to find the man who killed him. On a seer's advice, he takes seventeen men with him. His three foster brothers swim out and join the crew.
britannica-1911-malmesbury-james-harris-:
James Harris, first earl of Malmesbury, is tracked in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Salisbury in 1746, he was a scholar's son. He learned at Winchester, Oxford, and Leiden in his youth. In 1768 he joined the British mission at Madrid as secretary. Left in charge there, he learned of a Spanish plan in secret.

Spain meant to strike the Falkland Islands, Harris found out. His bold front helped to foil that stroke in time. Posts at Berlin and then St Petersburg made his name in full. He kept the trust of Catherine though she leaned to France. Later at the Hague he drove Pitt's plans for Europe. His diaries and letters, brought out by his grandson, close the tale.
britannica-1911-manchester-earls-and-duk:
Manchester, as earls and dukes, is the subject of a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The title, in the English peerage, belongs to a branch of the Montagu family. The first earl was Sir Henry Montagu, born about 1563 at Boughton in Northamptonshire. He was the grandson of a chief justice of the king's bench.

Henry was schooled at Cambridge and called to the bar, and in 1603 he was picked as recorder of London. In 1616 he became chief justice, and in that post he passed sentence on Sir Walter Raleigh in 1618. In 1620 he was made lord high treasurer and raised to the peerage. Charles the First made him earl of Manchester in 1626. He kept the trust of the king to the end and died in 1642.
britannica-1911-mar-earldom-of:
Mar, an earldom of Scotland, is traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The old province of Mar covered the larger part of Aberdeenshire. In Celtic times a chief called a mormaer ruled the district. An earl took that chief's place in the twelfth century.

No sure line of earls appears before the thirteen hundreds. From mid-century the earls of Mar ranked among the seven earls of Scotland. One earl married a sister of King Robert Bruce and gained the castle of Kildrummy. His son was made regent in 1332 and slain in battle a month later. The earldom passed by an heiress to the earl of Douglas. Her widowed daughter then held Kildrummy alone against her foes. A royal bastard stormed the castle and forced her to sign the earldom away. She revoked that deed, then married the man and granted him the earldom for life.
britannica-1911-mar-john-erskine-1st-or-:
Mar, John Erskine, 1st or 6th Earl of is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a regent of Scotland. Mar was a son of John, fifth Lord Erskine, guardian to two Scottish sovereigns. The younger John succeeded his father in 1552 and joined the religious reformers, though never with much ardour. He held Edinburgh Castle, and during the struggle between the regent Mary of Lorraine and the lords of the Congregation he acted steadily for peace.

The article follows his part in Mary's reign and fall. As guardian of the young James the Sixth he kept the prince out of Bothwell's hands. He joined the nobles who rose against Mary and helped govern Scotland during her imprisonment and after her abdication. He died at Stirling on the twenty-ninth of October 1572.
britannica-1911-mar-john-erskine-2nd-or-:
John Erskine, Earl of Mar (about 1558 to 1634), was a Scottish politician, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets him beside the king. He was the only son of the preceding earl of Mar. With King James the Sixth he was educated by George Buchanan. The young king, some seven years his junior, lived with him at Stirling.

On reaching his majority, Mar was in name the guardian of the young king. In truth he was a puppet in the hands of the regent, the earl of Morton. When Morton was imprisoned, Mar lost power and place with him. In 1582 he took part in the seizure of James, a plot known as the raid of Ruthven. When James escaped his new keepers, Mar fled into the west of Scotland. He then seized Stirling Castle, and the king marched against him.
britannica-1911-mar-john-erskine-6th-or-:
John Erskine, earl of Mar, a Scottish Jacobite born in sixteen seventy five, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of Charles, the fifth earl. He took lands from his father that were deep in debt. At first he stood with the side that backed the English state.

He was one of the men who set the terms for the Union of the two realms. He was made a state aide for Scotland and sat as a peer for his land. The Tory side made him a state aide for England too. Yet he seemed as ready to side with the Whigs. In seventeen fourteen he swore faith to the new king. He lost his post all the same. The next year he went in disguise to Scotland. There he led the men for the Old Pretender.
britannica-1911-march-earls-of:
March, Earls of, is a border title traced in a 1911 Britannica entry on great feudal houses. The name comes from the marches, or border lands, by Wales and by Scotland. Welsh March earls sprang from Roger de Mortemer of Normandy. His kin held wide lands in Shropshire and Herefordshire. Hugh de Mortimer built Wigmore Priory and fought King Henry the Second for his castles.

Roger Mortimer, first Earl of March, fills most of the shown text. He gained Ludlow Castle by marriage and great lands in Ireland. As lord deputy he drove Edward Bruce back and beat the De Lacy kin. He then turned on King Edward the Second and his close friends, the Despensers. That feud sent him to the Tower in thirteen twenty two.
britannica-1911-marignan-battle-of:
The Battle of Marignan was fought over two days in the autumn of the early fifteen hundreds. French troops under King Francis the First met Swiss troops near a village south east of Milan, by a small river. The 1911 Britannica entry sets out how the fight arose from the tangled wars and deals of Italy at that time.

The entry tells how the young French king led his host over a high Alpine pass by paths no army had used. His men seized a papal corps, joined with allied troops from Venice, and gained a hold on the Milan plain. It then notes the cash offer made to the Swiss to go home, and the fresh Swiss corps that came down keen to fight instead.
britannica-1911-marlborough-earls-and-du:
Marlborough, as earls and dukes, is the subject of a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The earldom was first held by the family of Ley, from 1626 to 1679. James Ley, the first earl, was chief justice of the king's bench in Ireland and then in England. He sat in parliament and was lord high treasurer from 1624 to 1628.

The third earl, his grandson James, was a navy officer killed in a fight with the Dutch. The title died out in 1679 with the fourth earl, an uncle of James. In 1689 John Churchill was made earl of Marlborough, and in 1702 duke. When he died in 1722 with no son left, an act of parliament let the titles pass through his daughters. His eldest daughter Henrietta took the dukedom first, and then her nephew Charles Spencer.
britannica-1911-marston-moor-battle-of:
Marston Moor is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a battle of the English civil war. The fight took place on the second of July 1644. The field lay seven miles west of York. Prince Rupert led the Royalist army in the fight. The earl of Manchester, Lord Fairfax, and Lord Leven led the other side. Their armies were those of Parliament and of Scotland. Rupert had just relieved the city of York.

Newcastle's army, which had held York, joined Rupert there. The besiegers drew off toward the south west in reply. Royalist troops followed close behind them. On the morning of the fight, Rupert struck their rearguard. That blow forced them to halt and deploy for battle. They took rising ground on the south edge of the moor. Their line ran between Long Marston and Tockwith. The Royalists held about eighteen thousand men in all.
britannica-1911-may-isle-of:
May, Isle of is an island article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an island of Fife, in Scotland. It stands at the mouth of the Firth of Forth, five miles south-east of Crail and Anstruther. It runs more than a mile from north-west to south-east. Saint Adrian, who had settled there, was killed by the Danes in the ninth century.

The ruins of his small chapel still stand, and it was long a place of pilgrimage. James the Fourth was often among the pilgrims. The landing place is still called Pilgrims' Haven, and old wells bear saints' names. In 1499 Sir Andrew Wood won a fierce sea fight by the island and took an English seaman and three ships. A coal beacon was lit on the May in 1636.
britannica-1911-mayenne-charles-of-lorra:
Charles of Lorraine, duke of Mayenne, who lived from 1554 to 1611, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the second son of Francis of Lorraine, second duke of Guise, and was born in March 1554. He was away from France at the time of the Saint Bartholomew massacre. The next year he took part in the siege of La Rochelle.

At that siege he was made duke and peer of France, the entry says. He went with Henry of Valois to Poland when that prince was chosen king there. Soon he came back to France to serve his brother, the third duke of Guise. The article calls him his brother's energetic supporter and chief helper in the struggles that followed.
britannica-1911-mercur-seigneurs-and-duk:
Mercœur, Seigneurs and Dukes of, is a short title history in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The estate of Mercœur in Auvergne in France gave its name to a line of strong lords. That line died out in the thirteen hundreds, and the estate passed by inheritance to the dauphins of Auvergne, the counts of Clermont. In 1426 it passed to the Bourbons by marriage.

Mercœur then formed part of the seized estates of the Constable de Bourbon. Francis the First and Louise of Savoy gave it to Antoine, Duke of Lorraine, and his wife Renée de Bourbon. Nicolas of Lorraine, the son of Antoine, was made Duke of Mercœur and a peer of France in 1569. His son was Philippe Emmanuel, whose daughter wed the Duke of Vendôme in 1609, carrying the title on by marriage once more.
britannica-1911-methuen-barony-of:
Methuen, Barony of, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on an English title created in 1838. The title, Baron Methuen of Corsham in Wiltshire, was made for Paul Methuen, who lived from 1779 to 1849. He had sat in Parliament first as a Tory for Wiltshire and later as a Whig for North Wiltshire.

Much of the entry looks back to his kin, above all John Methuen, lord chancellor of Ireland and envoy to Portugal. It explains his Methuen Treaty of 1703, which let English woollen cloth into Portugal. In return, Portuguese wines gained lower duties in England than French wines, which helped port displace Burgundy. The article then traces the title to the second and third barons.
britannica-1911-middleton-earls-of:
Middleton, Earls of, is the subject of a family entry in the 1911 Britannica. John Middleton, the first earl, lived from about 1619 to 1674. His kin had held lands at Middleton since the 1100s. He served as a soldier in France in youth. He then fought against King Charles the First. He stood out in fights against Montrose in Scotland.

He led a high post in an army sent to save the king in 1648. He was seized after the fight at Preston that year. He joined Charles the Second when that king came to Scotland. A public act of sorrow won him back royal favour. He was seized again after Worcester, where he led horse troops. He fled the Tower and went to Paris in exile. A planned rising in Scotland that he led failed in full.
britannica-1911-minto-earls-of:
Minto is the earldom held by a Scottish border family named Elliot. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the house from 1651 onward. Two early Elliots sat as judges under the title Lord Minto. The elder was condemned to death in 1685, then pardoned.

Later Elliots served as a naval chief, a governor of Newfoundland, and the last English governor of New York. A poet in the family wrote a famed ballad of Flodden. The third baronet sat in Parliament for over twenty years. His eldest son became the first earl in the line. That earl studied at Paris beside David Hume as a youth. He later governed Corsica and then served as governor general of India.
britannica-1911-misrule-lord-of:
The Lord of Misrule was, in medieval times, the master of the Christmas revels. One scholar holds that he follows the king of the Roman Saturnalia. That mock king played the god Saturn and was said to die at the revels' end. A like figure at carnival is destroyed at its close. A survey of London gives a full picture of the custom in its prime.

In the king's house at Christmas a Lord of Misrule led the merry sports. Each great house, lay or church, had its own such lord. The mayor and sheriffs of London kept Lords of Misrule as well. These mock monarchs began their reign on All Hallows Eve. They ruled until Candlemas, in the depth of winter. In Scotland they were called Abbots of Unreason and were banned in fifteen fifty five.
britannica-1911-monmouth-battle-of:
Monmouth, Battle of is a war article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a fight in the American War of Independence. It was fought in 1778. Word of a French alliance that year pushed the British to draw their forces together. Sir Henry Clinton chose to leave Philadelphia and march to New York through New Jersey.

Washington had wintered at Valley Forge and built his army back up. He marched at once to cut the British off and caught them near Monmouth Court House on the twenty-eighth of June. A strong force under General Charles Lee went ahead to hit the enemy rear. Lee hoped to cut off part of the long baggage train. Clinton strengthened his rear guard, which turned on the Americans and drove them back. Washington then rode up and formed a strong battle line.
britannica-1911-monmouth-james-scott-duk:
James Scott, duke of Monmouth, lived from 1649 to 1685 and led a failed rising against James the Second. The 1911 Britannica entry opens with doubt over who his father truly was. His mother Lucy Walters had been mistress to Charles the Second in exile. Yet the boy looked much like Robert Sidney, an earlier lover of hers.

Charles still owned him as his son and showered fond love on the child. Tutors Catholic then Protestant shaped his schooling in turn across his youth. At thirteen he was called to court and placed under noble care. The entry sets up the charm and claim that later drew men to his doomed banner.
britannica-1911-monmouth-robert-carey-1s:
Robert Carey, first Earl of Monmouth, who lived from about 1560 to 1639, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the youngest son of Henry Carey, Lord Hunsdon, a first cousin of Queen Elizabeth. As a young man Carey went on missions abroad and took part in campaigns of war.

He joined the bid to relieve Sluys in 1587, served against the Spanish Armada, and led a regiment in Essex's expedition to Normandy in 1591. That year Essex knighted him. He sat in Parliament for Morpeth, for Callington and for Northumberland at varied times. From 1593 he held posts in the government of the Scottish borders, and in 1596 he took his father's place as lord warden of the marches. In March 1603 he was at court and saw the queen's last illness, which he described in his Memoirs.
britannica-1911-montecucculi-raimondo-co:
Raimondo, Count of Montecucculi (1609-1680), was an Austrian general, born at the castle of Montecucculo in Modena, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. His family was of Burgundian origin and had settled in north Italy in the 900s. At sixteen he began as a private soldier under his uncle Ernest, a noted Austrian general.

Four years of hard service in Germany and the Low Countries made him a captain of infantry. He was badly wounded at New Brandenburg and again at Breitenfeld in 1631, where the Swedes captured him, and wounded once more at Lützen. Rising step by step, he won his colonelcy by a bold charge through a breach at Kaiserslautern. Taken prisoner again in 1639, he spent two and a half years in captivity studying war, Euclid, Tacitus, and building, and planning his great work on war.
britannica-1911-montferrat-count-of:
Count of Montferrat is a title drawn from a territory south of the Po and east of Turin, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article traces the family that held it. In the twelfth century that family was one of the most considerable in Lombardy. A count of Montferrat took part in the Second Crusade in 1147. The tie with the Holy Land grew close from 1176.

In that year William Longsword, eldest son of Count William the Third, went to Jerusalem. He married Sibylla, heiress of the kingdom, but died within months. His posthumous son became Baldwin the Fifth. The old count came east to guard his grandson's interests and was taken prisoner by Saladin at Hittin in 1187. Soon after, his second son Conrad reached Palestine, fled Constantinople, and saved Tyre from conquest.
britannica-1911-montpensier-counts-and-d:
Montpensier, Counts and Dukes of, is a French title traced through its houses in a 1911 Britannica entry. The lordship in the Puy de Dome lands rose to a countship in the thirteen hundreds. It was sold in thirteen eighty four to John, Duke of Berry. His child Marie brought it to her spouse, the Duke of Bourbon, in fourteen hundred. That house held it through the famed Constable of Bourbon.

King Francis seized the lands, then gave them back to the constable kin in fifteen thirty eight. A year later the hold was raised to a duchy of France. The heiress Marie brought it to Gaston of Orleans by marriage in sixteen twenty six. Her child, the Grande Mademoiselle, held the duchy next. The Orleans house kept the title from then on.
britannica-1911-montrose-james-graham-ma:
Montrose, James Graham, Marquess of, is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Scottish noble of the civil war age. He was born in 1612 and died in 1650. He became the fifth earl of Montrose on his father's death in 1626. He was schooled at St Andrews and wed at seventeen.

When the Scottish troubles broke out in 1637, he joined the party of resistance. For a time he was one of its most eager leaders. He had no puritan streak in him. What moved him was anger at the power Charles gave the bishops and at the bid to force a new prayer book on Scotland. He signed the Covenant. He was sent three times to crush foes of the cause around Aberdeen, in the country of the Gordons.
britannica-1911-montrose-marquesses-and-:
Montrose, Marquesses and Dukes of is a title history from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Scottish noble line. David Lindsay, fifth earl of Crawford, was made duke of Montrose in 1488. It was the first dukedom given in Scotland to a man not of royal blood. The gift rewarded his loyalty to James the Third in a revolt.

James the Fourth took the dukedom away, then gave it back in 1489 for life only. At Lindsay's death in 1495 the title died out. In 1505 William, fourth Lord Graham, became earl of Montrose. His line held that title till 1644, when the fifth earl was made marquess of Montrose. That was the famed marquess of the Civil War.
britannica-1911-moray-thomas-randolph-ea:
Moray, Thomas Randolph, Earl of, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Scots lord. He was the sole son of Thomas Randolph of Nithsdale. Through his mother, Lady Isabel Bruce, he was nephew to King Robert the Bruce. He joined Bruce in 1306 and was there at his crowning.

His path crossed sides more than once in the wars with England. Caught at Methven, he saved his life by swearing to Edward. Caught again in 1308, he came back to his uncle's side. Bruce made him Earl of Moray and lord of Man and Annandale. The entry tells how he took Edinburgh Castle by a bold night climb in 1314.
britannica-1911-morley-barons-and-earls-:
Morley, Barons and Earls of, is a title line traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In 1299 William de Morley of Morley in Norfolk was summoned to parliament as a baron. His son Robert, who died in 1360, was a famed warrior of his age. Credit for the English win at Sluys rests in large part on him, and he fought at Crecy as well.

The sixth baron left no sons when he died in 1443. His daughter Alianore wed William Lovel, who was summoned as Lord Morley in his turn. That line passed through a sister to the Parker family by marriage. Henry Parker became the tenth baron in 1523 on a summons to the Lords. He was a man of letters who turned works of Plutarch, Boccaccio, Petrarch, Seneca, and Cicero into English. Most of those versions live only in hand written form.
britannica-1911-morton-james-douglas-4th:
James Douglas, fourth earl of Morton, lived from about 1525 to 1581. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica casts him as a Scottish statesman of Mary's reign. He wed the daughter of the third earl and took the title in 1553. In 1563 he became lord chancellor of Scotland. In March 1566 he led the force that seized Holyrood palace. That raid set up the murder of Rizzio, the queen's secretary.

When Mary fled the palace, Morton fled to England. Pardoned, he came back early in 1567 with 600 men. He helped win her consent to give up the throne at Lochleven. His army beat her forces at Langside in 1568. Two regents leaned on him as their chief adviser. On the death of the earl of Mar in 1572, Morton won the regency at last.
britannica-1911-mulgrave-earldom-of:
Mulgrave, Earldom of, is a 1911 Britannica article on an English title and its holders. The title dates from 1626. In that year Edmund Sheffield, third Baron Sheffield, was created earl of Mulgrave. His grandson Edmund succeeded him as second earl. The second earl sat in Oliver Cromwell's House of Lords, as one of nine true peers there.

Edmund's son John became the third earl. He was created marquess of Normanby in 1694. In 1703 he was made duke of Buckingham and Normanby. On the death of his son, the second duke, the titles became extinct. That death fell in 1735, and the duke left no heirs. The second duke devised the Sheffield estates to his mother, Catherine. She was a natural daughter of James the Second. Her first husband had been the third earl of Annesley. The article traces how a title rose, flowered, and died with one line.
britannica-1911-nansen-fridtjof:
Fridtjof Nansen is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Nansen was a Norwegian scientist, explorer, and statesman, born near Christiania in 1861. He spent his childhood at Froen until he was fifteen. Then the family moved to Christiania, where he went to school.

He entered Christiania university in 1880 and made zoology his special study. In March 1882 he shipped on the sealing vessel Viking for Greenland waters. That voyage fixed his twin callings in science and the ice. On his return he became curator of the Bergen Museum. His chief there was Danielssen, a leading physician and zoologist. In 1886 he worked for a time at the zoological station in Naples. Papers and memoirs from his pen were already appearing. The entry opens the life of the man who would drift across the Arctic Ocean and serve his country in peace talks.
britannica-1911-neuchatel-lake-of:
