Lake of Neuchatel is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a lake in western Switzerland. Two neighbouring lakes, Bienne and Morat, are connected with it by canals. All three are the modern remnant of a far larger water. That great body once filled the lower valley of the Aar. Neuchatel is now the largest lake wholly within Switzerland. Parts of Geneva and Constance belong to foreign countries by contrast. No single canton holds the whole of this lake.

Its waters are split among four cantons in shares. Neuchatel canton holds the largest share of its area. Vaud, Fribourg, and Berne hold the remaining shares. The lake runs about twenty three miles in length. Its width varies from three to five miles across. Its greatest depth is given as 502 feet. Its surface lies 1427 feet above the sea. The Thiele river mainly forms the lake at its south west end.
britannica-1911-norfolk-earls-and-dukes-:
Earls and dukes of Norfolk form a long line traced in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The first earl was Ralph de Guader, a follower of William the Conqueror. He lost the title when he rose against William in ten seventy five. The next earl was Hugh Bigod, a backer of King Stephen.

Bigod kin held the earldom for more than a century. Through a marriage they gained the office of marshal of England. The line ended when the fifth earl died childless in thirteen oh six. The next earl was Thomas of Brotherton, a younger son of Edward the First. He got the earldom in thirteen twelve, with the old Bigod lands and the marshal office. He later helped bring down Edward the Second.
britannica-1911-northampton-assize-of:
Assize of Northampton is a 1911 Britannica article on a short code of English law. The code was issued in 1176. It is drawn up as instructions to six committees of judges. Each committee had three judges. They were to visit the six circuits into which England was divided.

The code claims to be a reissue of the Assize of Clarendon, from 1166. In fact, it holds many new rules. Set beside the earlier assize, it orders harsher punishment for crimes. Arson and forgery were now crimes the jurors must enquire into. Those who failed at the ordeal were to lose a hand as well as a foot. In one key section, the text sees the origin of a new action at law. That action, mort d'ancestor, let an heir claim land. Law readers get a landmark code in a tight account.
britannica-1911-northampton-earls-and-ma:
Northampton earls and marquesses form a title held by varied English houses. Their title entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. About ten eighty Simon de Senlis was made earl of Northampton by William. Simon, builder of Northampton Castle, also held the Huntingdon earldom then.

His son Simon was seen in the title in about eleven forty one. That second Simon died with no children to take the title on. In thirteen thirty seven William de Bohun was created earl of Northampton anew. His son Humphrey joined the title with Hereford and Essex earldoms later. Those joined titles died out at his death in thirteen seventy two.
britannica-1911-northumberland-earls-and:
Earls and Dukes of Northumberland are introduced in a 1911 Britannica entry tied to the house of Percy. The title reaches back before peerage rules were strict and fixed. Old Northumbria once covered far more land than the modern county of that name. For a century after the Norman Conquest it took in Durham and York as well.

That border land lay next to Scotland, so its earl held great power and duty. Guarding the north was no light charge for any lord of the marches. The entry notes that William the Conqueror and his heirs backed men of local right. It sets up a long tale of a border house and its sway.
britannica-1911-northumberland-john-dudl:
John Dudley, duke of Northumberland, lived from about 1502 to 1553. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his climb at court. His father was a grasping minister of Henry the Seventh. That father was attainted and put to death in 1509.

Dudley mother remarried into royal kin, and favor followed the match. The young man was restored in blood in 1512. He guarded Calais, held the Scottish marches, and led the fleet. He took Boulogne in 1544 and beat off a French attack in 1545. Court strife then turned on who would rule after Henry died. Dudley sided with the reform party against old rivals. He rose to earl of Warwick as the old king reign ended.
britannica-1911-northumberland-john-nevi:
John Neville, earl of Northumberland (c. 1430–1471), was an English soldier. He was the third son of Richard Neville, earl of Salisbury. He was a brother of Richard Neville, earl of Warwick, the man called the king-maker. At the battle of Blore Heath in 1459, the Lancastrians took John Neville prisoner. That was so though the Yorkists under his father had won the day. He was named among those attainted at the parliament of Coventry.

Neville was set free in 1460, when his own party gained the upper hand. Soon after, he was made Lord Montagu and keeper of the royal household. He was not at Wakefield, where his father was taken. He was caught once more after the second battle of St Albans in 1461, but Edward IV soon set him free.
britannica-1911-norwich-george-goring-ea:
George Goring, earl of Norwich (about 1583 to 1663), was an English soldier and courtier of Charles the First, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his civil war course. He was the son of George Goring of Sussex and of Anne Denny, whose brother held the Norwich title before him. Knighted in 1608, he became a favourite at court and grew rich on monopolies granted by the king.

He was made Baron Goring in 1628 and a privy councillor in 1639. When the quarrel between king and Parliament came to a head, he gave his fortune freely to the royal cause. In 1644 the king revived the earldom of Norwich for him. He went with the queen to Holland in 1642 to raise money. An intercepted letter betrayed his doings, and Parliament impeached him for high treason.
britannica-1911-nottingham-earls-of:
Nottingham, Earls of, is a family history in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English title held by three houses. The Mowbrays held it first, then the Howards, then the Finches. The part shown here deals with the Finch line.

The article centres on Heneage Finch, the first Finch earl. Born in 1621, he trained in law at Oxford and the Inner Temple. He rose through posts as solicitor general and attorney general. In 1675 he became lord chancellor of England. Peers on both sides praised his fair mind and his speech. He is still called the father of equity, the text notes. His best known work is the Statute of Frauds.
britannica-1911-orange-house-of:
The house of Orange takes its name from a small state now in the French department of Vaucluse. Orange claims a past as a free state that runs back to the time of Charlemagne. William, called le Cornet, is said to have been its first prince in the late 700s. The line of princes is sure only from Gerald Adhemar, who lived about 1086. In 1174 the state passed by marriage to Bertrand de Baux.

Nine princes of the Baux line held Orange in turn. In 1393 the house of Chalons took over through a marriage. The article lists the Chalons princes from John I to Philibert, who ruled from 1502 to 1530. Philibert was a great soldier and statesman held in high regard by the emperor Charles V. For his service the emperor gave him large lands in the Netherlands in 1522.
britannica-1911-orford-robert-walpole-1s:
Robert Walpole, first Earl of Orford, prime minister of England from 1721 to 1742, is the subject of a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is generally known as Sir Robert Walpole. Born at Houghton in Norfolk in 1676, he was the third but eldest surviving son of a Whig squire who loved outdoor sport and the pleasures of the table.

The father passed his chief traits to his son. Walpole was an Eton colleger and then a scholar at King's College, Cambridge. As a younger son he was meant for the church, but the deaths of his two elder brothers made him heir to an estate of about two thousand pounds a year. He then gave up his scholarship and was withdrawn from the university. When his father died in 1700, the family borough of Castle Rising sent him to the House of Commons.
britannica-1911-orkney-earl-of:
Orkney, Earl of, is a Scots title held by more than one house in this 1911 Britannica entry. The Orkney Isles were ruled by jarls under the kings of Norway in old times. Those jarls oft held Caithness as well under the Scots kings. Paul the Silent, one such jarl, helped build the church of Saint Magnus at Kirkwall. Kin ties bound the jarls to both royal houses.

In its new sense the title dates from near thirteen eighty. The Sinclair house held it first, with Henry Sinclair known as earl by the king of Norway. His grandson gave the title back to James the Third in fourteen seventy. Later holders span Bothwell, a love of Queen Mary, and a Stewart line whose harsh rule in the isles drew jail and death.
britannica-1911-orkney-elizabeth-hamilto:
Elizabeth Hamilton, Countess of Orkney (about 1657-1733), was mistress to King William III. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives her birth name as Elizabeth Villiers of Richmond. Her mother served as governess to Princesses Mary and Anne at court. That link placed Elizabeth among Mary maids of honor in Holland.

She became William acknowledged mistress in 1680 while still in that circle. After he took the English crown he granted her Irish lands of James II. Parliament took that grant back in 1699 after protest. She wed her cousin Lord George Hamilton in 1695. He gained the Orkney earldom the next year through that match.
britannica-1911-orkney-george-hamilton-e:
George Hamilton, Earl of Orkney, was a British soldier born in the late sixteen hundreds, fifth son of a duke. Trained for war by an uncle in a foot regiment, he rose fast to senior rank while still young. He fought in famed battles in Ireland and in Flanders, and led crack troops in the field.

The 1911 Britannica entry notes a grave wound at a siege, won him a generals sash. He wed a woman a famed wit called the wisest he ever knew, and was made an earl in the Scots peerage the next year. As a senior general he marched with a great commander in Flanders. At a famed battle it was his force that took and held the key village.
britannica-1911-orleans-dukes-of:
Orleans, Dukes of, is a French royal title traced through its holders in a 1911 Britannica entry. King Philip the Sixth first made the title for his son Philip. That son died with no true child in thirteen seventy five. A fresh grant in thirteen ninety two went to Louis, a son of Charles the Fifth. His son was the poet Charles of Orleans. That line gave France a king in Louis the Twelfth.

When that duke took the throne, the duchy merged with the crown lands. Kings made the title twice more for royal brothers in the next age. The line from Philip, brother of Louis the Fourteenth, holds it still. One of that line took the throne as Louis Philippe in eighteen thirty. Two side lines, Angouleme and Longueville, close the note.
britannica-1911-orleans-ferdinand-philip:
Ferdinand Philip Louis Charles Henry, Duke of Orleans, who lived from 1810 to 1842, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Palermo, he was the son of Louis Philippe, afterwards king of France, and of Marie Amélie of the Two Sicilies. Under the Restoration he bore the title Duke of Chartres and studied classics in Paris.

When the revolution of 1830 set his father on the throne, the young duke was colonel of a regiment of hussars. He took the title Duke of Orleans and was sent to put down riots at Lyons in 1831, then to the siege of Antwerp in 1832. He was made lieutenant general and campaigned more than once in Algeria. Back in France, he formed the battalions of light infantry known as the chasseurs d'Orléans. He died from a carriage accident at Neuilly in 1842.
britannica-1911-orleans-henri-prince-of:
Orleans, Henri, Prince of, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a French prince. Born at Ham near Richmond on the 16th of October 1867, he was a duke's eldest son. In 1889 his father paid for a long trip of exploration. With two mates he crossed Siberia on his way to Siam.

On that trip they crossed the high range of Tibet as well. Their notes won them a gold medal from the Paris Geographical Society. A book of the trip came out in print in 1892. In later years he probed East Africa and Madagascar on trips. His best feat was to find the source of the Irrawaddy river. That won him the Legion of Honour cross for his work. He died at Saigon in 1901.
britannica-1911-orleans-henrietta-duches:
Henrietta, Duchess of Orleans, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Exeter on the sixteenth of June 1644, she was the third daughter of King Charles the First of England. Her mother was Queen Henrietta Maria. She was born while civil war raged in England.

The article tells how she was smuggled to France in disguise in 1646. Raised at the French court, she wed Philip, duke of Orleans, in March 1661. She was liked at the court of Louis the Fourteenth but grew apart from her husband. In 1670 she won the signing of the treaty of Dover in England. Weeks after her return she died at Saint Cloud.
britannica-1911-orleans-jean-baptiste-ga:
Jean Baptiste Gaston, duke of Orleans, who lived from 1608 to 1660, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the third son of King Henry the Fourth of France and Marie de Medici. Born at Fontainebleau, he was first known as duke of Anjou. In 1626 he became duke of Orleans, and he led in name the army that besieged La Rochelle in 1628.

From that point his life was one long chain of plots, the text says. Twice he fled France for plots against his mother and Cardinal Richelieu, and he waged a failed war in Languedoc. Made whole with his brother the king, he plotted again, fled again, and gave in again. He urged Cinq-Mars to try to kill Richelieu, then left his partner to his fate. In the Fronde wars he swapped sides with ease until Mazarin exiled him to Blois in 1652.
britannica-1911-orleans-louis-philippe-d:
Louis Philippe, duke of Orleans (1725–1785), was a French prince born at Versailles on the 12th of May 1725. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sketches his life, first as duke of Chartres and then, from 1752, as head of his house. He served with the French armies and won praise in the campaigns of 1742 to 1744 and at Fontenoy in 1745.

In 1757 he retired to Bagnolet, where he spent his time on plays and the company of men of letters. His first wife, Louise Henriette de Bourbon-Conti, bore him Philip, later known as Égalité, and a daughter. In 1773 he secretly married Madame de Montesson, a clever woman and a writer of some note. He died at Saint Assise on the 18th of November 1785.
britannica-1911-orleans-louis-philippe-j:
Louis Philippe Joseph, duke of Orleans, a French prince who lived from 1747 to 1793, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born at Saint Cloud on April 13, 1747. In 1769 he wed the richest heiress of the time. Her wealth made it sure he would be the richest man in France.

As duke of Chartres he fought court plans in 1771 and was exiled to his estate. The new queen, Marie Antoinette, hated him, and he scorned her in turn. He served at sea and fought at Ushant in 1778, but was then kept from more war posts. He grew famed in Paris for gifts to the poor and for opening his gardens to all.
britannica-1911-orleans-louis-philippe-r:
Louis Philippe Robert, Duke of Orleans, born in 1869, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of the comte de Paris. He was born at York House, Twickenham, in February 1869. When the exile law was lifted in 1871, he returned with his parents to France.

He was taught first by a tutor, then at schools at Eu and in Paris. There he took a first prize in Latin translation. In 1886, his father now head of the Bourbons, both were exiled again. Queen Victoria placed the young duke as a cadet at Sandhurst. He gained a commission in a rifle battalion then serving in India. In 1888 he sailed out and was received by the viceroy at Calcutta. A grand tiger shoot in Nepal was laid on for him and his cousin. He left the Indian army in 1889 and came back to England.
britannica-1911-orleans-philip-i-duke-of:
Philip the First, Duke of Orleans, son of the French king Louis the Thirteenth, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He lived from 1640 to 1701 and was born at St Germain-en-Laye in September 1640. In 1661 he was created duke of Orleans. He married Henrietta, sister of Charles the Second of England, but the match was not a happy one. Her death in 1670 was ascribed to poison.

Orleans later married Charlotte Elizabeth, daughter of the elector palatine. He fought with distinction in Flanders in 1667. Known as Monsieur, he won a great victory at Cassel in 1677 and took St Omer. Louis the Fourteenth was said to be jealous of his brother's success. At all events, Orleans never commanded an army again. He died at St Cloud in June 1701.
britannica-1911-orleans-philip-ii-duke-o:
Philip the Second, duke of Orleans, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a regent of France. He lived from 1674 to 1723. He was son of Philip the First, duke of Orleans. He was born on the second of August 1674. His first taste of arms came at the siege of Mons in 1691. His marriage won him the favour of the king.

He wed Mademoiselle de Blois, a legitimized daughter of Louis the Fourteenth. He fought with distinction at Steinkerk, Neerwinden, and Namur. During the next few years he had no employment. He spent that time studying natural science. He was next given a command in Italy in 1706. He then served in Spain in 1707 and 1708. He gained some important successes in those campaigns. But he cherished lofty ambitions for the Spanish throne.
britannica-1911-ormonde-earl-and-marques:
Ormonde, Earl and Marquess of, is a title entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, tied to the Irish Butler family. The name comes from a district that is now part of County Tipperary. James Butler was made the first earl in 1328, helped by his wife Eleanor, a grandchild of King Edward the First.

The entry then walks through the line earl by earl. The second and fourth earls each governed Ireland more than once, and the fourth won fame as both a soldier and a scholar. The fifth earl backed the house of Lancaster, was caught after the battle of Towton, and died with no heir. Later pages cover loss of the title, its return, and Sir Thomas Boleyn, father of Anne Boleyn, who held the earldom under Henry the Eighth. The result is a compact family history of power in Ireland and England.
britannica-1911-ormonde-james-butler-1st:
James Butler, first Duke of Ormonde, who lived from 1610 to 1688, is profiled at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as an Irish statesman and soldier. Born in London, he lost his father by drowning in 1619. The boy was made a royal ward and raised in the household of the archbishop of Canterbury.

In 1629 Ormonde wed his cousin, which ended a long feud between their houses and joined their estates. He gained the earldom on his grandfathers death in 1632. Strafford, the kings man in Ireland, treated him with great favour despite his free spirit. In 1640 he took command of the forces there. When revolt broke out in 1641, he led the march that relieved Drogheda. Parliament thanked him in public and gave him a rich jewel. Wins at Kilrush and at New Ross followed in the next two years.
britannica-1911-ormonde-james-butler-2nd:
James Butler, second duke of Ormonde, an Irish statesman and soldier, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Dublin in 1665 and schooled in France and at Oxford. In 1688 he took his grandfather's title and sided with William of Orange. He led a horse regiment at the battle of the Boyne.

Under Queen Anne he led the land forces sent to aid Spain by sea. In 1703 he became viceroy of Ireland, a post he held four years. When Marlborough was cast out in 1711, Ormonde took his place at the head of the army. Secret orders bound him not to back the allies in the field. In 1715 he was charged with treason and fled to France. His vast estates were seized by the crown.
britannica-1911-orrery-charles-boyle-4th:
Charles Boyle, fourth Earl of Orrery (1676–1731), was an author, soldier, and statesman, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry gives his life. He was born at Chelsea in 1676, the second son of Roger, the second earl. He studied at Christ Church, Oxford, and soon stood out for his learning. He sat three times as member for the town of Huntingdon.

Boyle translated the life of Lysander by Plutarch into English. He also issued an edition of the epistles of Phalaris. That edition drew him into a famed dispute with the scholar Bentley. When his brother Lionel died in 1703, Boyle succeeded to the earldom. He joined the army and rose to major general in 1709. He was also sworn of the privy council that year.
britannica-1911-orrery-roger-boyle-1st-e:
Roger Boyle, 1st Earl of Orrery (1621-1670), was a British soldier, statesman, and dramatist, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. He was the third surviving son of Richard Boyle, 1st earl of Cork, educated at Trinity College, Dublin, and perhaps at Oxford. After travel in France and Italy, he fought against the Scots, then returned to Ireland when rebellion broke out in 1641.

Orrery served under the parliamentary side until the king's execution, then retired to Somerset. Cromwell, learning of his secret plan to restore the king, offered him a command in Ireland instead, which he took on terms of faithful service alone. His help there proved of great worth: he drove the rebels into Kilkenny, beat a relief force at Macroom in 1650, and helped at the taking of Clonmell and Limerick.
britannica-1911-orta-lake-of:
Lake Orta, in northern Italy, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article. It lies west of Lake Maggiore. It has borne the name Orta since the sixteenth century. Before that it was called the Lago di San Giulio, for the patron saint of the region.

The lake is about eight miles long. Its greatest depth is 482 feet, and its surface sits 951 feet above sea level. Its width shifts along its length. Rail lines near both ends tie it to Novara and to the Turin-Milan line. The text praises its scenery as characteristically Italian. The large island of San Giulio holds buildings called very picturesque. The village of Orta stands just east of that island. Travellers get a compact guide to a small lake with a long name history.
britannica-1911-oxford-provisions-of:
Provisions of Oxford were the articles of a first scheme of reform passed by a parliament at Oxford in June 1258. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out the plan. King Henry the Third had promised in May that the state of his realm would be set right by twenty four counsellors.

Twelve of those counsellors were chosen by the king, and twelve by the earls and barons. When parliament met, each twelve chose two from the other twelve. That committee of four was empowered to elect a king's council of fifteen members, subject to the approval of the whole body. The twenty four then provided that the new council should meet three times a year in parliaments. Twelve commissioners were to be summoned to speak for the whole community on the affairs of the realm. A further body was set to treat of an aid.
britannica-1911-oxford-robert-de-vere-9t:
Robert de Vere, 9th Earl of Oxford (1362–1392), was an English courtier and the only son of Thomas de Vere, the 8th earl. He became earl on his father's death in 1371 and married Philippa, daughter of his guardian Ingelram de Couci. He grew very close to Richard II, held the post of hereditary great chamberlain, and joined the privy council. He was also made a Knight of the Garter and received castles and lands.

In 1385 Richard planned to send his friend to govern Ireland. Oxford was given wide rights there and was created marquess of Dublin for life. Plans for the trip were made, but he did not leave England. By then, anger at the king's rule was rising, and the king's favour toward Oxford was one cause of that anger.
britannica-1911-oxford-robert-harley-1st:
Robert Harley, first Earl of Oxford, an English statesman who lived from 1661 to 1724, is the subject of a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of Sir Edward Harley, a large landowner in Herefordshire, and he was born in Bow Street in London. His small school in Oxfordshire bred high officers of state in the same years.

Whig and Nonconformist views were taught to him young, and though his politics shifted, he kept his family's faith. At the Revolution of 1688 he and his father raised a troop of horse for William the Third and took Worcester for his cause. That service brought him notice, and in April 1689 he was sent to Parliament for Tregony. He later sat for New Radnor till he was raised to the peerage in 1711. From the start, he gave close care to public business.
britannica-1911-paris-treaties-of:
The treaties of Paris of 1814 and 1815 are the best known of the many pacts signed in that city. Both rank among the chief acts in the politics of Europe. The first was signed on 30 May 1814. It set out the Allied bid to build a lasting peace after Napoleon gave up his throne at Fontainebleau. Louis XVIII of France was a party to that bid.

The second set of treaties was signed on 20 November 1815. It held the harsh and wary terms the Allies laid on France the next year. Napoleon's return from Elba had shown how weak the restored Bourbon rule was. Talleyrand signed the first treaty for France. Lords Castlereagh, Aberdeen, and Cathcart signed for Great Britain. Counts Rasumovski and Nesselrode signed for Russia.
britannica-1911-penthievre-counts-of:
Counts of Penthievre held a countship in Brittany, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces in brief. In the 1100s and 1200s the countship belonged to a branch of the ruling house of Brittany. Henry of Avaugour, heir of that line, lost the countship in 1235 to Duke Pierre Mauclerc. The duke gave it as dowry to his daughter Yolande on her marriage in 1238.

On the death of Yolande in 1272, her brother the duke seized the countship back. In 1337 it passed by marriage to Charles of Chatillon Blois. Later heirs lost it again to the duke of Brittany in 1465, then won it back in time. In 1569 it was raised to a duchy in the peerage of France for Sebastian of Luxemburg. From him it passed through heiresses to the house of Vendome, whose heir took it in 1669.
britannica-1911-perth-earls-and-dukes-of:
Earls and Dukes of Perth form a Scottish title line traced in a 1911 Britannica entry. James, fourth Lord Drummond, was made earl of Perth in 1605 by the crown. His line ran back to Sir John Drummond, made Lord Drummond in 1488. The fourth earl, later first duke, lived from 1648 to 1716 in harder times.

He rose against Lauderdale, then held top law posts in Scotland in the 1680s. As lord chancellor from 1684 to 1688 he stood high with James the Second. His turn to the Roman faith won royal favour but lost him the people. The entry notes the thumbscrew charge that blackened his name in Scotland.
britannica-1911-peter-epistles-of:
Peter, Epistles of, the two books of the New Testament ascribed by tradition to the apostle Peter, are the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The first epistle is addressed to the elect who are sojourners of the Dispersion. The provinces named are Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.

The entry weighs whether the readers were Jewish or Gentile Christians, and favours the Gentile view. Dispersion, it argues, is used as a figure for the lonely place of Christians among the heathen. The core aim of the letter was to stiffen the courage of readers who faced persecution. It also urged conduct that would give no fair ground to call Christianity a crime. After an opening of praise for a new birth and living hope, the letter calls its readers to holy lives. It then gives directions for life in the world.
britannica-1911-peterborough-and-monmout:
Charles Mordaunt is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English soldier and statesman born near sixteen fifty eight. As a boy he went to sea with a fleet in the middle sea. He won his first fame in a bold attack on an enemy fleet.

The entry follows his fierce work in party politics and his break with a king. He backed the Dutch prince who took the English throne and won high posts. Quarrels with the court then led to charges, prison in the Tower, and loss of office. He gained a new earldom from an uncle in the same hard year. The tale shows a brave but stormy public life.
britannica-1911-peterhof:
Peterhof is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a town of Russia west of Saint Petersburg, on the south coast of the Gulf of Finland. Founded in seventeen eleven, it grew up around a palace built by Peter the Great. The entry gives its population as eleven thousand three hundred.

Most people there lived in homes rather than working in large trades, the entry notes. Gem cutting and the making of farm tools were carried on. The palace, changed by later rulers, kept a clear mark of Peter's time. Set on a height above the sea, it held portraits of the royal family and other pictures.
britannica-1911-plymouth-earls-of:
Plymouth, as earls, is the subject of a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The title was first borne by Charles, a natural son of King Charles the Second. He was made earl in 1675, and the title died with him in 1680. In 1682 the title was made once more for Thomas Windsor, the seventh Baron Windsor.

Thomas had fought for Charles the First at Naseby and was, in name at least, governor of Jamaica from 1661 to 1663. His grandson Other was the second earl. The earldom died out when the eighth earl passed in 1843. The barony of Windsor came back in 1855 to a daughter of the sixth earl. Her grandson Robert rose through state posts and was made earl of Plymouth once more in 1905, the third making of the title.
britannica-1911-podebrad-george-of:
George of Podebrad is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a king of Bohemia. He lived from 1420 to 1471. His father was a Bohemian nobleman of Kunstat and Podebrad. That father led the Orphans in the Hussite wars. George fought at fourteen in the battle of Lipan. That battle marks the fall of the advanced Taborites.

Early in life he led the Calixtine party in Bohemia. He beat the Austrian troops of King Albert the Second. He soon stood out as a chief of the national party. On the death of Ptacek of Pirkstein, he led it outright. Bohemia was split in two during a royal minority. One side was Romanist and Austrian in its leanings. The other was the national side led by Podebrad. After failed talks of peace, he chose the appeal to force. The entry sets up his road to the throne.
britannica-1911-portland-earl-of:
Portland, Earl of, is an English title traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Weston family held it from 1633 to 1688. The Bentinck family then held it from 1689 to 1716, when it merged in the dukedom of Portland. Sir Richard Weston leads the account of the first line.

Weston came of a very old house in Essex and sat in parliament under James the First and Charles the First. James sent him abroad twice to treat for the elector palatine Frederick. After the murder of Buckingham, Weston became chief counsellor to Charles. He was made Baron Weston in 1628 and earl of Portland in 1633. Hard years of coaxing money from the Commons fit him for the post of lord high treasurer, which he took in 1628.
britannica-1911-portland-william-bentinc:
William Bentinck, Earl of Portland, is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Dutch born statesman who served the prince of Orange. He rose from page to chief of the prince bedchamber in youth. When the prince fell ill with pox, Bentinck nursed him with great care.

That care won him the trust of his master for the rest of his life. The entry tells how he wooed an English bride for the prince by proxy. He won German princes to back, or at least not block, a bold sea plan. He ran the whole prep for the fleet that sailed to claim a throne. High court posts in England crowned his work once the coup was won.
britannica-1911-powis-earls-and-marquess:
Powis, a line of earls and marquesses, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Before the Norman Conquest, Powis was a Welsh princely land covering Montgomery and parts of five other counties. Early in the twelfth century it split into upper and lower Powis. In 1283 its prince gave up his title and lands to Edward the First at Shrewsbury, and took them back as an English barony.

The article follows the barony as it passed by marriage through two families and fell into suspense in 1551. In 1587 a younger son of the Earl of Pembroke bought part of the lands, with the red castle near Welshpool that became Powis Castle. His son was made Baron Powis in 1629. The third baron rose to earl in 1674, then to marquess, with a viscount's title besides. The entry is a chain of land, marriage, and rank.
britannica-1911-pre-existence-doctrine-o:
Souls before birth are argued in a faith entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. One form of the claim treats the soul of Christ alone. It holds that his human soul stood first of all made things. That soul lived joined to God before his birth on earth. Dr Watts set out that claim most fully, the entry notes. Few have backed it in the age since he wrote it.

The wider form claims all men's souls were made at the start. Cast into bodies as a price for past ill acts, they wait. Schooling in the flesh may fit them for the spirit life. Justin Martyr and Origen held some such view in old days. A council at Constantinople cast the claim out in 540.
britannica-1911-proof:
Proof is a word whose two chief lines of sense come from the verb to prove. To prove means both to show a thing to be true and to test or try a thing. In the first line, proof is that which sets up the truth of a fact. In law, proof is the broad term for the setting up of the facts at stake in a case, by fit legal means, to the content of the court.

In a narrow sense, papers attested so as to serve as legal proof are called proofs. Copies in writing of what a witness is ready to swear are proofs as well. In Scots law the word names a trial before a judge alone, as set against trial by jury. From the broad sense of test or trial, more lines of sense have grown.
britannica-1911-ravenna-exarchate-of:
Ravenna, Exarchate of is a history article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the part of Italy that stayed loyal to the emperors at Constantinople. That rule ran from the late sixth century to the middle of the eighth. Its civil and military head, the exarch, was based at Ravenna. The land round the town, south to Rimini, lay under his direct rule.

Other districts were run by dukes and by officers called magistri militum, posts most often held by one and the same man. All of them answered to the exarch, so the name exarchate came to cover the whole imperial province of Italy. Its borders shifted with the ups and downs of the long fight against the Lombards. Sicily had its own government, while Corsica and Sardinia belonged to the exarchate of Africa.
britannica-1911-request-letters-of:
Letters of request, also called letters rogatory, are explained in a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The terms name a request from one judge to another for help. That help may be serving a summons, taking a witness's sworn statement, or enforcing a judgment. Any other act of a court may be sought in the same way.

Later Roman law laid a duty of mutual aid on the courts of the empire. That duty passed to the courts of separate states as Roman law spread. In England and the United States, the article finds only one old trace outside statute. A foreign admiralty court's sentence could be enforced on letters of request from its judge. The piece then takes up the taking of testimony abroad. Courts long sent commissions to private persons for that work. Objections grew, since such work gave no power to compel witnesses to attend.
britannica-1911-requests-court-of:
Court of Requests was a minor court of the king council in England for humble suits. A 1911 Britannica entry traces its roots to an order in council of 1390. Lords were told to form a body to hear the petitions of poor folk. Fair dealing at small cost made the court a favourite with plain suitors.

Cases too small for chancery found a cheap and ready home in its hall. Under Wolsey the court was fixed for good at Whitehall in London. Its judges bore the title masters of requests in ordinary course. Under Elizabeth two masters ordinary and two extraordinary held those posts.
britannica-1911-retz-seigneurs-and-dukes:
Retz is a tract in south Brittany whose lords and dukes are traced in one line. The land first bore its own house name, then passed to the Chabot line. From them it went to the house of Laval. One Laval lord was a friend in arms of Joan of Arc.

That lord fell to foul vice and was put to death at Nantes. The land then passed through three more houses in turn. In fifteen eighty-one it was raised to a dukes rank for a Gondi lord. That house gave Paris three church heads in a row. When its last male died, the rank died with him.
britannica-1911-riansares-augustin-ferna:
Augustin Fernandez Munoz, Duke of Riansares, is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the private husband of the queen regent of Spain. Born in New Castile, he was the son of a tobacco shop keeper. He joined the royal bodyguard as a young man.

The entry weighs three tales of how he first caught the queen eye. She wed him in secret soon after her royal husband died. To own the match in public would have cost her the rule of Spain. All at court knew of the bond, but it stayed hid in law for years. When troops rose and forced a charter, her guard was seized as a threat.
britannica-1911-rights-of-man-and-of-the:
Rights of Man and of the Citizen, Declaration of is an article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on the famous statement of principles issued in 1789 during the French Revolution. The Constituent Assembly drew it up as a kind of manifesto. It was meant to stand at the head of the new frame of government once that was done.

The article links the text to earlier rights statements in the American states, above all Virginia. It also links it to the writings of French thinkers of the age. The king accepted the final text on the fifth of October 1789, at first with conditions and then with changes. The text holds a preamble and seventeen articles. They set out equal rights and freedom in its many forms. The entry treats it as a base for modern civil law.
britannica-1911-rochester-john-wilmot-2n:
John Wilmot, second earl of Rochester, lived from 1647 to 1680 and was an English poet and wit. The 1911 Britannica entry spends much of its space on his father and forebears first. His grandfather Charles won fame in Ireland and became president of Connaught in 1616. His father Henry served Charles the First with skill in the Civil War.

Henry won the fights at Roundway Down and Cropredy Bridge for the king. He was made Baron Wilmot of Adderbury for that loyal service in war. Family feuds at court mark the tale as much as battles do. The long lineage sets the stage for the brief, bright life of the poet earl himself.
britannica-1911-rochester-lawrence-hyde-:
Lawrence Hyde, Earl of Rochester, an English statesman who lived from 1641 to 1711, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon. After the return of Charles the Second, he sat in Parliament for Newport, then for Oxford University, through to 1679.

Hyde was sent on a mission of compliment to Louis the Fourteenth in 1661, and he held the court post of master of the robes for thirteen years. In 1665 he wed Henrietta Boyle, daughter of the Earl of Burlington and Cork. When his father was charged in 1667, Lawrence and his brother Henry spoke for him, yet the fall of Clarendon did not hurt the sons. Kinship to the Duke of York helped them, and both were keen royalists. Hyde later served as envoy to Poland and at the peace congress at Nijmegen.
britannica-1911-rockingham-charles-watso:
Charles Watson Wentworth, second Marquess of Rockingham (1730-1782), twice prime minister of England, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry opens with the long family line behind his titles. His father was made Earl of Melton in 1733 and Marquess of Rockingham in 1746. The Watson line traced back to Sir Lewis Watson, who was made Baron Rockingham in 1645 for his service in the Civil War.

The article traces how the barony and the vast Wentworth estates passed from hand to hand. One earldom died out in 1746 when its holder left no heir. The barony went to a cousin, the father of the prime minister. That line had taken the added name Wentworth through marriage into the family of the Earl of Strafford.
britannica-1911-roland-legend-of:
Roland, the French epic hero known in Italian romance as Orlando, has his legend traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The tale rests on true history. Charlemagne invaded Spain in 778. He took Pampeluna but failed before Saragossa. News of a Saxon revolt called him back to the Rhine.

On the retreat through the Pyrenees, Basques lay in wait in a narrow pass. They cut off part of his army from the main body. The rear guard was driven into a valley, ringed round, and wiped out. The Basques looted the baggage and slipped away in the dark. Old annals tied to Einhard tell the event, and his life of Charles names the leaders who fell.
britannica-1911-romney-henry-sidney-earl:
Henry Sidney, Earl of Romney, is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English courtier and plotter born in Paris in sixteen forty one. Good looks and charm helped him rise at the royal court. He held posts in the royal wardrobe and in the army.

The entry shows a man whose light air hid a real gift for secret work. He ran missions to France and to Holland for two kings. He urged the Dutch prince to come to England and claim the throne. That prince did come, and Sidney stood close to the new rule. The tale weighs his skill in plots against the scandal of his private life.
britannica-1911-roscommon-wentworth-dill:
Wentworth Dillon, fourth Earl of Roscommon, an English poet who lived from about 1630 to 1685, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Ireland, he was a nephew of the earl of Strafford. He was taught in Yorkshire, at Caen in Normandy, and at Rome. He had succeeded to the earldom in 1649. After the Restoration he returned to England and was well received at court.

Parliament restored to Roscommon the lands his family held before the Civil War. As captain of the Gentleman Pensioners he had wide scope for his one vice, gambling. Disputes over his Irish estates took him to Ireland, where he showed business capacity. His fame rests on his blank verse version of the Ars Poetica (1680) and his Essay on Translated Verse (1684). That essay first stated clearly the principles of poetic diction.
britannica-1911-rosse-earl-of:
Rosse, as a title held by the Irish Parsons family, is traced in a family history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Sir William Parsons crossed to Ireland early in life and became surveyor general in 1602. He gained land in many places and was made a baronet in 1620. Later kin gained the titles of Baron Oxmantown and Viscount Rosse, and then Earl of Rosse in 1718.

That first line of earls died out in 1764, so the story turns to a second branch. Lawrence Harman Parsons gained the earldom again in 1806. His nephew Lawrence, the second earl of the new line, sat in the Irish parliament. He backed some relief for Catholics and spoke for reform of parliament. The entry helps readers untangle two lines that share one name.
britannica-1911-rosse-william-parsons-3r:
William Parsons, third Earl of Rosse, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rosse was an Irish star gazer and telescope builder who lived from 1800 to 1867. He was born at York, a son of the second earl. He studied at Dublin and then at Oxford. In 1821 he was returned to parliament for King's County. He later served as president of the Royal Society.

The article tells how he gave himself from 1827 to improving reflecting telescopes. In 1839 he set up a telescope of three foot width at his seat in Ireland. In 1845 his famed six foot mirror was finished. Famine and unrest kept the great tool idle for near three years. From 1848 it was in constant use, chiefly for watching nebulae. Its huge light gathering power suited it well to that work. He died in 1867.
britannica-1911-rosslyn-alexander-wedder:
Alexander Wedderburn, 1st Earl of Rosslyn (1733-1805), was Lord Chancellor of Great Britain, and his early career fills an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Eldest son of a Scottish judge, he was born in East Lothian and studied at Edinburgh University from age fourteen. He always meant to practise at the English bar.

The entry tells how he qualified as an advocate at Edinburgh in 1754 while also entering the Inner Temple in London. For three years he built a practice in Edinburgh, speaking in the church's General Assembly and in its debating clubs. In 1755 he edited a forerunner of the Edinburgh Review, whose pages carried Adam Smith's attack on Dr Johnson's dictionary.
britannica-1911-rosslyn-earls-of:
The Earls of Rosslyn take their line from a first earl who was a great lawyer of his age. The 1911 Britannica entry picks up the line with his heir, a nephew by his sister. That heir joined the army as a youth and served in wars in Portugal, Denmark, and the Low Countries, and rose to full general.

The entry notes his long years in the Commons before he took his seat as a peer. A Tory in his views and a friend of a famed duke general, he held high state seals in two spells of rule. He took a new family name when he came into the lands of an old Scots house. The piece then runs the line down through his son and great grandson to the fifth earl.
britannica-1911-rota-court-of:
The Court of Rota was one part of the medieval papal system at Rome. It stood beside other offices such as the Dataria and the two Signaturas. The Rota was the supreme court of Christendom in its day. It held twelve members drawn from across Italy and Europe. Three came from Rome, two from Spain, and one each from several other lands.

The court lost weight when a higher appeal court was set above it for Italy. It lost more as the pope's lands and reach shrank over time. After the Council of Trent, standing groups of cardinals took over its fields. Each such group dealt with a set branch of business at Rome. Yet the Rota was restored to its role as supreme appeal court in nineteen o eight. Pope Pius the Tenth made that change, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-rothes-earls-of:
Rothes, as earls, is the subject of a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The first earl was George Leslie, son of Norman Leslie of Rothes in Moray. He was made Baron Leslie of Leven in 1445 and earl of Rothes about 1458, in the peerage of Scotland. His line held a place in Scottish affairs for ages after.

The fourth earl, whose father fell at Flodden, was charged but cleared in 1546 over a share in the murder of Cardinal Beaton. His son Andrew, the fifth earl, stood with the lords of the congregation against Mary of Guise. He then turned on Mary queen of Scots and helped plot the murder of Rizzio. Yet he later fought for her at Langside. The seventh earl, John, fought for the king at Worcester in 1651. At the Restoration he rose to lord chancellor of Scotland for life.
britannica-1911-roxburghe-earls-and-duke:
Roxburghe, Earls and Dukes of, is the subject of a family entry in the 1911 Britannica. The entry traces the Ker line of Cessford in Scotland. Robert Ker, the first earl, lived from about 1570 to 1650. His forebears fought at Flodden and in border feuds. One forebear was killed near Melrose in 1526. That death was avenged by the killing of a Scott chief in 1552.

Robert Ker rose at court and went with King James to London in 1603. He was made an earl in 1616. He held the privy seal of Scotland for twelve years. His titles passed by a set plan to a grandson. That grandson took the Ker name as second earl. A later heir helped bring about the union with England. For that work he was made the first duke in 1707.
britannica-1911-rubruquis-william-of:
William of Rubruquis, who lived from about 1215 to 1270, was a Franciscan friar and a great medieval traveller. The 1911 Britannica article says next to nothing is known of him but what his own tale tells. His name has been much debated. Old writers tied it to Ruysbroeck near Brussels, home of a famed mystic. Fresh study points instead to Rubrouck, a village in French Flanders near Saint Omer.

Friar William went to Tartary by order of King Louis the Ninth of France. His trip of 1253 to 1255 took him deep into the Mongol world. His report of the road is the chief source for his life. Roger Bacon, a fellow friar of his age, also speaks of him. The article weighs the old printed forms of his name and of his book, as kept in a manuscript now in the British Museum.
britannica-1911-ruth-book-of:
Ruth, Book of, is a Bible study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a short book of the Old Testament. The book tells of Ruth, a woman of Moab. She was the great grandmother of King David.

The article deals chiefly with where the book sits in the Bible. In Jewish use it stands among the Writings and is read at the feast of Pentecost. In Greek and Latin lists it follows the book of Judges. The text argues that Ruth was not part of the old run of books from Joshua to Kings. Its calm tone and its tales of old customs set it apart. Talk of its date, and of its links to Ezra's time, fills the rest of the piece.
britannica-1911-rutland-earls-and-dukes-:
Rutland, Earls and Dukes of, is the subject of a family entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The first earl was Edward Plantagenet, who lived from 1373 to 1415. He was a son of Edmund, duke of York, and a grandson of King Edward the Third. He was made earl in 1390, but only for his father's lifetime.

On his father's death in 1402 the earldom died out, and Edward became duke of York. Later men of the house of York used the title with no clear legal right. In 1525 Thomas Manners was created earl of Rutland, and his heirs have held it since. Thomas was a favourite of Henry the Eighth, who gave him many posts and grants of land. Among them was Belvoir Castle in Leicestershire, which became the chief seat of his family. His son Henry served as an admiral under Queen Mary.
britannica-1911-rutland-john-james-rober:
John James Robert Manners, seventh duke of Rutland (1818-1906), was an English statesman, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces his long public life. He was born at Belvoir Castle, a younger son of the fifth duke, and was schooled at Eton and at Trinity College, Cambridge. In 1841 he entered Parliament for Newark in the Tory interest, on the same return as Gladstone. He later sat for Colchester and for Leicestershire seats until 1888.

That year he took his seat in the Lords on succeeding to the dukedom. In his first year in Parliament he brought out a book of poems, England's Trust, full of loyal feeling. By the end of 1841 he had joined the Young England party under Disraeli. That group hoped to curb the power of the middle classes and to rebuild the standing of the old nobility.
britannica-1911-ryswick-treaty-of:
Ryswick was the peace that ended a long war in 1697. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets France against the Empire, England, Spain, and Holland. William III of England led the fight to check Louis XIV of France. Fighting had spread across Europe, India, America, and the seas since 1689.

Talks met at Ryswick, with French envoys at the Hague and allies at Delft. A private deal between Portland and Boufflers broke the deadlock at last. France gave back towns seized since 1679 and kept Strassburg. Louis also agreed to accept William as king of England. A separate accord with the Empire followed weeks later.
britannica-1911-selborne-roundell-palmer:
Roundell Palmer, first earl of Selborne, who lived from 1812 to 1895, was an English lawyer and statesman. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Mixbury in Oxfordshire on the twenty-seventh of November 1812. His father was rector of the parish. His mother's kin, the Roundells, had sat in Yorkshire for four centuries. Palmer was schooled at Rugby and at Winchester. In 1830 he went to Trinity College, Oxford, as a scholar.

At Oxford he took a first class in classics and won the Eldon scholarship. A fellowship at Magdalen followed. He moved to London in 1835 to read for the bar, and was called in June 1837. Clients from his City kin soon filled his chambers with Chancery work. The article notes his wide life beyond the law. He wrote for The Times and dove for a time into the study of the early church fathers.
britannica-1911-shadoof:
Shadoof, from an Arabic word, is a tool for drawing water in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is used across the East, and most of all on the Nile to water fields. An upright frame holds a long pole hung at about one fifth of its length from one end. A bucket or skin bag hangs from the long end of the pole. A weight at the short end balances the load like a lever.

The full vessel is then swung round and poured into a channel. That channel carries the water where the farmer needs it to flow.
britannica-1911-sluys-battle-of:
Sluys was a sea fight told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was fought on a Saturday in June, in front of the town of Sluis, on the inlet between West Flanders and Zeeland. It was one of two sea fights in which King Edward the Third of England led in person. In those days the inlet was an open roadstead that could hold great fleets.

A French fleet had been drawn up to invade England. The king, in a letter to his son, puts it at one hundred and ninety sail. Part of it was Genoese galleys in French pay. English writers call the king's fleet the smaller, but he sailed from Orwell with two hundred sail and was joined by fifty more off Flanders. Some of the swarm were mere transports, and the queen's household came with the fleet.
britannica-1911-solomon-odes-of:
Odes of Solomon, a set of forty two hymns, is examined in a study entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The hymns most likely date from the close of the first century. The early church knew them, as quotes in later works prove. They were lost for ages and found again in 1908 in a Syriac manuscript.

Nothing is known of who wrote the odes, and the name Solomon is a pen name. A few odes are missing in the found copy, and the first has been restored from quotes. Many odes are plainly Christian in tone, yet they hold few traces of the New Testament. The words gospel and church never appear in them. A feel akin to the Gospel of John shows in places. The odes share a buoyant mood of Christian joy, and may be the work of a school of writers.
britannica-1911-somerset-earls-and-dukes:
Somerset, Earls and Dukes of, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on holders of English titles. It opens by noting that Somerset and Dorset long shared one sheriff. For a long stretch, titles drawn from each shire were held by the same person. The Somerset earldom in the Beaufort family dates from 1397.

In that year Richard the Second granted the earldom to John Beaufort, eldest son of John of Gaunt. His three sons held it in turn after him. The second of them also became duke of Somerset in 1443, a title that died with him. The third gained yet higher titles, becoming duke of Somerset in 1448. When that duke's son was put to death by the Yorkists in 1464, the titles were taken away by law.
britannica-1911-somerset-edmund-beaufort:
Edmund Beaufort, duke of Somerset, lived from about 1404 to 1455 and was a grandson of John of Gaunt. The 1911 Britannica entry opens with his capture at Bauge in 1421 on his first campaign. He stayed a prisoner until 1431 before he came home to England at last. Envoy work at the council of Basel followed in 1432 for the crown.

He served at the relief of Calais in 1436 and led with some success in Maine. Harfleur was recovered under his hand in 1440 in the French war. Earl rank came in 1441 and a marquess title two years after that. The entry traces the rise that made him a chief power in the realm.
britannica-1911-somerset-edward-seymour-:
Edward Seymour, Duke of Somerset (about 1506-1552), was protector of England. He was the eldest son to live of Sir John Seymour of Wolf Hall in Wiltshire. His mother was Margaret Wentworth, whose line ran back to Edward III. His father was knighted by Henry VII for service at Blackheath in 1497. The father died in December 1536.

Edward went to France as a young man with Mary Tudor at her wedding to Louis XII in 1514. He served in the French campaign of 1523 and was knighted there. He went with Wolsey on a mission to France in 1527. Henry VIII made him an esquire of the body in 1529. From there he rose fast in the king's favour, and in June 1536 his rise took a sharp step up.
britannica-1911-somerset-robert-carr-ear:
Robert Carr, earl of Somerset, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a Scottish politician. He lived from about 1590 to 1645. The date of his birth is not recorded in the entry. He was a younger son of Sir Thomas Ker of Ferniehurst. His mother was Janet, sister of Walter Scott of Buccleuch. He accompanied King James the First to England as page. 

For a time he sought to make his fortune in France. Returning to England, he broke his arm at a tilting match. The king was present and recognized the young man. Carr lacked all high intellectual qualities, the entry says. But he had good looks and excellent spirits. Those advantages were enough for King James at once. The king knighted him and took him into favour. In 1607 a chance let the king enrich him further.
britannica-1911-southampton-earl-of:
Southampton, Earl of, in the 1911 Britannica, is a title entry that tracks two families who held the name. Sir William Fitzwilliam was made earl in 1537. A boyhood friend of Henry the Eighth, he was knighted at the siege of Tournai in 1513. He served as vice admiral and keeper of the privy seal, died on the march into Scotland in 1542, and left no sons, so the title lapsed.

In 1547 Thomas Wriothesley was made earl, the first of a new line. He rose as chief secretary to Henry the Eighth and gained rich lands when the monasteries were shut. As lord chancellor from 1544 he became known for his harsh acts against Anne Askew. He lost his post in 1547 yet helped bring down Somerset before his death in 1550. His son Henry joined plots to free Mary Queen of Scots.
britannica-1911-southampton-henry-wrioth:
Henry Wriothesley, third Earl of Southampton, was a friend and backer of Shakespeare in this 1911 Britannica life. Born at Cowdray House in fifteen seventy three, he was a second son. He came to the title in fifteen eighty one and grew up a ward of the crown. He read at Cambridge and took a degree in fifteen eighty nine. At age seventeen he came to court and won the queen grace at once.

He gave rich gifts to poets of his day in great count. Nashe gave him a prose tale, and Markham gave him a sea poem. Two plays of praise from Shakespeare bear his name on their first leaves. The praise in the second of those gifts runs warm and full of love. One late tale credits him with a gift of a thousand pounds to the bard.
britannica-1911-st-albans-earls-and-duke:
St Albans, Earls and Dukes of, is a title history in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The English title of earl of St Albans was first borne by Richard Bourke, fourth earl of Clanricarde, who died in 1635. He was lord president of Connaught and governor of Galway. In 1628 he was made earl of St Albans in the English peerage. His English titles died out with his only son Ulick in 1657. The title was made a second time in 1660 for Henry, Baron Jermyn, but it died out again in 1684.

The dukedom of St Albans was created in that same year, 1684, for Charles Beauclerk. After the battle of Landen, William the Third made him captain of the gentlemen pensioners. His Whig views kept him from favour under Queen Anne, but George the First restored him. He died at Bath in 1726.
britannica-1911-st-albans-henry-jermyn-e:
Henry Jermyn, earl of St Albans (about 1604 to 1684), was a courtier of the Stuarts, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces his service to Queen Henrietta Maria. He was the third son of Sir Thomas Jermyn of Rushbroke in Suffolk. Young, he won the queen's favour, becoming her vice-chamberlain in 1628 and master of the horse in 1639.

He sat for Bury St Edmunds in the Long Parliament and acted as a keen, rash royalist. He took a leading part in the army plot of 1641 and fled to France when it came out. Back in 1643 he waited on the queen again, was raised to the peerage, and went with her to France in 1644 as her secretary. Made governor of Jersey, he conducted the prince of Wales to Paris.
britannica-1911-st-bartholomew-massacre-:
Saint Bartholomew Massacre is the name for a killing of Huguenots in France. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lays the plan at one queen door. It began in Paris on 24 August 1572. Catherine de Medici drove the crime from first to last.

Fear of Admiral Coligny grip on her son moved her. A first try at his murder only wounded the admiral. Huguenot anger then scared the court into a wider plot. At a night council she wrung the king consent from Charles. The killing ran at daybreak and lasted weeks in Paris. It spread to the provinces until early October that year. Some governors flatly refused to pass the order on. One count puts the dead of France at fifty thousand. Coligny was among the first and greatest victims.
britannica-1911-st-pol-counts-of:
Saint Pol is a count land in France whose holders are traced in one line of houses. In the eleven and twelve hundreds it was held by one house line. An heir of that house bore it to her spouse in twelve five. Past a wed match it then passed to the house of Luxemburg.

One lord of that house, chief guard of France, was put to death in fourteen seventy-five. His lands were seized, then gave back to his heirs in the next age but one. Past more wed ties the land went to a branch of the royal house. A sale in the past age but two moved it once more.
britannica-1911-st-vincent-john-jervis-e:
John Jervis, earl of Saint Vincent, who lived from 1735 to 1823, was a British admiral. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Meaford in Staffordshire on the ninth of January 1735. His father was a lawyer for the admiralty. Jervis entered the navy in January 1749. He rose to lieutenant in 1755 and served at the taking of Quebec. He gained his first commands in 1759 and 1760.

In the American war Jervis fought at Ushant and at the reliefs of Gibraltar. His great feat was the capture of the French ship Pégase in 1782, after a long chase. A knighthood marked that win. He sat in parliament from 1783 and held strong Whig views. Flag rank came in 1787, and command in the West Indies in 1793. In 1795 he took the Mediterranean fleet and held the blockade of Toulon.
britannica-1911-stafford-earls-and-marqu:
Stafford, earls and marquesses of, is the subject of this 1911 Britannica entry, which traces a title through creation, loss, and revival. The earldom of Stafford was created in 1351 and held first by the Stafford family. It died out in 1521. In 1640 Sir William Howard, son of the earl of Arundel, married Mary Stafford, sister and heiress of the fifth Baron Stafford, and was made Baron Stafford and then viscount.

Accused by Titus Oates of a share in the popish plots, Howard was found guilty and beheaded in December 1680, and his titles were forfeited. His son Henry, who but for that attainder would have inherited, was created earl of Stafford in 1688. When the fourth earl died in 1762 the earldom died out again, while the claim to the barony, still under attainder, fell into abeyance.
britannica-1911-stamford-henry-grey-1st-:
Henry Grey, first earl of Stamford, is drawn in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born about 1599, he came into his grand-father's barony in 1614. He wed Anne Cecil, heiress of the town and manor of Stamford. In 1628 the king made him earl of Stamford. When the Civil War neared, he sided firmly against the king.

Stamford led the side of parliament in Leicestershire and held Hereford. Royalist troops beat his men at Stratton in 1643. Besieged in Exeter, he gave up the city after three months. Charged with a lack of nerve, he fought no more. Poor and out of trust, he later backed Charles the Second and died in 1673.
britannica-1911-state-great-officers-of:
State, great officers of, is a name for the chief officers of the British Crown, and this 1911 Britannica entry sorts the loose use from the strict one. In common talk it covers all the principal ministers of the Crown. Strictly it fits only nine offices, from the lord high steward and the lord high chancellor to the earl marshal and the lord high admiral.

Those three are the lord chancellor, the lord-president of the council, and the lord privy seal. Two more offices, the lord treasurer's and the high admiral's, are now carried out by boards of commissioners. The heads of those boards sit in the cabinet, and the first lord of the treasury is usually the head of the government. The entry notes that nothing but custom keeps those two great posts in commission.
britannica-1911-stone-river-battle-of:
Stone River, called Murfreesboro by the Confederates, was a battle of the American Civil War fought at the turn of 1862 into 1863. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives General Rosecrans leading the Army of the Cumberland from Nashville toward Chattanooga. General Bragg left his quarters at Murfreesboro to meet him north of the town.

Each side planned to crush the other's right, and on the 31st of December the Confederate left bent the Union right back onto its centre. There Thomas's corps held fast, and the 1st of January passed quiet. On the 2nd they attacked again and failed to shift the Union left from high ground above the river. Bragg withdrew on the night of the 3rd, leaving Murfreesboro to the Union. The article calls it a drawn fight but a Union gain, with losses above 11,000 men on each side.
britannica-1911-strafford-earls-of:
Strafford, Earls of, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a line of English lords. The first earl was Thomas Wentworth, friend and aide to Charles the First. He was attainted and put to death in May 1641, and his titles were lost. Later that year his son William was made earl in his place.

William died with no heir in 1695, and most titles died with him. The lands passed to kin in the Watson line. That line rose in time to the marquess of Rockingham. The barony of Raby went to a cousin, Thomas Wentworth. His work as a soldier and as envoy at the Hague from 1711 is also told.
britannica-1911-strafford-thomas-wentwor:
Thomas Wentworth, earl of Strafford, an English statesman who lived from 1593 to 1641, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the son of Sir William Wentworth of Wentworth Woodhouse, near Rotherham. Born in London in April 1593, he was educated at St John's College, Cambridge. He entered the Inner Temple in 1607.

In 1611 Wentworth was knighted and married Margaret, daughter of the earl of Cumberland. In 1614 he sat for Yorkshire in the Addled Parliament. Only in the parliament of 1621 did he take a known part in debate. He did not share the popular party's zeal for war with Spain. But James's denial of the rights of parliament moved him to join in defending the claims of the House. His first wife died in 1622, and in 1625 he married Arabella Holles.
britannica-1911-suffolk-charles-brandon-:
Charles Brandon, first duke of Suffolk, was born about 1484 and died in 1545. The 1911 Britannica life calls his father the standard bearer of Henry the Seventh. That father fell at Bosworth Field, slain by Richard the Third in person. Young Charles was raised at the court of Henry the Seventh. He grew comely, bold, and very like Henry the Eighth in temper.

That likeness made him a great favourite of the young king. Posts in the royal household came to him one by one in turn. In 1513 he was made master of the horse for the king. That same May he was raised to the rank of Viscount Lisle. He won fresh fame at sieges in the French campaign of 1513.
britannica-1911-suffolk-thomas-howard-1s:
Thomas Howard, first earl of Suffolk, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English noble. He was born in 1561 and died in 1626. He was the second son of the fourth duke of Norfolk. He showed great gallantry in the attack on the Spanish Armada. He became an admiral in the year 1599.

He was made Baron Howard de Walden in 1597. In 1603 he became earl of Suffolk. He served as lord Chamberlain from 1603 to 1614. He then held the post of lord high treasurer for four years. In 1618 he lost that post on a charge of theft of funds. He was tried in the Star Chamber and fined heavily. His wife Catherine shared both his trial and his fall. The entry blames her greed in part for his ruin. She took bribes from Spain.
britannica-1911-suffolk-william-de-la-po:
William de la Pole, duke of Suffolk, lived from 1396 to 1450 and fought in France for Henry the Fifth. The 1911 Britannica entry notes his father fell at Harfleur and his brother at Agincourt. Young as he was, Suffolk held high command on the Normandy marches by 1421. Wins at Cravant and Verneuil followed in campaigns with Salisbury and Bedford.

When Salisbury was killed before Orleans in 1428, Suffolk took the chief command. After the siege was raised, Joan of Arc beat and captured him at Jargeau in 1429. Ransom freed him soon after that sharp reverse in the field. The entry opens the rise of a soldier who later steered the realm itself.
britannica-1911-surrey-earldom-of:
Surrey earldom is an old English title whose first date is in doubt. Its title entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. A Norman count, William de Warenne, is most often seen as first holder. William the Second is thought to have made him earl in about ten eighty eight.

Holders were styled earls of Surrey or Earls Warenne with no set rule. That first house died out when the third earl died in eleven forty eight. A second house came through Isabel de Warenne and Hamelin Plantagenet wedlock. Their line held the earldom until Earl John died in thirteen forty seven. The title then passed to the Fitzalan earls of Arundel by kin.
britannica-1911-surrey-henry-howard-earl:
English poet Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, born most likely in fifteen eighteen, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Lord Thomas Howard. In fifteen twenty four his father became Duke of Norfolk, and the boy took the Surrey title.

His youth was spent in Howard houses, chiefly at Kenninghall in Norfolk. A tutor taught him the old Latin and Greek works. The tutor also gave him a love of the verse of Italy. He grew close to Henry Fitzroy, the young son of King Henry the Eighth. The two boys lived at Windsor for a time. A planned match with the Princess Mary was raised, then dropped.
britannica-1911-sussex-earls-of:
Sussex, Earls of, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on an English title borne by several families. Its early history is tangled in obscurity, the entry says at the start. Under the Norman kings, earls' titles were often drawn loosely from a county, its chief town, or the earl's main home. The true mark of an earl was his right to a third of a county's court profits.

So one man in the twelfth century may appear as earl of Sussex, of Chichester, or of Arundel. A further tangle came from Sussex and Surrey sharing a single sheriff for a time. That muddled the earldoms of the two counties as well. The Crown's ruling in 1433, that holding Arundel castle carried a title with it, is also weighed and doubted.
britannica-1911-sussex-kingdom-of:
Sussex, Kingdom of, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Anglo-Saxon kingdom. The name means the South Saxons in the old tongue. Its bounds matched, in the main, the modern county of Sussex. Much of that land was once covered by a great forest. That forest was called Andred in the old records. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle gives the tale of its founding. It says Ella led invaders ashore in the year 477.

Ella beat the folk who held the shore at landing. A second battle is set down under the year 485. In 491 Ella and his son Cissa sacked Anderida. The record says they slew all who lived there. Bede names Ella first among kings who held sway over peers. The entry treats him as a real man of history. It warns that the Chronicle's dates carry little weight. After that, the record goes blank until 607.
britannica-1911-sussex-thomas-radclyffe-:
Thomas Radclyffe, 3rd Earl of Sussex (c. 1525–1583), was lord-lieutenant of Ireland. He was the eldest son of Henry, 2nd earl of Sussex, by his first wife. She was a daughter of Thomas Howard, 2nd duke of Norfolk. He was born about 1525 and was styled Viscount Fitzwalter after his father took the earldom in 1542. After service in the army abroad, he was used in 1551 to treat for a match. The match was to be between Edward VI and a daughter of Henry II of France.

Sussex stood among the men who signed the paper of June 1553 that set the crown on Lady Jane Grey. Yet he won the favour of Queen Mary all the same. She used him to set up her match with Philip of Spain, and she raised him as Baron Fitzwalter in August 1553.
britannica-1911-sutherland-earls-and-duk:
Sutherland, Earls and Dukes of, is a house entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It traces a Scottish title from its first earl in the middle ages. The first earl took the name from a district his father had gained. His line wed into the house of a famed Scots king.

The entry follows the title as it passed by marriage to a new house. One earl of that line was killed by poison at a rival hand. A later earl won praise as a good lord and fought for his faith. He then served the restored king well in his last years. The next earl backed the great change of sixteen eighty eight.
britannica-1911-swartz-olof: Swartz, Olof is a brief life entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a Swedish botanist. Olof Swartz was born in 1760 and died in 1818. He studied plants at Upsala, under Linnaeus and Thunberg. In 1783 he sailed to America, and in 1788 he visited England. Back in Sweden in 1789, he was made professor of natural history in Stockholm. The entry credits him with many works that set plants in order and widened what was known of flowering plants and cryptogams alike.
britannica-1911-swold-battle-of:
The Battle of Swold was the most famous sea fight of the ancient Norsemen, and a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its frame. The fight took place on the ninth of September in the year 1000. The place of the battle can no longer be fixed with sureness. The Baltic coast has changed much in the centuries since.

Silting of the sea and great storms of the fourteenth century reshaped that coast. Swold was an island, likely on the north German coast near Rügen. On one side stood Olaf Trygvesson, king of Norway. Against him stood a league of his enemies in arms. They were Eric Hakonson, his cousin and rival, and two kings. Those kings were Olaf of Sweden and Sweyn Forkbeard of Denmark. Poets and saga writers are the only sources for the tale.
britannica-1911-tempe-vale-of:
Tempe, Vale of is a place article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a famed narrow valley in the north of Thessaly, in Greece. Through the vale the river Peneus runs down to the sea. The name itself means a cleft, from a Greek verb for cutting, and old fable said the sea god Poseidon split the rocks with his trident, between Mount Olympus and Mount Ossa.

The article gives the vale as about four and a half miles long. Cliffs on the Olympus side drop so steeply that they block the path, while those from Ossa rise in places not less than fifteen hundred feet. Yet the scene is soft as well as grand, with a broad winding river and rich plant life. The entry also notes the pass could be held by a small force, though an invader could still force a way through.
britannica-1911-thanet-isle-of:
Kent's far north east corner forms the Isle of Thanet, set out in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Two arms of the river Stour cut it off from the rest of the county. Its name may come from a Saxon word for a beacon or fire.

The isle is roughly oblong, about eight miles long and five miles wide. A sea channel once ran where the Stour now flows. Roman forts at Reculver and Richborough guarded that old channel. When the channel dried up, marsh land was left to the south and west. High cliffs face the sea, and the North Foreland marks the east tip. Ramsgate, Broadstairs, and Margate draw crowds to the coast.
britannica-1911-tongues-gift-of:
Tongues, Gift of, is a church article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a strange form of speech in early Christian groups. The Greek name for it is also given. It names speech that pours out in broken sounds under strong religious feeling, with no plain sense.

The article draws its picture chiefly from the letters of Paul. Such speech was counted a gift of the spirit, yet not a clear one. Paul sets it beside a pipe or harp played at random, with no tune. A trumpet blown with no set call helps no one, he says. So Paul lays down firm rules for its use. In church, no more than three should speak in tongues, and each in turn. A man who can render the sense must be at hand, or the gift should stay at home.
britannica-1911-toreno-jose-maria-quiepo:
Jose Maria Queipo de Llano, Count of Toreno, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Toreno was a Spanish statesman and historian who lived from 1786 to 1843. He was born at Oviedo into a rich family of old nobility. He gained a better schooling in classics, maths, and modern tongues than was usual then. Reading Voltaire and Rousseau shaped his young views.

The article tells how he was in Madrid when the city rose against the French in 1808. That rising began the Peninsular War. He escaped to Asturias and sailed to England to ask for help. The mission was warmly received in London. During the war he served chiefly as a member of the Cortes. He helped frame the constitution of 1812 while still under the legal age. When the king returned in 1814, Toreno fled into exile.
britannica-1911-torrington-arthur-herber:
