Arthur Herbert, earl of Torrington, a British admiral who lived from 1647 to 1716, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a judge, Sir Edward Herbert. He joined the navy in 1663 and served in the Dutch wars of Charles the Second and against the Barbary pirates. From 1680 to 1683 he held command in the Mediterranean.

His record was good and he had been wounded in action. King James the Second, who counted on his Royalist kin, made him rear-admiral of England. But Herbert would not back the repeal of the Test Acts, and the king struck him from his posts. He then dealt in secret with the agents of the prince of Orange and carried the call to William in 1688. The Revolution made good his losses. He was named first lord of the admiralty and took the home fleet to sea.
britannica-1911-trade-board-of:
The Board of Trade is the British body that watches over commerce and industry, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its growth. Its formal name is the Committee of Privy Council for Trade. Most state oversight of trade and industry in the United Kingdom runs through it. Councils on trade go back as far as the fourteenth century.

Those early councils were set up from time to time to advise parliament. No lasting department was tried until the middle of the seventeenth century, under the Commonwealth. Cromwell set that pattern, and it was kept after the Restoration. In 1660 a committee of the privy council took charge of trade matters. Its task was to gather facts on imports and exports. It was also to find ways to improve the trade of the country.
britannica-1911-trafalgar-battle-of:
Trafalgar, Battle of, is a war entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It tells of a great sea win for Britain off a cape in Spain. The fight took place in the fall of eighteen hundred and five. It grew from the wreck of a French plan to invade the British Isles.

The entry sets the scene with fleets at watch off the port of Cadiz. A French fleet gave up its push for the Channel and fell back there. Small British squadrons held the watch and drew out pursuit in turn. Allied ships lay still in port while London weighed how to strike them. The full tale of the clash is told step by step from that tense start.
britannica-1911-trent-council-of:
Trent, Council of is a church history article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the great council of the Catholic Church held from 1545 to 1563. The article starts far back. Through the fifteenth century and the first half of the sixteenth, the idea of a general council stayed alive. Men hoped such a council would solve the grave troubles of the Church.

The councils of Constance and Basel had fallen short of that hope. Still, trust in a council grew deeper as the popes of the Renaissance showed less will to make the reforms many thought due. The papacy did not grant that a council held power over it. In 1459 Pius the Second banned any appeal to such a court, on pain of being cast out of the Church. That ban changed no minds.
britannica-1911-trenton-and-princeton-ba:
Trenton and Princeton, two battles of the War of American Independence, are told together in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They came in the winter of 1776 to 1777. The entry calls them the first wins in the open field for Washington. They followed close on a run of defeats, and their effect on troops and folk at large was marked.

The first half tells of the retreat through New Jersey and across the Delaware. On Christmas night Washington crossed back through floating ice. At dawn his two columns fell on the Hessian post at Trenton by surprise. Some nine hundred and fifty men gave up, and the American loss was a handful of wounded. The piece then turns to the march of Cornwallis and the clash at Princeton.
britannica-1911-tweeddale-marquesses-of:
John Hay, 2nd Earl and 1st Marquess of Tweeddale (1626–1697), heads this account of the family. He was the eldest son of John, 8th Lord Hay of Yester, made earl of Tweeddale in 1646. The line runs back to a lord of the Scots parliament of 1488. Before he took the peerage in 1654, Hay fought for Charles I in the Civil War. He soon changed sides and stood in the Scots ranks at Marston Moor.

Hay changed sides once more and stood with the royalists at Preston. Yet he sat in Cromwell's parliament in 1656 and was jailed just after Charles II came back. The king soon took him into favour. In 1663 he became president of the Scots council, and in 1664 a lord of session. In Scotland he sought to soften the harsh rule used on the Covenanters. That stand led to his loss of office.
britannica-1911-urmia-lake-of:
The Lake of Urmia is a great lake in north western Persia, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry measures its shifting shores. The lake takes its name from the town of Urmia, near its western shore. It is also called the Deryacheh i Shahi, or Shahi lake. Its bounds run from about eighty to ninety miles in length.

The width of the lake runs from thirty to forty five miles. Both length and width grow in the season of high water. That season comes in spring, when the snows melt. In the low water season the lake shrinks far back. A rise of a few inches can push the shore miles inland. The entry reckons the high water surface at half as much again as the low water surface. Few lakes change their map so much with the seasons.
britannica-1911-warwick-sir-robert-rich-:
Robert Rich, second earl of Warwick, lived from 1587 to 1658. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows the Puritan admiral and colonizer. He took the title in 1619 as eldest son of the first earl. Colonial ventures seized his interest from an early age.

He joined companies for Bermuda, Virginia, and New England. His fights helped crush the Virginia Company in 1624. He helped win the patent for the Massachusetts colony in 1628. A Connecticut patent grant followed from his hand in 1631. At home he fought forced loans, ship money, and church policy. Parliament made him admiral against the king veto in 1642. He won the whole navy over to Parliament that July. As lord high admiral he cut off royal ships and ports. He also worked to secure freedom of worship in the colonies.
britannica-1911-wellington-arthur-welles:
Arthur Wellesley, first duke of Wellington, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He was the fourth son of the earl of Mornington. The family had been settled in Ireland for two centuries. Its name was once Colley, then Wesley. The spelling Wellesley came in about 1790. Arthur was born in Ireland in 1769. He was sent to Eton, then to a military college at Angers.

He entered the army in 1787 as an ensign. He rose fast through posts in five regiments. In 1793 he bought the rank of lieutenant-colonel. His brother lent him the money for the purchase. Yet he did little duty with his regiment. He served as aide to the lord-lieutenant of Ireland instead. He also sat in the Irish parliament for Trim. His first real campaign came in 1794. In 1796 he was sent with his regiment to India.
britannica-1911-westmeath-earl-of:
Earl of Westmeath is the title covered in a family history entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The title had been held by the Irish family of Nugent since sixteen twenty one. The entry traces the line back to Sir Gilbert Nugent in the reign of Henry the Second. He gained the lordship of Delvin in Meath.

That lordship passed by marriage away from the Nugents and later came back. Sir William Nugent wed Catherine, daughter of John Fitzjohn, in the early fourteen hundreds. The barony is held to date from his time rather than from Gilbert's. His son Richard served twice as lord deputy of Ireland. The line is then traced through later barons.
britannica-1911-westminster-marquesses-a:
The title of marquess of Westminster was given in 1831 to Robert Grosvenor, 2nd Earl Grosvenor (1767-1845). His grandson, Hugh Lupus Grosvenor (1825-1899), was made duke of Westminster in 1874. The Grosvenor family is of great age in Cheshire. Deeds prove a knightly house of that name in the county as early as the twelfth century.

A legend gives the family descent from a nephew of Hugh Lupus, earl of Chester. That tale lives on in the first duke's name. An even wilder tale makes the family's forebears the chief huntsmen of the dukes of Normandy. Research by W. H. B. Bird has blown up both tales, as the article notes. The Grosvenors of Eaton, near Chester, were a younger branch of that old knightly house.
britannica-1911-westminster-statutes-of:
Westminster, Statutes of, two English statutes passed under Edward the First, are the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Parliament met at Westminster in April 1275 to take up the first statute. It was drawn up in Norman French, not Latin. Stubbs, quoted in the entry, calls it almost a code by itself, with fifty one clauses.

Its clauses cover the whole ground of law making for the realm. Common right is to be done to all, poor and rich alike, with no respect of persons. Votes are to be free, with no force, malice, or threats to sway them. The act curbs heavy fines, abuse of wardship, and unfair feudal demands. The second statute, passed in 1285, is called a code in itself as well. Its famous clause on gifts shaped the land law of medieval England.
britannica-1911-wight-isle-of:
The Isle of Wight is the subject of a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. The isle lies off the south coast of England. It forms part of Hampshire. The Solent and Spithead split it from the mainland. It has the shape of a diamond when seen on a map. It spans just over twenty two miles from east to west. Its full area is just under one hundred and fifty square miles.

A ridge of high chalk downs runs across the isle. Three streams cut through that ridge as they flow north. The south downs rise still higher at one peak. Below them lies the Undercliff, a shelf formed by fallen rock. That shelf is warm and calm, and fine plants grow well there. Gulfs cut by streams, called chines, mark the south coast. Three tall chalk stacks called the Needles stand off the west tip.
britannica-1911-winchelsea-anne-finch-co:
Anne Finch, Countess of Winchelsea, is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was an English poet born in April of sixteen sixty one. Both her parents died while she was still a small child. She served as maid of honour to a duchess at the royal court.

The entry tells how she wed a court colonel in sixteen eighty four. Verse notes to her husband fill much of her work, with pet names for both. When a new king took the throne, the pair lost their place at court. A kin earl gave them a home in Kent for long years. She took his title in time and died in London in seventeen twenty.
britannica-1911-winchester-earls-and-mar:
The title earl of Winchester was first borne by Saier de Quincy, who got it from King John in twelve o seven. The gift joined the earldom with the county of Southampton. Saier was one of the twenty five barons named to enforce the Great Charter. He served in the Crusades at the siege of Damietta. He died soon after, most likely in November twelve nineteen.

His second son Roger held the earldom next and fought in the barons' struggles. Roger died with no male heir in twelve sixty four, and the title went back to the crown. It was revived in thirteen twenty two for Hugh le Despenser, a favourite of Edward the Second. He lost it when the barons put him to death as a traitor. Later grants and the marquessate of fifteen fifty one follow.
britannica-1911-worcester-earls-and-marq:
Worcester is an earl title that passed through many English houses. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica unrolls its holders from the 1100s. A Norman count likely held it under King Stephen. He lost it, turned crusader, and died a monk.

Thomas Percy held the earldom from 1397 to 1403. He revolted with his kin and lost his head at Shrewsbury. The title lapsed and woke again for short spells twice. In 1514 Henry the Eighth gave it to Charles Somerset. That earl was a son of a duke of Somerset. The Somerset line then held it in direct descent. The fifth earl lent great sums to Charles the First. In 1643 the king raised him to marquess for that aid.
bygone-beliefs-being-a-series-of-excursi:
H Stanley Redgrove subtitled Bygone Beliefs a series of excursions in the byways of thought, with Novalis and Blake on magic and belief as mottoes. His chapters begin with medieval thought and Pythagoras. They turn to medicine and magic, superstitions concerning birds, and the powder of sympathy. That last was a cure worked by treating the weapon rather than the wound.

Talismans, ceremonial magic in theory and practice, and architectural symbolism follow. Redgrove, a chemist, treats white magic's disguised goetia and Waite's judgments with a scholar's care rather than a debunker's scorn. The book surveys occult belief as a serious chapter in the history of ideas, and collectors of folklore still mine it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximus-von-i:
Maximus von Imhof, a German physicist born at Rissbach in Bavaria in 1758, died at Munich in 1817. The son of a shoemaker, he studied at Landshut and joined the Augustinian Order in 1780. At the Munich monastery he taught physics, maths, and philosophy from 1786 to 1791. He joined the physics class of the Munich Academy of Sciences in 1790 and became its director in 1800.

That same year he became professor of physics and maths at the Electoral Lyceum, and in 1792 the academy asked him to lecture in public on experimental physics and chemistry. Elected prior of his monastery in 1798, he left the order in 1802 and became canon of Munich's Frauenkirche. For twenty-one years he oversaw the fitting of lightning rods across Bavaria. His books cover electricity, physics, chemistry, and lightning rods, the last published in 1816.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-proof:
Proof settles a disputed matter through lawful means or arguments. Proof is evidence's fruit.  Proof is perfect when it breeds full conviction and lets the judge sentence with no further inquiry. It is imperfect if it breeds but probability.

Canonists count six kinds of perfect proof: two unshaken witnesses above all suspicion. The rest are a public document, or a paper with its force; conclusive presumption of law; the decisive oath; judicial confession; and notoriety of the fact. Imperfect, or semi-proof, flows from one witness alone, or several singular witnesses, or two witnesses not wholly unshaken or not past all suspicion. It also flows from private papers, from a paper held true but on handwriting alone, from the necessary oath, from merely probable presumption, and from public report when lawfully proved. Two imperfect proofs cannot make perfect proof in criminal cases.
ceremonial-of-hasjelti-dailjis-and-mythi:
James Stevenson reached the Navajo Reservation in the summer of 1885, near Keam's Canyon in Arizona, days before a great healing ceremonial began. Some 1,200 Navajos gathered on the plateau. A man of standing in the tribe faced losing his sight to inflamed eyes, and curing the sick was the gathering's prime cause.

Stevenson's account follows all nine days and nights in order. A medicine lodge is built, sweat houses raised, masks and prayer sticks prepared, and sacred reeds made. Personators of the gods Hasjelti and Hostjoghon enter the lodge in ceremony. Four sand paintings, shown in plates, anchor the middle days. Navajo myths close the report, among them the creation of the sun.
corporal-cameron-of-the-north-west-mount:
Ralph Connor, the Canadian novelist and Presbyterian minister, tells this tale of the Macleod Trail in three books. The first opens in Scotland under the heading The Quitter. Allan Cameron, heir to the glen of Cuagh Oir, has thrown away his chances, and the family solicitor and a question of honour send him across the Atlantic to begin again.

Book Two puts him to a man's job on a ranch in the foothills, among harvests, chivarees, and Sabbath days. Book Three takes him into the North West Mounted Police at Macleod, under Sergeant Crisp, where the making of braves among the Stoney Indians and a nurse named Haley fill the chapters. The quitter of the first page earns the corporal's stripes of the title. Connor built the book on the formula he was known for: disgrace, exile, and redemption under western skies.
correggio-a-collection-of-fifteen-pictur:
Fifteen pictures by the Italian painter Correggio, plus a supposed portrait of him, form the heart of this art book by Estelle M. Hurll. Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York issued it in 1901 in the Masterpieces of Art line. Hurll opens with a study of Correggio's character as an artist.

Each plate gets notes that point out how the figures are grouped and lit. The Holy Night, St. Catherine Reading, and The Marriage of St. Catherine are among the works shown. Front matter adds a list of books to consult, a table of dates from the painter's life, and a list of painters of his time. The book suits readers who want guided looking, not just plates.
democracy-and-education-an-introduction-:
John Dewey published Democracy and Education in 1916 as an introduction to the philosophy of education, and it became his most read book. The opening chapters treat education as a necessity of life, a social function, direction, and growth. Chapter seven states the democratic conception that organizes the whole argument.

Dewey attacks fixed aims, rote fact-loading, and the split between interest and discipline, arguing instead for learning through experience and thinking. Mere assent to presented facts, he warns, is lazy acquiescence, not knowledge. Schools, for Dewey, are small democracies where habits of shared inquiry form citizens. The book still anchors debates about progressive education, vocational training, and what public schools owe a free society.
doe-osti-17019154-abbreviated-final-repo:
Abbreviated final report from Lawrence Livermore, dated September 2026, covers project 24-ERD-008 on why pulsed laser diodes fail when light strikes back at them. Will Fenwick and Bob Deri studied this back irradiance failure in diodes that pump solid state lasers. Such failures were widely reported, but the physics behind them was poorly understood.

Over one hundred diodes from two makers were driven to failure while pulse length, temperature, power, packaging, and coatings varied. Heat and light modeling plus post failure study pointed to thermal runaway at the diode output face. Shorter pump pulses and certain pump light delivery designs improved resistance, as did packaging details that improve heat sinking near the face.
doe-osti-17076846-three-dimensional-nume:
Sajjan Pokhrel, Christine Doughty, and Xiaobing Liu of Oak Ridge modeled a plan to heat a courthouse with warm water from a flooded mine in report ORNL/TM-2026/4581, dated April 2026. The abandoned mine shaft sits in Butte, Montana, near the Mansfield Courthouse. Closed loop U-shaped heat exchangers would hang in the shaft, and a heat pump would lift the warmth to building use.

A three dimensional model in the TOUGH3 simulator tracked outlet temperature, shaft temperature patterns, and pumping cost as loop counts changed. In the base case, outlet temperature stayed in the heat pump comfort range even at peak winter demand. Sideways groundwater flow toward the Berkeley Pit improved performance further by renewing the heat.
doe-osti-17084207-development-and-attemp:
Nathan Brown and a Sandia and Georgia Tech team report in October 2026 on a laser method for reading gas coming off pulsed power electrodes. The method, femtosecond laser induced breakdown spectroscopy, fires an ultra short laser pulse to spark a tiny plasma, whose light reveals what gas is present. Desorption, gas released from a surface under heating, matters for electrode behavior.

Early chapters prove the method on single and mixed low density gases, with spectral models and deep learning analysis of the light lines. Electron density over time was measured in hydrogen and methane. The team then tried the method on heated wires as stand ins for electrodes, varying wire size and probe distance, and modeled heating, desorption, and diffusion to judge the attempt.
doe-osti-17120795-thermo-chemical-mechan:
William Neilson, Michael Cooper, David Andersson, Topher Matthews, and Los Alamos colleagues present SWIFT, a simulation tool for hydrogen inside metal hydride reactor moderators, issued 30 September 2026. Hydrides such as yttrium and zirconium hydride slow neutrons well, but hydrogen slowly escapes them, which sets operating limits. Knowing where the hydrogen goes is a safety and life question.

Built on the MOOSE framework, SWIFT follows hydrogen as it diffuses through the bulk, absorbs and desorbs at surfaces, and leaks through cladding barriers. Uneven temperature fields drive a drift called the Soret effect. Tested against past closed vessel experiments on zirconium hydride, the code matched measured hydrogen loss. The team also shows the standard heat of transport value for the Soret effect is too high, and calls the tool ready for microreactor design work.
doe-osti-17152723-an-updated-sesame-mult:
Joshua Leveillee and Scott Crockett of Los Alamos rebuild the Sesame equation of state table for Vascomax Maraging 250 steel, in a report issued 5 October 2026. An equation of state tells simulation codes how a material responds to pressure and heat. This steel is ultra strong and wear resistant, a candidate for extreme settings, but measured data for it are scarce.

Four phases are built separately to match what measurements exist: room condition alpha martensite, a high pressure epsilon phase, high temperature austenite, and liquid. Shock data from this steel and from the stronger 350 grade, plus the iron table, guided choices where data ran thin. The update tracks shock behavior better than the 2016 version it replaces. It enters the Sesame database as material 4396.
doe-osti-17152726-an-updated-sesame-mult:
Joshua Leveillee, Patricia Kalita, and Scott Crockett of Los Alamos update the Sesame equation of state for pure nickel and add new shock data, in a report issued 6 October 2026. Nickel parts appear across technology, and nickel also fills much of Earth's core, so its high pressure behavior feeds both engineering and planetary models. New experiments since 2022 called for a rebuild.

Shock shots on Sandia's Z pulsed power machine traced the Hugoniot curve to near 1 terapascal. Atom scale calculations supplied extra constraints, and Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling turned them into parameter ranges with stated uncertainty. Recent diffraction work shows the crystal form holds to 322 gigapascals, then melts across a broad range. The new table, material 3105, draws the melt line from a free energy crossing instead of the older rule.
doe-osti-2583519-engineering-yeast-for-t:
Lygos and NREL joined forces on an unusual yeast under CRADA CRD-17-00718, closed out in report NREL/TP-2800-94279 dated February 11, 2025. Jeffrey Linger was the laboratory's contact; Eric Steen represented Lygos. Their organism was Pichia kudriavzevii, a yeast well suited to making acids and esters such as butyric acid and ethyl butyrate, building blocks for fuels and bioproducts. Few labs work with it, so public genetic tools are scarce.

Lygos brought years of strain-specific know-how and its own genetic toolkit, developed while pursuing malonic acid products. NREL brought its immediate focus on butyric acid and ethyl butyrate, plus broad bioprocess experience. The pairing let each side move faster than either could alone: Lygos gained a route into molecules it wanted long-term, and NREL gained access to a hardy acid-tolerant host. The final report records the collaboration's structure and shared direction rather than production data.
doe-osti-2583533-durability-and-accelera:
A Solar Prize participant coating polymer mirror film with liquid metal sent its prototype to NREL for a durability verdict. Report NREL/TP-5700-93249, dated February 7, 2025, closes CRADA CRD-21-17856, with Guangdong Zhu and Tucker Farrell as the laboratory's contacts. Concentrating solar plants use heavy, costly glass mirrors. Polymer film is lighter and cheaper, but making it is expensive; the participant's room-temperature liquid-metal deposition aimed to cut expenditures by eighty percent and film cost in half.

NREL's job was the hard question: does it last? The laboratory ran durability and accelerated aging tests on the prototype film, compressing years of sun, heat, and weather into laboratory time. Monthly check-ins with the principal investigator kept the test program aligned with the design. A mirror that delaminates in year three is worse than no mirror, so this unglamorous aging work decides whether the cost breakthrough is real.
doe-osti-2588041-efficient-and-accurate-:
Erin O'Neil and Joshua Basabe wrote this report, LA-UR-25-28888, at Los Alamos National Laboratory in July 2025. It comes out of a ten-week student workshop, and the authors say so up front: the findings are preliminary and reflect a learning process. The topic is equation of state data, the tables that tell a simulation how a material responds to density and temperature.

Simulations rarely use raw table values; they interpolate, and they often need the table inverted, swapping which variable is looked up. The report compares three interpolation strategies on SESAME tabular data: EOSPAC, and two SpinerEOS variants keyed to different variable pairs. Accuracy and speed are weighed against each other. One thread works out how to transform the grid itself so the specific-internal-energy variant can look up values accurately. It is a careful student study of a trade-off every hydrocode user faces.
doe-osti-2589893-reconceptualizing-off-r:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2011168, by Michael Albertson, dated September 2025, rethinks how a United States-China crisis could be ended short of full war. Off-ramps are negotiated pauses or pullbacks taken mid-crisis, when fighting realities have sobered leaders on both sides. The paper draws on arms control history and recent Chinese writings on nuclear learning.

Much is unknown about how such a war would unfold: both sides field modern systems never tested against each other. Lessons from the Russia-Ukraine land war fit an air and sea contest poorly. The report argues for planning cooperative steps in advance, at the turning points where each side can accept a stop. Strategists get a framework for building exits into war plans before a crisis removes the time to invent them.
doe-osti-2997754-design-construction-and:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/CFCT-25/23, by Nora Shaheen, Amber Polke, Denis Johnson, and co-authors, documents building pumped molten salt loops inside a glovebox. The loops circulate hot, actinide-bearing salt so instruments can be tested under flowing, uneven-temperature conditions like a real molten salt reactor. Most monitoring tools for these reactors are still too immature for licensing, and loop testing is how they grow up.

Design and construction details fill the report, down to joint choices: connecting points were built from 316 stainless steel. Because the loops run at ambient pressure, pressure vessel codes for materials, welding, and inspection do not apply, a point the authors make explicitly. Partitioned glovebox layouts are shown as renderings and photographs. Test teams at other laboratories can copy the platform to qualify their own sensors.
doe-osti-2999148-evaluating-pulse-shapin:
Brian Hutsel, Andrew Porwitzky and Jean-Paul Davis of Sandia National Laboratories, with Western Michigan University partners, evaluate pulse shaping in next-generation pulsed power machines, in report SAND2025-12806R, printed October 2025. Future machines must deliver current pulses with carefully sculpted shapes, since the pulse profile steers experiments on how materials behave under extreme squeeze. Each forming line should fire with its own timing and mode.

The team built a circuit model of a proposed point design. Its pulse forming lines are modelled one by one, so timing and mode can vary per line. A two-dimensional mesh stands in for the radial impedance transformer, catching uneven flow around its ring. Runs showed the design family can serve dynamic materials experiments. Automated design help is also explored, including a learning-based model detailed in an appendix. The report gives designers a way to test pulse shapes before metal is cut.
doe-osti-3002209-report-on-updated-prope:
Peeyush Nandwana, Selda Nayir, Caleb Massey, Geeta Kumari, David Collins, and colleagues update a reference work in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4107, dated August 2025. The reference is a properties handbook for 3D-printed stainless steel 316. Designers turn to handbooks for tested values of strength, ductility, and other traits before they trust a material in service.

The update folds in new data gathered across wide ranges of printing settings. It builds on earlier work that deposited and tested material at the extremes of the process window. A standard process-parameter procedure for the alloy is part of the background. Keeping the handbook current matters because printed steel varies with machine settings. Engineers comparing printed 316 against conventional stock get one checked source here.
doe-osti-3003300-building-partnerships-f:
Daniel Foti of the University of Memphis reports on a partnership-building grant, DE-SC0023267, which ran from September 2022 to February 2025. The university had deep experience in energy systems but little contact with the Energy Department's environmental science facilities. The grant set out to connect Memphis researchers with the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement user facility and its boundary-layer science.

The work targeted a shared problem: forecasting atmospheric conditions across scales, from the lowest boundary layer up to aerosol layers that shape clouds. Renewable energy systems live or die on those forecasts. Products listed include a random forest model of optical turbulence in the boundary layer, presented to an aeronautics audience. The report is a final account of the collaboration and the joint research directions it opened.
doe-osti-3010299-advanced-manufacturing-:
Optimax report by Jennifer Coniglio documents a Phase II effort to manufacture diffraction-limited x-ray mirrors for synchrotron beamlines. The mirrors bounce x-rays at grazing incidence, and their surfaces must be smooth to 0.3 nanometres RMS in the fine roughness band.

The HERMES robotic platform smoothed diamond-turned silicon and polished optics, cutting mid-spatial-frequency error on every part from small coupons up to the 500L demonstrator optic. A companion Grolish polishing platform scaled to the demonstrator as well. Smoothing of the 500L optic was still unfinished when the project expired, so its final ion beam finishing never ran. The process line was aimed at a one-metre optic as the end goal.
doe-osti-3012016-solar-scale-improving-t:
Local rules for large scale solar are the focus of the Solar@Scale project in a final report by Debra Perry of the International City/County Management Association. The award DE-EE0009000 ran from August 2020 to July 2025. United States solar deployment grew about 28 percent per year over the past decade, leaving many communities without solar planning or permitting experience.

Tools and resources target planning, siting, permitting, and inspection for local governments and other authorities having jurisdiction. A project guidebook went through advisory committee review and three external reviews before final release. The project weighed local benefits such as economic growth and resilience against project trade offs.
doe-osti-3012869-constraining-microphysi:
Colorado State University's final technical report for award DE-SC0021167, by principal investigator Jui-Yuan Christine Chiu, dated January 12, 2026, tackles a stubborn cloud measurement problem. Drizzle forms inside marine clouds as droplets collide and merge. Radar signals from drizzle drops swamp the signal from the far smaller cloud droplets, so the two are hard to measure at the same time.

The project improved the ENCORE ensemble retrieval method to pull cloud and drizzle properties out of ARM observations together. From those paired retrievals, users can derive autoconversion and accretion rates, the speeds at which cloud water turns into drizzle and drizzle grows by collecting cloud water. A machine learning model now predicts those rates for warm clouds, with formal uncertainty estimates attached.
doe-osti-3013404-modular-system-for-dire:
Stanford University's final report for award DE-FE-0031867 covers October 2020 to September 2025. Arun Majumdar served as principal investigator, with partners Susteon and Casale. The team pursued direct conversion of methane into methanol by photocatalysis. Methanol is a valuable chemical feedstock. Methane, by contrast, is often flared as waste gas. The modular system would run at flare sites. It would use light rather than high heat and pressure.

The team built a bifunctional catalyst. A semiconductor photocatalyst uses ultraviolet light to make hydroxyl radicals, which activate methane. A co-catalyst then steers the fragments toward methanol. Tests varied the silica coating thickness on the catalyst, at 9 and 13 nanometers. They also varied the ultraviolet flux. The runs mapped how those choices trade conversion against selectivity. Techno-economic and market assessments accompany the reactor design.
doe-osti-3014158-crossing-the-finish-lin:
The Water Research Foundation's final technical report for award DE-EE0009508, submitted December 23, 2025, closes the Crossing the Finish Line project, led by principal investigator Jeff Moeller. Partners included DC Water, Hampton Roads Sanitation District, Metro Water Recovery, three universities, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The project brought data-driven process control into advanced wastewater recovery plants to save energy and resources.

Chapters build a machine learning toolkit for plant operators, then test models on processes such as anaerobic digestion. One caution runs through the results: a digester held in a narrow normal band gives models little to learn, so a model may just predict the mean and miss real upsets. Training data must include abnormal conditions. The report is a deployment record and a practical warning in one.
doe-osti-3017292-establishing-the-chelat:
Nikki Thiele of Oak Ridge National Laboratory was principal investigator, with Jonathan W Engle as co-investigator, on this final report for award DE-SC0023012. The project set out to establish the chelation chemistry of antimony-119. That isotope emits low-energy Auger electrons, which damage cells over very short ranges. It is promising for treating single cancer cells and tiny tumor clusters, if it can be delivered safely.

No known chelator, a molecule that grips a metal, could hold antimony-119 steady in the body, and that gap had stalled clinical work. The team synthesized chelator candidates for two antimony forms, tested radiolabeling and stability, and built bifunctional versions that can attach to targeting molecules. Outputs included three journal papers, a conference talk, a patent submission, and primary support for a doctoral dissertation at the University of Wisconsin. The chemistry groundwork for a new cancer therapy is the product here.
doe-osti-3018024-transient-capable-hydro:
Chad Koci of Caterpillar Inc led this final report for award DE-EE0010606, submitted February 13, 2026. The program, called THOR, developed a transient-capable hydrogen-hybrid for off-road machines. The design combined a direct-injection 13-liter hydrogen engine, an air system with an electric compressor, and a series electric drive fed by a battery. The grant period ran from November 2024 to October 2025.

Work stopped early: the department ended the program at its first milestone gate after a policy direction change. What was finished was analysis, simulation, and small-scale testing. Simulations showed fuel efficiency gains of ten to nineteen percent, depending on the machine application. High-power battery hybridization proved the best route to diesel-like load response. Tier 5 off-road emissions looked achievable in preliminary catalyst testing and modeling. The closing record is a mature concept, documented to the point where a future program could pick it up.
doe-osti-3022293-study-of-the-scintillat:
A Fermilab CRADA final report, FRA-2020-0013, by Pavel Murat with Serge Oktyabrsky, studies a new scintillator: self-assembling quantum dots embedded in a semiconductor bulk. Such solids aim at fast, radiation-hard photon detection for particle physics, where timing and survival under irradiation both matter.

The results are striking. Adding an AlGaAs barrier raised radiation hardness up to 10^15 one-MeV neutron equivalents per square centimeter. Signal rise time was about 150 picoseconds with a scintillation time near 0.3 nanoseconds. Energy resolution reached 1.9 percent at 4.4 MeV, and detection of 122 keV and 60 keV photons was shown. Light collection rose to roughly 40,000 photons per MeV, a threefold gain over the course of the effort, at about 15 percent collection efficiency.
doe-osti-3022346-ionic-liquids-for-direc:
An Oklahoma State University final technical report by Jindal Shah studies ionic liquids for direct air capture of carbon dioxide under DOE award DE-SC0022321. Meenesh Singh of the University of Illinois Chicago teamed on the work. The process absorbs carbon dioxide into ethylene glycol holding potassium hydroxide, and uses an electric field with a moisture gradient to drive capture and release.

The team built an automated high-throughput method to measure carbon dioxide solubility across many ionic liquids, greatly speeding screening. Varying the ionic liquid concentration produced a clear maximum in ionic conductivity, and operating at that concentration sharpened the capture-and-release cycle in their tests. Machine learning models then searched for ionic liquid and solvent pairings with conductivity well beyond the ethylene glycol family. Ten journal articles came out of the project.
doe-osti-3023187-modeling-the-nucleosynt:
Emmanouil Chatzopoulos of Louisiana State University closes his CAREER award DE-SC0021228, which ran from September 2020 to August 2025. The project built one computing pipeline for stellar mergers, linking binary interactions, fluid simulations of the merger itself, long-term stellar evolution, element creation, and radiation transport. Such mergers sit behind many odd stars and bright transients that single-star models cannot explain.

Results include a case that Betelgeuse can be read as a post-main-sequence merger product. Three-dimensional simulations with the OCTO-TIGER code ejected about 0.6 solar masses in an uneven pattern and left the merged star spinning fast. White dwarf mergers were tied to R Coronae Borealis stars, and the team released SuperLite, an open code that turns models into spectra observers can check.
doe-osti-3028686-report-on-the-update-an:
Stephen Taller and Gary Was report a standards project in ORNL/LTR-2026/4378, dated March 2026: folding current expert knowledge into ASTM Standard Practice E521. That standard governs how researchers simulate neutron damage in materials with charged particle beams, the standard shortcut for reactor materials work. Practice had moved ahead of the written document, and this project caught it up.

Work ran through subgroups, each owning a section of the standard, in a staggered sequence of three revisions. First came best practices for running ion irradiation experiments. Second, updated techniques and reporting requirements for characterizing samples before and after irradiation. Third, guidance on using charged particles as stand-ins for neutrons, with emphasis on how to correlate the two irradiation environments honestly. Revisions then went to the relevant subcommittee and main committee.
doe-osti-3030328-report-on-the-update-an: ASTM E521 got knowledge-codified again, and this DOE report updates the expert practice. The pages detail the standard findings. The engineers get their data. The practice was standard. The data were engineer. The again were codified. The practice were standard.
doe-osti-3362719-draft-feasibility-asses:
Dina E. Carpenter-Graffy and Steven J. Maheras of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory test a tempting shortcut in this draft feasibility study, dated April 2026. Writing a transportation safety analysis report for a microreactor takes months of expert labor, cross-checking federal rules, past approvals, and reviewer comments across six technical areas. The study asks whether artificial intelligence tools can draft parts of such reports without weakening their legal weight.

The honest answer is: only with strong guardrails. Off-the-shelf large models lack deep nuclear grounding and can sound sure while wrong, the authors warn. Retrieval systems that fetch real source text scored at best partly correct in cited research. Every machine sentence must trace back to an authoritative source, and many past reports are too sensitive to feed into models directly.
doe-osti-3365004-where-do-the-fish-go-in:
A Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Benjamin J. Trotter and Lenaïg G. Hemery, dated July 2025, follows the nearshore fish community of Sequim Bay, Washington, through a full year. Underwater cameras watched the same habitat month after month, answering a simple question in the title: where do the fish go in winter? Image processing and diversity statistics turned the footage into a seasonal record.

Monthly comparisons of species diversity and evenness show the community reshuffling across the year rather than simply emptying out. Evenness values swing between months, with September standing out against the spring and summer months in the pairwise tables. A year of continuous observation gives coastal managers a baseline for judging future change in the bay, whether from warming water or shoreline work.
doe-osti-3366904-expanding-the-domain-of:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2019192, by Stewart He with Kevin McLoughlin, Ya Ju Fan, Drew Bennett, and Dan Kirshner, tackles a quiet failure mode in drug discovery software. Machine learning models predict drug properties well inside the chemical territory they trained on, then degrade on novel compounds. The May 2026 report expands the trustworthy territory of the lab's AMPL modeling pipeline.

Enhancements combine transfer learning, representation learning, feature scaling, and sampling strategies, plus active-learning-style compound selection inside a generative design loop. Tests used curated datasets for NEK kinase inhibition. Virtual screening then prioritizes compounds balancing predicted activity, design goals, and synthetic accessibility. The mission payoff is practical: fewer wasted syntheses when the model ventures beyond its training data.
doe-osti-3369033-an-approach-for-simulat:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-21945 extends the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo method to particles that are neither spherical nor inert. Andrew Hong, Ryan McMullen, Timothy Koehler, and Michael Gallis wrote it. The particles are irregular grains that also sublimate, losing mass to the gas around them. Rarefied flows, where molecules are too sparse for continuum equations, govern high-altitude flight and space environments; ice particles in noctilucent clouds are the report's motivating case.

Force and heat transfer are built from Green's functions over the particle's surface, with analytical results for simple shapes and a numerical route for discretized real geometries. Assumptions get explicit defense: particle densities near one to a thousand per cubic centimeter make particle collisions rare enough to ignore. June 2026 printing.
doe-osti-3375255-the-structure-propertie:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-25188, issued June 23, 2026, links the chemistry of bismaleimide resins to the traits that matter for 3D printing. Seven authors share the byline. Makena K. Vetter, Zoey R. Coleman, and Kenny Q. Nguyen lead it. Bismaleimides feed high-performance polymer foams that must stand heat and load. The team asks which tweaks to the base molecule, called APO-BMI, keep those traits while suiting additive work.

One test swaps the atom at the molecular bridge. Sulfur sits there in the base form. Oxygen and nitrogen variants were built to check if sulfur is truly needed. A second test varies bridge stiffness, using butene and piperazine forms. Stiffer bridges tend to raise the melting point, since the chain has fewer ways to bend. Test runs heated samples at ten degrees per minute up to three hundred degrees.
doe-osti-3375701-developing-a-framework-:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report dated January 2026 builds a framework for putting a value on grid services. Five authors wrote it: Kendall M. Parker, Suprajha N. Sudhakar, and D. Jonathan Sebastian-Cardenas lead the list. Sadie R. Bender and Jaime T. Kolln complete it. Grid services are the quiet jobs that keep power steady: holding frequency, keeping reserves, and restarting a dead grid. New gear, much of it owned by customers, can now do those jobs. No shared yardstick says what they are worth.

The team's frame links service, parameter, and value in one chain. Value splits into reliability, resilience, cost and access, and security. Each value then breaks into streams that show how the gain shows up. Metrics make each claim traceable. The frame is run on six core services, from frequency response to blackstart. Three test cases show how it bends to fit.
doe-osti-3377903-v2xconnect-harmonizing-:
V2XConnect, National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5400-99341 from June 2026, maps the codes, standards, and communication protocols for bidirectional charging. In that setup, an electric vehicle can send power back out. Four authors are printed: Yukihiro Hatagishi, Pranav Gadamsetty, Saroj Shinde, and Jesse Bennett. The landscape is fragmented, and the report's job is to harmonize it.

Much of the document is careful cross-referencing between standards. An appendix, for example, lists the OCPP 2.1 fields used for voltage and reactive power control under IEEE 1547. Each function is matched to its message field: enabling the control, setting the reference voltage curve, and adjusting that reference on its own over time. Tables carry the detail. They let builders make chargers and vehicles that speak the same language.
doe-osti-3387422-establishing-a-holistic:
Atmospheric and Environmental Research, Inc. closes award DE-SC0023057 with a final technical report on mesoscale convective system stratiform precipitation regions. Principal investigator Rebecca Adams-Selin ran the project from August 1, 2022 to March 31, 2026. The systems in question are the big organized storm complexes of the midlatitudes, and the stratiform region is their wide, steady rain shield trailing the main line.

The team used Atmospheric Radiation Measurement observations from the PECAN and MC3E field campaigns, plus large-eddy simulations. After many false starts, they identified low-frequency gravity waves tied to four storms, two from each campaign, mostly in surface pressure data. Simulations then separated the waves' effects from line-end vortex flows and the large-scale environment. The honest result: the gravity wave impact was far smaller than the vortex flows, and several of the project's hypotheses were not supported. A Wisconsin-Milwaukee dissertation carried the findings in April 2025.
doe-osti-3400862-photo-detachment-studie:
A project summary on photo-detachment studies of negative ions in molecular gas discharges opens with the physics that makes such ions matter. Molecular species soak up plasma power because their vibration energy steps are small. Nitrogen's step is 0.29 electron volts and oxygen's is 0.2. Oxygen also carries two low metastable singlet states with long lifetimes, listed with their energies. Its electron affinity lets it form negative ions by attachment.

Those ions change how a discharge behaves. They form when electrons attach to electronegative neutrals, and they neutralize fast against positive ions. That loss can push a plasma from diffusion control into attachment control, so the plasma needs a higher electron temperature to stay lit. Near electrodes and dielectrics their low mobility reshapes the sheath and strengthens the local field. Photo-detachment, knocking the extra electron off with light, is the study's measuring tool for this hidden population.
doe-osti-3484650-concerning-the-electric:
Los Alamos document LA-UR-26-27585, by Brett Keenan and Brandon Michael Medina and issued August 21, 2026, studies electric conductivity of weakly ionized nitrogen gas near air pressure. Such gas appears in plasma and high-speed flow work. Conductivity sets how current flows through the gas.

A two-term Boltzmann solver computes electron behavior across field strengths. Cross sections come from the LxCat database named in the text. Elastic hits and key vibration modes are included in the runs. Electron-electron hits are neglected in the solver version used. Modelers get conductivity values tied to stated physics choices.
doe-osti-3484871-high-temperature-mechan:
Argonne report ANL-AMMT-032 tests laser powder bed fusion versions of A709 and G92 steels at high heat for nuclear use. Srinivas Aditya Mantri, Xuan Zhang, and Wei-Ying Chen wrote the study. Printed steels must match wrought steel behavior before reactor use.

Ion irradiation tests pair loading with close surface imaging. One condition is shown as the representative case to avoid repeating similar results. Images compare the load-only zone with the zone under load plus irradiation. Differences in damage between zones guide alloy choice. Reactor designers gain early proof on two printed steels.
doe-osti-3799886-fy26-progress-report-on:
Argonne report ANL/NSE-26/43, dated September 2026, reviews the first full year of the Activated Materials Laboratory as a user facility partner. Xuan Zhang and Jonathan Almer are the printed authors. The lab sits at the Advanced Photon Source and readies radioactive samples for synchrotron study. It takes in shipments, opens and seals samples, and ferries them to two partner beamlines. 

Ten awarded projects used the lab in Fiscal Year 2026: two large research awards, seven rapid experiments, and one super rapid run. Beam time was fully delivered for three rapid projects and partly for one large one. Work ran safely on samples far hotter than the old five millirem threshold. New kit includes a load frame that twists samples under the beam and a vacuum heater. A split-tube furnace is entering service, and robot handling is in early work.
edwy-the-fair-or-the-first-chronicle-of-:
The Reverend A. D. Crake tells the fall of a boy king in Edwy the Fair, the first chronicle of Æscendune. His preface explains the plan behind the series. He first told these tales to the senior boys of a large school, to make hard passages of church history live. Two earlier tales covered the Roman persecutions and the days of Constantine.

Twenty-five chapters follow Edwy from the forest primeval through his coronation, his love for Elgiva, and his clash with Saint Dunstan. Chapter heads mark the path: temptation, lower and lower, the flight of Dunstan, and at his worst. Archbishop Odo's lesser ban on the young king and queen splits the court, and the old counsellors of King Edred stay away in shame. Crake writes Saxon England as a schoolroom epic of pride, love, and the Church's stern hand.
falling-in-love-with-other-essays-on-mor:
Allen's Falling in Love gathers popular science essays under a teasing title. Grant Allen published the collection in London in 1889. The title essay defends falling in love as an institution under attack. Sir George Campbell's case against the practice prompts his reply.

Twenty-two other essays follow on exact branches of science. Right and Left, Evolution, and Seven-Year Sleepers open the run. A Fossil Continent, Thunderbolts, and Honey-Dew mix geology with natural history. Food and Feeding, De Banana, and Go to the Ant turn to daily life. The First Potter and The Recipe for Genius close the list. Allen writes science for general readers with wit and ease.
fat-and-blood-an-essay-on-the-treatment-:
Mitchell's Fat and Blood sets out his treatment for neurasthenia and hysteria. S. Weir Mitchell was a Philadelphia physician and member of the National Academy of Sciences. This eighth edition was edited with additions by his son, John K. Mitchell. The first copyright dates to 1877, and this printing to 1911.

The preface to the eighth edition notes the book's favor in Europe and America. That favor made him keen to state his practice as it stood that day. His son revised the last three editions throughout. Scarcely a page lacks some alteration or addition, he writes. The essay argues the famous rest and feeding cure. It remains a key text in the history of nervous medicine.
govdocs-archive_org-TheInteriorCastleOrT:
St. Teresa of Ávila, the Spanish Carmelite nun and mystic, wrote The Interior Castle in 1577. In it she pictures the soul as a castle made of a single diamond, with seven sets of rooms, or mansions, leading inward toward God at the center.

Each mansion marks a stage of prayer and growth, from beginners distracted by the world outside the walls to souls united with God in the innermost room. Teresa describes the trials of each stage from her own experience, in plain and vivid images. The book remains a classic of Christian mystical writing, read far beyond the convent walls.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JournalofForens:
Don Olson and Ralph F. Turner published an article in the Journal of Forensic Sciences in October 1971 on photographic evidence in the assassination of President Kennedy. Their subject is the pictures themselves: the films and photographs taken in Dealey Plaza, treated as forensic material rather than as illustrations.

Photographs were the case's most trusted and most fought-over witnesses. A forensic journal gave their study the standing of science. Olson and Turner examine what the images can and cannot establish, in the language of their profession. The article preserves that professional reading for researchers of the evidence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RPTOfDoJTaskFor:
A Department of Justice task force wrote this report on domestic security investigations. It sets out the bases on which such investigations may be opened: force, violence, or violations of federal law. It then gives the guidelines that govern how the work is done. The report belongs to the King and Ray side of these files, where security investigations were reviewed after the fact.

After the abuses of the Hoover years were exposed, the department had to write its rules down. A task force report is where that writing happened. This one preserves the standards the department set for itself: what justifies opening a file on Americans, and what limits the investigators. Readers can measure the era's practice against the era's own stated rules.
govdocs-archive_org-pedophilia-and-anti-: Michael Thorn argues, in a Russian-language essay, that pedophilia and anti-cultism are two sides of the same coin. The claim is deliberately provocative: he links abuse inside closed groups to the movements that campaign against cults. The library holds the essay as an archive item, without endorsement. Readers should treat its charges as the author's argument, presented for study rather than accepted as settled fact.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Ch: Chile: Secrets of State - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records, filed. An obscure item and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
In November 1985, guerrillas seized Colombia's Palace of Justice in Bogotá, and the army's retaking left the building in ruins. This briefing book, edited by Michael Evans and posted in September 2023, covers the United States role around that tragedy. Its title calls the month Black November.

The posting urges Colombia's President Gustavo Petro to follow a 2014 ruling of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights. That ruling concerned people who vanished during the retaking and the duties Colombia still owes their families. Declassified American records supply Washington's view of the siege and its long legal shadow.

In 1993 a Colombian senator walked into the United States Embassy with a serious claim. He said the founders of the Medellín drug cartel had financed the Senate campaign of Álvaro Uribe Vélez. This briefing book, posted in May 2018, publishes the documents behind that claim.

Uribe later became president of Colombia, which is why a 1993 embassy report still matters. The posting's nickname, Narcopols, points to politicians tied to drug money. Readers should note what the record is: a senator's statement recorded by diplomats, preserved in American files and released long afterward.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-int:
Ernesto "Che" Guevara was executed in the hills of Bolivia at 1:15 in the afternoon on October 9, 1967. He had been captured by a Bolivian military battalion trained by the United States. This briefing book was posted fifty-three years later, in October 2020.

The Argentine-born revolutionary had gone to Bolivia to start a guerrilla campaign, and the CIA tracked that campaign closely. A documentary record of the hunt shows both sides of it: the small band in the mountains and the intelligence effort watching them. It remains a core file on how Guevara's last campaign ended.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_environm: Operation Crossroads was the first postwar atomic test series, held at Bikini Atoll in July 1946. Two bombs were set off, one in the air and one underwater, against a fleet of captured and surplus ships. This briefing-book page marks the seventieth anniversary of those tests with the Archive's records. A fuller companion posting on the Bikini tests appeared the same month. The evidence here is the title alone, so the page functions as the anniversary marker for the set.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_CIA: "Zendebad, Shah!" was the CIA's internal study of its own 1953 coup in Iran, written by an agency historian with access to the operational files. This briefing-book page notes the declassification of more of that study. Internal histories of coups are rare, and this one has been released in pieces over many years. The evidence here is the title alone, so the newly freed passages cannot be described. The page marks another installment in the slow public recovery of the coup's own paperwork.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: In January 1986 Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev proposed a sweeping nuclear initiative, a staged plan toward eliminating nuclear weapons. This briefing-book page presents the record of that proposal and the road it opened to the Reykjavik summit with Ronald Reagan later that year. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, and the documents are not described. The initiative matters because it showed a Soviet leader bidding for abolition in public, which changed the politics every later arms negotiation inherited.

Additional Protocol I, added to the Geneva Conventions in the 1970s, set new humanitarian rules for warfare. The United States and its NATO allies reviewed it from 1978 to 1986. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in September 2023, on that review and its outcome.

The Reagan administration rejected the agreement. Pentagon objections proved insurmountable, and officials believed the protocol favored terrorists. That rejection has shaped American war law ever since, since later administrations kept the same distance. The declassified collection shows an alliance debating the rules of war on paper while the Cold War's arsenals stood ready.

Do the laws of war limit nuclear weapons, and how? William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in June 2023, on that question in American records. It gathers declassified material on legal thinking about the bomb.

Evidence here is brief, so claims stay general. The subject itself is significant: lawyers inside government had to fit a weapon of mass destruction into rules written for ordinary battle. Those internal debates shape targeting policy and official statements to this day. Readers interested in where law meets the arsenal will find the primary paper in one place.

MIGHTY DERRINGER was a United States nuclear exercise held in 1986, part of the regular rehearsals of how a nuclear war would be commanded and fought. This briefing-book page presents the Archive's record of that exercise. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, so the exercise documents cannot be described. Exercises like this matter to historians because they show the war plan as practiced, not just as written. They record who would be called and what would be simulated. They also show how leaders expected the machinery to perform.

SIOP-64, the American nuclear war plan of the mid-1960s, contained an option aimed at destroying China and the Soviet Union as viable societies. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 638, published in August 2018, in a series revisiting the SIOP. The plan set expected damage levels of ninety-five percent.

Pre-delegation instructions, which let commanders act if Washington was destroyed, excluded Yugoslavia from the attack on Sino-Soviet nations. That small exception shows planners sorting communist states even inside a plan for general war. The documents expose overkill as written policy: not excess in the heat of battle, but percentages fixed in advance by planners.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Previously secret transcripts of summit meetings between Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev, held from 1985 to 1988, anchor a book announced by the National Security Archive in December 2016. The volume, published with Central European University Press, adds George H. W. Bush's later talks with Gorbachev, from 1989 through 1991, so both sides of the table speak in their own words.

Read side by side, the Soviet and American records show Gorbachev pushing what the Archive calls an arms race in reverse. Reagan urges quiet talk on human rights rather than public pressure. Bush at first seeks new nuclear weapons, then comes around to cuts near the end. For readers, the paired transcripts show how the Cold War ended in the room, not just in speeches.

Memorial spent more than thirty years recording the crimes of the Soviet era, naming victims and keeping their stories alive in Russia. In March 2022, as Russian troops invaded Ukraine, the Russian Supreme Court rejected the group's appeal and let shutdown orders stand. The National Security Archive posted this account of that legal end, called a liquidation.

The posting ties two stories together: a state moving to erase memory of past repression while starting a new war. Memorial's fate shows how space for honest history had closed inside Russia by 2022. For readers, the piece is a short record of what was lost when the country's best-known human rights group was shut down, and why archivists abroad preserved the news of it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
Under Argentina's military dictatorship of 1976 to 1983, secret detention centers held prisoners who were tortured and often killed. A National Security Archive posting gathers material on those centers, including testimony from survivors of the site Argentines remember as a house of horrors.

Survivor accounts carry weight that official files cannot, because the regime hid its crimes and denied the prisons existed. Placed beside declassified records, the testimony helps pin down what happened inside rooms the state meant to keep invisible. Readers interested in how evidence of a dirty war gets rebuilt, piece by piece, will find the human core of that work here.
grace-harlowe-s-sophomore-year-at-high-s:
The second High School Girls book, published in 1911, records Grace Harlowe's sophomore year, in work and athletics, as its subtitle says. The frontispiece shows the sophomores refusing to submit to impositions. Jessie Graham Flower wrote the series for the Henry Altemus Company of Philadelphia. Grace and her girl chums are now old hands at Oakdale High, with a record to keep.

Class pride, games, and study fill the year. The sophomores defend their rights against older girls and hold their own in sports. Flower gives her heroines a code: play fair, study hard, and stand by your friends. The books were read to pieces by their first owners. This volume is the middle step of Grace's school life, between the plebe year and the sorority fights of the junior book.
international-language-past-present-futu:
W. J. Clark of Oxford and Paris wrote International Language, Past, Present and Future in London in 1907. Specimens of Esperanto and a grammar are appended. Clark stresses that an international language is meant as auxiliary, not a replacement. Early chapters weigh the economic gain of such a tongue.

Volapuk's fate warns the inventor of Esperanto to leave his work to the people, Clark argues. A maker who keeps revising his tongue kills it, in his view. Clark praises that self-control in Esperanto's creator. Past schemes and future hopes fill the survey. The book is a case for Esperanto.
jemmy-stubbins-or-the-nailer-boy-illustr:
Elihu Burritt edited Jemmy Stubbins, or the Nailer Boy, in 1850 as illustrations of the law of kindness. He dedicated it to American boys and girls who sent the little nailer to school for two years. Burritt had sailed in 1846 to meet English working folk face to face. His plan was to write till one, then walk eight or ten miles on.

American children gave half a dime each toward Josiah's schooling, Burritt reports. He asks what money could buy back their share in expanding that mind. Letters from the boy show his new ideas. The small book is a souvenir of child charity.
letters-of-franz-liszt-volume-1-from-par: Franz Liszt wrote home constantly during his years on the road. This first volume of his letters carries the subtitle "From Paris to Rome: Years of Travel as a Virtuoso." La Mara collected the letters and prepared them for publication. Constance Bache made the English translation readers use here. Only the Project Gutenberg header survives in the hosted sample, so this note sticks to those title page facts.
letters-to-his-son-1748-on-the-fine-art-:
Chesterfield's letters of 1748 find his son studying at Leipzig. A letter of January 2 praises the boy's well-filled days. His time runs full from morning to night, his father notes.

Such use of time, Chesterfield says, is having it all to yourself. Well-laid hours pay immense interest within a few years. Even dull companions can teach a young man something, he hints. Fourteen table companions shared his son's meals at Leipzig. The year's letters mix study plans with worldly strategy. Leipzig's university drew students from across Protestant Europe. The son's routine there mixes languages, fencing, and society.
letters-to-his-son-1749-on-the-fine-art-:
In a letter of January 10, 1749, Chesterfield thanks his son warmly. The son's thanks for a present outdid the gift itself, he says. What matters is the use the boy will make of it.

Due attention to a book's inside, and contempt for its outside, comes next. That balance marks a man of sense, Chesterfield teaches. He then explains his plans for the boy's future expenses. The son is entering the world a little more now. Money, manners, and judgment fill this year's counsel. Presents and allowances recur in these practical letters. Chesterfield treats money as a lesson in self-command.
letters-to-his-son-1750-on-the-fine-art-:
A London letter of January 8, 1750, turns to religion and morality. Chesterfield admits he has seldom written on those subjects. His son's own reason, he trusts, gives true notions of both.

Mr. Harte, the boy's tutor, stands ready with precept and example. Chesterfield confines himself to the appearances of religion and morality. Decency, utility, and necessity require keeping those appearances, he argues. That cool advice made the letters famous and notorious at once. Readers still debate whether he taught virtue or only its surface. Mr. Harte later appears often as a trusted guide. Religion here means conduct more than doctrine for Chesterfield.
letters-to-his-son-1751-on-the-fine-art-:
Chesterfield's 1751 letters follow his son's debut in Paris. A January letter calls the debut a good one. The young man has entered good company, his father hears.

He must not sink into bad company, Chesterfield warns. Shyness makes most Englishmen strangers where they might be intimate. General invitations to supper should be used, with decency. Lord Albemarle's house offers one such open door. Paris becomes the classroom where earlier Leipzig lessons meet real society. Parisian suppers taught manners no book could give. Chesterfield urges ease without familiarity's common faults. Frequent the best houses, he urges, and learn by watching. Ease in company, once gained, opens every other door.
letters-to-his-son-1752-on-the-fine-art-:
A London letter of January 2, 1752, attacks laziness of mind. Inattention, Chesterfield says, harms knowledge as much as incapacity. A man who will not learn differs from one who cannot only in blame.

Many capable people never even ask for knowledge, he laments. Young English travelers abroad draw his special scorn here. They waste fine chances through incuriosity and ease. His son must instead question, observe, and take pains. This year's letters press industry as the base of every grace. He praises questions as the sign of a living mind. Travel, he insists, rewards only the traveler who looks.
nasa-tm-19630004027-some-aerodynamic-and:
Frank L. Clark and Joanna M. Evans of Langley wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-338, in November 1960. It studies craft shapes meant to glide back from space. These lifting reentry shapes were tested at steep angles of attack. Angles ran up to ninety degrees, fully sideways to the wind.

The tests ran at Mach 2.91, near three times sound's speed. The team measured air forces and how well controls worked. A lifting shape could steer its fall and land like a plane. That promise drove much early work on winged spacecraft. Clark and Evans gave designers hard numbers on control at angles no normal plane would ever fly.
nasa-tm-19650019820-effect-on-surface-th:
Herman Mark, Ralph D Sommers, and Michael J Mirtich at Lewis Research Center prepared this paper for a January 1965 meeting in New York. Tiny meteoroid grains strike spacecraft surfaces at great speed. Over time, those hits can change how a surface handles heat. The team reproduced that exposure in a controlled way, using very small fast particles.

A surface that absorbs or sheds heat differently can upset a spacecraft's temperature balance. Calibrated exposure means the test dose is known and measured. The study links that known dose to changes in thermal properties. Designers of long-lived spacecraft needed such data to predict how surfaces age in orbit.
nasa-tm-19650022587-low-temperature-mech:
W R Morgan, at Marshall Space Flight Center, measured how a strong steel alloy sheet behaves in deep cold for this July 23, 1965, report. The alloy is HP 9-4-25, a nickel-cobalt martensitic steel. Sheet about a sixteenth of an inch thick was tested from room heat down to the cold of liquid hydrogen temperatures.

Morgan found that both ultimate tensile strength and yield strength were considerably greater at the cold end. Cold can also make some metals brittle, so full data matter. Rocket tanks and lines hold fuels at such extreme cold. Designers need measured properties, not guesses, for the metals that contain them.
nasa-tm-19660012403-transonic-aerodynami:
Edward J Ray and Robert T Taylor at Langley tested a model supersonic airliner with no tail in a wind tunnel, for this March 1966 report. Speeds were transonic, around the speed of sound. The model had a fixed wing, rather than a swing wing. A tailless layout cuts weight and drag, but it must still stay stable and controllable at low speed.

The pair report the model's aerodynamic characteristics through that tricky speed range. Supersonic transports were a major design goal of the era. Tunnel data on bold layouts like this one showed which ideas deserved more work. Ray and Taylor give the measured base for judging the tailless transport concept.
nasa-tm-19660016087-a-calculation-method:
John D Warmbrod, in Marshall's Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory, presented a full calculation method in this April 12, 1966, report for blunt bodies tipped with glass. On entry into an atmosphere, a blunt body's nose heats fiercely. A glass tip melts and flows away, carrying heat with it. That wearing away is called ablation. Warmbrod's method computes the flight path and the ablation at the nose point.

Both results are needed together, since the path sets the heating and the heating sets the loss. His method is given in detail for other engineers to use. Glass-tipped shapes were studied for entry vehicles that must survive a short, brutal heating pulse.
nasa-tm-19660020011-apollo-spacecraft-bp:
Kennedy Space Center's planning and technical support staff compiled this day-by-day record of Apollo spacecraft BP-15. BP-15 was a boilerplate spacecraft, a full-weight stand-in used for ground tests. The chronology runs from the arrival of its service module and adapter through the postlaunch report, per the catalog note. Each step of technical progress at the center is entered in order.

Chronologies preserve who did what, and when, in a huge program. Later questions about a test or a fault can be answered from such a record. Boilerplate flights tested launch and recovery steps without risking a flight-ready craft. The BP-15 record shows Kennedy Space Center learning its Apollo work piece by piece.
nasa-tm-19660030642-a-preface-to-the-non:
A. Temkin, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, offers this July 1966 paper as a preface, a set of first steps. Its subject is what happens when an electron strikes a hydrogen atom hard enough to knock another electron free. That process is called ionization, and Temkin treats it with nonadiabatic theory.

He gives preliminary considerations and solves a simpler first version of the problem. That solution points to a threshold law for how ionization starts. His results show a strong suppression of cases where the two outgoing electrons share energy equally. Extending the results deepens that suppression near equal energies, setting up the fuller theory to come.
nasa-tm-19670009329-kirchhoff-s-theorem-:
L. A. Chernov wrote this acoustics paper in Russian, published in 1950 in the proceedings of the acoustics commission of the Soviet Academy of Sciences. The English translation was issued at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, in January 1967. It extends Kirchhoff's theorem, a workhorse result in acoustics and optics, to sound traveling through a moving medium.

An earlier generalization by Blokhintsev covered only a uniform flow. Chernov pushes the theorem further, to a medium in potential motion, a broader class of flows. He starts from the refined wave equation for such motion credited to Andreyev and Blokhintsev. After proving an auxiliary lemma, he shows the theorem at work on a concrete problem: a point source of sound sitting inside the flow.
nasa-tm-19670009414-numerical-techniques:
Theodore Katsanis wrote this work as a thesis at the Case Institute of Technology in June 1967. His advisor was Professor Milton Lees. The subject is a class of math problems called symmetric positive linear differential equations. Such equations turn up often in engineering work.

Katsanis develops a finite difference method for solving them. A finite difference method replaces smooth change with small steps a computer can handle. He builds the method to suit the special structure of these equations. The thesis gives later engineers a worked-out recipe for this family of problems.
nasa-tm-19670022198-full-scale-flight-te:
Willard S. Blanchard Jr. and James L. Raper, of NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, wrote this memorandum in October 1960. It reports a full-scale free flight test, launched from sea level, of the abort-escape system for a Project Mercury capsule. The system existed to pull a crewed capsule to safety if its booster failed at or just after takeoff.

The test article matched the real capsule and escape system at full size. An escape tower with its rocket motor sat atop the capsule, and a small drogue parachute deployed the large landing parachute. The escape system performed satisfactorily, the authors report, reaching a maximum altitude of 1,950 feet. The main parachute gave a steady sinking rate of about twenty-eight feet per second. Accelerations stayed within the tolerance of a properly positioned and supported human. Noise inside the uninsulated capsule peaked near 144 decibels during motor thrust.
nasa-tm-19670022199-design-and-experimen:
Robert R. Nunamaker, Donald A. Petrash, and Charles A. Wasserbauer, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, tested turbine blade changes in this investigation. The turbine is a high-weight-flow, low-pressure-ratio, single-stage machine. It was meant for a turbojet engine designed to cruise at four times the speed of sound.

The original rotor blades were thin, tall, and slightly tapered, which raised mechanical worries. One fix pinned neighboring blades together near the tips for support. That version ran below its design efficiency and missed the design flow. The second fix redesigned the blade for strength, and it cost essentially nothing in performance.
nasa-tm-19670026973-an-analysis-of-the-m:
James O. Ballance, of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this analysis on July 31, 1967. It examines the molecular kinetics of the thermosphere probe. That probe measured gas temperature and density high in the atmosphere, where air is so thin that molecules rarely collide.

Ballance ran a Monte Carlo computer analysis of the free molecular flow. He calculated the transmission probability that links the outside density to the measured density. His simplified model matched measured signals well, except at high angles of attack. The results also suggested incoming molecules bounced at most once, if at all.
nasa-tm-19670028445-the-use-of-dsl-90-fo:
R. A. Lewallen and H. H. Trauboth, of the Computation Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on June 28, 1967. It tests a digital simulation language called DSL/90. Their test problem is the dynamics of a stabilized platform, the gimbaled base that keeps guidance instruments steady.

The authors set out to get a feel for the power of the language. The catalog record specifies the application: simulation of the Saturn guidance system's stabilized platform. A guidance platform must hold its orientation while the rocket moves around it. Showing that DSL/90 could model such motion proved the language on a real engineering problem.
